**TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MEN, THE CONSULS**
**AND ILLUSTRIOUS SENATORS**
**OF THE REPUBLIC OF NUREMBERG,**
**GREETINGS.** [Handwritten note: I began to read on June 29, 1583]

[Large historiated initial P depicting a figure in a landscape within a decorative frame] That saying of Plato, most distinguished Fathers, has been widely spread: that republics will then at last be happy, if either philosophers rule, or kings philosophize. For since the right administration of the state depends entirely on the perfect use of reason, and according to Aristotle's opinion, he who is most excellent in virtue and wisdom is, by the silent consent of all nature, most worthy of universal rule: just as this honor belongs per se to God alone and to Christ, the best and greatest, so too, by a certain participation, it belongs to those whom He willed to be His vicars on earth, and whom He honored with the name of Gods. (In reality, it also participates) Moreover, since He has been accustomed to specially arouse, call, and instruct these very men for right governance, as the examples of Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Jephthah, (Exod: 22. Ps: 82.) Samson, Maccabee, and similar figures teach: (Exod: Josua Jud: Jud: Machab:) then truly, by a popular method, that good author of good nature is accustomed to explain and illustrate the rules for right living inscribed in the minds of all men, by the efficacy of His spirit, in certain individuals born to rule, and who therefore possess 'golden souls' according to Plato's opinion: so that He may make them participants of His essence, and also of truth and virtue, as far as is permissible.

Indeed, there are two norms of virtue and truth: (Two norms of Virtue and Truth) Sacred Authority, constant by eternal reason, and profane reason, relying on mortal authority. Of these, the former, Theology, rejoicing in its unfeigned name, like the most splendid sun, can dispel and illuminate all the darkness of the human mind even by itself: but it is granted only to those who, by the singular benevolence of the Divine Will, have obtained the revelation of divine oracles, first outlined by the Mosaic Law, and then explained by the Evangelical Law. The latter, however, which they called philosophy from the imitation of the Wise God, gathering the remnants of human shipwreck, investigates the law of incorrupt nature: and while it understands and deplores the adventitious depravity of man, it strives to escape to the idea of native beauty, if not by acting, at least by contemplating. But even frustrated by this attempt, while it recognizes what it lacks, it nevertheless ignores the cause of the ailment, and sees no way to dispel it; it turns entirely to the good author of nature, and to His goodness which envies no one, so that from Him, to whom it owes the principles of its origin, it may also supplicantly and devoutly seek the aids for its restoration and preservation. This end of its philosophy-

Socrates assigned primacy to reason.

PROLOGUE.
This end of his philosophy Socrates, judged by the oracle of Apollo to be the wisest of all mortals, established when he taught that all things should be referred to that highest good and beautiful, and defined philosophy as a meditation on death. But he also did not hesitate to assert that philosophy holds primacy among all things we have received from the Gods. He was deceived in this one thing, that through ignorance of divine Authority (although he perhaps tacitly insinuated that this very thing was placed outside the reckoning of human gifts), he assigned primacy to reason, which nevertheless ought to be counted only in second place.

Now indeed, since human reason itself (for divine reason completely dulls and obscures the eyes of men like owls with its splendor) deduces universal theory and contemplation from the history and observation of particulars, and observation, in turn, cannot be done in a short time nor by any one person; unless, to speak thus, experience is to serve and assist in furnishing reason, and therefore, the constant order of nature persuades that the Authority of those who, with observed reason, discovered, established what was discovered, and taught what was established, must be held in the highest regard. Wherefore, that admirable mystic and interpreter of nature, Aristotle, who asserts that there is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the senses, pronounced that "the learner must believe" (τὸν μανθάνοντα πιστεύειν). For although the freedom of reason and speech, dedicated to no authority, devoted solely to truth, befits a philosopher, yet this very freedom can only apply to a few, whom just Jupiter has loved, and who have surpassed all authority by the perspicacity of their divine mind. Meanwhile, for the mediocre, who constitute the largest part, it would be much more advisable to serve the opinions of their predecessors, than, by an ill-considered zeal for liberty, having rejected the authority of their elders, to invade the tyranny of novelty.

And so that we may omit the Germanas and Brahmans of the Indians, the priests of the Egyptians, the Chaldeans of the Babylonians, the Tarabosteseos of the Scythians, and the Druids of the Germans and Gauls: certainly the two most famous schools of the ancient Greek philosophers—the Ionian, from Thales to Epicurus, and the Italian, derived from Pythagoras to Socrates—gave much to authority, and while they followed the footsteps of reason, they often turned aside into the precincts of authority; even that Pythagorean saying, "he himself said it," more than sufficiently proves this. Socrates indeed, when he undertook to restore mutilated philosophy to its completeness, and to investigate not only the obscurity of nature but also the depravity of morals, and to seek a way to repair it, propagated from himself various colonies of later philosophers because of his elegance in philosophizing and and the sanctity of his life, while his astute disciples strove either to understand more correctly or to cultivate more diligently the natural seeds of virtue and truth that they had drawn from him.

--- Page 13 ---
**PREFACE.**

Consequently, the sect of Academic philosophers from Plato, and of the Cynics from Antisthenes, which soon also produced the Stoic school from itself, were established. Plato's disciple Aristotle led the Peripatetic colony from its metropolis into the Lyceum, a colony in no way inferior in perpetual succession for so many centuries now, on account of the light of its order and method. Meanwhile, Speusippus with his successors preserved the name and dignity of the Old Academy; Arcesilaus introduced the Middle, and Lacydes the New. Afterwards, with the constitution of the Athenian school disturbed along with the empire, the Academy, roused by its own origins, began to spread its branches, more than other sects, first throughout Greece, then also throughout Italy: with such benevolence of sky and soil, that these living roots grew into very wide forests; and after Greece, though captured, captured its fierce victor, as he says, the harvest of Platonic philosophy was especially abundant in Rome: wonderfully attested and celebrated not only by living tradition, but also by the writings of very learned men. This can be demonstrated by Plotinus [Marginal note: Plotinus of Lycopolis] of Lycopolis, whom we here bring onto a more cultivated and more elegant literary stage, a diligent auditor of Ammonius of Alexandria, the greatest philosopher [Marginal note: Ammonius of Alexandria, Plotinus' teacher.], for eleven years from the 28th year of his age, when he first approached philosophy, and a fellow student of Origen and Erennius [Marginal note: Origen and Erennius, Plotinus' fellow students.]. It had been agreed among them long ago that they should not publish the esoteric doctrines of their teacher, but only by communicating them orally to legitimate students, they should preserve the authority of the school. But after Erennius first, then Origen, broke their faith, and also because Plotinus' students (of whom he had many and learned ones in Rome for 26 years [Marginal note: Plotinus taught in Rome for 26 years]) were following only tumultuous oral instruction without a reading of the doctrines: Plotinus, already over forty, finally, at the 66th year of his age (which was the second year of Emperor Claudius II, certainly fatal for both), applied his mind to writing. Since Porphyry has diligently and copiously written his life, there is no reason for us to repeat what has already been done; but let us note this one thing: that Plotinus fell upon those times in which profane Philosophy, roused by emulation of the Christian religion then emerging far and wide, and moreover compelled by the truth of its doctrines, could most easily have submitted to the yoke of Christ, had not the ambition and wickedness of those who philosophized only as far as their beard and cloak, and swollen with the opinion of their own wisdom, and who considered it most shameful to obey the unlearned and simple, stood in the way. For when they strove to defend the authority of profane wisdom, they observed meanwhile that Christian piety rested not so much on the subtlety of arguments as on the sanctity of morals and the frequency of miracles: they did not hesitate to move Acheron itself, that is, under the pretext of human philosophy, to call Magic to their aid. Therefore, after Apollonius of Tyana (whose admirable [Marginal note: Apollonius of Tyana, adversary of Christ] deceptions the most cunning evil spirit of Christ, the Best and Greatest, a miracle...

P R E F A C E.
...to undermine the authority of [Christ's] miracles, and tried to oppose him with this one (Apollonius) as an antagonist) Julian the Chaldean, called the Thaumaturge, Iamblichus of Chalcis, Maximus of Ephesus, Libanius the sophist, Amelius and Sopater of Apamea, Aedesius the Cappadocian, Chrysanthius of Lydia, and that impious Porphyry from Tyre, with the blasphemous Proclus of Lycia, put on the philosophical mask of impious magic. And this indeed caused that, although Saint Paul seriously commands the pious to abstain from vain philosophy, the followers of the Christian religion in that century not only philosophers (and deservedly so), but also philosophy itself, though innocent, condemned as impious; and the matter came to this, that out of hatred for magic, divine Theology was entirely stripped of the service and ministry of sincere Philosophy, a service as honorable as it was necessary.

But since the more excellent a thing is, the worse its abuse usually is, these things had to be carefully distinguished from each other, lest what was due to the morals of men be imputed to the art itself. More rightly did those (among whom were Melito, Bishop of Sardis, a disciple of the philosopher Fronto, Patenus, also an Alexandrian Stoic, with Clement of Alexandria, and Alexander, Bishop of Jerusalem, their disciples, Quadratus likewise, and Aristides the Athenian, Justin Martyr, Cyprian of Carthage, a magician before he was a bishop, Origen moreover the Egyptian, with many others) who, having rejected philosophical vanity, compelled philosophical truth to serve revealed truth, and thus transferred the otherwise forbidden use of Egyptian gold to the worship of the true God, with such success, that Julian the Apostate thought this to be the only way to extirpate Christianity, if the pious were kept away from pagan literature, who, instructed by these, would defend the truth itself much more probably and effectively, and defeat the impious with their own weapons.

Although it seems absurd that men turned away from God, and openly enemies of true piety, could have attained any knowledge of sincere truth, even if profane: yet great is the indulgence of that eternal giver of good things, who, just as he illuminates the impious equally with the pious with his sun, so to the prophets of the pagans, by an admirable counsel, he gave much clearer revelations concerning the Messiah (as can be seen from the Sibylline Oracles) than to the prophets of the Jews themselves. Therefore, although Plotinus thought impiously about our revealed religion, and perhaps also attacked it with magical attempts (even if Porphyry trifles that in evoking his guiding spirit, not a demon but God appeared to the Egyptian priest), yet in that kind of philosophy which is consonant with human reason, and is an emulator of nature, that is, of God's works, in knowing and expressing every kind of being, he was preeminent after Plato: and therefore if, as someone says, Platonists can become Christians with a few changes: Plotinus certainly,

certainly, who, having investigated and interpreted Platonic doctrines much more accurately and diligently, deserved the first place among these, since if he is compared with others of the same profession, he seems no less worthy of the appellation *theios* than Plato once, when compared with the *daimonios* Aristotle. But if indeed, either because he was unwilling, or because, deprived of divine benevolence, he could not attain the knowledge of eternal piety: yet we, upon whom a more generous grace of the divine spirit has shone, let us compel his philosophy, consonant with right nature and to that extent not alien from divine Authority, to serve Theology; and let us learn to refer the very treasures of nature, extracted from these innermost recesses in both contemplation and action, to the glory of the one God, and to rest in the light of Him who illuminates every person, but in a different manner. With this intention, most illustrious Sirs, we wished to give Plotinus, who some years ago had come forth from our workshop with Marsilio Ficino as interpreter, now speaking in his own language, both augmented and emended, relying on the trustworthiness and aid of four Greek manuscript copies—three Italian indeed, and the fourth belonging to Io. Sambucus of Tirnauia, Imperial Historian, whose literary excellence makes them preferable to all private copies and comparable to most princely ones: so that we might give students of both languages the opportunity for understanding, judging, and translating Platonic philosophy—that is, the philosophy most akin to the Christian religion—to the use of true piety; since it abounds in richness of thought and brevity of words, so that sometimes it can be understood more correctly from the Greek than from the Latin, certainly not due to any fault of the interpreter, but because of the obscurity of the subject matter itself and the peculiarity of the language. But this same author, most eminent Fathers of your Republic, I wished to offer especially, so that since likeness begets friendships, this prince among philosophers, and an outstanding teacher of truth and virtue in his kind, might come forth under the title and patronage of that Republic, which
      *Among the cities of Germany, has raised its head as high*
      *As cypresses are wont to do among pliant viburnums;*
and which, by a constant succession of many years now, has expressed both Corinthian opulence and the best discipline, much holier than Spartan, in the midst of Germany, and by long-lasting benevolence has bravely preserved it amidst so many plotters against liberty. But just as these are ancestral praises of your city, so what now comes to be said is proper to you, the generous posterity of good parents: that with a spirit no less regal than philosophical, at this time, when we see most people—lest I say something more serious—indulging in either shameful or idle leisure and neglecting public affairs, you have founded the Altdorf Academy, and most learned

**MARSILIO FICINO, THE FLORENTINE, ON PLOTINUS, TO THE MAGNANIMOUS LORENZO DE' MEDICI, SAVIOR OF THE FATHERLAND,**

**Proemium**

[Large decorative initial M] AGNUS COSMUS, by decree of the Senate, father of his country, at the time when the Council between the Greeks and Latins was being held in Florence under Pope Eugenius, frequently heard a Greek philosopher named Gemistus, surnamed Plethon, as if another Plato, disputing on Platonic mysteries. From whose fervent mouth he was immediately so inspired, so animated, that from it he conceived in his lofty mind a certain Academy, intending to bring it forth at the first opportune moment.

Then, while that great Medici was in a manner giving birth to such a concept, he destined me, the son of his most chosen physician Ficino, still a boy, for such a great work; he educated me daily for this very purpose; moreover, he took care that I should possess all the Greek books not only of Plato but also of Plotinus.

Afterwards, however, in the year one thousand four hundred sixty-three, when I was in my thirtieth year of age, he first entrusted to me Hermes Trismegistus, and soon after Plato, for translation. I completed Hermes within a few months while he was still alive; I then also undertook Plato. Although he also desired Plotinus, he nevertheless said not a word about translating him, lest he seem to burden me with too heavy a weight at once. So great was the clemency of such a man towards his own, so great his modesty towards all.

Therefore, I myself, as if not a prophet, never thought of undertaking Plotinus. But meanwhile, Cosimo, what he once kept silent about while living on earth, at last expressed, or rather impressed from on high. For at the time when I gave Plato to the Latins to be read, that heroic spirit of Cosimo somehow instigated the heroic mind of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, so that he came to Florence, and he himself, as if not knowing how.

Indeed, he was born in the very year I undertook Plato; then, coming to Florence on the day, and almost at the very hour, I published Plato, he immediately after our first greeting asked me about Plato. To him, I said, "Indeed, our Plato has today departed from our threshold." Then he, greatly congratulated me on this very fact, and soon, with I know not what words, and he knows not what words, he did not merely persuade me, but rather incited me to translate Plotinus.

It truly seems to have been divinely brought about that while Plato was, as it were, being reborn, the hero Pico, born under his Saturn possessing Aquarius (under which I too had similarly been born thirty years earlier), arriving in Florence on the very day our Plato was published, wonderfully inspired in me that ancient vow of the hero Cosimo concerning Plotinus, a vow entirely hidden from me, but divinely inspired in him.

Since indeed we have now touched upon divine providence concerning the duty of philosophizing, it seems worthwhile to pursue it a little more broadly. It is certainly not to be thought that acute and, in a way, philosophical human minds can ever be gradually attracted and led to perfect religion by any other bait than a philosophical one.

For acute minds generally commit themselves solely to reason, and when they receive this from a certain religious philosopher, they readily admit a common religion; indeed, imbued with this, they are led to a better form of religion comprehended under its genus

PROLOGUE.
And so, not without divine providence, wishing, namely, to wonderfully recall all to itself according to each individual's genius, it came to pass that a certain pious philosophy was born once among the Persians under Zoroaster, and among the Egyptians under Mercury, in both places consistent with itself. Then it was nurtured among the Thracians under Orpheus and Aglaophemus. And it soon grew up under Pythagoras among the Greeks and Italians, but finally it was perfected by the divine Plato in Athens. Now it was the ancient custom of theologians to cover divine mysteries with mathematical numbers and figures, as well as poetic fictions: lest they be common to anyone rashly. Plotinus finally stripped Theology of these veils, and was the first and only one, as Porphyry and Proclus testify, to divinely penetrate the secrets of the ancients: but because of the incredible brevity of his words, the abundance of his ideas, and the profundity of his meaning, he needs not only a translation of the language, but also commentaries. Therefore, we, in the higher theological matters concerning Plato

**EXHORTATION OF MARSILIO FICINO**
**THE FLORENTINE TO THE LISTENERS AND**
**READERS OF PLOTINUS.**

[Large decorative initial P] FIRST of all, I admonish all of you who come here to hear the divine Plotinus, to consider that you are about to hear Plato himself speaking under the guise of Plotinus. For whether Plato once lived again in Plotinus (which the Pythagoreans will readily grant us), or whether the same Daemon [Marginal note: Comparison of Plato and Plotinus.] first inspired Plato, and then Plotinus, which no Platonist will deny: in any case, the same inspirer breathes upon the Platonic mouth and the Plotinian. But in Plato, by inspiring, he pours forth a more abundant spirit; in Plotinus, however, a narrower breath; or rather, lest I say narrower, at least no less august, sometimes almost deeper. Therefore, the same divine power pours forth divine oracles to the human race through both mouths: worthy in both cases of a most sagacious interpreter: since there [in Plato] he indeed applies himself to unfolding the fictions in a flowing manner; here [in Plotinus], however, he labors more diligently both in expressing the most sacred meanings everywhere and in explaining the briefest words. Remember, moreover, that you will penetrate Plotinus's exalted mind not at all with sense as your companion, nor with human reason as your guide, but with a certain more sublime mind. Indeed (to speak Platonically), we call other men rational souls: but Plotinus, not a soul, but intellect. Thus all philosophers, in his time, especially the Platonists, named him. And would that in interpreting his mysteries, the help of Porphyry, or Eustochius, or Proclus, who arranged and expounded Plotinus's books, were available to us. I hope, however, that which is much more fortunate, that divine aid will not be lacking to Marsilio Ficino in translating and explaining Plotinus's divine books. But now, with heavenly auspices, let us happily proceed both to translate Plotinus's first book and briefly expound its argument, and then the rest. And you should imagine Plato himself exclaiming thus concerning Plotinus:

Οἷος πέπνυται, τοὶ δ᾽ ὡς σκιαὶ ἀΐσσουσι
*He alone is wise, the rest flit about like shadows.*

**MARSILIO FICINO**
**TO THE MAGNANIMOUS PIERO DE' MEDICI,**
**GREETINGS.**

[Large decorative initial C] WHEN on the Ides of November, in the Careggi countryside, I was walking with the Great Lorenzo de' Medici, and we were interpreting many of Plato's mysteries back and forth, I happened to fall, while speaking, from wisdom into fortune, and began to accuse the latter more sharply: because it had for many centuries now hindered Plato, who was striving for light. Then he said, "Marsilio, do not call our Plato unfortunate, unless perhaps you think I will be unfortunate." Indeed, we then concluded our conversation with these words. But is it permissible to consider Lorenzo unfortunate because of the death that followed? And at the same time, that Plato's fortune has utterly collapsed? Far be it from me to think that soul less fortunate, which, flying forth from the chains of the body, the joyful ether received with a new kind of applause, a larger star falling upon the Laurentian roofs, and wondrous flames flashing from above through the Careggi fields for three days. But two days before his death, Jupiter, with a reddened right hand, hurled bolts at sacred citadels, terrifying the city, soon to be orphaned of so great a father: he terrified enemies, lest perhaps they should plot anything serious against the invincible house of Medici. Therefore, neither the hero Lorenzo, nor the heroic Piero, son of Lorenzo, is to be judged less fortunate hereafter because of what recently happened: nor for that reason is our Plato unfortunate. Whose head until now was cherished by the wholly salutary shade of the laurel, now his feet rest on the firmest rock. Finally, Plotinus, now grasped by your hands, will meanwhile sustain the elder Plato on pious shoulders; and with you as guide, he will bring him forth into the light.

**THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS, AND THE SERIES OF HIS BOOKS, BY PORPHYRY AS AUTHOR, BUT WITH MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE AS INTERPRETER.**

[Left column: Greek text with decorative initial Π]

[Middle gutter section markers: A, B, C, D, E, F]

[Right column:]

Plotinus scorned pleasures, empty glory, and life. He died of angina; a dragon appeared.

PLOTINUS, a philosopher singular in our age, seemed to be affected by a certain shame, because his soul was in a body. When therefore he was thus affected, it is no wonder that he would not calmly relate from where he drew his lineage, nor by what parents he was born, nor even from what country he originated. He likewise so greatly disdained to hand over the likeness of his body to painters and sculptors to be rendered, that when Amelius implored him to permit his image to be made: "As if indeed," he said, "it were not enough to bear this image which nature has surrounded us with from the beginning: do you also think that an image of this image should be left to posterity, more lasting, as a work worthy of spectacle?" Since therefore he diligently denied this, and refused to wait for the painter's work by sitting, Amelius ordered a friend named Carterius, the best painter of his time, to enter Plotinus's schools. For it was permitted for anyone to attend the assemblies of those disputing there. Amelius therefore accustomed the painter, through a certain long attention, to conceive more vivid images in his mind from observation. Then, while Carterius duly rendered the likeness from the image committed to memory, and Amelius at the same time corrected the lines to achieve the likeness, by the skill of this painter, a most similar image was produced, unknown to Plotinus. Furthermore, when he was often troubled by colic, he always refused enemas, saying that such treatments were not fitting for an old man. Nor did he ever accept theriac antidotes, since he said he would not even take food from the bodies of tame animals. He also abstained from baths; but he used daily rubdowns at home. But when a plague, beyond measure, grew worse, and those who rubbed him had already departed from life, and he himself had entirely neglected that kind of treatment, he gradually fell into angina. This evil, indeed, never gave any indication of itself in my presence before. But when I had departed, the plague of this disease so greatly intensified (as my friend Eustochius, who did not abandon Plotinus until his death, later reported to me upon my return) that, due to excessive hoarseness, all that clear and resonant vigor of his rounded voice departed; his sight also grew dim, and his hands and feet became ulcerated. Wherefore, since his friends no longer greeted him, because he himself was accustomed to address everyone by his own mouth—

He departed from the city; and having set out for Campania, he was taken to the estate of Zethus, his old friend, who had already departed this life. But necessities for him were supplied from the possessions and heirs of Zethus, and also brought from Minturnae from Castricius's lands. For Castricius had estates in Minturnae. But when Plotinus was approaching death, as Eustochius, who lived in Puteoli, told us, and who had arrived rather late to him, Plotinus said: "I am still waiting for you, and indeed I am now striving to bring that which is divine in us back to the Divine itself which is active in the universe." And with these words, he breathed his last. Meanwhile, a serpent, wandering under the bed where he lay,

Spreading an inner light even to his face. Indeed, he was amiable in appearance, but while he was debating, he seemed much more beautiful: then truly a certain thin sweat, like dew, distilled from his face: then a benign gentleness shone forth: then a calm mildness appeared for receiving questions, and a very robust vigor was demonstrated for resolving them. Now indeed, when I, Porphyry, questioned him for three days about the condition by which the soul is especially joined with the body, he persevered in demonstrating it. When also a certain person named Thaumasius entered the schools, intending to discuss common topics, he declared that he wished to hear Plotinus's opinions expounded in writings; but that he could by no means tolerate such a discussion with Porphyry questioning and answering. But Plotinus objected: "Unless we resolve doubts with Porphyry questioning, we will not be able to comment on anything in a continuous discourse in any book." He writes with a certain most intense sharpness and a multifaceted intellect. Indeed, he is brief, but everywhere abounding more in senses than in words. He pours forth many things inspired by divine power; often he wonderfully suffers from the very subject he is discussing; nor does he speak with such simple instruction as with a mind ardently affected by the subject itself. Hidden doctrines of the Stoics and Peripatetics are likewise inserted into his books; but especially the opinions of Aristotle compiled after his Physics are more frequently found there. Nothing at all escaped him that pertained to geometry, arithmetic, mechanics, perspective, or music; although he never rendered himself ready to execute these works. In his schools, commentaries of the Platonic philosophers Severus, Cronius, Numenius, Gaius, Atticus were read; likewise of the Peripatetics Aspasius, Alexander, Adrastus, and whatever commentaries happened to come up: but nothing from these was discussed in a continuous discourse. For he was his own master and independent, and different from them in contemplation. But in discussing matters, he carried the understanding of Ammonius. As soon as he emerged imbued with the reading, he would rise, bringing with a few words a profound understanding of contemplation. When the book of Longinus and Philarchus on principles had been read: Longinus is indeed a man of letters, but by no means a philosopher. When Origen had come to the schools, Plotinus immediately, suffused with a blush on his cheeks, wished to rise, but being asked by Origen to continue the discourse, he replied: "The desire to speak ceases when he who speaks perceives that he will be speaking to those who themselves already know the same things." And so, after having discussed a few things, he rose from there.

When I had recited a poem on the sacred marriage on Plato's birthday, and a certain person present objected that Porphyry was mad, inasmuch as many things there had been spoken with a certain divine inspiration and secret mystery: Plotinus openly said to all who were listening: "You have shown him to be at once a poet, a philosopher, and a priest." There, on one occasion, the orator Diophanes read a defense for Alcibiades, raging in Plato's Symposium, proving that it was fitting for the sake of learning virtue to expose oneself to a lover: he would demonstrate this very thing, even if he (the lover) had sought a venereal encounter. But during the reading, Plotinus rose several times, as if about to suddenly depart from that assembly; nevertheless, he restrained himself;

Eubulus, a follower of Plato, wrote in Athens and sent his writings to Rome concerning certain Platonic questions. He applied himself to the rules of astronomy, although not in a very mathematical manner; but he applied himself more diligently to the judgments of astrologers. And when he discovered that their predictions were not trustworthy, he did not hesitate to often refute their prophecies in his writings.

Although many philosophers existed in our times, O Marcellus, indeed a greater number of them existed in the early years of our age. For it is by no means possible to say how few the present time possesses. But while we were young men, not a few excelled in the studies of philosophy,

**LIFE OF PLOTINUS.**

[Marginal note: unclear mark]
Therefore, of those who have written, some indeed composed nothing further than a collection or a certain transcription of what older authors had already composed: such as Euclid, and Democritus, and Proclinus. Others, however, commending very little from ancient history to memory, following the same topics, undertook to compose books, like Annius, and Medius, and Phoebion. These, indeed, thought glory was to be gained more from the very arrangement of their discourse than from the mere mental concept; to whom Heliodorus also may be added, who himself, besides those things which had been heard from older authors, seems to have contributed absolutely nothing more to a distinct structure of discourse. Plotinus and Gentilianus Amelius, however, are filled with an abundance of propositions, which they diligently discuss, and seriously chose the task of writing, using a certain peculiar method of contemplation. And Plotinus indeed, as it seems, expounded Pythagorean as well as Platonic principles more certainly than his predecessors. And indeed, the writings of Numenius, Cronius, Moderatus, Thrasyllus, where Plotinus writes about the same things, in no part come close to his exact diligence. Amelius, however, resolved to observe Plotinus's footsteps and follows many of his discoveries; but while he is more prolix in explaining things and wanders in a wider scope of interpretation, he assumes a form contrary to Plotinus. We consider only the books of these men worthy of consideration. For why should anyone strive to follow others, meanwhile neglecting to investigate those from whom these men, receiving these things, committed them to their own writings, and they themselves added nothing to these, not even the main points of things, nor indeed any argument? Therefore, they cared for nothing further than to gather what belonged to many, or by discussing many things, to choose the better ones. Now indeed, through other means, we have also achieved the same, just as when we contradicted Gentilianus concerning justice as posited by Plato, and when we considered Plotinus's book treating of Ideas: I mean our common friend and theirs, Tyrian Basil, who himself also treated not a few things imitating Plotinus, and approving Plotinus himself more than our way and rule, by the composition of a certain book, he tried to show that the Platonic opinion on Ideas was [Marginal note: to be truer] truer than ours: this man, I say, by a certain opposing re-writing, seems to have moderately refuted, as one who had not, of course, correctly presented his argument. We, indeed, in these matters, have discussed not a few opinions of these men, as also in the letter to Amelius, extended to the size of a book, responding indeed to some things which he had sent and written to us from Rome, which letter he himself inscribed in the manner of Plotinian philosophy. We, however, were content with a merely common inscription of the book, inscribing the book itself "To Amelius's Letter."

(A) Beware of claiming for oneself the safe (teachings) of Numenius; Plotinus, however, decided to follow the mysteries of the Pythagoreans. But the works of Numenius, Cronius, Moderatus, and Thrasyllus, compared to Plotinus's works on the same subjects, are to be considered inferior as far as absolute reason is concerned. Therefore, when he (Longinus) had said that Amelius indeed progressed in Plotinus's footsteps, but was led in opposition to Plotinus by a certain excessive prolixity of exposition, he then made mention of me, who had recently attained familiarity with Plotinus, and added: (B) "But our and their common friend, that Tyrian Basilius, he himself indeed treated and composed not a few things after the example of Plotinus."

In these words, Longinus truly indicates that he perceived that I had most diligently avoided Amelius's digressions, which were too alien from a philosopher, and that in writing, I had embraced Plotinus's form. It is enough, therefore, that such a great man, and foremost in judgment, be brought forward thus far as a witness for us, writing such things about Plotinus.

(C) Indeed, if I had been able to approach him then, when he summoned me, he certainly would never have written against those things which he began to write before he had diligently examined the doctrine itself. Golden lyre had these things to say, to one living well.

In this oracle it is contained that Plotinus was good, gentle, and mild above all, and sweet, such as we have also proven him to be by true experience. Furthermore, that he was vigilant, and with a pure soul always directed upwards to the divine itself, which indeed he ardently loved with his whole soul. Likewise, that he strove with all his might to emerge completely from the bitter wave of this bloody life. Therefore, by this reason, by this blessed light, when he often raised himself with his whole mind to the first God, superior to mind, and ascended through all the steps arranged by Plato in the Symposium to divine things, that God immediately shone forth to him, having neither form nor any idea, but being beyond intellect, and the whole intelligible subsisting in itself. To whom I, Porphyry, also once drew near, and was united, when I was already completing my sixty-eighth year of age. Therefore, that ultimate goal appeared to Plotinus as close as possible. For the end and sign for Plotinus was to which he directed the keenness of his mind to approach, and to be united with God himself, present everywhere to all. But four times while I was with him, he attained this end: not merely in potential, I say, but attained by a certain ineffable act. Moreover, the oracle adds that the gods often, seizing Plotinus as he wandered about, directed him into the right path, while they benignly extended the most abundant rays of divine light to the lights of his eyes: so that it may truly be said that Plotinus composed his books by contemplation and intuition divinely shining. Now indeed, it is said by the oracle that he beheld many things with his eyes, both inwardly and outwardly, with vigilant intuition, and most beautiful things, which indeed no professor of philosophy would easily have beheld. For human contemplation can indeed be superior to other human contemplation; but compared to divine knowledge, it can indeed be pleasing, yet it cannot penetrate the depth which the higher beings penetrate. Thus far the oracle has shown what things Plotinus accomplished while he was enclosed in the body, and what he attained. After this, it prophesies that Plotinus, freed from the body, arrived at the blessed assembly, where...

--- Page 37 ---
**PLOTINUS'S LIFE.**

**A** Pure charity, sweet desire, and joy and love joined with God. Moreover, that Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus, sons of God, have been appointed judges of souls: to whom Plotinus goes not indeed to be judged, but to converse, with whom also other excellent gods converse. Where also Plato and Pythagoras and others live, whoever firmly established the chorus of immortal love: there also the most blessed Daemones have their origin. Likewise, that he lives there a festive life, most full of freshness and joy, and that he continues blessed by divine bounty.
**B**

Thus far, let it be said about the life of Plotinus in a historical manner. [Marginal note: *Arrangement of Plotinus's books digested by subject matter in order.*]
Since Plotinus entrusted to us that we should take care of the order and emendation of his books: and I indeed promised him while he was living, and I pledged to others to accomplish it: first of all, I considered it worthwhile not to allow the books to lie scattered in confusion, just as they were composed in succession of time: but just as Apollodorus the Athenian collected Epicharmus's comedies into ten volumes, and Andronicus the Peripatetic distributed the books of Aristotle and Theophrastus into treatises, gathering their own suppositions into one: so also I have divided Plotinus's fifty-four books into six Enneads, rejoicing in the occasion of the perfect number six, namely, and nine. And to each Ennead, that is, to each nine, assigning its own, I thus simultaneously gathered related ones, always placing the lighter ones first in numerical order.

work itself can signify it.

SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK

The rational soul is a medium between divine and natural forms; it is not inherent in the body, but
is present to it

and where, with an end proposed and the diversity of paths discovered, it consults about the choice of those. Indeed, this whole fa-

The rational soul, although it consists in itself, nevertheless in a certain way inclines towards the body, which least of all suits an intellectual substance.

III. Since indeed he had indicated that the soul consists in itself, lest anyone therefore think it differs not at all from the mind, he adds that the soul, although it exists in itself, just like the mind, nevertheless cherishes the body, and by cherishing forms it, and fills it with life: which indeed the mind itself does not accomplish. Then he says the soul already vivifies by using the body as a certain natural and conjoined instrument. After this he investigates whether, while it uses the body as an instrument, it receives the same sensations and passions, and gradually inclines to the view that it does not receive them: because, namely, it uses the body not as relying on the body, but as ruling it. Then indeed he signifies that the soul is separable from the body by nature, and that this is especially proven in reality by philosophy: finally he asks, if it is joined to the body in some way, how it is joined. Is it as a certain temperament of the body? Or because it itself propagates itself through the whole body? Or because it is a form lying in the body? Or a species presiding over

IN BOOK I OF THE FIRST ENNEAD

I feel another law in my members warring against the law of my mind, and leading me captive. But even reason itself, since it is also concerned with things to be done, should have long ago so trained its imagination as to rush less rashly, and to tame the animal: and to have directed and formed itself towards the intellect first. For this intellect certainly does not concern itself with individual things that are done: and therefore is entirely free from fault. But we, that is, defined by rational power and action, sometimes arrive at intelligible and ideal reasons, and species of things, which are first in the divine mind: then they are also in ours, but we very rarely rise to them. Then, however, in our reason they are only in potency: but in both minds they are always in [marginal note: act]. He said that the discursive reasonings are most proper to us, that is, to the soul: because since it is a medium between divine things which always remain, and natural things, which by a certain lapse and motion, as it were, straightly depart from themselves, it deservedly has a circular motion and discursion, properly a medium between straight motion and rest. Intelligence is also said to be proper to the soul, not so much because it is of its nature, but because it understands without the instrument of the body. Thus the soul also reasons without it. But this at least is the difference, that discursive argumentation, even if it is not through a bodily instrument, almost always has some images of sensible things before its eyes. For motion naturally tends towards such things: but intelligence neither uses bodily instruments, nor contemplates such images. Reason, moreover, when it turns itself entirely to the intellect, contemplates universals without images of particulars. But we discuss these more broadly in our Theology. While he uses the word of Aristotle here, it signifies that Aristotle in these matters does not at all disagree with Plato. He adds that the discourse of reason, intellect, and imagination are engaged, and do not touch bodily passions, but certain images of passions are engaged by their own sense, that is, by primary imagination. Likewise, that reason, or thought, is a certain act of intelligence. For true thought is a certain intelligence more broadly explained: and sometimes reaching the intellect, it contemplates universal species: sometimes inclining towards imagination, and through it to the animal, it derives universal species down to particulars: sometimes comparing these with those, it discerns and judges wherein they agree or disagree. And if it begins from the intellect, and thence departs, then it descends from universals to particulars by composing. But if it takes occasion from imagination, and rises higher, it ascends from particulars to universals by resolving. Finally, you will observe this order in the soul, so that you remember it has species in the mind, both universal and stable. But in reason, species are indeed universal, but in a certain way mobile: while in imagination, they are already particular and mutable. He concludes that passions, disturbances, and the causes of sins properly consist in the animal: but in the soul, the awareness of these and often a certain consent. You, however, in the words of Plotinus, observe the Mosaic allegory: namely, the persons whom, that is, man himself as Adam: and the human animal drawn thence and degenerating as Eve. Add also the drawing from the sleeping soul. For this then propagates from itself, when, lapsing from its pristine vigil with God to natural things, and having forgotten divine things, it now sleeps and dreams. Therefore, it then generates corporeal life as Eve. Consider also this one first sinning, then that one consenting: but the intellect presiding over it as an angel, and soon rebuking, and God to the angel. And finally, consider two in the flesh, that is, as it were, two souls in the same body. But since Plotinus, Origen, and Ammonius understood Moses thus, let us proceed to the rest.

How the animal in us relates to the soul, and whether any life perishes.
X Chapter X of the book teaches that what is proper to our animal also pertains to us in a certain way. Likewise, that in the rational soul there are virtues sought by reason: in the animal, virtues acquired by habit. Again, that life bestowed by the rational soul upon the body is not extinguished when the body is dissolved, but almost follows its soul, just as light seems to follow its candle. Numenius had also felt the same.

How the soul relates to the intellect, through which it always understands, even if reason does not always perceive it. Also concerning children and brutes.

XI After having discussed in the preceding chapters how we relate to the animal which is below us: now in the eleventh chapter, how we relate to the intellect, which is superior to us by reason. He says therefore, that our intellect always acts in itself concerning the divine, and by perpetual intellection always contemplates all intelligibles: which Iamblichus asserts to have been an Egyptian discovery. For which reason it also acts the same in children. But I believe Plotinus understood that thus: "The angels of little ones always see the face of the heavenly Father." For Ammonius and Origen were accustomed to interpret sacred writings in the Platonic manner. He says moreover: in children, the animal powers operate most intensely due to the necessary structure for body growth, and around these same powers, and the same ministry, the imagination of the higher soul is also greatly occupied: but the smallest sparks of reason flash forth into these, as they are turned towards opposites. He adds that the act of reason, being free from these, operates meanwhile concerning the intellect: since a power so effective cannot be entirely idle. Nevertheless, neither the act of the intellect concerning intelligibles, nor the act of reason concerning the intellect, is then recognized by us: because the imagination proper to the higher soul, by whose ministry perception occurs in us, being entirely turned towards the opposite, does not receive any images of intelligences, which it might reflect to the eyes of reason like a mirror: by which images, thus reflected, reason is accustomed, and therefore we are accustomed, to perceive the actions of intelligence

--- Page 44 ---
COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO.

...soul, to be supplied to the rational part, but it is itself meanwhile said to be present: yet it is not present, indeed, as much as it provides life, it is by no means present: because it does not perform there the customary office of reason, although in the higher realms intelligence performs it: and the very substance of the rational soul consists in itself, and does not become part of a composite. This last point pleased Proclus, and before him Porphyry, who denied that the rational soul of man becomes the proper soul of a brute, yet conceded that the souls of sagacious animals have some reason and always live. Origen also attempted the same, namely, when he heard that demons frequently insinuate themselves into men and are sometimes sent into pigs, he dared to send human souls into animals, perhaps for purgation. But let them see to these matters themselves. It must be noted, however, that Plotinus here tempers his judgment in this matter, when he says: "If our souls are in brutes." Likewise where he says, "As it is said," namely by the Egyptians. Again when he adds, "Which have sinned": as if to say, "in place of purgatory." Finally, when he denies that it becomes the proper form of a brute, and part of a composite. But we will amend this opinion in what follows. And in general, how Platonic sayings are to be purified, we have declared in the books of our Theology, especially the last ones.

In the rational soul, there is neither sin proper, nor punishment: but in the irrational life, which is an image of the soul, which, when the soul departs from here, although it is no longer an image, is nevertheless a certain vital act of the soul rooted within.

XII. CHAPTER TWELVE raises and resolves doubts concerning the aforesaid, by saying that in the proper essence of the soul itself, there is neither sin nor punishment, because it is a simple form existing in itself, never falling from its proper state: but rather in the life emanating therefrom, and properly in the animal, because it is composed of this life and the body. Indeed, it says elsewhere that the soul sins, elsewhere that it does not sin: to sin, that is, to somewhat relax the intention previously turned towards higher things: not to sin, however, that is, neither to lose natural faculties, nor to admit foreign elements within. Then indeed it declares how the generation of an animal occurs, that is, when a certain life results from the soul into a body already affected by a certain condition: and that this is something natural, neither sin, nor does the soul properly fall in this way, but rather assents and fosters. Furthermore, this life, which is both an act and a certain image of the soul, when the soul departs from here, does not perish as far as it is an act of the soul, but ceases to be an image: just as if an image is formed in a mirror from a face, and when the face departs, a certain act remains in the face, and the effective, radiating vigor of the image, but the image itself does not remain. Then indeed this act of the soul ceases to be an image when both the body prepared for the image to result is absent, and the soul is entirely converted to the intelligible: yet such an act does not cease as far as it is the vigor of life, just as even with a severed hand, the vivifying act itself does not cease, which would equally govern the hand again if it were restored: as appears in regrowing hair. Remember that Numenius and Plotinus believed that nothing of life ever perishes: because life is a certain splendor of eternity, that is, of the first intelligence, and an indissoluble bond of the universe.

The rational soul reasons by itself, not through a bodily instrument. It also understands through its own intellect: it also understands through the common intellect, which is, as it were, a certain form of every individual intellect.

XIII. CHAPTER THIRTEEN declares what was almost the last point proposed in the question, namely, what it is that considers these things in the present. It asserts, however, that it is not some composite thing that considers these in the present through the soul as a part, but the soul itself existing in itself meditates on such things: therefore, it is not similarly changed when the body changes, but its motion is its own essential act of life, or a vital and perennial act of its essence. It adds: just as rational consideration is ours, that is, proper to the soul, and not performed through the body, so intelligence is proper to the soul: because, namely, the soul is intellectual, so much so that intelligence in the soul is life, and the summit of the soul's life: which indeed is itself a part of us, and acts in us, that is, our most proper reason, just as the common intellect acts in ours. Here note that life in all things is almost the ultimate splendor of the mind: but the supreme mind is the highest degree of life. Hence that prophetic saying: "Give me understanding, and I shall live." It adds that the soul understands both through its own intellect and through the common and divine intellect, and that reason strives towards our intellect, and finally our intellect towards the divine: and both are indeed a part of us, but in different ways. Our intellect is indeed a part of us, because in a certain way it is the apex of the soul: but the divine is seen as a part in a certain way, because our intellect is subjected to the divine as to a form, like a certain matter

when they are at rest as far as we are concerned, they meanwhile operate towards the higher realms. Indeed, they act upon us when they proceed all the way to the middle. What then? Are we not also that which is before this? Nevertheless, attention must be paid. For we do not constantly use whatever we have. But when we turn the middle, either to higher things or to contrary things: or whatever we bring from potentiality or habit into act. But how do brute animals have a soul? Perhaps if human souls **D**
(as is said) that have sinned are in them, this [separable part] does not become a characteristic of brutes, as far as it is separable, but it is not present to them. But the common sensation itself has an image of the soul together with the body; a body, I say, such as is made for the image of the soul itself. But if the soul of man has not entered by some illumination, such an animal is produced by the soul of the whole itself.

**XII**
BUT if the soul is not a sinner, how are there judgments and punishments? But this discourse differs from every discourse **E**
that says it sins and is purified, and pays penalties in the underworld, and transmigrates through bodies. Therefore, one must adhere to whichever discourse one prefers. Perhaps someone might find how they do not contradict each other. For he who teaches that the soul does not sin, posits something entirely simple, taking the soul to be one and the same as being soul. But he who says that it sins, joins to it and **F**
moreover fuses another species of soul having grave passions. Therefore, the soul itself becomes a composite something from all these, and indeed suffers according to the whole, and the composite sins: and it is this that pays the penalties, not that [the simple soul]. Hence Plato says: "For we see it, just as those who look upon marine Glaucus." But if one wishes to inspect its nature, one must separate what is joined to it, and consider philosophy in relation to those things which **G**
it touches, and to which it is akin, so that what it truly is, may be revealed. Therefore, life is one thing, and actions are another, and that which is punished is another. But withdrawal and separation ought to be not only from this body, but from every adjunct. For in generation, an adjunct occurs, or altogether, the generation of another species of soul seems to happen. But as to what is asked, in what manner generation occurs? The answer would be, that the soul descends—

MARSILIO FICINO'S ARGUMENT
FOR THE BOOK ON VIRTUES.

SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK,
One must strive, by fleeing from here, to become like God through virtue.

THE end of this book, indeed, is for the soul to become like God. The subject matter, however, is virtue, through which such likeness is attained. Finally, the form of the book is its division into seven chapters, and in the first, a certain exercise for finding virtue, and in the following, its discovery, definition, and distribution. The first chapter begins with that golden saying of our Plato, placed in the book on Knowledge, that is, the Theaetetus: That we may avoid evils, we must forthwith flee from here. To flee from here, however, is to become like God. The soul becomes like God through virtue. But lest anyone err concerning the knowledge of the end, he argues that the soul will be like God through virtue not because, as you see, virtue exists in God as it does in the soul, but because God is the principle and exemplar of virtue, and virtue itself. God, I say, the divine mind, the artificer of the world, presiding over the world itself and its soul. And although among the principles of argument he grants that the soul becomes similar through virtue to the world's soul and its mind, which is also true, nevertheless, as the discussion progresses, he asserts that the end of this likeness extends higher, namely, to the divine intellect. And to this end, as if to a fourth degree, where the exemplars of virtues are, the soul arrives through three degrees. Firstly, by civil virtues, secondly, by purgative virtues, thirdly, by the virtues of the soul already purified. And this is the summary of the entire book.

Although the soul becomes like God through virtues, yet God does not possess virtue: but He is the exemplar of virtue: and what is a quality of virtue in the soul, with God is essence: likewise, ideas are confirmed here.

Showing meanwhile that civic [virtues] should rather be called dispositions

which the soul ascends through the three already mentioned steps, and is to be formed from there. And indeed, just as there are three steps, so there are three kinds of exemplary virtues. First, when the soul turns its imagination to its reason, to be better formed there or from there. Second, when it translates the formulas of reason to forms inherent in its own intellect, so that it may know better there. Third, when it completely adapts its own intellect to the divine mind, and conforms its own understanding to the ideas of the divine mind. This it achieves by a certain eternal contact. From this it follows that they can in time conform both reason to their intellect and imagination to reason properly. The existence of the primary forms of all things in one intellect, namely the effector of all, is signified by the congregation of natural forms in one matter subject to all. That they are distinct in some way there, is shown by the formal difference between natural forms: which is neither from unformed matter, nor by chance, since it is always most orderly, nor from one certain species of form among these, because it is ordered to one most common to all. [III] Since, therefore, the formal distinction of all forms proceeds from one form, the effector of all, it is necessary that the principle of distinction exists there, by which forms are distinct from each other in a certain way. That intellect is therefore both uniform and omniform at the same time. But there, since there is also the greatest unity, indeed, the essence of all forms is one, and the principles are diverse. But in any intellect after that one, forms are certain essential, eternal, and deeply intimate contacts of ideas. From this contact, then, in the soul, that is, in the rational faculty, formulas of ideas, as if conceived from that union, are indeed always inherent, but passing from habit to act and vice versa in time: and they are universal formulas, designating what each thing is and why it is. Furthermore, from these, other formulas flow into the imagination, now inclining more closely to individual things: which show more of the 'what kind' rather than the 'what it is' about each thing, and if they show 'what kind of thing,' they do not, however, reveal 'why it is'. But you, where Plotinus elsewhere denies that figures of things are received by the soul, lest this contradict itself in this book, understand that figures are not impressed upon the soul by inferior things, and do not recently arrive, and then again recede, and are utterly deleted. For these forms, which it draws from an intimate source, are as it were the very nature of the soul, or the natural power of the soul, and not something adventitious and added. For the soul proceeds from the author of its nature, and one power of it emerges from another, always endowed with its natural function. Remember, Plotinus here is properly discussing the intellectual good of the soul, and considers the end of virtues to be that the soul may thereby become a universal intellectual world, the end of which world is the good itself, simply speaking. For just as above the soul, as if corporeal, is the soul itself simply, so also above animal intelligence is the intellect itself simply: and above the intellectual good, if the good itself simply exists. But in explaining the words, where he says that figures, or impressed forms, must be accommodated to their exemplars, already brought into act, and submitted to the illuminator, understand that the formulas of imagination are to be subjected to the forms of reason and to reason. Likewise, the formulas of reason are to be applied to the proper intellect and its forms, or rather, to its formations. For this is always formed by the divine mind. Where he says that the intellect is not alien to the soul, understand that it has its own inherent intellect, and its own intellect is always joined to the divine, and joined to itself in a certain proper way. That forms are naturally inherent in the soul, and that our intellect is always conformed to the divine, we have sufficiently proven in Theology.

*In the proper imagination of the rational soul, images are often aroused according to the first movements of the imagination, which is in the animal before it consults or perceives.*

V He defines the virtues of the purified soul in a sufficiently clear order. What he here calls 'prefigured phantasy,' understand that from the first impulses, certain images prone to the senses are often aroused even in our imagination, before reason sufficiently perceives them.

*Wisdom in the divine mind is like a touch, in our mind like a contact, in reason like a visible figure.*

VI He confirms that the end of the soul is not innocence, but to become God: and says that he in whom only the first movements now remain, is a certain god and a demon at the same time: For demons are touched by certain affections. But he in whom even the first movements now seem to be entirely lulled to sleep is merely a god, that is, a wholly intellectual soul from among those who properly accompany the divine mind. He adds that when the soul has turned entirely to itself, with purification, that is, preceding, it is such as it had proceeded from the divine mind: and is suddenly and completely restored there: For even having departed from this long ago, it did not entirely leave it. Indeed, reason adheres to its own intellect and its proper guide at will, and the intellect is naturally coupled with the divine mind. After this, he defines exemplary virtues, insofar as they are accommodated to us in some way. For insofar as they are in the divine mind, they are indeed exemplars, but not virtues. But where he says that wisdom in the soul is indeed the inspection of those things which the intellect possesses: and that the intellect has wisdom by a certain touch: understand 'intellect' here as twofold, namely ours and the divine, and wisdom in the divine is called a touch, that is, not the possession of some image, but of the thing itself, or rather its existence. In our intellect, however, it is rather called a contact, that is, a real (so to speak) union, not an imaginary notion. For in the rational nature, which is properly called soul, the possession is more imaginary: but in the intellect (so to speak) it is substantial: but this possession is first in the divine mind, then it is transferred also to ours.

*The divine intellect is primarily that which it has: our intellect is secondarily that which it has: reason is not similarly that which it has. Likewise, a comparison of virtues is made here: and some precepts are handed down.*

VII He accommodates exemplary virtues, adapted to the soul, in a certain order corresponding to the divine exemplars: and declares what the exemplar of each virtue is in God: and in what way exemplary virtues in the soul rightly correspond to the divine exemplars of virtues. And where he says that the soul is not similarly what it has, as the intellect is, understand the soul as rather already discursive, in which essence is one thing, forms or images are another, and habits and acts are another. But in the divine mind, essence is reduced to act from eternity: and that essential act itself fulfills all things which are accomplished in the soul through certain additions. Moreover, our intellect is in a certain way what it has, to speak from Plotinus' mind. It is

--- Page 55 ---
IN BOOK I. OF THE FIRST ENNEAD 31

For it is reduced to the act of all ideas by eternal and intimate contact: into the act of which the divine mind proceeded from eternity. After this, it compares virtues with each other in a certain way, and delivers certain precepts, or resolves doubts. It says therefore: Those things which precede perfect purity of soul are paths to virtue, rather than virtue itself. Likewise, purity itself is not considered virtue, unless it is referred to God, both to be imitated and to be attained according to one's strength. Again, in the lower degrees of virtues, the higher ones are not present except through an image. But in the higher ones, the lower ones are contained by an exemplar, and virtue itself. Likewise, where principles are changed, the species of virtues also change. Principles, I say, are two: namely, the proper end of each virtue, and its rules and laws, to which it is formed: especially when the principles of prudence are changed, which is judged to be the rule of other virtues. From this it follows that civil temperance is of one species, purgative of another, also purified of another, exemplary of another, and the rest similarly. Finally, it concludes that the common and principal end of all virtues is not in external things, not in virtue, not in the soul, but in God. Indeed, nothing more sacred can be said by this conclusion. Which also testifies to us the divine mind of our Plotinus.

A To be purified is the removal of everything alien. But the Good seems to be something else besides this itself. Perhaps if it was good before the loss of purity, purification itself would suffice: but purification will indeed suffice: yet what remains will be good, not purification itself. Then indeed it must be asked what that remainder is. For perhaps the remaining nature is not good: otherwise it would never have been in evil. Is it therefore permissible to call it good-formed? Or rather, by no means sufficient to remain in that which is truly good?

That it may perceive: or having become similar to it, or having revered it, so that it dares to do nothing of those things which a good person would not dare. Therefore, there will be no struggle. For the present understanding suffices, which that inferior part will fear, so much so that it will be angry with itself if, in any way disturbed, it has not maintained quiet in the presence of the master, and reproaches its own inconstancy.

Therefore, there is no such sin, but a correction for man, and his duty. But the very striving and desire is not merely to be free from sin, but to be God. If, therefore, something of this kind happens only inadvertently, then such a god and a demon will exist, being twofold; nay, rather having another with him, endowed with another virtue. But if nothing (inadvertent happens), then God alone. God, I say, from the number of those who follow the first. For he himself is the one who proceeded from there. And if it happens according to himself, as he came, he is there; but having progressed here, he adheres to the intellect. And moreover, his power will assimilate this to himself, so that, if it is possible, he is either not moved, or does not do anything of those things which least please the master.

What, therefore, is any virtue for this (person/being)? Wisdom, indeed, is the inspection of those things which the intellect possesses. But the intellect has by a certain touch. And each is twofold: one existing in the intellect, the other in the soul. And there (in the intellect) it is not virtue, but in the soul, it is virtue. What then is it there? It is its own action and what it is; but here (in the soul) it is what is in another, hence virtue. For neither justice itself, nor temperance itself, nor any similar thing, is properly a virtue, but rather an exemplar. But what is done by it (the exemplar) in the soul, that is already virtue. For it is the virtue of something. But each thing itself is of itself, not of another. But if justice is indeed the action of its proper function, is it therefore always in a multitude of parts? Nay, in a multitude, whenever there are many parts. But simply, it is the action of its proper function, even if it exists in one. Therefore, true justice itself is of one towards itself, in which there is not one thing and another. Wherefore, for the soul itself, a greater justice is to direct itself by acting towards the intellect. But temperance is an intimate conversion to the intellect. Fortitude is a habit free from passion, through its likeness to that which it looks up to, naturally constituted outside of passion. But the soul, by virtue, overcomes passion, lest it suffer together with an inferior companion.

18 COMMENTARY. MARSILIO FICINO.
we proceed to divinity by a valley, by reason, sight, hearing. And three natures of souls are carried there more readily, namely, the philosophical one dedicated to reason, the amatory one to the eyes, and the musical one to hearing. Which Plato attests in *Phaedrus* and *Phaedo*.

On the three contemplations in the intelligible world, and
then on the three types of genius.

Furthermore, in the divine world, three things are primarily conceived: species (form/kind), number, and mode (measure). For the divine mind itself is the first species, and every idea is a species or form. There is a certain number there, both of forms, and in each form, of those things which are proper to the form. There is also a certain mode or measure of virtue and a certain proportion, both of forms in themselves or to forms, and to the numbers of numbers. Although these three are distinguished from each other by a certain reason, nevertheless in the species itself or form, both number and mode are contained, but by a formal reason. Likewise, in number, there is both form and mode, by a certain condition especially numerous. Again, in mode and measure, similarly there is both form and number, by a proportion, so to speak, mensural. Wherefore, contemplators of divine things, although each one sees and loves all things, some nevertheless, both by cognition and affection, refer the two remaining things to the species itself: others indeed to number by a similar reason: others finally to the mode itself and measure. From the first, indeed, comes the philosophical genius, from the second, the musical, and from the third, not inferior, the amatory. Although these three types of genius are almost thus conjoined among themselves, just as species, number, and mode are interconnected. The philosopher, therefore, in conceiving numbers and measures, rather admires the species itself and nature. The musician, however, in natures, and modes, and measures, is vehemently affected by sonorous numbers. Finally, the lover ardently pursues mode and measure in all things. All three in summary, Plotinus says, are elevated to sublime beauty, that is, to the divine mind, which is the first beauty, the eternal splendor of the good itself, in which both species, number, and mode, like three Graces embracing each other, equally lead to complete beauty and full grace. Likewise, he says, one is excited differently from another. Again, after they have risen to the divine mind, which is also the intelligible world, there they proceed through all genera of ideas in a certain order of their own: finally, they emerge from that world to the good itself, which is the beginning and end of that world. After this, he explains by what reason the musical genius turns there by nature and is carried there by art. For nature is inclined to beauty, so that, namely, through beautiful voices it is especially aroused to the numerous beauty of proportion. Here, therefore, he must be taught that that very thing which he admires in the modulations of voices is not vocal, or similar matter, otherwise all sounds everywhere would equally please him, but rather a proportional and numerous reason, as if it were a certain form in the matter of voice and sound. Wherefore, if in any way matter could be separated from it, and such a form remain either in itself or in the mind, then the form alone would please: and it would please more, because there the reason of numerous proportion would be more perfect and a more absolute unity: for the sake of which grace and proportion please. He must therefore be led from a beautiful voice to the beauty which exists in the voice: hence again to that which consists in a certain proportion within the rational soul: then from this and that proportion, which are something beautiful, or a certain beauty, to the beautiful of this order itself, and to beauty itself, that is, the idea: and first to the idea of numerous and vocal beauty, then to the simple reason of beauty, finally to the good itself, from which beauty, that is, its splendor and grace, almost thus shines forth: just as external comeliness from internal health, and external light from internal light.

The Philosophical, Musical, and Amorous types of genius easily converge.

II In the second chapter of the book, he says that the musician often conspires with the lover, and both with the philosopher, and not without reason: for the aspirations of these are close both in position and motion: the Sun, Mercury, and Venus. Again, close are hearing, and sight, and imagination serving reason. Likewise, he who naturally loves the beautiful, by what reason he loves

--- Page 63 ---
IN BOOK III, ENNEAD I, 19

...deals with distinctions, concepts, propositions, and syllogisms. Metaphysics, however, deals with things themselves, using logical tools in the meantime. The task of the Metaphysician is to resolve, divide, compose, define, demonstrate, and by doing so, to progress through all beings, especially to the incorporeal, since these are truly beings: then to the One itself, the principle and end of these: after this, to contemplate the procession of beings from the highest to the lowest, returning again through all grades of beings: finally to return to the highest, and there to rest. Among these things, you can learn how the Platonic division is made in Plotinus's three books on the kinds of being: Also in Parmenides, Sophist, Politicus, Philebus.
      The Metaphysician indeed has innate principles in the intellect, but brings them into action in reason, and by the rules of truth refutes sophisms, and holds to the rules of logic.
V. The fifth chapter of the book teaches that the intellect itself, which always exists in act, and similarly possesses the principles of all sciences, sometimes transmits these to reason turned towards it: through which the mind becomes metaphysical, while reason is formed by the intellect, and perfected into it. Moreover, it says that the metaphysician detects and refutes the falsehoods and cavillations of sophists by the very rule of truth: but does not very attentively meditate on the minute and, as it were, literal rules of logic: nevertheless, because it grasps both the movements of minds themselves, and the agreement and disagreement of things among themselves, it can therefore rightly discern the force of propositions, and the congruence of affirmations and negations.
      All faculties draw principles from metaphysics, without which sciences do not exist, and morals are imperfect.
VI. He says furthermore in the sixth chapter that the other faculties, both mathematical, physical, and moral, derive their principles from metaphysics: likewise, that metaphysics holds entirely universal and very material laws of morals: which it hands over, as a geometer to prudence, or as an architect: prudence, however, serves other virtues as if in building. He concludes that other virtues are imperfect without wisdom, and vice versa. For wisdom and the remaining virtue almost equally coalesce simultaneously: and the natural beginnings of virtues in the soul, with wisdom approaching, emerge into perfect virtues, whether wisdom arises before others, or the reverse: for from wherever you begin, one virtue leads to another. Finally, the natural beginning in rational nature for wisdom or prudence is an imperfect eye: but the former is indeed the right, the latter the left. Again, the natural beginning for other virtues is called a certain imperfect custom. The principle of both kinds of virtues is indeed drawn especially from those things which we naturally possess in mind, or reason, or even imagination.
