[Marginal note:]
Dialectics, that is, metaphysics, contemplates the entire order of beings, and progresses beyond, and uses logic as an instrument.

WHAT is dialectics, which must also be applied to the former things? It is indeed a habit which, by reason, can say of each thing what each thing is: and how it differs from others, or how it agrees. Moreover, how and where anything is: and if it is, what it is: and how many beings there are: and again, non-beings, but things other than beings. The same also disputes about the good itself, and about **B** what is under the contrary of the good. Likewise, what is eternal: or what is not always. I say, treating of all things not by opinion, but by knowledge, free from error which occurs concerning the sensible, it adheres entirely to the intelligible: and diligently acts concerning it, setting aside the false, nourishing the soul in the very field of truth, relying namely on Platonic distinction for the discernment of ideas and species, and for defining anything, and for the primary genera, and those which are from **C** them, weaving and complicating with intellectual reason, until it progresses through the whole intelligible: and again resolving into that from which it had proceeded from the beginning. Then at last, acting in quietude, as it were, inasmuch as it reaches that point, it attains quietude: no longer striving about many things, but reduced to one, it looks upon that which is called logic, occupied with propositions and syllogisms, just as if it concedes the knowledge of writing to some other art, some of which it considers **D** necessary and preceding by art: but it judges these things itself, like the others, and considers some of them useful, others superfluous, and these pertaining to the appetitive faculty.

[Marginal note:]
The metaphysician receives principles from the intellect, and by the most true rules refutes sophisms. Then he comprehends the rules of logic.

BUT from where does this science get these principles? Perhaps the Intellect gives clear principles, if the soul can receive any. Then indeed the soul composes, connects, and divides until it reaches perfect intellect. For this is, as he says, the purest of intelligence, and of prudence, or wisdom. It is necessary therefore, since it is **E** the most excellent habit among those which are in us, to be concerned with being, and with the most excellent: prudence or wisdom indeed with being: but intellect with that which is superior to being. What then is philosophy? Undoubtedly the most excellent. But is philosophy the same as dialectics? Indeed, dialectics seems to be the most excellent part of philosophy. For it must not be thought that this is merely an instrument of the philosopher. Since **F** it does not contain bare propositions and relations, but is concerned with things themselves, and as it were has beings as its matter. Yet it progresses towards them, having the things themselves along with notions. But it recognizes falsehood and sophism with a certain accidental respect: namely, when another introduces this, it judges it as alien, recognizing falsehood through the truths it possesses, whenever someone objects to it as if it were contrary to the rule of truth. Therefore, what properly pertains to a proposition, it hardly knows. For these are letters. But knowing the truth, it has known **G** that very thing which they call a proposition: and commonly it has known the motions of the soul: what it posits, or what it removes, and whether it removes what it also posits, or something else. Likewise, whether different things, or rather the same things are brought forward among themselves, as if touching by the manner of sense: but it concedes these things, which it values highly, to another faculty.

MARSILIO FICINO'S ARGUMENT
FOR THE BOOK ON HAPPINESS.

SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK,
He is blessed who lives by mind alone.

HE begins the book on happiness from that opinion in which all agree. Indeed, all
proclaim happiness to be living well. But because they are utterly ignorant of what life is, and what good is: therefore, as
often as they define living well, so often are they compelled to err. Plotinus detects their errors in the first and second
chapters of the book: admonishing us, namely, that we should begin the discussion from the definition itself.
Therefore, in the third chapter of the book, he describes life, and the good, and happiness. In the fourth, he raises and resolves doubts:
asking whether a blessed life is fitting for man. Likewise, by what reason again it might be impeded:
meanwhile signifying that it cannot be impeded. Then in the following chapters, he brings up similar questions, and finally resolves them:
proving from all, namely, that only he is blessed who, living by mind alone, is already entirely intellect, depending on nothing else
than on the divine intellect, and on the good itself, the beginning and end of all things. This is the purpose of the entire book.

Various opinions on what it means to live well.

I The first chapter therefore deals circuitously with those who, ignorant of what life itself is, and what the good itself is, nevertheless strive to define living well, saying namely: To live well is to pass life without impediment: likewise, to be well: again, to perform one's proper work: moreover, to achieve the end naturally desired by appetite: then, to live tranquilly: finally, to live according to nature. In all these things, therefore, he leads those ignorant of the true definition to the point where they are compelled to grant the divine gift of blessedness to even the most abject little beasts, indeed even to plants, and to attribute happiness, that is, the highest good of life, to those in whom there is the least life.

Just as in the first, so in the second, he discusses false opinions, and from them chooses something true: in which note concerning sensation in animals and plants.

II IN

--- Page 67 ---
IN LIBR. III. ENNEAD. I. 23

II. In the second chapter of the book, while it achieves almost the same thing as in the first, it attempts meanwhile, without doubt, to gather some conjectures here and there from the errors of others for finding true happiness.

They had said, however, that happiness is a certain condition of nature, according to which someone is usually said to be well off.

After this, some among them deny that happiness is present in plants, although they attribute it to all animals. Hence Plotinus says, "Those who deny happiness to plants because they do not feel, seem also likely to deny it to certain animals, that is, oysters and similar creatures, which scarcely seem to feel; and the Pythagoreans thought that plants feel perfections almost in the same way, so that the highest degree in plants corresponds to the lowest in animals. Moreover, in plants there is a distinction of sex; and plants situated close together as spouses sprout more fruitfully; and by some sense, I know not what, they turn towards moisture and heat; and if violently cut or handled, they dry up."

But we think that sense is twofold: The lower one, by which no nature or quality of a thing is discerned, but only a certain affection brought about by it is felt; which is also a dull sense, like

--- Page 68 ---
24 COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO
can be considered life. For it seems that essence is a kind of nascent life, and cognition, especially intellectual cognition, is a life fully mature. Moreover, we see certain traces of these three extending through all things that exist. For everywhere, under the aspect of form, a trace of essence is found: since each thing seems to exist through form. Likewise, under the same aspect, a trace of life: since through form there is inclination and motion, and generation. Again, by the same aspect, a trace of intelligence appears: for since through form there is order everywhere, it is a proper sign of intelligence. Therefore, since these three extend through all things by means of one thing, that is, by form, it is necessary that there be one first form of all: which itself is the first essence, and likewise the first life, and the first intelligence. For it is for this reason that these three extend through all things by the single function of form: because one form exists above all things, embracing these three within itself. Now, that the first form is the first essence, is evident from the fact that through form, essence is everywhere produced and exists, and where there is more form, there is a greater function of being. Likewise, that the same first form is also the most perfect life, and the most perfect intellect, we infer from this: that both life is the perfection of essence, and intellect is the perfection of life. Therefore, with the highest perfection of essence, the highest perfection of life and intellect concurs. Especially since the most perfect

--- Page 69 ---
IN LIBR. IIII. ENNEAD. I. 25

so that it appears to have generated itself in a certain way. For in that where being, living, and understanding are in reality one, here, while it understands itself, it seems meanwhile to generate, or unfold, or preserve something essential and vital within itself. From all these things we can gather that the most intimate and most perfect motion and generation flourish in the mind: and therefore life is most perfect. In the divine mind, I say, primarily and through itself; in our mind, however, proximately and through itself. Therefore, we consider the blessed life to be, not indeed such and such a life, as if lacking some addition, but life itself flourishing at the highest degree of living. Life, I say, that is, the act of the first essence naturally directed towards the good itself, and thus perfect. And at this very degree of perfection, we think that understanding is simultaneously achieved, and life itself is entirely completed by understanding itself. In this understanding, however, to live, to understand, to will are the same, although in rational nature it is one thing to live, another to think, and another to choose. just as in celestial light it is the same to shine, to sparkle, to be warm: although in our light of the air it is one thing to gleam, another to reflect, and another to glow. For what an inferior nature is compelled to do through diverse means, a superior nature accomplishes through one. Just as what the exterior five senses perform with instruments, imagination accomplishes with a certain single act. And what imagination devises through multiple and individual forms, reason gathers into one universal species. Finally, what reason traverses with multiple acts, intellect attains with one stable act, indeed, it possesses with a perpetual act. Therefore, for this [intellect], to live is to understand: for this, to understand is to will: or if perhaps there is some distinction in the will, nevertheless by the same instinct of its nature (so to speak), while it strives towards the good, it is naturally said to will: while it attains the good, it is said to understand: again, while it embraces the good it has attained, it is judged to will again. This first life, and first mind, always enjoying the paternal good, is considered a blessed life. Hence also, any mind whatsoever becomes perpetually blessed by adhering always to the first mind, and through it, to the good. Hence also, reason becomes happy as often as it is joined to its own mind, and through its own mind, to the divine mind.

Rational nature can attain the blessed life: namely, when it is formed and acts by intellect.

IIII. Since, therefore, the blessed life is perfect life, and perfect life is true intellect, and perfect in act: the question then arises: Whether man, that is, the rational soul, can attain this mind, this life, by its own rational power. To this question, therefore, it is answered in the fourth chapter of the book that it can sometimes attain it: which we indeed explain more broadly in Theology and in the book On the Mind. This rational faculty has two principal acts: namely, intuition and argumentation. By intuition, it resolves and abstracts forms from the conditions of matter: and from individual forms of imagination it withdraws to universal forms: again to more universal ones, until it arrives at the most common forms, proper now to intelligence itself: where it seems to make an end in the mind, from which it also derives the power of argumentation, while it prescribes to itself the principal rules of sciences and arts naturally inherent in the intellect, as principles of argumentation. Thus, by intuiting, it establishes an end in the mind: and by arguing, it draws a principle from the mind: and deservedly so, since as a posterior, it naturally depends on it. Therefore, the end of reason is to possess the mind to the best of its ability. Hence, it strives daily, as much as it is not hindered, to be formed more gradually and more by the mind. But since this faculty, as natural to this species, is not empty, it can sometimes attain the mind: and finally be perfected by the virtue by which it daily progresses. But when the rational faculty has already advanced to the ideal forms and rules of intelligence, then, like a certain matter, it will itself be formed by the mind as a form, and will now act under the mind's act: And so at last, it will live that life, and live a blessed life. But if it cannot acquire these things in this life, as if occupied by diverse matters, it will attain them in another: and he will attain them more quickly who has more readily prepared himself for it. In Plotinus' words, you will note that intellect is a certain intimate and proper part of the soul itself. And before reason is entirely converted to the mind, intellect and reason are still in the soul, as two parts of the soul. But after it has been converted, intellect is no longer a part, but the soul itself is then intellect: which soul is certainly not happy until it entirely becomes intellect in act. Almost as the sublime air under the sphere of fire is fiery and acts like fire. Moreover, a human is not a human unless he at least has intellect in potentiality. Which, indeed, I believe is said on account of brute animals: in whose imaginations, if any argumentative power is present, it nevertheless cannot be formed by the mind. For since the proper forms of the mind are entirely stable and most common, deservedly the imagination of a brute, through its forms, which are only particular and mobile, can never be formed by the mind. Reason, however, through its forms, although in a certain way mobile, yet universal, can sometimes be led to the forms of intelligence. After this, he argues that such happiness is minimally disturbed by the care of the animal and its inconveniences: since the soul, thus affected, considers the animal not to be a part of itself, but something either made from it.

--- Page 70 ---
minimally disturbed, since the soul, when so affected, does not consider the animal to be part of itself, but something made from it... let us not deviate at all [from this understanding]. Indeed, as long as the soul is connected to this [state], he says it is equally blessed, even if the body is meanwhile tormented by pains. I, for my part, believe Plotinus learned this not so much from the words of the Stoics, as from the deeds of the Christian martyrs who were frequent in his century. Moreover, he denies that happiness is to be placed in a certain accumulation of greater and lesser goods; which lesser things, though called goods, he himself rather names necessities. God, truly the author of nature, willed our animal, that is, the living body, to be subject to the soul as something more imperfect. Furthermore, in the soul, He subjects imagination to reason, reason to the mind, and finally the mind to Himself. In the same way, He established that the good and proper end of the animal should serve the end and good of the soul. And in the soul, He commanded the proper end of imagination to serve the proper end of reason, and likewise the familiar end of reason to serve the end of the mind; which indeed, just as it is the proper end of the intellect, so too is it the common end of what follows, and the end of ends. Therefore, the end of the rational soul is not composed of diverse goods, but is the good of the intellect itself: to which, as to an end, subsequent goods are referred.

The foregoing are confirmed, that in every mind wisdom is eternal, and how

The soul often, either by intuition or by reasoning, considers profound things, not only that they are eternal, but also by what reason they are eternal; and conceives (so to speak) the proper reason of eternity itself. But the reason itself is of greater importance for eternity than the manner. Since, therefore, there is such great virtue in the soul that it thinks eternal things and eternity itself by an eternal reason, much more is that virtue in the soul which considers eternal things in a certain eternal manner, that is, eternally and always. 28               COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO
from which it follows that recognition here follows cognition as something posterior, and perhaps as something consequent and accompanying, and often causes a certain distraction of the soul to make the prior action somewhat more remiss. Therefore, Plotinus not without reason says that recognition and such perception are accomplished through a consequent and posterior faculty and form. And we do not doubt that the faculty accompanying later is imagination itself. Similarly, the form that accompanies the prior form, we call an image. Let there therefore be natural forms in the mind, or reason: although in the mind they are eternal, in reason however perpetual. Let there therefore be adventitious forms in imagination, images of natural forms, through which the soul, as if marveling, attends to them as new things, and perceives what is happening in reason and mind: indeed, just as the eye is contained in the face, so is reason in the mind. And just as the eye neither sees the face, nor perceives its movement, unless when the linear rays of the face are directed into a mirror placed in a certain way opposite to us, and from there are reflected at similar angles to the eye, and the mirror thus shows the image, if it has any image: in a similar way, reason, like an eye, neither sees the mind, nor perceives it acting, although it always acts, unless its act acts somewhat into imagination, which is otherwise diverse, but turned towards it. By which act indeed, an image of the superior action results from imagination into reason. Here you will note first indeed where Plotinus says, that we are not the act of the vegetative faculty, but rather the act of intelligence: that this is especially true in the blessed: true also in any soul: which Plotinus considers more connected to the intellect than to the animal. Then where he says, that the act of understanding is then without phantasy, when no image is made and results from it in the latter: not that intelligence is pure from phantasy, but that phantasy depends on intelligence: although rational intelligence, that is, thought, and mobile reason are often excited by phantasy, especially active reason: which alone Aristotle says phantasy always needs: as Themistius and Simplicius prudently interpret. Finally, know that Plotinus assents, while he recounts certain words of Aristotle, that this was his opinion concerning the mind: where in the third book of "On the Soul" he writes, that the Intellect always understands, and its intelligence is its substance, and truly exists as immortal. For immortality is not so true in inferior virtues. For even if some are perpetual, they are nevertheless involved in motion. But as for the fact that he denies that we, that is, our rational faculty, remember after death, Plotinus will diligently examine this elsewhere. Finally, remember that Averroes, although not the same, nevertheless indicated something similar: where he says, that our Intellect has a twofold intelligence in itself: one eternal, the other temporal: the former indeed through its own being, the latter however through our images: and that we never perceive the former, because it communicates nothing with our imagination: but we recognize the latter, because its forms correspond with the images of our imagination. And since he places a twofold intellect in the same substance, namely the forming and the formable, he says that this formable intellect does not recognize through us what that forming intellect does, until it itself is perfectly formed by it through us. Then finally and simultaneously with it, it will be happy in us. But let us dismiss Averroes: for Porphyry and Proclus themselves omitted Plotinus in this part, not approving that the intellect of our soul always acts as Plotinus says: and we in the preceding parts have expounded not so much approvingly, as interpretively. Indeed, it must be thought that there is sufficient stability and excellence in our mind, if the essence and inherent forms of things and the principles of sciences remain.

        Up to this point, ten chapters of the book are completed. The remaining six chapters of the same will become clear to one who considers them diligently. In these, he raises and solves questions: and also responds to unspoken objections: and everywhere confirms that the blessed depends on nothing other than the mind and God.

Since we establish living well and being
happy as one and the same thing, do we
also grant this to other living beings? For if
it is given to them to live their life without impediment, in the manner they were born, what prevents them from also
living well, that is, happily? For whether one posits
living well in being in a good state, or in perfecting one's
proper work, according to both, it will also be fitting for
other animals. For it will be possible both for them to be in a good state, and also to perfect their natural work:
just as many musical animals are in a good state in other respects: and
as they are naturally apt, they sing: and in this way
it seems possible for them to attain a desirable life.
Furthermore, if we posit happiness as a certain end,
which is indeed the ultimate goal in the appetite of nature,
in this way too we will confess that they will be happy,
namely when they have reached the ultimate goal. When
they have proceeded to this, nature ceases its movement in them:
which has already completed their entire life for them, and has
entirely fulfilled it from beginning to end. But if anyone
takes it ill that happiness is transferred to beasts,
asserting that it would thus be fitting even for the most abject,
and moreover for plants, which also live and bring their life
to its proper end: that person indeed might seem
absurd, saying that other animals cannot live well:
because they themselves do not seem to be considered of much worth.
However, he will not be compelled to grant to plants what he grants to all animals,
because they lack sensation. Nor perhaps will there be

But if tranquility will be the end, it will happen similarly.
Likewise, if living according to nature is said to be living well itself,
the same will seem to follow.

A ...they seem also not to grant it to all animals. If indeed they say that to feel this is, namely, for an affection not to lie hidden, then the good itself must be the affection itself, before that very thing which is said not to lie hidden, as if it is in accordance with nature, even if it has lain hidden; and to be proper, even if you do not yet know it to be proper. who enjoys the best, desires to have that alone, and nothing else whatsoever along with it. For since he considers whatever prosperities may be present not great: such as kingdoms, and empires of cities and nations, and the founding of cities, even if they are done by himself: why then would he consider the loss of dominion or country a grave evil? But if he considers such a thing to be a huge evil, or altogether an evil, he will be considered ridiculous: nor will he any longer be upright, deeming wood, and stones, and by Jove, the deaths of mortals, a great thing: whom we think ought to consider death altogether better than corporeal life. But if he himself is sacrificed, will he think death an evil for himself, because he is to be slain near the altars? Unless this is granted, will his body not be dissolved altogether, both above and below the earth? Will he also make much of the fact that he is buried at slight expense and ignobly, judged utterly unworthy of a grander monument? But altogether, it is the mark of a faint-hearted person to make much of such things. Furthermore, if he is led captive, there will be the faculty of release, if it is not granted to be happy there. But if his household members are led captive, such as his granddaughters and daughters, will he be less happy? What then shall we say, if he departs from life having foreseen none of these things, will he depart from life with such an opinion, as if these things cannot happen? But thinking so, he would be absurd. Will he not therefore suppose that it is possible for his own people to be overwhelmed by such misfortunes? Will he then, because of this very opinion, as if it were about to happen, be not at all happy? Indeed, even having thought so, he will be able to be happy. Therefore, even if it happens in the present, he will trust that it is the nature of the universe to bear such things, and that one ought to follow it. Many, furthermore, even when led into captivity, will fare better. Moreover, it is in the power of those who are bound to release themselves. But if they remain, either they will remain for some reason, and thus nothing very grave will have happened: or without reason, then indeed it is not fitting that they themselves should be the cause of their own disturbance. Certainly, an upright man will never be oppressed by evil because of the baseness of his own people, nor will he be carried away by the fortunes of others, whether adverse or prosperous.

**MARSILIO FICINO ON**
**BOOK V. WHETHER HAPPINESS**
**IS INCREASED BY TIME.**

What is eternity: what is blessedness: how all minds enjoy eternity eternally, but rational natures sometimes: and how long they enjoy it, they act stably.

I [S]UPERIOR to being itself, the Platonists place the principle of being itself: and they name it the One and the Good. In being, however, they conceive of the first essence, the first life, and the first mind. That life, indeed, we can call both eternal and blessed, but for different reasons. For life is the first, innermost, perpetual act of essence. Insofar, therefore, as such an act is wholly affixed to its essence simultaneously, and the essence itself simultaneously rests always on the One, it is called eternal life, nay, eternity itself. But insofar as the same act, never departing from its source, turns inward, it is called mind itself: which, thus immediately joined to the Good, is deservedly called blessed life, nay, blessedness itself. By this mind, this eternity, this blessedness, all minds, because they enjoy them most directly, therefore enjoy them eternally. But rational natures, since they possess the next degree, therefore indeed possess eternity and blessedness of this kind, but (to speak Platonically, or rather Plotinically) they do not enjoy them eternally. Thus, at times they are blessed, at other times again not blessed. Nevertheless, while they are blessed, they no longer live changeably, but stably. For since primary eternity and blessedness are in reality one, rational natures, insofar as they possess blessedness, similarly attain eternity. But since the very state is most proper to eternity, namely, as long as they, as if happy, possess eternity, they act immovably, and embrace all the gifts of action simultaneously as if in a single intuition. But to speak sometimes in my own opinion, the soul cannot enjoy eternity unless it enjoys it eternally. Therefore, when it first reaches the state of eternity, being placed there outside time and motion, it acts so stably that it cannot be moved from it in any part any longer. Having once established this opinion of ours, let us proceed with the Plotinian interpretation.

**Rational nature lives happily for much longer ages in the sublime spheres than unhappily around the earth.**

II Therefore, they judge that the souls of men living mostly on earth, or in thicker air, are not happy, but miserable, being placed, that is, in a place of sin, of purgatorial punishment. But then all will be blessed, when from here they have ascended to the pure spheres with a pure body, or to the higher air, or ether, and heaven. For then, due to the prosperity of the body and place, and the easy provision for the body, they are least distracted from divine contemplation. Now, indeed, by how much greater is the virtue and amplitude in the higher spheres than in the lower, and by how much more excellent is the virtue of the soul living there than here, by so much longer do they think souls live there than here: and therefore, by so much longer are they happy than miserable. Which Plato testifies to in the Phaedo, where he speaks of long-lived beings: and Olympiodorus confirms. Added to this is: that by how much more powerful is the mind, which raises to the sublime, than the animal imagination, which tends to opposites, by so much longer is the life of the rational soul, already elevated to the sublime through the mind, than the life of the same through imagination to the lower.

42          COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

Since a wretched person seems to become more wretched over a longer time, why should not a happy person, by similar reasoning, become happier? He concludes that evil itself, because it occurs in a subject naturally susceptible to suffering and weak, continuously infects that subject more. Indeed, if this subject always remained the same, and no greater detriment occurred, only the present evil itself would be weighed in the judgment of evil. But if the subject thus perseveres in distress, so that evil increases in it, then misery is judged more severe, not so much because the time is longer, as because a greater degree of evil has accrued. Supreme happiness, however, possesses a certain fixed limit, that is, the highest degree in good. Likewise, it always has the same limit, namely the highest itself, neither greater nor lesser, that is, as soon as and as long as there is happiness; otherwise, it is not supreme happiness. Finally, the state of evil exists in time and in a temporary subject, to which diversity occurs. Happiness, however, exists in eternity and an eternal subject, to which indeed identity itself (so to speak) and a proper state properly belong. An eternal state there also belongs to the rational part already made happy; otherwise, it would not have been made happy, nor would it live securely if it thought it would depart from there.

Seventh Question.

Since in time we count the past and the future along with the present, and thus call it a greater span of time, why do we not do so in happiness? He concludes that it is permissible for us to count non-being with being in the length of time, since the very nature of time revolves in a certain number and flux. But also counted are those things which no longer exist, but which have long since passed. Likewise, in every flux, being is, as it were, joined with non-being, since the present moment, which is in a way called being, falls in the middle between the past which is no more, and the future which is not yet. He denies, however, that the same happens in the very nature of happiness, since its essence consists in a present life and a stable act, having already in a way attained the gift of eternity. Otherwise, if it still runs through some motion and time, it is not yet an absolute state; the soul has not yet attained its end. Since therefore the nature of happiness includes the present itself and a state, it certainly excludes temporal computation far from itself. Now indeed, since eternity is of the first essence and the life of being itself, whether it is in the first mind or already communicated to some mind, it in no way admits anything of non-being. Therefore, it utterly expels temporal flux from itself. Therefore, in eternal life the act is one and stable, but in time, whether in the soul or then in the body, acts are both many and succeed one another in a certain flux, just as in the center of a circle there is one and stable point, from which diverse mobile points are produced to the circumference along the length of lines. Where it seems both that the one is dispersed into many, and

beheld it once, gains equally.

saying the same thing that we are seeking.
Therefore, longer pleasure always has only the present:
but what is said to be past from it, has now utterly vanished.

MARSILIO FICINO
ON THE BOOK CONCERNING BEAUTY,
SUMMARY.

From the first essence, life, mind, influences emanate through all things, like rays, sounds, words, through six grades.

[Illuminated initial I]NFLUENCES of a certain kind emanate from Being itself through all beings everywhere: but in so far as essence is in Being itself, they flow forth especially in the manner of a solar ray: but in so far as life is there, they burst forth in the manner of sound and voice: finally, in so far as intellect is there, they are carried in the manner of a significant word: and in so far as they are like rays, they seem to move sight: in so far as they are voices or sounds, they strike the ears: in so far as they are like words, they especially stir souls. But everywhere, as certain beautiful things, or certain beauties, meet us: for they proceed from the very form of beauty itself. But when we name beauty itself, by way of form, that is, as the formal beauty, we properly wish Being itself to be understood: but by way of cause, that is, as the cause of beauty itself, we wish the Good itself to be thought of. For we believe the Good to be light itself, or the source of beauty shining forth and flowing therefrom. But beauty we believe to be the splendor emanating from the light of the Good itself, that is, Being itself depending on the One Good itself. From Being itself again, as I was saying, we do not doubt that influences proceed through all things like rays, voices, words. Such influences are first indeed in the idea of the divine mind: secondly, they are received in every mind thereafter: but through universal providence in the mind of the mundane soul: thirdly, in the reason of the same soul: fourthly, in its principal imagination: fifthly, in the subsequent imagination: sixthly, in the vegetative power, which is also called universal nature. Up to this point, they retain a certain ideal character in themselves. For up to this point, they are living and effective and fruitful, and eternal. For in this last divine grade are the seminal reasons of all things: by which the species of things themselves are propagated. For since the first life, and the first formal reason of all things, in the first essence itself is the principle of each essence, in which principle both reason and life were: deservedly, insofar as the influences emanating therefrom preserve life and formal reason in themselves pure and integral and effective, they are called essential, ideal, divine. But they preserve such a great function even in nature, that is, in the vegetative power of the soul: therefore, on this sixth day, the proper works of God receive their end: but thereupon those influences strike the matter subject to the soul. But since they can neither proceed further, nor, in it, as if next to nothing, retain the nature of true essence and life, they now pass from forms into images. Images, I say, resembling true and divine forms. Which, indeed, under the generative nature of the soul itself, acting entirely upon matter, result from the suffering matter itself, and are, as it were, reflected from a mirror in the manner of a ray, and reflected from an arch in the manner of a voice, and returned from some flatter wall in the manner of a word, like Echo. To this lowest grade, the formal efflux of the Moon seems to be favorable, the mistress of ultimate generation: but to the seminal reasons thriving in nature and nourishing matter, Venus: but to the same (reasons) hastening to motion in the lower imagination, Mars: again, to the same (reasons) reigning in the imagination, the Sun: but to those thriving in reason, Mercury: but to those dominating in the mind of the soul, Jupiter: finally, to those resting in the divine mind, Saturn. In this seventh grade, indeed, as on Saturn's day, the creator of the world rests, that is, the idea itself, deeply intimate to itself. For it does not refer this (idea) to other things that are made from it, but refers other things to this as an exemplar.

Formal beauty itself is the mind itself: to whose allurements are mixed admiration, power, diffusion, pleasure.

Since this exemplar is the all-forming reason of all forms, it is therefore considered the first and universal form and species. And for this reason, it is the first formal beauty: whence we are accustomed to call beauty everywhere both form and species, and beautiful things 'formosi' (well-formed): whose opposite we call deformity and deformed. From which it is clear that matter, by its nature utterly formless, is deservedly to be considered deformity itself. But of this elsewhere. But formal beauty itself arises indeed with the first essence: but it grows while essence proceeds into life: finally, it is judged adult when life is completed into mind. For through the very act of the mind, essential life is perfectly formed, and becomes an all-forming form. Therefore, in the order of things, there is most beauty where there is most mind: whether a certain nature of mind is present, or its proper artifice, or a trace, or an indication. And all that moves more vehemently there, where it meets us more vividly. For true beauty of the form itself is life itself, thoroughly perfected through the act of the mind. But the proper quality of beauty is to attract and to ravish simultaneously. Whence in Greek it is called 'Calon' (καλόν), as if 'provoking' or 'calling forth'. And since beauty exists as an intellectual gift/function, therefore it attracts only those who know: those who know, I say, whether by some intellectual reason, or by sight, or by hearing, which are mostly ministers of reason. But admiration and power are mixed with the allurements of beauty

desire the good: not all things desire the beautiful, but only those who have a certain judgment of beauty: and these

good is most common and perpetual, it follows that the good itself is the most common and
most powerful principle of all: and that the form of beauty itself is as close as possible to the good. And since the provocation from and to beauty is as it were something new: seeing that it happens only to certain ones, and sometimes, and after nature,
and knowledge occurs, a certain admiration is deservedly mixed with the allurements of beauty. Likewise also a certain violence (as I might say): for although the appetite for the good, which is common and perpetual, is most intimate to nature and draws
from within, nevertheless the desire for the beautiful as it were snatches from without, necessarily following knowledge: and therefore since it is less

...it gladly embraces. That form in bodies is congruent which is composed according to the very norm and rule of the Idea: while the seminal reason, which is in nature as the former of bodies, largely dominates matter, and renders the form in it indeed minimally material, but maximally formal. Indeed, as we learn from Timaeus: Intellect itself is divinely the father of forms, matter the mother. But reason and the fomes of forms thriving in nature can rightly be called the paternal and effective seed: and the form born from it is the offspring. Beauty, however, is nothing other than the very nature of this offspring, more expressively reflecting the father's image. Deformity, on the contrary, is a certain dissimilarity of the deficient form to the father's form, and also the origin of this defect of matter: especially when, by some impeding chance, the subject is not at all overcome by the forming reason, that is, it either does not sustain the act of the former, or receives it most ineptly. Therefore, in any element, even if there are many accidental forms, there is nevertheless one substantial and principal form. Similarly in mixed things, such as stones and metals, if there are several substantial forms in potency, one is nevertheless principal in act, and common. So in plants and animals: if there are many substantial forms in each in a certain act, there is nevertheless one principal act commanding many. Everywhere, however, beauty is a certain absolute perfection, or grace, and as it were a certain flower of the form itself, especially of the form dominating others. It is therefore something divine and imperious: because it signifies both the dominion of the reigning form, and refers to the victory of divine art and reason over matter, and clearly represents the Idea itself.

*Beauty in bodies is a more expressive likeness of the Idea: and if matter is subtracted, it is*
*the Idea itself. Likewise, the beauty of any species is judged by the soul through an innate*
*formula of the Idea itself, according to which the species is constituted.*

**III** Who then is a beautiful man? or a beautiful lion? or a beautiful horse? Certainly, one who is primarily so formed, so born, as both the divine mind instituted through its Idea, and universal nature thence conceived by seminal virtue. Now, our soul has an innate formula of that Idea in its mind: and it likewise has a seminal reason in its own nature. Therefore, by a certain natural judgment, it is accustomed to judge concerning a man, or a lion, or a horse, and other things, that this one is not beautiful, but that one is beautiful: because, namely, this one entirely dissents from the formula and reason, while that one assents: and among the beautiful, that this one is more beautiful than that one: because this one assents more to the formula and reason than that one. And indeed, since a natural and sudden judgment about these things cannot be more conveniently expedited than through formulas and reasons innate in us, it is probable that divine providence, disposing all things in the best possible way, has imprinted such characters upon us from the beginning. But when we judge concerning beauty, we approve as most beautiful among others that which is animated and rational, and so formed that it satisfies the formula of beauty which we have in mind through the soul: and responds through the body to the seminal reason of beauty which we possess in nature and in the secondary soul. The form in a beautiful body is indeed similar to its Idea, just as the figure of a building in matter is similar to the exemplar in the architect's mind, and speech in voice is similar to the speech which is in the soul. Therefore, if you were to remove matter from a man, but leave the form, this very form which remains to you, that is the Idea itself, according to which man is formed. Just as if you were to remove its matter from a building, leaving the figure: or if you were to remove the broken air from speech, preserving the meaning: certainly, the remaining figure there is nothing other than the exemplar itself existing in the architect: and the preserved meaning here is nothing other than the speaker's own thought. Hence, he who gathers such meaning is said to possess and interpret the mind of the speaker. Therefore, we too ought to disregard matter in beautiful things, but by selecting forms and order, to divine the Ideas in these things, and to interpret divine art and mind. He believes that the beauty of a composite body consists in this: that both the individual forms in it overcome the informity of matter, and the common form entirely excels the individual forms: but the beauty of a simple body, in which there is a single substantial form in act, such as gold, or silver, and similar things, he believes to be situated in the greatest portion of light. He certainly wants light to be the form of fire, that is, of heaven, which is a certain image of the life of heaven, so much so that what is intellectual in celestial life is luminous in the celestial body. Likewise, light beneath the moon is the act of form, that is, of celestial light, and (so to speak) its image. Hence it is clear how great is the virtue of heaven, since the image of its form produces and preserves all things among us. He also believes fire beneath the moon to be an igneous, or ignited body, rather than pure fire. Nevertheless, because it is more similar to heaven to exist as lucid, and as it were the form of other bodies, and near to corporeal things, and therefore most beautiful, and by its participation other things become most beautiful: especially those which derive light from it. Such things are those which have either the least earth, or the most temperate nature. For that which is either most earthy, or least temperate, being as it were far removed from heaven, is most inept for receiving light and luminous color, as something celestial. What has been said concerning bodies which appear beautiful, similarly applies to those things which are heard as beautiful, whether it be a single voice, or a certain pleasing composition of voices. And just as the beauty of visible form proceeds from its ideal and seminal reason, so the beauty of voice and harmony is perfected both by the spirit itself and by the harmonic conception of the mind. And everywhere beauty is the dominion of form over the subject: and corporeal form proceeds from incorporeal form.

*Beauty that is seen represents the beauty of the mind: beauty that is*
*heard refers to the beauty of the soul. Likewise, no one ought or can*
*speak of the beauty of the mind and soul,*
*unless they themselves possess it.*

**IIII** There is a twofold beauty: namely, incorporeal and corporeal. And just as corporeal beauty is again twofold: one in those things which are seen, and the other in those things which are heard, so too incorporeal beauty is twofold: one in the intellect, the other is in the soul. The beauty of intellectual light is primarily represented to us by that which is seen in light as an image. The beauty of the soul, again, constituted in a certain harmony, is rightly referred to by that which is heard, by harmonic beauty as an image. But altogether, just as no one can speak of corporeal beauty unless they have known it by sense, so neither can they speak of incorporeal beauty unless they have perceived it with the mind. But one who is to know corporeal beauty is carried outside themselves: one who is to perceive incorporeal beauty, however, must be brought back within themselves: and having been recalled to themselves, they will not perceive it unless they possess it. Therefore, be beautiful in intellect and soul before you dare to dispute about incorporeal beauty. Remember, if you delight in sensible beauty, which is an image of insensible beauty, you will perceive much greater pleasure,

--- Page 93 ---
...pleasure, when you shall have known the very beauty of the soul and mind; nay, when you shall have possessed it.
Matter indeed has natural deformity, but foreign comeliness. But the soul indeed has adventitious ugliness, but native beauty. Likewise, the beauty of the divine mind is like light. The beauty of the human mind, namely in intellectual virtue, is like some most brilliant color. The beauty of the soul, namely in moral virtue, is like a figure.

¶ Since beauty, that is, comeliness, is the very flower and vigor and grace of form, certainly matter, just as it is formlessness itself, so it is also deformity itself. To this, therefore, deformity is indeed natural; but beauty is foreign, inasmuch as matter receives form from elsewhere. But to the soul, on the contrary, beauty is indeed native, because by its very nature it is true form, that is, an act subsisting in itself. For the remaining forms under the soul are rather certain formations than forms, that is, actions of the soul upon matter, and conversely, passions of matter. Therefore, the soul's comeliness is indeed natural, deformity adventitious. For just as matter, while it borrows something formal from the soul, seems to become beautiful, so conversely, the soul, while it receives something formless from matter, becomes deformed. But it receives (it) inasmuch as it yields to the body in affection and concedes in cognition. Therefore, the mind does not become beautiful by some acquisition of a new gift, but by purification alone, by which it is restored to its pristine nature, in which its own idea formed it, and the divine intellect; whose beauty indeed is like light; but the beauty of our intellect, thence flowing, called intellectual virtue, is like some most brilliant color; but moral beauty, proceeding from here and there, is like a figure.

Virtue and beauty in the soul are natural; and its very purity restored to the soul: thus immediately shining forth with the beauty of the divine mind, and most happily enjoying the good itself. Likewise, the first form, the first mind, the first being is the same.

to create for the eyes, and that the beauty of all things is situated in this, that they are moderate and well-proportioned. But among those who hold this opinion, nothing simple, but only what is composite will necessarily be beautiful, and the whole itself will be beautiful. But the individual parts will have no beauty of their own; but only insofar as they contribute to the whole will they be called beautiful; although it is necessary, if the whole is beautiful, that the parts also be beautiful, for the beautiful does not consist of ugly things. **B** However, all parts ought to have received beauty. Moreover, beautiful colors, just like the light of the sun itself, since they are simple and do not have beauty from proportion, will be left excluded from beauty by them. How then will gold be beautiful to them? And the nocturnal twinkling, and the spectacle of the stars? Similarly in sounds, what is simple will be alien from beauty. Although any whole in these **C** songs, which are beautiful as a whole, is itself beautiful. Therefore, when the same proportion remains, and the same face sometimes appears beautiful, but at other times not beautiful, ought we not to say that beauty in that which is proportioned is one thing, and proportion itself is another? And that the proportioned thing itself is beautiful on account of something else? But if they, turning to beautiful studies and beautiful discourses, have assigned the proportion of measure in these also as the cause of beauty, **D** what proportion of measure will be said to exist in beautiful studies, or laws, or disciplines, or sciences? Furthermore, how are the speculations themselves said to be proportioned to each other? But if someone assigns this very thing, because, namely, they are harmonious, we will certainly say that there is also a certain agreement and harmony among evil things. For these two things agree with each other (as is said), namely, that temperance is foolishness, **E** and that justice is noble ignorance. Therefore, the beauty of the soul is every virtue, and this very kind (of beauty) is much truer than the preceding ones. But in what way will there be proportion here? For it is not a matter of magnitude, nor a matter of number. But since there are many parts of the soul, in what kind of reason will the composition, or the tempering of parts or speculations, be situated? Finally, the beauty of the intellect itself, namely, separated, and of that which is alone in itself, what will it be? **F**

Let us return again to the beginning, asking what beauty itself is in bodies. In the first place, it is something that reveals itself to the sense at first glance; and the soul, apprehending and familiarly recognizing it, receives it, and as if most suitable, approves and embraces it. But falling upon the ugly, it withdraws itself; and as if abhorring it on account of its discord, rejects it as alien. **G** For the soul, existing as that which is natural, and nearly and essentially most excellent in the order of things, whenever it has beheld something kindred, and a trace of its kin, it rejoices and is amazed, and brings it back to itself, and remembers itself and its own. What then is the similarity between those things which appear beautiful among us, and those things which are beautiful above us? For if there is any similarity, if-

Whoever, then, has seen *that*, with what love, O Jupiter, he burns, with what desire he blazes, vehemently longing to unite into one: how wonderfully he mingles pleasure with awe. Thus indeed is it ordained by nature, that he who does not yet see, desires *it* as good; but he who already sees, is delighted by *it* as beautiful, and is equally filled with admiration and pleasure: he is moved by a certain salutary awe: and is affected by a true and supreme love: he scorns keen affections and other loves: and despises what were previously held to be beautiful. This indeed almost happens also to those, who, when they have encountered the forms of gods or daemons, thereafter value the forms of other bodies as nothing. What then shall we deem him to be, eternal, who has contemplated the Beautiful itself? It itself, I say, pure in itself: neither weighed down by flesh, nor by any other body: nor encompassed by earth, nor by heaven: so that it may exist as pure. For all these things are adventitious and mixed, and therefore not primary, but proceed from *it*. If therefore anyone contemplates *that* which indeed offers gifts to all, and meanwhile remains in itself while it bestows, nor receives anything from another, and remaining in its contemplation, and so enjoys it, that he becomes like it, what further beauty will he need? For since *it* is the chief and primary beauty itself, it makes its lovers beautiful and lovable. Where indeed the greatest and ultimate contest is proposed to souls, for the sake of which we must absolutely strive, lest perchance we be left devoid of the best contemplation, whoever attains this, becomes blessed by a happy vision: on the contrary, he who does not attain it, is unhappy. For he is not miserable who does not attain beautiful colors and comely bodies: nor he who falls from power and dominion and kingship: but he who lacks the possession of *this* alone, for which alone one must certainly cast aside kingdoms, and empires of the whole earth, and sea, and heaven: if, having abandoned and scorned all these things, one turns and contemplates *it*.

VIII
How the soul
may see
Beauty.

What then is the way? What device? What method? By which one may contemplate inestimable beauty: beauty, I say, established in sacred inner sanctuaries, and not coming forth outside, lest any profane person behold it. Let him therefore enter, and let whoever can advance into the innermost parts from without, abandoning the gaze of the eyes: nor looking back any further at the usual spectacles of the senses. For it is necessary for one contemplating this to look no further at anything of corporeal beauty, but knowing that these corporeal things are images, traces, and shadows, to flee entirely to that of which these are likenesses. For if anyone rushes towards these things, as if grasping at what is true, which nevertheless appear as beautiful images in water, he will undoubtedly suffer the same thing that (as the fable relates) that one suffered, who, striving to grasp a shadow, plunged himself into the water and perished. For in a similar manner, he who embraces the forms of bodies and does not depart from them, is plunged not so much in body as in soul into a dark abyss, dreadful to the mind: where, blind both among the dead and remaining here, he will dwell everywhere among shadows. Here therefore someone will most truly exclaim, "Let us depart from here, friends, within!"

MARSILIO FICINO ON
BOOK VII, CONCERNING THE FIRST GOOD,
AND OTHER GOODS,
A SUMMARY.

SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.
The Good itself is above essence, life, intellect.

IN the universal order of things, no essence rests in itself, but every (essence) naturally and always strives with its whole power to act; and this natural and proper function all essences derive from nowhere else than from the first essence, because, namely, it itself proceeds into action with a similar kind of effort. Moreover, any essence and essence itself proceeds into action, so that it may be better off thereby. Therefore, neither this nor that (any essence) is the Good

--- Page 103 ---
IN BOOK VII. ENNEAD. I. 59

the first and highest [Good] is able properly, then continuously, to emanate, and then finally, to be reached. But in order that what the Good itself is may be understood, two things especially must first be understood: First, that there is some principle of things, and that it exists as one. Second, that it is itself the end of all things. Indeed, in our Theology, we assert and conclude this whole matter with many arguments: that unless a first and highest principle is granted, but instead one proceeds from one thing to another successively without any end, whatever you find will depend on another, and therefore by its very nature will be mutable and wavering: and there will be no stable foundation for wavering things, nor a fixed pivot for mutable things. And for this reason, there will be no stability in things, no order, no union, and no harmony. But since all things perpetually maintain a certain stable order, and everywhere converge into one form of the universal work, and towards one common end of the universe, it is established that there is some highest principle of all things, and that it exists as unique. And that it is the end of all things is evident from this: that the highest principle, since it depends on nothing, neither looks to nor acts for another, nor establishes all things for any other end than itself. Therefore, the principle and end of the universe are the same: And this is nothing other than the Good itself. For if it is the highest principle, certainly all things are made,

60          COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO
of evil, nevertheless evil itself (if indeed it is right to speak of evil itself) is compelled under the immense empire of the good itself to desire good and to be called good. The third gift of the good is form/species. For this is a certain determination, or distinction, or act of essence. But you, when you hear here that the gift of the one and the good is propagated more widely than the gift of being and essence, conclude that the one and the good itself is superior to being; moreover, just as unity, essence, and form are in things, so too is the participation of the good. Indeed, in the first mind, in other minds, in animals endowed with reason, there is a true participation of the good, because there is true unity, essence, and form. For unity in them, even if it has a certain multitude mixed in, nevertheless truly constitutes a unity there, because it overcomes the multitude and renders it an indissoluble one. Therefore, there is also true essence there, since it can never not be. And true form/species, since form there cannot be resolved into something formless. However, in inferior things, the soul and unity are often overcome by multitude, and therefore can very much be dissolved, and in essence there is a certain privation, and some lapse into non-being; and form is mixed with a completely formless subject, and collapses into it. For this reason, in these things there is not true unity, not true essence, not true species and form; and therefore not a true, but a certain imaginary portion of the good.

          Just as life is not simply good in itself, but rather, if it is directed to the highest principle,
          it is good; but if to matter, it is evil: so death is not simply evil in itself,
          but rather, if it separates the soul from evil, that is, from matter, it is good.

III Chapter III introduces three questions. The first is of this kind: If life is good, is living good for everyone and in every way of living? Certainly not: because life itself is not the first and simply good in itself, but insofar as it powerfully and directly rises to that first good itself, to that extent also does life become perfect. But wherever it falters and strays, while it falls from the good itself, it simultaneously degenerates from the perfection of life. Hence that saying of Democritus: To live imprudently, intemperately, impiously, is not so much to live badly as to die for a long time. Second question: Since life for us, insofar as it is mixed with the mortal and thereby disturbed, becomes a certain evil for the soul, although it is good for the body and the universe, is not death an evil, seeing that what is mortal makes life evil by its proximity? In responding, he asks for whom is death an evil? Certainly, evil, since it is either an accident or even weaker than an accident, and therefore cannot subsist in itself, necessarily happens to something. But it does not happen to that which subsists in no way, or which by nature can exist without life. Again, it does not happen to the soul if it is immortal; and however else it may happen, it will benefit the eternal soul, which will perform its proper actions more perfectly without the impediment of the body. But if the soul, after the death of the body, performs not so much its own actions as common ones, as if a colleague of the world-soul, much less will any evil be able to happen there to that which is already living with the universal life. On the contrary, for a soul gravely ailing from disturbances either here or in the underworld: death is rather to be desired, and life is an evil. Here that question is resolved: whether souls that are utterly miserable prefer to die than to live. And this, without doubt, nature teaches: by its prompting, those gravely tormented prefer to lose sensation than to feel dreadful pains. Finally, since the soul has its own life, and is by its essence a certain life living in itself, it neither borrows life from elsewhere, nor undergoes death. If anyone, however, defines living as being joined to the body, and dying as being separated from the body, then both will happen to the soul in this sense, but neither will properly change its substance. Third question: If life is good, why is not death also evil? He responds that death is not simply evil, because life is not simply good. For life is judged to be similar to a certain motion; and motion, of whatever kind it may be, ought to be denominated from the very end towards which it properly tends. Therefore, insofar as this vital motion perhaps lapses into evil, that is, into matter, to that extent it is also judged evil; but insofar as it directs itself to the good itself, that is, to the highest principle of the universe, to that extent it is considered good.

ON THE FIRST GOOD, AND THE OTHER GOODS.
On the First Good and Other Goods.

[Right column]

[Decorative woodcut initial A] Can anyone call anything else its own good for each thing besides the natural action of life? And if something is composed of many parts, for this thing, its good is the action of that which is better in it, always proper and consistent with nature, and in no part deficient? Therefore, the action of the soul according to its nature is good.
But if it acts towards the best, since it is itself the best, not only is that which pertains to itself good, but it also simply exists as good. If, therefore, something acts minimally towards anything else, since it is itself the most excellent of all, and above all things, and other things act towards it, it is clear that this very thing is the Good, by whose power other things also partake of the good. Other things, moreover, have the good in two principal ways: both because they are made similar to it, and because they work towards it.
Therefore, if appetite and action towards the best is good, it follows that the Good itself does not look to anything else, nor desire anything else: but is a stable and entirely quiet principle of all things, the natural beginning of actions: which indeed makes other things good in its own likeness. It makes them, I say, not by any action concerning them: for they act concerning it. Thus, it is clear that the Good exists neither by intelligence, nor by any action whatsoever, but only by itself.
For because it exists above essence, it again exists above action, and intellect, and intelligence. Moreover, it is necessary to assert that this very Good is that to which all things are referred, but it itself is not referred to anything else. For thus it is also clear that it is true that the Good is that which all things desire. Therefore, it must remain firmly, and turn all things towards itself: just as a circle revolves around a center, from which individual lines are produced.
As an example for us, the Sun can be, which is like a center for the light, which depends on it, and is simultaneously connected to it, and therefore exists everywhere together with it, and is nowhere separated from it: and if you were to separate it

**MARSILIO FICINO ON**
**BOOK VIII, WHAT EVILS ARE, AND**
**WHENCE THEY COME,**
**ARGUMENT.**

Four questions concerning good and evil.

[Marginal note: 1] [Decorative initial L]IBER (The Book) seems to be entirely concerned with this: that we may avoid evils with all our might; let us pursue good things; that is, let us flee matter, let us follow divine things separated from matter; let us recognize that the very principle of the universe is the very good, but that the last thing of the universe, that is, matter, is evil itself. And how evil comes to us, and by what reason we can finally avoid it. The first chapter of the book raises questions: What evils are, and whence they originate. But in order to find this out, it inquires what good things are; so that again, it undertakes to investigate what good itself is, or what evil is. It also asks how we recognize evil, since, due to its infirmity, it is entirely alien from the very form of the knowing soul. And it teaches that the formlessness of evil is discerned through the very form and light of good. Finally, it asks in what way evil is contrary to good. Whether, namely, as the last of the universe is to the first of the universe, and the highest abundance to the highest scarcity. But what it says, the knowing power...

--- Page 108 ---
64 COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO.

calls and limit: just as Plato also names in the *Philebus*. God measures all things, as principle: the same God limits all things as end. If God is the measure of all things, certainly the order of things does not ascend from principle to principle without some first principle of all things: for that would indeed be to adhere to principles without any reason of a principle, to wander. For the reason of a principle is that it be first. Indeed, through God as a measure, we perceive that intellect is better than soul, and soul than body: because the former [intellect] is closer to God as the highest good than the latter [soul], and the latter [soul] than the former [body]. But if nowhere a first and highest goodness were to exist, but one were to imagine it proceeding through innumerable degrees, nowhere indeed would there be any reason, measure, or rule by which some things are preferred to others: nor would some things approach and agree with the measure more than others. Therefore, let God be the principle, let Him be the measure: moreover, let Him also be the limit of all things, because He is the end: a limit, I say, who both limits subjects by forms, and the movements of forms by their ultimate ends, lest nature perchance wander from end to end without end: for that would indeed be nothing other than to wander through ends without any reason of an end. But the principal reason of an end is that it be ultimate and extreme. After these things, however, he places essence in the second degree of goods, and mind within essence: then soul in the third degree, and life within soul. He says all these things are good, because they are from the Good itself, and because they act around the Good by the virtue of the Good. He also wants those forms of bodies alone to be considered in the fourth place of goods, which never depart from the soul, and which the soul itself never departs from God. Such indeed are celestial bodies, or those similar to celestial bodies. To these points, he posits a difference between divine intellect and rational intellect: namely, that the divine intellect itself is the fullness of all things: while the rational intellect strives to be filled from it. Therefore, when you hear here that our intellect is said to be as if empty, do not take it to mean our simple intellect, which is always filled by the divine: but rather our rational intellect, that is, the power of the soul that ranges through universal species. This power, indeed, is in a certain way the potentiality of the intellect, and a potentiality for the intelligible, and it proceeds into act by the virtue of a superior intellect, which always exists in act: the intellect, I say, by the virtue of both the divine and our own. For just as that which is simply all things in potentiality becomes actually all things through that which is simply all things in act, or matter through the divine mind, so also must this power, by which the human intellect is in potentiality, become human intellect in act, through the human intellect also always vigorous in act. Just as this living man in act is generated not only by universal nature, which holds the seminal reasons of all animals reigning in act, but also by his own nature, that is, human nature, already possessing the seminal reason of man vigorous in act. For the generation of perfect things demands this. And this is Plotinus's opinion everywhere. He adds, that the divine intellect thus contains all things within itself, so that it itself is all things. Which indeed you should understand with this example: If all vessels of different shapes are submerged in the sea, the water will immediately fill them all, and in filling them, it will assume as many similar shapes as it fills vessels. But such shapes will be nothing other than the sea water, accommodating itself in different ways. Thus the intellect is all species that it is thought to have: and much more is it itself its own species, than the sea water is the shapes: both because no novelty, no dimension, no distance impedes union there: and because it does not assume or produce species from another, nor in another, like water, but from itself, and in itself, or rather, it entirely exists as them. But in what way species are distinguished from each other in the mind, and yet all are in each one, we will often discuss elsewhere. He adds, that to be a participant of the divine mind is not to have all species simultaneously vigorous in act: understand this as the rational power, which sometimes becomes a participant of the divine mind. For the intellectual nature itself, even in us, is not sometimes a participant, as Plotinus wishes, but is always composed of the divine mind. Moreover, he calls the divine mind the first act of the Good itself and the first essence. For he does not want there to be any act in God through which God does something: otherwise, such an act would differ from the very substance of God at least in some respect: yet from the first unity, all difference, all number, ought to be entirely absent. Therefore, he believes the very act of God to be outside God: just as light is outside light: and that God is of such great virtue that His act is not any motion or accident, but substance and first essence: and that there, both act and the acted (or the object of the act) are the same, that is, it itself is the most complete fount of all things' essence: so that while one thing seems to be made from divine unity, all things are simultaneously brought forth in the one. For deservedly, from the unity which is above all things, and equally regards all things most proximately, comes this one which is equally all things. Finally, he wants the act of essence itself around God to be His life, and the perfection of life to be mind. He adds, namely, that the pure soul, through the mind, both its own as an eye, and the divine as light, beholds the light of the good itself: and up to this point, no evil occurs. But if either the soul or nature itself were to stop its descent here, no evil would occur: nevertheless, the very fecundity of nature causes there to be many further degrees of things beneath the soul itself and nature itself. But since by gradually descending, the portion of good is little by little diminished (for effects cannot equal their causes), eventually from a lesser good, one arrives at evil. And what he says, that all things are 'around God,' means equally 'from God' and 'to God.' Likewise, the first and principal orders of things, that is, ideas, are around God, from whom they come into the mind, and into whom they are reflected back from the mind. But the second orders, that is, rational notions, are around the second, that is, the intellect, from which they flow into the soul and similarly flow back. Moreover, the third orders, that is, seminal reasons, are around the third, that is, the soul, from which they flow forth into nature, and from which they flow back again into the soul. Finally, he wants the fourth orders to be understood as around the fourth, that is, natural forms around nature, from which they glide into matter, and into which they return as much as possible. All this, I say, we have discussed more fully elsewhere, and will discuss again.

What is beyond being: what is true being: what is not true being: what is true non-being: how far goods extend: where evils first arise: and in how many ways evils are spoken of: and many reasons why matter exists.

III Chapter III discusses what evil is: how many evils there are: where evils are. He denies that evil exists in that which transcends beings. For that is the Good itself: which is indeed known to be beyond beings from this: that the very nature of desiring and choosing not only desires many things to be, but also wishes many things not to be, not to have been, not to be in the future: yet it always chooses under the aspect of the good. From which it is clear that the lot of the desirable, that is, of the good, is not only to be present, but also to pertain to non-being, and therefore the Good itself exists more universally and superior to being. But since essence is the first receptacle of the good, and therefore through it the good is derived into other things, it follows that as far as the participation of true essence extends, so far also the true portion of good extends. And up to this point, there are no evils: just as insofar as true heat is vigorous, coldness is absent from it. But the portion of true essence extends even to the very substances of the spheres of the world, in whose essences no privation is found. Therefore, in these, evils cannot exist. Whatever

--- Page 109 ---
IN BOOK VIII, ENNEAD I, 65

But whatever among composite things is sometimes dissolved, is not truly called being: because its very being was preceded by a long privation, and a similar one follows, and the course of its being, while it passes through motion and time, as far as it properly pertains to being, has an individual present (moment), because it pertains to non-being, it suffers a long past and future. Therefore, such a composite, to which much privation of being is mixed, is thus called untrue being, just as something is not truly hot, in which, to a minimum of heat, a maximum of cold is applied. Therefore, evil befalls these, because, being untrue being, while it falls too much from the first essence, and therefore slips away from the very lot of good, meanwhile it is precipitated into evil. But evil itself is that which is most distant from the good, that is, the formless matter of the world itself. In the second place, evil is a form or quality suffering while lying in matter, which is also called a certain passion or externally agitated affection of matter. Three degrees of evils: how evil is in the soul, how matter has nothing good.

IIII In the fourth chapter, he continues the degrees of evils, placing matter in the first degree, and the form of corporeal matter in the second: which Plotinus briefly indicates here is not a true form, and which we demonstrate more extensively in our Theology. In the third, however, he establishes the evil of the soul, saying that the soul itself is not evil in itself: otherwise, every soul would be evil, and would be evil from the beginning, and always. He believes that the second soul, that is, life sometimes adapted to the body from the first soul, immediately becomes corrupt at the very beginning of this adaptation. For when it is thus bound to the body, so that from it and the body one animal is composed, it is deservedly infected by matter at once: so much so that it becomes subject to passions, and undergoes immoderate movements, like the body, in excess and defect. Indeed, the Platonists think that all such life becomes like this, yet that even this can hardly ever be tempered at last: but before moderation

then by the counsel of the rational faculty choosing matter, then by the command of the superior imagination: or by falling into matter, namely, through the influence of the inferior imagination: or finally, by suffering, namely, through the lowest sense. Indeed, since all things, insofar as they are such in some respect, are judged as such, inasmuch as they are simply referred to that very quality, Plotinus rightly considers all things evil through some relation to matter, which is evil itself, both in the soul, as has already been said, and in the body, and in circumstances, which he subsequently shows, where he raises and resolves the second question. From these things, he concludes that the soul is not the principle of evil: because, namely, its nature itself is not evil, since it is an intellectual nature, and intellect itself is as close as possible to the Good itself: since both intellect turns most directly to the Good itself, and the soul turns through intellect. Here he implies that souls do not fall away from God by a certain purpose, as if rebellious, but rather from a certain contingent consequence: insofar as, namely, they are affected by matter and something material. From this, the mind is secretly turned away from God, while it willingly turns to the opposite. Indeed, if in this place of our wickedness
