...of all things, Plotinus necessarily holds that a worldly work follows from it. If the world exists, necessarily there is matter, which is evil. If therefore the Good exists, evil necessarily follows. Furthermore, since the Good itself has inestimable efficacy, it diffuses its power and effect very far and very wide. If it extends very far, it certainly produces a series of innumerable successive grades, so that the last grade, as if most distant, is contrary to the first, i.e., the Good, that is, entirely different and most dissimilar. It will therefore be evil: evil, I say, simply and universally. Likewise, if it diffuses its power most widely, very many grades through the breadth of things cause one to be most different from another, and often truly contrary. And [this results in] evil not indeed simply evil, but rather mutually [evil]. If therefore the Good exists, consequently, then in length, evil itself finally creeps in, and then in breadth certain evils occur among themselves. From the inestimable fecundity of the Good itself, necessarily, a Good that is again most fecund follows. And of this, in turn...

IN BOOK VIII. ENNEAD. I. 69

Now, what Plotinus brings forward concerning good and evil, and the grades of good and evil, both in previous discussions and here, so that you may grasp it summarily, consider it thus. Diverse goods, in whatever kind of things they may be, we call by the common appellation of good; and not by chance, but led to this by a certain condition. For thus in all things we divine a common share, not one in species or genus; for in all genera, however diverse, we perceive and name good. Therefore, this appellation is one, namely, on account of a certain unity of order towards the same, because they are from the same principle, and have something of it, and are carried towards and contribute to the same as a goal. Similarly, through all genera we find some evil; and all evils we denote by the same name of evil, not by chance, but by a certain reason. Nor can this be done more truly than if we refer all things to one supreme evil, namely, because they either arise from it, or have something of it, whether of likeness, or inclination, or nature; or because they are carried towards it and contribute to it. That which is good itself is the highest grade of the universe; therefore, evil itself must be the lowest grade of all. Nor indeed is it proper to judge evils solely by their departure from good itself and by their distance; but much more rightly by their approach to evil itself. For not whatever immediately departs from the first (principle) do

Whether evil itself is not pure evil, and whether it is in the soul?
It is answered that it is pure, and not in the soul.

Question XII, the third in Chapter XII, inquires whether it is permissible to judge evil itself and the first evil as not pure evil in every respect, and thus to place it in the soul? I answer: the first and highest evil, according to Plotinus, is understood to be the extreme emptiness of forms, which, as far as forms are concerned, is both pure emptiness and prime matter. Indeed, if it had anything formal intrinsically, it would not be true matter, just as a true form is not one that admits anything material into itself. Conversely, if matter is not true matter, if any formal quality has emerged intrinsically within it: so neither is a true form, whatever turns out to be material. Especially because if matter, while being fashioned for the better, that is, to be transformed into a formal state, ceases to be true matter: much more does a true form cease to exist as a form, while it is transferred to the worse, that is, into matter. Therefore, in order that we may arrive from the non-true to the true, it is necessary both to ascend to pure forms above matter, and to descend to pure matter below forms. For this reason, matter always

--- Page 115 ---
IN BOOK VIII OF THE ENNEADS. I. 71
it is itself, that is, abundantly COMMUNICATING itself, but rather insofar as that (matter/evil) is that very one, that is, wonderfully separated from all things. Thus, therefore, matter becomes utterly destitute and formless, separated from all gifts whatsoever. Thus again, matter is denominated something one rather than good, and indeed has intrinsic unity, but goodness appearing extrinsically. But altogether, since all effects of the supreme principle are both from it and are compelled to exist outside and below it, certainly insofar as they are from it, they derive forms and acts therefrom. But insofar as they are outside it and inferior, they suffer a certain material lot (so to speak) mixed within themselves, and the condition of a lesser good; and finally, they end in matter, the lowest and most inferior subject of all, and the origin of evils. Now indeed, when the soul generates matter, it is not yet evil, but good, nor yet deficient, but fertile, and therefore can generate. But when it now embraces matter too much, from this it becomes weaker, as if by a burden, and worse; but that it embraces matter is brought about both by the destitution and appetite of matter, and by the soul's fecundity. Four questions

[Decorative initial Q containing a figure of a man] HOEVER inquire whence evils have arisen, whether concerning things, or concerning some kind of things, will make a suitable beginning of investigation if they first propose what evil is, and the nature of evil. For thus it will appear whence it came, where it is founded, to whom evil happens: and altogether it will be established wherever it is in the nature of things. But it is doubtful: by which of the powers within us can we especially perceive the nature of evil? Since the knowledge of individual things is perfected through a certain likeness. For intellect and soul, since they are certain species, also know species, and naturally desire species. But indeed, no one can fashion evil under the form of reason, since it is conceived in a certain absence of all good. But if, because there is the same knowledge of contraries, and evil is contrary to good, therefore there will be the same knowledge of good and evil, it is certainly necessary for those who are to know evils, to discern good: since superior things rightly precede inferior things: and species precede those things which are judged not species, but rather privations. BUT for the present we must say what the nature of good is, as much as the present discussion demands. This is that from which all things depend, and which all things desire, receiving from it their beginning, and utterly in need of it: but it itself is in need of nothing, sufficient to itself, desiring nothing utterly, the measure and end of all things, producing from itself intellect, essence, soul, life: and again, action concerning intellect. Up to this point all things are beautiful, but beauty itself, and above those things which are best, reign in the intelligible world: which is indeed intellect: intellect, I say, not such as one might perhaps think, supposing it to be similar to those which among us are called intellects, which from

III
Evil is not in those things which truly are, but in those which either are not truly, or incline towards those which are not truly.

D IF these are beings, and this [evil] is what is above beings, certainly evil will nowhere be in beings: and much less in that which transcends beings. For all these things are good. It remains therefore: if evil is anywhere, it is to be found in those things which are not, as a certain species of non-being: and around something of those things which are mixed with non-being, or in whatever way they have commerce with non-being. Non-being, I say, is by no means entirely non-being, but only different from being.
E Not indeed non-being in the way that motion and rest are said to be around being, but as an image of being, or even more remote from being. That, however, is the sensible universe, and whatever passions are around the sensible: or something posterior to these, and as it were accidental to them, or the principle of these, or something of those things which complete it, such indeed as I shall now describe. For it is permissible to conceive of it as a certain immoderation if referred to measure, the infinite
F also to a limit, the formless again to a former: likewise, always needy to the sufficient, always indeterminate, nowhere at all resting, suffering all things from all sides, insatiable, uttermost poverty. Nor do such things happen to this, but they seem to be its very essence. Moreover, whatever portion of it you see, you will find all these things summarily in each: but whatever other things participate in it, and are assimilated to it, indeed become evil,
G yet it is not evil itself. Therefore, these things are inherent in a certain foundation, not as something other than itself, but as itself. this happens to another. What then, someone will say, is immoderation, if not in that which is immoderate? And what, in turn, is measure, if not in a thing participating in measure? But just as measure exists in no measured thing, so too immoderation exists outside an immoderate subject. Therefore, a nature subjected to figures, species, forms, measures, terms, and endowed with an alien ornament, possessing nothing good from itself besides: an image again, if compared with beings, and indeed the very essence of evil, if an essence of evil can exist at all, this, I say, reason rightly convinces to be the primary evil, and evil in itself.

IV
Three degrees of evils:

THE NATURE of bodies, insofar as it participates in matter, is indeed evil, though not primary: for it has a certain appearance, though not true; it is also deprived of life; and it brings mutual corruption among bodies, and disorderly collision from them; furthermore, it brings impediments to the soul for its proper action; moreover, by perpetual flux it flees essence, and therefore obtains the second degree of evil. But the soul in itself is not evil, nor is every soul depraved. But which is depraved? That, namely, as Plato says, which serves that to which the depravity of the soul can naturally belong: as if the irrational species of the soul undergoes evil, immoderation, and excess, and defect: from which intemperance and timidity, and other depravity of the soul, arise as involuntary passions: from which also false opinions, by which one thinks things good or evil, which one pursues or flees. But what brings about this depravity? And how can you reduce it to that principle and cause? First, it will be said that such a soul is not outside matter, nor is it such in itself: and so it is mixed with immoderation, and becomes devoid of the adorning and moderating form: for it is immersed in a body possessing matter. Moreover, if the rational faculty is offended, it is prevented from discerning, obscured by disturbances, and overwhelmed by the darkness of matter, inasmuch as it assents and slides into matter: and altogether looks not to essence, but to generation, whose origin is the nature of matter, so utterly evil that even that which is not yet in it, but only looks to it, it fills with its evil. For it becomes utterly devoid of good, and a privation of good, and a pure defect, indeed whatever touches it in any way, it renders similar to itself. Therefore, the perfect soul, tending towards the Intellect, is always pure, eliminating matter far from itself, and all that is indeterminate, immoderate, evil, neither approaching these nor even looking at them: for this reason it remains pure, by intellect...

But if the good itself is essence, or rather super-essence, what then can be contrary to it? That therefore nothing is contrary to essence, this is sufficiently manifest in individual essences through induction. But what then could be contrary to universal essence itself, and indeed to the very first principles of the universe? Perhaps indeed, to essence itself, non-essence will be contrary: but to the nature of the good, the contrary will be, if there is any nature and principle of evil. For both are principles, the one of good things, the other of evil things: and all things which are in either nature are contrary to each other. Wherefore they themselves are entirely contrary, and more contrary F than other things. For other contraries are placed either in the same species or in the same genus, and in whatever they are, they agree in some common aspect: but those which are separate, and are so disposed that those which fill the nature of one are contrary to those which fill the nature of the other: what prevents them from being most contrary to each other? if indeed those are contraries which are separated by the longest interval from each other.

Indeed, to limit, and to measure, and to other things which are proper to the divine G nature, are contrary infinitude, immoderation [marginal note in Greek: not itself], and all other things whatsoever that are said to be in the nature of evil. Therefore, the whole is contrary to the whole. One indeed possesses being as most fallacious, and primarily and truly false and a lie: but the being of the other is truly being: and so the falsity of the former resists the truth of the latter. that which is entirely devoid of measure: but that which

dark: then indeed, depravity, since it is ignorance

either similar to or a participant in the good itself. **F**

**A** ...leaving behind what is deprived from the defined.
But indeed, looking at matter itself as if it were a deformed face, since reason does not dominate there, nor can it cover the ugliness of matter, we naturally conceive deformity from a certain defect of form. But how do we know that which has obtained no form in any part? Perhaps by completely removing form, we assert all that remains, in which forms are not present, to be matter, and meanwhile we admit a certain formlessness within ourselves, while we remove all form, if indeed we are to inspect matter. Therefore, this understanding is different, and almost not an understanding, while it dares to inspect what is not its own; just as an eye turning away from light, to see darkness, and not see: because in order to see darkness, it leaves the light; for it cannot see darkness together with light, nor again can it see anything without light, so that, as far as possible, it may see.
**C** Similarly, the intellect, hiding its own light in its inner chambers, and as if going outside itself, departs into those things that are alien to it; nor meanwhile does it apply its own light; and therefore it subjects itself to a condition contrary to its nature, so that it may inspect what is contrary to itself.

**D** UP TO THIS POINT enough has been said about these things.
But since matter is entirely devoid of quality, under what condition is it said to be evil? Perhaps it is said to be empty of quality because it possesses no quality from itself, which it is about to receive, as future qualities in itself as a subject; nor, however, is it said to be non-qualitative as if it had no nature at all. But if it has some nature, what prevents us from saying this nature is evil? And I do not mean evil as if endowed with some quality, since that very thing is a quality, by whose presence another thing is also denominated as having a quality.
**E** Quality, therefore, is an accident, and it lies in another; but matter is not in another, but is the subject around which every accident revolves. Since therefore that which is called qualitative has the nature of an accident, indeed, matter, having by no means obtained that, is said to be non-qualitative. Furthermore, if quality itself is non-qualitative, in what way will matter, not having obtained quality, be able to be called qualitative? Therefore, it will rightly be called both non-qualitative and evil. For it is not considered evil because it has quality,
**F** but rather because it has no quality, lest if it were a form, perhaps it would be evil in some way, but not by a nature contrary to form.

**G** BUT the nature contrary to universal form is privation; but privation is always in another, and in itself it is not a substance. Evil, therefore, if it is situated in privation, certainly in that which is deprived of form, there will be evil. Therefore, it will not be able to exist by itself. If, therefore, evil will be in the soul, privation in it will be evil and depravity, and it will not be necessary to receive anything from outside whence evil comes into it; because other reasons completely remove matter, but these (reasons) do not even think matter itself, when it exists, is evil. Therefore, nothing is to be sought from elsewhere as evil; but whoever places evil in the soul, let him place it so that it is the absence of good. But if privation is of a certain form pertaining to being:

For depravity is still something human, mixed with a certain contrary. Therefore, the vicious person dies by that very condition by which the soul can die. But the death of the soul is, both while it is immersed in the body, to slip into matter and be filled by it, and after it has laid aside the body, to wallow in the same mud, until at last it returns to higher things, and lifts its gaze upwards from the mire: otherwise, this very thing will have been what is said, that the soul, having fallen to the underworld, slumbers.

MARSILIO FICINO'S
ARGUMENT ON BOOK IX
CONCERNING THE SEPARATION
OF THE SOUL FROM THE BODY.

[Decorative initial V]HETHER it is ever permissible to violently separate the soul from the body or not: some Platonists dispute among themselves; and on both sides they bring forward Plato and Plotinus as patrons for their cause, but especially two, Olympiodorus and Macrobius, seem to disagree. Indeed, certain arguments of Socrates in the Phaedo favor Macrobius's side, and more of Plotinus's. Socrates' argument relies especially on Orphic authority. Orpheus places providence, that is, nature, under the universal providence of Jupiter, that is, of Dionysus, the world-soul: to whom the Titans, that is, the Daemons, minister: who, persuaded by Juno, that is, by the process of generation, are imagined to diligently tear Dionysus apart: because, differing from his common office of equally generating and moving all things, they divide it among themselves into lots, and bring forth species of things for individual generation. Furthermore, Orpheus imagines that the Titans, because they devoured the torn Dionysus, were struck by lightning: that is, converted by Jupiter to higher things, and men were born from their burning, that is, begotten by their divine mystery. And because men were born from the Titans, who had been nourished by the body of Dionysus: therefore he calls them Dionysiacs, as if they were certain members of Dionysus sprouting forth anew from the Titans who generate them: so much so that the human body is also a part of the Dionysiac, that is, the mundane body: and human nature of life, is a certain portion of that nature and life. And if any proper form or proper function exists in us, which indeed it does, it ought to obey the common [principle]. Therefore, as guardians of the providence of Dionysus, that is, of universal nature, we ought to remain in this guardianship: and not depart from here before God commands it: likewise to preserve what we have received from there, inasmuch as we have received it to be preserved: and not to dissolve what God himself has bound: and not to inflict violence upon the very members of God. Socrates first brings forth this Orphic opinion in the Phaedo, then confirms it with the authority of Philolaus the Pythagorean. For Philolaus says, "Do not divide the wood on the path," that is, do not separate the body from the soul in the very space of life, while the path still has its end. Again, "When you have arrived at the sacred place, do not look back": that is, do not turn back again to lower things a life that has already attained the highest contemplation. Indeed, in the first precept, he commands that just as nature has bound the body to the soul, so you should permit nature to separate the body from the soul. But in the second, he commands: that just as our will has bound the soul's intention to the body, so the will should release this intention from the body, and once released, not permit it to be bound again. These Pythagorean [teachings], Plato

--- Page 128 ---
64 COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO.
But souls who have departed from this life burdened by the defilement of sins are rather to be compared to those who, having fallen headlong from a height into an abyss, lack the ability to rise again. Therefore, they warn to use the allotted spans of life, lest the opportunity for perfect purification be lacking. Therefore, Macrobius, persuaded by these arguments of Plato and Plotinus, thus interprets the mind of both, that they would not under any condition permit anyone to lay hands upon themselves: Porphyry also seems to hold the same opinion in his book 'On Abstinence': Olympiodorus understands and approves of the same arguments, but from their very words, both here and elsewhere, he believes that it can sometimes be permitted. Indeed, to prove this, he brings forward certain words of Socrates in the Phaedo. First, what he says: "Perhaps a philosopher will not lay violent hands upon himself." Where he said this very word "perhaps", he seems to have left the suspicion that it is sometimes permissible. Then what he added in this manner: "Philosophers ought not to inflict death upon themselves, unless God has imposed a great necessity, such as He has now imposed upon me." As if to say: "A philosopher, placed in a similar necessity, can rightly free himself from life by death." He again brings forward Plato's testimony in the Republic, where he seems to permit a person utterly oppressed by a long-standing and incurable disease to release himself from this life, because he is useless to the state. For he says that citizens ought to live not for themselves, but for the state. Likewise, he adds Plato's testimony in the Laws, saying: "a man gripped by an incurable crime, such as lust for his mother, or a desire for sacrilege, or a similar impulse, which he sees he cannot restrain, it is fitting for him to remove himself from this world." Similarly, Olympiodorus seems to have understood some words of Plotinus: First, where Plotinus says: "If someone perceives impending madness, he will choose [it], then this very thing is to be chosen not as desirable in itself, but as a necessary condition." Olympiodorus seems to have understood this as if to say, to cast off the soul from here rather than to live with madness: for if that (madness) persists, a person does not live, but an animal: nor is any opportunity for progress given. Someone will further confirm this by what Plotinus says in the book 'On Happiness' in this manner: "If a happy man should perchance be led captive, a way out is prepared: if not, it is given to live happily there." Macrobius will be able to respond to these points thus: first, that Plato used that expression 'perhaps' (as is his custom) for the sake of modesty: then, regarding what he says 'unless God has imposed a necessity': then he will say that it is permissible for the Philosopher not to kill himself, but to choose from several conditions of death placed in his option, whichever he prefers. Furthermore, he will explain Plato's words in the Republic and the Laws thus: that Plato did not so much wish to permit anyone to kill himself, as to appeal to a great love for the fatherland, and to sharply recall from impious crime. He will also take Plotinus's words thus, that in the book 'On Happiness' he frees the happy man from his chains, by rather withdrawing the mind from the senses, than life from the body. Finally, what he says in this book, 'to be chosen as necessary', someone will explain it as enduring madness, as a thing necessarily to be borne, rather than doing violence to nature. This opinion will again be confirmed by Plotinus's words at the end of his disputation against the Gnostics: where he forbids departing from this life before the natural time. Against these points, Olympiodorus will again bring forward, that Plato's and Plotinus's words are thus excessively twisted: indeed, it is fitting for the safety of the fatherland, for honor, for the sake of bearing truth, to undergo certain death, even by one's own hand. Likewise, sometimes to separate the soul from the body by starvation rather, than to permit it to live uselessly through long-lasting madness and a completely incurable disease, indeed with harm to oneself and others, and far from every duty of reason. For thus, although someone may not follow the order of inferior nature, he will nevertheless follow the order of superior nature, and always the more perfect to the less perfect: and this indeed is to be preferred not by impulse, but by counsel. These things they bring forward back and forth, and the case is still before the judge.
PLOTINUS

--- Page 129 ---
**PLOTINUS. ENNEAD I. BOOK IX.**

**ON THE EXTRACTION OF THE SOUL FROM THE BODY.**

[Large decorative initial N containing an illustration of a figure]
**A** Let no one forcibly expel the soul from the body: lest perchance it depart to a similar place, intending to migrate: otherwise it will depart carrying something corporeal, by means of which it will migrate through similar things. For to migrate is to pass from one place to another. But one ought to wait until the whole body fails from the soul itself:
**B** when the soul does not need transmigration, but is entirely outside. How then does the body fail from the soul? When, namely, no power of the soul is any longer bound in it. Since the body can no longer bind it, having lost, namely, the harmony which it once possessed, and by which it also held the soul. What then, if someone endeavors that the body be dissolved from the soul? But thus he will use force: nor would the body then release the soul, but the soul itself would abandon it. Added to this,
**C** that when someone dissolves the body, he is not free from passion, but is compelled either by distress, or by pain, or by anger. Nothing of that kind, however, is to be done. But if someone perceives impending madness, what will he do? Perhaps indeed this will not happen to a sensible person. But if it should happen, it must be placed in that class of things which are called necessary: and to be chosen because of the circumstances, but not simply. For the devising of poisons compelling the soul to depart, perhaps does not benefit the soul. And although a fated time is given to each, before it, this will not happen happily, unless (as we said) it is considered as necessary. If finally, as each person departs, such an order he also retains there, the mind is not to be extracted from the body, since there may still be an opportunity for progress.

MARSILIO FICINO
ON BOOK I OF THE SECOND ENNEAD,
CONCERNING HEAVEN,
A COMMENTARY.

SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

[Decorative initial D in a square frame with floral patterns] PLOTINUS'S DISPUTATION on the heavens has eight chapters. In the first and second, he raises several doubts, and meanwhile brings forward certain things conducive to solving the questions. In the third, resuming the doubts, he gradually begins to unravel the uncertainties, and similarly in the others, and summarily concludes from all that heaven is fire, and indeed pure and sole: whose sensible form is. First indeed light, then truly harmless and vital heat: but he wishes this twofold form to proceed from the insensible form of the same heaven: heat indeed from life, light from intellect to be its eternal substance, and he wishes the perpetual motion of this immortality to be caused by that intellectual life, that is, its soul never departing from divinity. But the corporeal nature of heaven itself, although it is not properly the cause of immortality, nevertheless by a certain accommodation contributes to its perpetual perseverance, as long as it aptly, opportunely, and willingly obeys the always preserving cause. Let this be the summary of the entire book thus far.

Since the world is corporeal, it is neither from itself, nor by itself
eternal, but through a cause entirely
incorporeal.

1 Therefore, at the outset, it seems astonishing how the world, being a body, can be eternal: as very many wise men have agreed. For this entire body cannot be perpetual by itself, since it cannot even exist by itself: which we sufficiently prove in Theology. Nor is it easily convinced how it can be eternal through another cause: especially under the singularity of the same substance, which can be seen by its dimension and motion: finally, it is subject to division and change of substance. Moreover, the matter of the entire world is one. For the work of one craftsman is one. One, I say, through one matter and form, and everywhere agreeing with itself, and sympathetic. Indeed, the unity of form and matter itself brings about this communion of acting and suffering among all things. Finally, since the very nature of matter is entirely formless, and distinction usually occurs through forms, there seems to be no reason why matter should be distinguished from matter anywhere. But since matter is the lowest subject of all, entirely formless, equally avid for all forms, even those repugnant to each other, it is perpetually mutable. Therefore, just as below the moon, so also in heaven, a certain potential for change of form always lies hidden in matter, since the matter is the same everywhere. This we indeed prove thus: Since the motion that thrives in the soul is the primary motion: and therefore there is action there: but motion in the body is secondary, and therefore passion: indeed, this passion threatens the body with destruction, especially because motion in the soul, as in an individual thing, does not tend towards dissolution: but in the body, as in something divisible, it tends in a certain way. Nor is it permitted for anyone, in the manner of Averroes, to place dimensions in heaven without matter. For if the primary forms of all things, that is, the ideal forms, have, as it were, something material joined to them, I mean the formative essence of the mind, much more do the lowest forms of all, that is, dimensions, have something material, indeed entirely material, everywhere with them. And if substantial forms are placed in a subject, much more does dimension need a subject: which is rather accidental and utterly ineffectual. Now indeed, no corporeal form is anything other than a passion of matter, while this matter is affected from elsewhere. Nor is dimension again anything other than the extension of matter itself, while it is extended by the same from which it is formed, so that it can be formed more distinctly and abundantly. Therefore, the foundation of the world is matter and dimension simultaneously: from matter indeed mutable, from dimension divisible, from both ineffectual and passive, and necessarily dependent on something else. The world, therefore, is not eternal by the inherent faculty of its own body, but both from the soul as an intrinsic cause of immortality, and from the divine will as an extrinsic principle and end. If the nature of God is considered as always existing in the same act, and entirely immutable, the world seems from that to have always been and to be. Hence Mercury and Plotinus, because to be and to act are the same for divine things, and effect immediately follows that action, judge the world to be entirely eternal. But if the free will in God is considered, and this is judged to be the principle of the world, which Mercury, Plato, and Plotinus believe, it seems that the world can be made new by God without a newness of divine nature, without a new will. Thus, therefore, Plutarch, Severus, and Atticus consider the world to be new, accepting the saying of Timaeus of Locri in this sense, where he says: God created the soul of the world, prior to its body both in power and in time: Whence Plato also says in Timaeus: the soul of the world was created prior to its body, both in virtue and in generation. Although Plotinus, Porphyrius, Proclus, and others explain these words of Timaeus and Plato thus: that the time and generation by which the soul precedes the body is not an extrinsic interval: but that a certain succession in the soul, in the very discourse of forms, precedes the motion of the world's origin: so that this motion is from that, and that is the age of ages. I now omit the opinion of Heraclitus, that every body of the world, even of the spheres and stars, always flows out and flows back: and therefore either ceases to be, or is perpetually renewed: which Plato also touched upon, where he says the world is always becoming, but never is: and Plotinus here and Proclus in Timaeus: which Phleton also does not deny to be probable, and we ourselves prove in Theology that the same can happen. But if the entire body of the world thus always flows and flows back, while the substance of the soul remains, then not undeservedly will the soul also be prior in time and generation to any new body of the world, if the world is always made new from old. Hence perhaps the Prophet and the Evangelist say: I saw a new heaven and a new earth. Likewise the Evangelist: the world indeed passes away. But let us now return to Plotinus. Since the matter in heaven is the same as that below heaven, Plotinus asks whether celestial things, like others, are subject to change, and whether the species of any sphere or star always remains, while the singular nature of each is gradually changed and somehow renewed, as if it happens below the moon? To these questions, if someone responds that the universe is perpetual for this reason, that nothing can flow out of it, nor flow into it, since

--- Page 131 ---
IN LIBR. I. ENNEAD. II. 87

...since it embraces all things: that person has not yet sufficiently discovered why any spheres and stars are eternal: for no sphere and no star contains all things: nor has he granted sufficient eternity to the whole world. For perhaps the world can still, even if not externally, yet internally be so changed, that, like our animals, it often changes its individual substance: while nevertheless retaining the eternal nature of its species. Finally, doubt remains: whether either this whole (world), or at least something celestial, is eternal: and for what reason: and why in heaven both the species and the individual remain, but under heaven only the species itself remains, while individuals change.

**The soul is indeed the cause of heaven's immortality: and heaven, for its part, does not resist the soul in this.**

II Therefore, in the second chapter, he (Plotinus) doubts the same thing, implying everywhere that nothing in the world can remain perpetual by its own nature: so that you may remember that all these things are made and preserved from elsewhere. But what the Peripatetics say, that heaven is eternal because it is a fifth body besides the four elements, he passes over here negligently. For by the very fact that it is a body, since it is not simply by itself, it certainly is not always by itself: especially since its nature is divisible and mutable. Finally, he signifies that the cause of immortal life for heaven is the soul itself, which is also simply the cause of life: but that the celestial body and the universe are naturally prepared for immortal life, if not to effect it, at least to receive it: or at least that they do not resist receiving it in the slightest.

But let us again take up the whole matter from another principle. If you consider heaven, which entirely fills the world, in its form and motion, far removed from extended matter, you will undoubtedly be contemplating the very soul of the world: of which heaven is indeed the image, and the rest is merely a shadow. That, therefore, is the undivided heaven; but heaven itself is the soul now extended. Therefore, let us relate each individual thing, as from an image to its exemplar, to its corresponding individual thing. That indeed is a simple form; this is similarly a simple body. That has no parts; this is never separated into parts. That (the soul) by a single act, that is, by its self-awareness, completes its principal function; this (heaven) by perpetual turning upon itself accomplishes all things. but either infinite in number or in magnitude, we thus briefly conjecture. We conceive of a fourfold infinity. First,
of virtue and perseverance simultaneously, especially in the supreme God: Second, of perseverance at least in divine works
perpetually enduring therefrom: Third, of number: And finally, fourth, of bulk. Indeed, the infinity of number seems
to arise gradually through a certain perpetual succession of individual things, but never to exist actually all at once. For it is
defined by the unity of the species as a limit, and an innumerable multitude actually admits no order. Nevertheless, all
things are defined by a certain order under a first principle, which is both common to all and proper to some. If there is no
disorderly crowd in the lowest things, much less is it found in the highest, where order is supreme. Therefore, there are
not innumerable worlds, nor innumerable parts of one world. Moreover, infinite bulk is further removed from the divine
mind than infinite number. Since, therefore, the divine mind least desires an innumerable number, much less will it tolerate
immense bulk. Otherwise, this would have received no order or limit from God. Nor indeed is it permissible to imagine
corporeal bulk existing entirely from itself, or from several causes entirely diverse from each other. Which we frequently
refute in Theology. Nor that under one cause of all things, the work should not be one; nor that there should be multiple worlds,
one disconnected from another. For we refute this in the Timaeus.

For this soul is not so much a part as the cause of the animal, and primary matter is rather the subject in which the animal exists. It is made, I say, properly from its own certain matter, already entirely adapted to its own form. But where it says that what is within the heavens are not parts of the heavens: understand 'below' not so much in place as in order. For the heaven, although it thrives everywhere, is never separated from itself. Where it says that the heaven extends up to the moon, understand 'up to the lunar condition'. For the lunar lot is the last in the degrees of celestial dignity. For the ancients call the entire region above the moon 'solar', but the following (region) 'lunar'. 92 COMMENTARY ON MARSILIO FICINO

If none, then earth will be nowhere, and water will not be able to bind earth which is found nowhere. Likewise, the nature of air is one thing, and the nature of earth is another, indeed, their natures are very diverse. If anyone therefore says that earth, in order to be earth, needs air intrinsically, he will say that coldness, dryness, density, gravity, in order to be what they are, need their opposites. Again, air is something in itself before it is infused into earth: earth similarly is something in itself before it absorbs air. Then indeed, air exists in its own rarity before it is condensed into earth: and earth consists in itself before it condenses air: which if it is condensed by another, namely water, it will pass into water. Therefore, Timaeus did not say that earth, in order to be earth, needs fire: lest coldness and gravity, in order to be coldness and gravity, should ridiculously be said to need heat and lightness; rather, he said it needs fire to be visible. For by light both eyes see, and things themselves are seen, which are also colored by a certain participation of light. Light, however, is proper to fire. For since earth is naturally opaque and neither shines by itself nor receives light within: while water and air, being diaphanous, that is, translucent and permeable to light, do not indeed have light themselves, but suddenly receive it: it follows that fire immediately has light by itself: especially since other things manifestly have light from it, and it itself, as if its own light, leaves it in nothing when it departs, although it leaves heat for a time. From this it is clear that fire is heaven. But since fire projects light, as if its principal attribute, sooner and more quickly and further than heat, it can undoubtedly apply this act of its own, that is, light, and the passion produced from it, that is, especially bright color, to other things by which they may be seen, although it does not mix itself with them. Indeed, it provides more light and luster to the more humid things, as being more similar to heaven: but to the drier things, it provides heat, and this heat is already consuming, made such by dryness, constriction, and violence. Up to this point, we have shown that earth is that very thing which it is, without intimate mixture of fire, air, and water. Again, it is clear by similar arguments that water can be water without participation of earth. Indeed, when water is forced to an earthly density, it ceases to be water, and becomes crystal: after it has evidently received a new and substantial form: for before that, it becomes ice. Therefore, earth does not make it water, but rather makes it not water. Again, whoever considers that nothing is softer, more yielding, or more penetrable than air, and nothing is more unsuitable for these qualities than earth, will discover that air is not a participant of earth. Therefore, earth does not make air to be air itself: since it has a contrary property. But if lower things are something in themselves apart from others, much more so is fire, which is impatient of mixture, and the most excellent of all, that is, heaven. Nor does earth need it to acquire dimensions and continuity from it: for because of its own most efficacious nature in matter, it wonderfully amplifies its own matter into dimensions. Likewise, since it suffers mixture least of all, it preserves its own continuity: but a certain resistance and consistency, which they call solidity in it, it has neither because of earth, nor simply because of its three dimensions: but through a certain density proper to itself somewhere, by which it not only reflects the rays of the eyes, but also more congenially and appropriately adapts the forces of higher things to lower ones: but it is clear that nothing earthly is present in celestial lights: because nowhere in heaven is seen such redness as in the color of clouds, which have something earthly: but rather such as a more frequent flame, or the gathered pallor of saffron usually renders. Indeed, Plotinus wants solidity, resisting in whatever way, to be one way in earth, and another way in other things. In earth, indeed, along with a certain rough and dry hardness proper to earth, inasmuch as it is most distant from heaven, which is the smoothest and most agile of all: Elsewhere again in its own peculiar way: in fire, namely, its solidity is not through earth, but through a certain density proper to itself somewhere: just as in water, often not through earth, but through its own coherence and union, crystal is formed, and metal, namely gold. Which here seems to be considered not a participant of earth, but to be formed only from water in the manner of crystal, but more tightly compressed within itself, in which there is some viscous substance similar to oil: whence it happens that gold is then indissoluble because of its very tight concretion: then it is melted by fire and liquefies because of its viscous humor: then because it is not a participant of earth, it does not acquire rust: but it derives its brilliance from its solar species and idea. Silver behaves almost similarly, except that it follows the Moon rather. For the authors of alchemy attribute gold to the Sun: silver to the Moon: lead to Saturn: tin to Jupiter: iron to Mars: bronze to Venus: and quicksilver to Mercury, which they call "living silver". But I approve this distribution more at present than that which I followed in the compendium of Critias. Plotinus indeed seems to have received this opinion about metals especially from Timaeus, where metals are called concrete and fusible waters: and gold is said to emerge from water compacted among adamantine veins, like a flower. Bronze is added, because it is a participant of earth, it is worn away into rust by age while the earth is separated. Plato, therefore, although he seems to place nothing of earth in gold and similarly in silver, can nevertheless probably be understood according to the opinion of others, that what is earthly in gold is so tempered with other elements, and so exactly mixed, that it can never be separated from others. Let it be said also that both gold and all metal are formed from water by a certain viscous humor, from which, as from a mother, all metals are made, which they also call the first and hidden quicksilver, which they believe is cooked and formed by sulfur as the father of metals: and from this all metals are made, and they are diverse, inasmuch as in such a union there is more of one or the other: and according as this or that of the two is purer or more impure there, and according as the cooking is lesser or greater. Therefore, these two (elements) are in gold most pure, most equal, most tempered, most thoroughly mixed, almost similarly in silver: in other metals, these behave very differently. Indeed, all metals liquefy in fire: because their mother is a plentiful, oily, and viscous humor. But rocks do not liquefy, because they have a great deal of earth, yet do not have such a rich humor, nor one as viscous as oil: thus we can explain Plato. And where Plotinus says: "Gold, since it is water, is compressed into itself without earth," it can be understood thus: that is, when it is poured into fire like water, it again solidifies into itself without the addition of earth when removed from the fire. But let anyone accept these things as he wishes. Finally, let us return to our purpose. If condensation alone in moisture either forms crystal or restores the form of metal, why should not the soul, like a glue, continue fire and connect it to itself, and contain it under the form of life? Now indeed there are also fiery bodies of demons, not compelled by earth, nor by concretion as by ice, but held in their proper form by the connecting power of the soul, and reduced to a spherical figure. For above us are demons, each in their own sphere, like stars: although mostly hidden from us, they express a naturally orbicular figure in their bodies through the inner circle of the mind, contributing to the same affection and place. Although they often show us whatever figures they wish, either by easily transfiguring the agile matter of their body in various ways, and then very easily refiguring it into their former shape: or by the vehemence of imagination and affection, like pregnant women, they fashion any forms in their inner body. I omit that they often do not so much change their own body as they excite various images in our imagination. Although demons are properly aerial animals, they are nevertheless often called fiery and watery. For properly three

--- Page 137 ---
IN BOOK I. ENNEAD. II. 93

properly are orders of demons assigned to three regions of the air: The first inhabit the sublime air nearest the Moon, heated and shining by the heat, motion, and light of the sky, which they call fire and ether: The second the middle: The third the lowest. The highest air is called fiery: the middle air, aerial: the lowest air is watery: and similarly the demons. Again, over the air thus distributed, (as they say) a certain aerial triplicity of stars presides. Over the highest air, Gemini: over the middle, Libra, and Aquarius over the lowest, and similarly over the demons. The ancients sometimes call these gods: not simply, but divine demons. Just as some call similar animals in the sky demons, not simply, but demonic gods. I indeed believe that celestial demons are not in the region of fixed stars, but of planets, as companions to the planetary stars: observing proportion, they follow the motions of the stars and planets: and similarly, demons in the pure air complete a celestial dance with appropriate progression. For perhaps, just as demons, so too stars and planets, one might think, move through the sky by their own motions like animals.

and to obtain light from heaven. After this, he says the entire heaven is light, although invisible to our eyes due to its subtlety, yet in it the lights of the stars appear due to some density: Indeed, pure light cannot be seen entirely, but mixed: either under heaven with foreign materials, or in heaven with a certain solidity and resistance, as if earthly – I do not mean a solidity in heaven, as some believe, which resists touch (for this is truly characteristic of earth), but one that either gathers or reflects rays. This invisible light, as is taught in the Xth book of the Republic, extends throughout the entire world, everywhere, like the sight of the mundane soul, by which it perceives, touches, and nourishes its whole being. The Platonists also believe that the sphere of the Sun is the sight of its soul, and likewise other spheres and globes are the sights of other celestial souls. Hence we see that in all eyes, sight is nothing other than a ray, and the shapes and qualities of eyes are very similar to heaven, or what appears to be light, or is primarily a participant of light, that is, colors. But stars and planets are not only visual eyes, but visible ones: by which animals see, and are thence governed: for through denser rays their virtues are more accommodated to us. The remaining spheres, however, are invisible eyes, I mean to earthly eyes: for they can be perceived by ethereal eyes, that is, by the sense that thrives in our ethereal body.

Plato, in the Timaeus, indeed proves that this hidden light, or fire and vital spirit, is diffused throughout the universe. The circuit of universal nature, he says, since it has embraced the other kinds of things in its circular ambit, and strives to meet with itself within it, constrains all things and nowhere allows a vacuum to be left. Therefore, fire has penetrated most of all things: then air, as being closest to fire in subtlety: and other things in a similar manner thereafter. Here it seems to be thought that the very first nature of hidden fire proceeded from a certain breathing of the mundane soul, and flowed from the innermost circuit of the soul into a circle, by whose virtue the remaining elements coalesced: which, soon encompassed by the ambit of the fire itself, and as it were restrained, left nothing empty within themselves. Likewise, when that fire, amplified into an orb, desired both to meet with itself everywhere within, and to leave nothing empty anywhere, it thoroughly penetrated all things, itself being least penetrated: then air similarly penetrated water, and water finally earth: so much so that if you ascend gradually through the middle orbs from the center, where earth is, there you will find the three remaining elements present to each other rather than confused. Then where water is, there are the other two: where air is, there is also fire. Thus the orbs of the four elements are compared to each other, so that the narrowest orb is the earthly one: the wider is the watery one, both filling the earth internally and rising above the earth's surface. The aerial one is likewise wider than earth and water: and finally, the fiery one, by a similar reasoning, is the widest of all, both nourishing all things externally and sustaining them internally.

Arnaldus and Raymundus, believing this fiery and vital spirit to be inherent in all things, and calling it the fifth essence, most diligently investigate by what means they might separate it from foreign matter, and by what custody they might best preserve it, once segregated, for uses which they hope will be most salutary for all. I omit what they hope, that if they carefully extract this from wine, as something very celestial, they will apply it to celestial gold as much as possible: which gold will then drink it up as its closest kin, and always retain it, becoming potable. But let them see to these things. Indeed, I know for certain that unless such a spirit is inherent in all things, many cannot accomplish what they promise: nor is that Platonic idea true, namely, that the navel of the world can be fire. It is indeed probable that the center and hinge of the universe is not an earthly torch, but rather fire. What is again written in the Phaedo, where it speaks of mountains surpassing the clouds, namely, that pure earth lies in pure heaven, in which are the stars, cannot be true: unless either heaven there is infused with pure air, or only heaven is there, as if there were a single orb above the clouds. But for now, let us dismiss the unity of the orb. Perhaps indeed that supreme Theologian, when he says the celestial city has twelve foundations, understands the city to be this vital spirit reigning everywhere: and the twelve foundations, the twelve spheres of the world: namely, eight heavens above the aether: and again, four heavens diffused through the aether, namely air, water, and earth. He also describes twelve gates: three from the East, three likewise from the West, three from the South, three again from the North, so as to show the four triplicities of the signs: one of which is Oriental, that is, fiery: containing Aries, Leo, Sagittarius. Another again is Occidental, that is, airy: comprising Libra, Gemini, and Aquarius. Another likewise Southern, earthy: Taurus and

A It exists, and a horse, though not the same. Therefore, not one thing in the world, namely the heavens, will endure eternally, while another, namely the genus of earthly things, will suffer destruction: but all things will behave similarly, differing only in the span of time: for celestial things are more lasting. If, therefore, under this condition, we were to accept eternity both in the universe and in its parts, less ambiguity would follow this opinion:
B indeed, all doubt will be far removed, if we demonstrate that the divine will is sufficient, and if it is in such a way and by such a pact to perpetually contain the universe. But if we say that anything in the world possesses perpetuity in its own substance, it will remain for us to demonstrate whether the divine will can effect this. Doubt will also persist as to why some things remain eternal in species and number simultaneously, while others remain eternal only in species:
C moreover, by what reason the parts that are in heaven are perpetually the same: since in this way all things will also be the same.
D IF we admit this opinion, and say that heaven and all celestial things have eternal perseverance according to the singular substance of each: but that things which are beneath the moon possess this only according to species, it will need to be demonstrated how a body can always preserve the same nature under a singular property, when the nature of the body itself continuously flows. For this is an old opinion, both of others who disputed about nature, and of Plato himself, that there is a perpetual flux not only concerning other things, but also concerning celestial bodies. For he says: how, since they are bodies and visible, will they be able to preserve an immutable and always the same nature? agreeing with Heraclitus in this matter, who says that the sun itself is also continually coming into being.
E Indeed, with Aristotle, this would not be very difficult, if one has already granted his suppositions about the fifth body. But with those who do not posit this, by what reason will a celestial body be able to be eternal under a singular property of substance? since, however, with them, heaven is constituted from the same elements as those animals which are here. Moreover, it will be much more to be doubted
F concerning the sun and the other parts that are in heaven. Indeed, since every animal is composed of a soul and the nature of a body, it is necessary that if heaven has always been the same in number, it must have this [sameness] either according to both, or according to one or the other of those things which are in it, namely, either through the body or through the soul. Whoever, therefore, attributes incorruptibility to the body, will need the soul for nothing, unless perhaps for this one thing, that the soul always be with the body to constitute the animal itself.
G But for him who posits the body as corruptible in itself, and attributes the cause of eternal salvation to the soul, it will be necessary to try to show that the very nature of the body in no way resists such a constitution and perseverance. For since in those things which are constituted by nature there is nothing dissonant: but the matter itself must also be entirely accommodated to the intention of its effect.

But in the mind indeed and in any intelligence, it occurs in an eternal moment; whereas in the soul's own discursive movement, it occurs at least in particular time; finally, in heaven, it is compelled to need not only a body, but also a place, whatever that place may be. It is asked, however, what kind of motion this was? Not the body of heaven itself, for the body, insofar as it is body, does nothing; therefore, the soul produces motion from itself into the body, yet the motion in the soul and in the body simultaneously is not of the same kind. For also in our body, through the spirit, expansion occurs indeed through pleasure, and contraction through pain, leading to a certain motion of the soul, which can be neither expansion nor contraction in the soul as an individual entity. Now the soul is, namely, secondary, from which motion immediately arises, so as to be, as it were, continuous with the body, so that from it and the body, one animal, namely heaven, is made. And while it itself, by a certain formal motion—that is, from one act of form to another act and affection of form—is turned and turned back again, meanwhile, heaven is figured differently and differently by a quasi-local motion. Therefore, if the soul were to stand still, the body would also stand still,

--- Page 149 ---
IN BOOK II. ENNEAD. II. 105

Individual motions indeed occur in certain times: but the first and universal motion is almost the same as time, just as the first state is eternity. Therefore, that something of itself remains in this perfect and continuous orb, perfectly moved in a circle, is evident from this: because it has no straight motion at all, nor does the whole itself change its place from elsewhere. Likewise, that no part of this spherical and solid dimension, which has dimension, can remain while the whole moves, is clear from this: that it is not broken by motion, but everywhere remains whole and continuous at the same time. This very thing, therefore, which remains in the orb while it is agitated, is indivisible. And that indeed is the center of the orb. For since slowness truly increases gradually towards the center, it is certain that the center itself completely rests. And if you imagine some dimension placed in the middle to be the center: certainly, when this is conceived, it will be shaped spherically. Then indeed I will ask: does this whole little sphere remain or not? If you say the whole remains, the entire orb is already broken: but if it revolves by the circumference, and rests by the center, I will ask again about the center. If you say it is divisible, the previous question will return: and you will be forced to err infinitely, nor will you ever find a center: but if you confess it to be indivisible, you must admit that only something indivisible acts as rest in a continuous sphere. And this is not so much some sign or point, as the very heart of the sphere and the power of the soul, or rather the soul itself. But since it hastens by natural desire towards this indivisible, as if a life-giving foundation of the whole orb, and does not wish to be forced into the indivisible, lest it lose its natural figure, it deservedly revolves. For thus, through every point and line marked in the sphere, the whole sphere gradually inserts itself, so that at least it seems as if it becomes indivisible, and whole everywhere like the soul, and from all sides the whole contemplates the whole soul. Now indeed you will not deny, I think, that this whole lives, when you consider that in its womb, and by its power, even the smallest things live. But if the whole lives, heaven lives most of all, which is the greatest part of the whole, and the whole itself. But if you say heaven is an instrument of a more divine life for generating living things, you will still confess that this natural and proximate instrument, as it were, generative of a more divine life (if I may say so), already lives with its own life, by whose nourishment, and in whose womb, all things coalesce into life. Indeed, in no other way than through this already made living thing, is the benefit of living transmitted to the rest. This life proper to heaven is the very nature of heaven and the universe, through which the motion of heaven, as the first and leader of natural motions, is most natural and intimate, and most voluntary, so that heaven wishes to move as willingly as either a superior life, or heaven's own life consenting with the superior one, studiously decides to move. Hence it happens that this motion is most easy and perpetual: both because in the sphere and its motion, whatever you mark as an end, will be similarly as a beginning: and because the power and act of moving in the soul is the very natural life of the soul. Therefore, by this life, by this soul which is whole everywhere, and as it were moves, it renders itself whole everywhere present like light in a moment: heaven also, as much as it can, by revolution

For all [souls] perpetually enjoy the divine mind and God by a certain act of intelligence, though hidden from us. All, by a certain rational discourse, either do the same thing or strive to do it. Here, however, you will observe that every act proceeding from one term to another, even if it happens suddenly and without an intermediary, can be called motion: thus, you will in a way name the intelligence proceeding from the divine mind into God himself, motion and circuit. But an act proceeding from one thing to another suddenly, but through an intermediary, you can call motion by a more proper name: by this motion, I say, the intellect of the soul turns around God through the divine intellect as if it were an intermediary. Finally, an act proceeding from one thing to another both through an intermediary and through time, you will rightly call motion by the most proper name. By this circuit, rational nature turns, both within itself around forms, and from itself to its own intellect, and through the divine, it turns itself to God. congratulating, it is moved with exultation; and since it desires to occupy itself with the good, and the good itself is everywhere, it indeed dances everywhere. Similarly acts reason directed to the understood good; similarly intellect, most closely stirred by the good. But it is the circumference insofar as it is superior, undoubtedly exceeding the inferior [soul] by many degrees of virtue. By this excess of virtue, as by some wider compass, it overtops that inferior [soul], as if it were narrower, and embraces and preserves it, and leads it forth and brings it back in equal measure.

On the motion of the heavens.

[Marginal note:]
The motion of the heavens,
because it is made by the intellectual
soul, and occurs in a circle,
both because both the soul and the intellect
make a certain circuit within themselves,
and because the circular shape
of the heavens contributes to the circuit.

[Decorative initial 'Q']
WHY does the heaven move in a circle? Because it imitates mind. But whose is that motion? Of the soul or of the body? What then? Is it because the soul is in a sphere, and this [sphere] hastens to proceed around it [the soul]? Also, is it in it as if not continuous, or rather in such a way that, being moved itself, it moves others? But perhaps it was fitting that the moving soul should not move further, but should have already moved. But this is rather to make it remain, and not to agitate it always in a circle. For perhaps it will also stand still, or if it is moved, it will not, however, be changed in place. In what way, therefore, does it move locally, when it itself is moved in some other way? Perhaps circular motion may not seem local to someone. But if such a motion is accidental, what kind of motion, then, is this essentially? Indeed, a certain harmony consenting in itself, and conscious of its own things, and vital, neither tending outwards in any way or anywhere, nor elsewhere, in which all things ought to be comprehended. For what is principal in an animal comprehends all things in itself, and brings them together into one. But it does not embrace vitally if it rests; nor, when it has a body, will it preserve its inner parts, for the life of the body is a certain motion. But if such a motion is also local, it will be agitated as much as it can; and not as soul alone, but as an animated and living body, so that such agitation is mixed from corporeal and animal motion at the same time;

Questions are solved:
How the soul moves,
and the body of man.
Again, How the heaven
moves in a circle.

A Indeed, since the body by its own nature is carried in a straight line, but the soul contains it: and so from both a certain motion is produced, in which there is both being carried and remaining at the same time. But if circular motion is said to be the motion of the body, in what way will it be rightly said, since every body, even fire itself, is carried by straight motion? Perhaps it must be said that it proceeds in a straight path, until it reaches where it is naturally established to be. For as it is established in order, so it seems both to remain according to nature, and to be carried to that which is ordered.

B Why then does fire not rest, after it has reached its proper place? Is it because the very nature of fire is to be in motion? Therefore, unless it revolves, it will certainly be immediately dissipated, being drawn in a straight line; does it then remain that it is agitated in a circle? But indeed, is that already the function of providence? Let it be so: for is fire itself placed in itself by providence itself? Therefore, if it happens there, it will revolve circularly from itself. Or perhaps if it desires straight motion, where it no longer has a place to be carried to, it necessarily, as if circling, revolves in the places where it can.

C For no place beyond itself is open to it. For this is the outermost place. Therefore, it runs around in the seat it possesses: indeed, it is its own place, thus naturally constituted, not indeed to remain, but to be carried. Hence, in a circle, the center naturally rests: but if the outer circumference rests, the center will be immense. Rather, therefore, it will be present around the center, namely, to a living body, and one naturally disposed.

D For thus it will continuously conspire towards the very center, not indeed by settling, otherwise it would lose its orb, but when it cannot do that, at least by wandering around. For by this reason alone will it completely satisfy its desire. But if the soul revolves, it is never fatigued: for neither does it itself drag, nor is the body moved contrary to nature. For that very thing is nature, which is ordered by the soul of the universe.

E Moreover, the soul of the world, existing everywhere, not divided into parts, but whole everywhere, grants to heaven also, that it too, as far as it can, may be everywhere. But it can only do so by passing through and progressing through all things. Indeed, it would rest, if the soul were to rest somewhere, when it had finally reached the soul. But now, since the soul itself, which it desires, pours itself out entirely through the whole, it too, of course, everywhere follows the soul.

F What then, will it never attain the soul? Perhaps indeed it always attains it thus; nay, rather, the soul itself, always drawing heaven to itself, by always acting, moves it, and always. Not indeed moving elsewhere, but to itself and in the same place, not indeed in a straight line, but leading in a circle, and therefore it grants to it that wherever it arrives, it finds the soul there. But if the soul were to rest, as if only remaining there, where anything rests, heaven too would rest. If therefore the soul is not only somewhere, but everywhere, then of course heaven moves through all things. And since it is not carried outwards, it is rightly turned back into a circle.

G BUT how are other things moved? Certainly, not everything is a whole, but each is a part and contained in its own place: but heaven is a whole and as it were a place, and nothing hinders it: for it is the universe itself. How then are men moved? Perhaps by the reason that each is a part dependent on the whole: but in what way we ourselves are, each is its own whole. Likewise, if wherever a body is, it finds the soul, what is it compelled to wander about for? Perhaps because it does not only thrive somewhere...

MARSILIO FICINO'S
COMMENTARY ON BOOK III OF THE SECOND ENNEAD,
"WHETHER THE STARS DO ANYTHING."

SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

Species and individuals within species are generated, especially by seminal virtues in species and individuals; celestial bodies, however, dispose matter in one way or another.

PORPHYRY writes in the Life of Plotinus: that when he had devoted diligent effort to astrology, he discovered that the judgments of astrologers were not to be believed; and that he had often refuted them both in speech and in writing. This he indeed did in the book On Fate, and in the books On Providence. But in this book, finally, "Whether the Stars Do Anything," he seems to have accomplished it more diligently. In this, Plotinus's intention is certainly, first of all, to assert that whatever things are generated and moved by nature, are especially made and guided, both by the seminal reasons of universal nature, and by reasons and seeds very much proper to universal nature, which are by no means discordant: and therefore he argues that neither the influx nor the nature of the stars alone, as being too universal:

--- Page 155 ---
IN BOOK III. ENNEAD. II. 111

because the causes are immense and powerful, and the movement is most effective and swiftest. Plotinus will indeed concede that qualities concurring into such a form are led forth by one certain cause, entirely stable and everywhere active, namely by the seminal virtue which thrives in the life of the world, lest one arrive at unity either by chance or unstably. But rays flowing together in one way or another either affect matter in one way or another, or provoke the active cause, that is, the seminal reason, to its proper effect. Nor can a new form, however, be produced from many things by the confluence of rays, which is always different at another moment, a form which requires a certain time, and perhaps to be begun and perfected, not merely such as that confluence is, but also such as the preceding disposition of matter, and finally, such as the seminal reason, both of its own and of universal nature, decrees for such a condition. Finally, however the matter stands, it will be very difficult to judge about future things. For if it is hidden from us what new thing arises from the mixture of natural things which we handle daily, it will certainly be much more hidden what new communion and form is forged by the casting of rays. Indeed, since they confess that something different is produced from the conjunction of two celestial rays than from the casting of only one ray, they confess and undoubtedly that something different is produced from a certain conjunction of planets than from two. And thus, something far different happens from the confluence of all stars. But the

However, a figure having five angles cannot be formed from the twelve whole signs. But otherwise, aspects seem to be able to be formed. For there are three hundred and sixty degrees in the Zodiac, which, divided into five parts, will form a figure possessing five angles: and in the same way, an angle will aspect an angle, as it is in a trine and square aspect. For this reason, to present only five aspects is more the work of an inventor than of someone truly counting.
