116          COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO.

Why, pray tell, do they wish Saturn, whom they consider earthy, to be exalted in Libra? It would be tedious to recount other things of the same kind. Let us now return to Plotinus' conclusion. He states first, indeed, that astrologers believe each star acts on its own: but from all conspiring together, something new is moreover produced. From which it is clear that no one can clearly judge what precisely results from these. Then he indicates that astrologers do not have a method by which planets act, whatever they are said to effect. For neither does each one need its own counsel, nor all together a common counsel, to act: since natural causes below the moon are sufficient by their nature to act, and do not require any counsel beyond nature. Nor again, when the stars do these things according to the manner of nature, do they do them differently, or other things, than could be done by the tenor of nature, although they do them more excellently and produce more excellent things, namely, by a more excellent nature. Therefore, they do not produce prophets, nor miracles, which must be done by divinity: nor theologians: nor geometers, who are made by mind and art: nor the rich: nor kings: nor those twice opposed who are made or hindered by prudence, opportunity, favor, or their opposites.

Errors of astrologers concerning Saturn, Mars, and the Moon.

V In the fifth chapter of the book, he pursues and follows up on the errors of astrologers more extensively. They teach that Saturn, because he is cold, is harmful to nature, and therefore they separate him from the ascendant (as they say), the principle of life. And to separate him most from there, they foolishly place him too much in the twelfth house. Which position, although by some method of their calculation it seems most remote from the first of all, is in reality nevertheless the closest. For it is continuous with the East upwards, and whatever star ascends soon hastens into the twelfth: therefore they would have more probably placed Saturn in the seventh house as the most distant of all. But they do not even want that, lest he be opposed to those being born: but in both cases they seem to contradict themselves: for they are accustomed to accommodate both the ascendant and the beginning of the first conception to Saturn for another reason. Furthermore, they say that Saturn and Mars, both when conjoined and when opposed to each other, are harmful to us. Perhaps they would have said more correctly that in this way the coldness of Saturn is most tempered by the heat of Mars, and the fervor of the latter by the coldness of the former. They add that Saturn, if he is above the earth or near the East for those born during the day, tempered by diurnal heat, then turns out to be propitious to us. And also if he ascends thus: especially in Aquarius, he is not harmful to nature. But Mars, as being fiery, should be placed at night, or under the earth, lest he become more vehemently hot from the sun's heat. And in this, similarly, as often, they rave. For since the shadow of the earth, from which night comes, scarcely reaches as far as the moon, all the lights of all stars above the moon continuously touch each other without anything intervening: and similarly they are always in day, never truly under night. But above all, Saturn exists separated from shadow and coldness, which two are proper to the earth: so that nothing seems more absurd than to call him dark and cold. Furthermore, they are accustomed to blame the conjunction of the Moon with Saturn or Mars. Although if she approaches Saturn full of light, or Mars empty, they do not dare to condemn. For if she conjoins with Saturn full, then she cherishes him with her light, and he does not cool her when full. On the contrary, if she submits herself to Mars full, she is burned and consumed by him at the same time: if empty, she is tempered in turn and tempers him. Here too, as elsewhere, they err more boldly. First, indeed, celestial bodies, as always harmonious, never burn or cool each other: then, if that perhaps be granted, the opposite should be done. For when the Moon is full with the semicircle facing us, meanwhile she is empty with the other, and vice versa, therefore, so that that inconvenience might be avoided, they ought rather to subject her to Saturn in this way. For when she is empty to us, then she offers herself full to him, but to Mars when she is full to us, for then she shows herself empty to him. Among these things, it is expedient to note that many clauses in the Greek codex seem to have been transposed: and words often changed: these indeed I have diligently corrected to the best of my ability, relying on the office of a prophet (so to speak) rather than an interpreter. Therefore, what immediately follows in the text can admit a double meaning. For either they signify that Saturn does not greatly help us sometimes, because he is far away: and therefore the Moon is falsely, then she ought to be full towards us, so that at least she may help us. Or rather they signify that Saturn does not help the Moon, because he is far from the Moon, nor does she in turn help him if she is ever empty towards him. And therefore she ought to extend herself full to him: and then make herself sufficient to us with her half-orb towards us, although empty towards us. Likewise, although Saturn is far from us. The first meaning indeed seems to follow the words more clearly: which I fear are perverse. For it seems to agree neither with Plotinus' preceding nor subsequent sayings and opinions, but rather to contradict them.

That in heaven there is only light, and heat, and moisture: but cold and dryness are around the center: nor does anything celestial by itself bring cold, or dryness, or anything harmful to life.

VI Since heaven is closest to life, and therefore most living, and most life-giving: it must be thought that by itself and primarily it heats and moistens. For these two properly lead to life: but never by themselves do they cool or dry, which by their very nature are contrary to life. And if they contribute, they contribute in some accidental way: cold indeed lest excessive heat suddenly dissolve moisture: and dryness, lest moisture flow away too much. But these two are sufficiently supplied to us by the earth. This will moreover be confirmed from that, if what most people think is true. Just as death is nothing other than the privation of life: so cold and dryness, as deadly qualities, are nothing other than the privations of heat and moisture. Which Plotinus himself indicates elsewhere. It is also probable: just as darkness occurs at the greatest distance from heaven merely as a privation of light: so cold and dryness perhaps occur from an excessive distance from heaven due to the absence of heat and moisture. But that the whole heaven is hot is clear, because it is all fire: that it is all fire again, is shown by its sublimity, mobility, light, and heat, even if hidden, cherishing all things. But heat, being most ample in space and suffering no violence, has a familiar moisture. Indeed, in the soul of heaven there are three most powerful things: life, and intellect, and motion. For the soul is a certain life, both intellectual and mobile, and all this is one. Therefore, what is life in the soul, is heat in heaven. What again is intellect there, here is light. What finally is vital motion there, here is vital moisture. Therefore moisture is nothing other than agility (so to speak) for motion. Therefore, celestial fire can not only be called hot, but moreover moist, that is, liquid, fluid, agile, and slippery, and gentle, and pleasing: since in dryness we understand a harsh rigidity: such as even more vehement coldness brings. Wherefore nothing else in heaven is in any way similar to our qualities, except heat, moisture, light. Light, I say, is there in place of intelligence: heat there is the efficacy of life: moisture is the motion and nourishment of life. Nor is that heat felt there otherwise than as favor, fomentation, recreation, vigor: nor moisture otherwise than as augmentation, and amplification, and sweet agility. From this, these

And certain similar things are among us. Furthermore, to that humid heat and to moisture temperately hot, is somehow similar the vital spirit and heat and moisture, either manifest in animals or hidden in plants, universally implanted from heaven: from heaven, I say, implanted in all. But dryness and cold certainly happen to our things from here, not from there: dryness indeed because of the very narrowness of this place, and its dense, harsh, resistant, impacting nature, unfit for formation and motion: but cold because of the distance, both by nature from the whole heaven, and by position from the stars, the greatest possible. Therefore, as far as cold is concerned, we strongly approve Averroes saying: heavenly things bring no cold, but all bring heat: but those which are said to bring cold, are those which heat less. These things in the book 'On the Heavens', according to his and Aristotle's opinion, Abraham Avenazara calls Saturn cold, which brings heat less intense than ours. But to return to the Moon, when it decreases in light, more learned astrologers say that it does not indeed diminish the substance of humor, but rather restrains it towards the center, just as in growing it dilates, which appears in the sea, whose amplitude also dilates while the Moon seeks the middle of the sky from the East; but when it tends from the middle to the West, it flows back into narrowness. Nor meanwhile is it likely that it is so easily, so suddenly increased or decreased in substance.

Moreover, the heat of the Sun and Mars move and affect in different conditions: that of Mars, indeed, as if in a pyramid; that of the Sun, in an orb. In two, therefore, that is, in Jupiter and Venus simultaneously, the portion of humor and heat is almost equal; but since in two others, namely the Sun and Mars, heat far exceeds, why then are there three, namely Saturn, Mercury, and the Moon, in which humor exceeds? Because both heat is more efficacious than humor, and the mass of the Sun and Mars together is immense. Therefore, rightly, the operations of the two combined are balanced by the three.

So great, moreover, is the efficacy of heat on humor, that the very maker of the world willed that in the very masses of the spheres which contain the stars, humor should exceed heat by a balanced proportion: so that at least by a portion, as if by weight, humor might equalize its nature to the efficacy of heat. For this reason, therefore, all spheres above the earth are called waters, and just as the sea is water and liquid to the earth, so air is humor to the sea; so the Moon's circuit is liquid to the air; so the higher ones seem to relate to this and to each other in succession, so that the higher always nourish and happily sustain the lower.

Therefore, stars neither arrange the smallest earthly things by design, otherwise they would be miserable with such great solicitude: nor by natural condition do they immediately descend from their most common nature to the most distinct things. ...portents are not judged as causes. Similarly, the face of the sky can be a book, in which figures divinely written present future events, but do not act: especially if, by considering celestial bodies, those things are foreknown which cannot happen by the tenor of that corporeal nature, namely, certain dignities and depressions of men at certain times, discoveries of treasures, thoughts of counsels, and changes of our own fortunes and those of our people. Fourth indication: If, through the present constitution of the stars, either immense crimes or proper works of divinity are portended, it will be said much more probably that the stars rather declare both, than that, when they are best, they commit the worst, or when they are bodies, they make incorporeal things: and that they effect things which are either against or above corporeal nature. Fifth indication: The questions that are daily asked of astrologers, whether about past events, "have such things happened?", or about future events, "will they happen?", or about present events, "are they happening?", concerning matters both foreign to us and far distant, confirm that whatever is answered from the present hour of interrogation is not answered by cause, but by sign. The foregoing is again confirmed by this, that of all things that happen to us or are done by us, we find manifest and sufficient causes within ourselves, in the proper nature of our kind, in custom, affection, counsel, action, and the concurrence of surrounding causes, nor does anything ever happen from heaven without these causes: so that there is no need to scrutinize the causes of these things in heaven, which are often evident on earth, and yet are not found in heaven. But if we grant that the present figures of the sky always do something in us hourly, we will say that it pertains only to bodily affections and first impulses. And this indeed is of little moment, if it is acted upon by a momentary cause: Again, it is received according to its own nature, and changed to our own, as it were, stronger (principles). From the fact that the constitution of the stars signifies, but does not effect, whatever it signifies, the proper action of divinity, and nature, and art is confirmed. Therefore, whether the conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn portends a new religion, nevertheless, a true religion can be perfected by God in the meantime, or a false one invented by man: or if, through celestial movements, things that happen below the Moon are sometimes designated by nature, nevertheless nature makes such things, and effects them by the tenor of nature: or if human actions are portended by the same movements, they nevertheless proceed by human counsel and according to our free will, and signs sometimes become vain, when the efficient cause changes the signifying cause within itself. Therefore, what Plotinus and Origen say, that the letters of future events are, as it were, written in the sky either from the beginning and gradually unfolded, or perpetually written, they understand to mean the stars, and figures both formed from stars and imaginary ones: Likewise, the degrees and minute parts of the signs: finally, the aspects and movements of plants, and whatever follows or accompanies these everywhere. You, however, understand the whole sky here. For the sky is everywhere: and Timaeus calls the whole (universe) sky. Indeed, above the Moon, just as the causes of inferior things are common, so too are the common signs: but below the Moon are proper causes, by knowing which the common signs are derived into proper indications, and all this exists as if it were the body of a single animal. Therefore, in this mundane animal, one must look around at all things both above and below the Moon, and weigh them against each other. For just as there are diverse agents among themselves, both above and below, and sometimes superior to inferior: so too are signs often diverse among themselves everywhere: just as in any animal there are both natures contrary to each other, and diverse members, and signs repugnant in some to others. Therefore, Rafis commands the physiognomist not to believe one sign, but to comprehend all, and weigh them against each other: and where they are contrary, to follow the more numerous and more certain ones. The same should be observed by one who divines from the world in the world: whom Aristotle, in the book "On Sleep and Waking," admonishes to be cautious in judging with these words: "Often there are signs in bodies, even from heaven, like those of rains and winds, yet the signified event does not occur, when another, more vehement motion happens." Therefore, Origen and Porphyry took away such divination from men, granting it to demons, to whom that celestial book to be read is open. I say, not to all demons equally: for Porphyry, in his book "On Oracles," after proving that whatever fatal events the gods announce through oracles, they predict by observation of the stars, adds that the gods also often lie, and that an exquisite knowledge of future events is not only uncertain for men, but also for many of the gods: and for those gods to whom it can become known, it is not fully perceived at every hour. Thus, therefore, it is pleasing to arrange demons, as far as the present is concerned. Ethereal demons, inhabiting the higher air, contemplate celestial rather than terrestrial portents: but watery demons, inhabiting the lowest air, hunt for arguments of things more from our (terrestrial) realm than from celestial ones: Finally, the middle ones more conveniently observe signs on both sides: therefore, they are much more suitable for prophecy among us. And from these, Origen says, men have sometimes received premonitions: yet whether they received them from these, or learned them by observation, they see confusedly, and wander in a certain fog.

For many reasons, judgment about future events is most difficult.

That neither man nor demon can discern the minutest things among us by the mere inspection of celestial bodies, we argue in this way: Just as any celestial nature is more common than any terrestrial nature: so any motion of the sky is more common than any terrestrial motion. there is a harmony, and he judges such a harmony to exist in the world itself, in the spheres, in the stars: For everywhere the intellectual soul governs the body through a life closer to the body, flowing from the soul. For inasmuch as it is intellectual, seeking separate and higher things, it is too distant from the body: but it approaches the body through something which, in or from itself, already degenerates from the intellect. I say "from itself": because if an elemental nature, like fire, approaching a subject not only applies its substance to it but also inserts some quality similar to itself, much more does the soul, as a more powerful nature, by the presence of its vital substance, infuse a certain vital faculty into the body. Let there be therefore in the world, in the spheres, in the stars, twin souls everywhere: Let the first hold the place of good angels and gods everywhere: but let the subsequent ones be judged to play the role of angels who fell into bodies, and of demons: All angels accompany such a first, that is, the angel of the mundane soul, always adhering to God. Angels again incline mostly towards incorporeal things, demons towards corporeal things, and they attract souls. Therefore, angels free souls from fate: but demons bind them to fate. In demons is placed the proximate dominion of this corporeal world. Hence it happens that if a comparison is made from here to angels, this world is rightly said to be placed in evil. From this, too, the error of the Manicheans easily arose. Therefore, just as he asserts our intellect always to be engaged with divine things, although reason is meanwhile occupied with human things: so he affirms that reason and the entire higher soul in celestial beings enjoy perpetual contemplation of divine things, while the lower souls of celestial beings govern bodies, and imagine bodies. In these, therefore, he judges the affections to be demonic. Indeed, divine affections are primary: human affections are in us, and often bestial: but what kind are the demonic ones there? Imagine a wise person constantly engaged in divine contemplations: but in him meanwhile, in his vegetative nature, an affection for bodily nourishment thrives, sometimes a craving of hunger creeps into the stomach, natural procreative desire titillates: but the reason of the wise mind, meanwhile dedicated to separate things, by no means perceives such affections: and imagination too barely feels them stupidly: almost as it usually happens in one in whom these things are excited in sleep almost without dreams: such, therefore, are the demonic affections for these things in heaven. Therefore, nothing evil or vile proceeds from the prior souls: but from the subsequent ones, not truly evil things, but certain vile and less good things follow: inasmuch as from them, sometimes less orderly changes occur in bodies, and frequently incitements arise in souls enslaved to the body by nature, through which, even if souls do not necessarily become wicked, they nevertheless indulge more freely in bodily incitements, or at least foster the body more readily and care for it more diligently daily. But he says that the higher souls of the stars are not parts of this universe: For since they are entirely turned towards the intellectual world, they seem rather to be able to be called parts of that. But he calls the lower souls of the stars parts of this universe, because they are enslaved to the bodies of the world, which, since they are made of the same matter among themselves and under the same common form of the whole, are considered parts of the universe. In this common matter and form of the world, therefore, all such souls conspire everywhere in one work, both among themselves and with the soul of the world, and communicate with each other through a common, though hidden, sense and a certain latent compassion. Then, whatever works are done by them, they exist as individual parts of the world, or pertain to parts and the whole. But nothing proceeds from them anywhere that is separate from the natural condition of this world: but whatever they do, they do almost by animal nature, just as elements by elemental nature, and plants and animals by vegetative nature, with absolutely no choice. For since choice is different from life, and life is posterior, if the life of inferiors accomplishes its own things by itself without the function of choice, much more does the life of superiors accomplish its own things entirely by itself. But if there is any intellectual and rational choice there, it chooses not indeed this ministry, but a higher office. And perhaps even before that choice, something proceeds internally from a prior life without choice: but entirely without any necessity of counsel, even if some imagination accompanies the work, and from the first soul there proceeds a second, and from the second similarly a singular power in the body, and from the body light, and in the light a power generating and governing lower things. Therefore, what is generated and happens daily in this world is distant by many degrees from the intelligible world, so it should not seem strange that these things of ours do not turn out to be most orderly or most fortunate. For such things would succeed if they were done directly by the divine intellect, or at least by intellectual souls: but now they are done from bodies living by an irrational soul, and through powers emanating from bodies. If, therefore, anything occurs in the world that is troublesome, laborious, that you do not approve of, remember that all of it happens to us from the "woman," that is, from the soul enslaved to the body, from the matter of the body, and again from the contrariety of elemental qualities.

XII. The twelfth chapter shows that various influences coming from heaven converge into one among us, although differently elsewhere; and from this confluence, whatever is generated under it carries something away. Indeed, what is born is commonly aided towards birth by the common favor of heaven; but for a human or a horse to be born, it does not derive from a common influx, which favors all equally, nor does it obtain it from this or that specific influx. For under any [celestial configuration], humans and horses are born equally. Therefore, a human comes into being because he is born from a human, and a horse because it is made from a horse: but for a human to be such, like sanguine or choleric, more or less beautiful, tall, or short, and the rest: partly indeed they seem to have from heaven, but certainly very much from parents: which Ptolemy confesses, compelled by the effect. Hence he forbids judging about the born from the sole consideration of celestial things: but he commands diligently to consider the nature of its parents, nourishment, and place, and custom. I omit for now how much variety the imagination of the generators brings to their children. Certainly, for the very property of substance and natural quality, the nature of both the species and the individual generator is much more potent than celestial influx: which manifest experience teaches in all things, especially from the very resemblance by which the offspring reflects the species and person of the generator. Therefore, common and celestial causes have very great authority concerning the most common conditions: but proximate and proper causes can undoubtedly do much more concerning proper ones: especially since what is brought from superior causes is received according to the nature of the subject and place, and according to the determination of proximate causes, and is transmuted into another form. Hence Ptolemy says, with Aristotle also testifying, that celestial effects can be changed due to the matter and nature of inferior things, and do not inevitably occur. Therefore, a human is made as if from a cause, from the seminal reason of a human, which is indeed in the soul and proper nature, and is governed under the ideal reason of a human, which, being active in the common nature and soul, is finally governed by the idea of the divine mind itself. But while a human is conceived from the very power of the seed, in the meantime, either from heaven, or from proximate or surrounding matter, some impediment or aid can be brought, by which the one to be born receives either a worse or a more perfect quality. Nevertheless, it mostly comes forth similar to the generator, always in species, and frequently in person. But since an impediment can arise either from heaven or from matter, that which happens from matter is much greater: for it often produces certain defects. But the greatest [impediment] is that which arises from imagination: for this usually produces monsters. If, therefore, a greater impediment comes from matter, and place, and causes surrounding us, then undoubtedly aid also primarily comes from here: and absolutely no celestial influx, but the seminal reason possesses the authority of generating: for even where living beings seem to arise spontaneously under the Sun and moisture, they necessarily arise from the seminal virtue which the life of the world possesses: which we declare more broadly in Theology.

**From the common life of the world and its seminal reasons, and simultaneously from the proper reasons of each thing, all things are generated. Likewise, besides the common action of the world's soul, there are proper actions in most things: but the influxes of celestial motions seem to approach as if from outside.**

XIII. Since he had already descended to the causes of things, both common and proper, therefore in the thirteenth chapter of the book he duly pursues the principles of things. Just as, therefore, in every living being, so in the world as a very great animal, the whole body is formed under the form of the whole by the seminal reason, which is in the vegetative virtue of the soul, and by natural and vital spirit; and the members are formed by the proper forms of the members, and individual parts are conformed, both by mutual communion among themselves and by relation to the form and end of the whole. Since, therefore, all things are formally contained in the very form of the whole, but in the forms of individual things, other things are not formally comprehended, although they seem to be present by a certain participation, deservedly whatever is done or acts or suffers in the world, as its own familiar property, conduces to its good: yet not everything that comes from one part to another part comes equally as domestic. For what comes from one part of the world to a part distant either by situation or nature, seems to offend as something more alien: what comes otherwise, to aid. But all things, whatever they do to each other, always, besides what they consist of in themselves, or what they do by their own faculty, undoubtedly conspire everywhere towards the common spirit of the whole life. Therefore, distinguish concerning agents thus: Those things in this living body of the world which, besides a certain small trace of common life, possess no proper life, are not properly agents, but instruments of agents, namely of the world itself and of the principal parts of the world. Nor is this unjust: for natural action depends on motion: but the principle of motion is life. For life, just as it is the first, innermost, perpetual motion of essence, so it is the principle of any motion, and thus it is also the origin of natural action. Therefore, for those lacking proper life, motion and proper action are certainly absent: where they seem to act, they are acted upon. Thus, heavy and light things, and things that heat, and similar things are drawn to motions and actions by the very life of the world, no differently than iron is drawn by a magnet, and heat or humor in an animal is led and drawn by vital virtue. But those things which, beyond the common life of the world, have obtained some gift of proper life, these seem to have something of their own motion and action, as it were. But distinguish these living things: Since the principle of motion is inherent in all living things, I say, indifferent to motions differing among themselves, it is either determined to a certain condition of motion by another, or rather from itself. By another, indeed, plants, namely by universal nature and by a certain daily need, opportunity, occasion, and concurrence of surrounding causes. Again by another, namely brute animals, by the encounter of things perceived, while they impel the imagination here or there, serving moreover the necessity of nature. But the rational animal often defines the innermost principle of its motion to certain movements by its own notion conceived by itself and by choice: and the more intelligence advances, the more it is counted in the order of agents, and is separated from patients. But both kinds of animals, namely those having reason and those lacking reason, as certain parts of the world, conduce to the glory of the world. Again, distinguish animals thus: Celestial and ethereal animals are said simply to act rather than to suffer: but brute animals have very little action, and very much passion (suffering). But aerial daemons and humans hold almost a middle ground between action and passion. From these three kinds of animals, the glory and function of the mundane animal are fulfilled. And the highest genus indeed stands in the world as intelligence in us: but the middle as reason, whether universal or particular, in us: finally, the lowest as

But everywhere in the universe, the higher souls of the spheres and stars offer things more excellent to the universe than the lower souls of the same, and are called by Plato colleagues of Jupiter, that is, of the mundane intelligence. But absolutely everything that exists anywhere in the world lives in a certain way, either by its own life or by a common life, no less than whatever is in any animal. They live, I say, and all things become living according to life, I mean corporeal life: principally by some benefit of the mundane soul, in whose seminal reason all reasons of living things are contained: And everywhere the seminal reason active in the soul, both in the common soul and in any particular one, is the principal origin of motion and generation, and of formation. For the fact that certain special virtues are inherent in things, which cannot be referred to elemental causes, this simply arises from the confluence of many things: otherwise they would happen by chance, or would not be firm. But of this elsewhere. Let us return to the soul. We are accustomed to argue that the rational soul is an essence, namely a form

...its being and existing in itself completely and beautifully, is contained in the reasons by itself, and properly proceeds from them: whatever, however, happens to be deformed, that seems to arise first from unformed matter, or consequently from those things which are infected by it. But what does he mean by saying that "the defects of things are contained in the reasons not according to act, but according to potency"? Certainly not according to act, because defects are not produced from them: because there is no proper form of defect there, but it is said to exist there at least according to potency: because from the complete form, as from an exemplar, it can be conjectured in what way, or to what degree, something can deviate from it. Therefore, whatever things are evil or less good, can indeed be foreknown there, but cannot be predestined. For whatever is determined from there, is defined by form: but what comes from there, does not emerge in matter as it is possessed by the soul: but also because it is external, it degenerates: and because it is in unformed matter, it becomes deformed, and again is confused by the mixture of diverse things. The soul therefore acts through reasons as far as things correspond in beauty to the reasons, although it can also conceive further, that is, deformity, generally by intelligence, but specifically by reason, or by a certain imagination joined to nature: but in it too, not so much by discoursing through particulars, as summarily. He says here too that forms in matter deviate from the forms of nature by a certain shock, that is, partly because they seem to depart from the reasons, partly because they become deformed by unformed matter, partly because they are mixed with opposites, partly because they gradually degenerate from their pristine dignity: Plotinus says in earlier works that natural things gradually degenerate through the ages, and Plato in the Politicus, Protagoras, Critias, Menexenus: and we have assigned the causes there, and here we assign them briefly. Some degeneration of things is more enduring, extending from the beginning of the cosmic cycle even to its end: some is long-lasting, less so, persevering from one great terrestrial illusion to another. Consider therefore the twelve signs which in the firmament appear to be subject to the twelve signs marked in the ninth sphere: which sphere Plato, although he did not explicitly posit it, nevertheless thought could exist: inasmuch as he does not deny its possibility. So once the signs corresponded everywhere to the signs: Aries to Aries, Taurus to Taurus, Gemini to Gemini, Cancer to Cancer, Leo to Leo, Virgo to Virgo, Libra to Libra, Scorpio to Scorpio, Sagittarius to Sagittarius, Capricorn to Capricorn, Aquarius to Aquarius, and finally Pisces to Pisces. Then it was a happy omen for the age of ages, happy as long as the same things corresponded to the same. But then Aries transgressed Aries by a motion towards the east, and the remaining signs consequently transgressed. Meanwhile, natural things began to degenerate in a similar degree. Although in some ages they also seem able to regain something of their pristine vigor for a time: when these signs, even if not precisely the same as those, at least come to similar ones. Aries to Leo, or at least to Gemini: or Leo to Sagittarius, or to Libra: Gemini to Libra, or Libra to Aquarius, and the rest similarly: or at least aspects arise there which Astronomers report to be more concordant. Meanwhile, certain great conjunctions of planets contribute, although it also happens that they sometimes harm in turn. Similarly, the motion of the images towards the south and their recession, restored over many centuries, contributes to the changes of things: but things will not recover their pristine happiness until the same things return to the same. Indeed, the motion of the signs manifest to us, tending towards the east, passes one degree of the superior signs in a hundred years. Thus, the age of ages will be completed in thirty-six thousand years. Meanwhile, another change of the age occurs, when the earth is either diluted by an illusion of waters, or devastated by a conflagration of flames. So whether after the waters the sun's powerful heat presses upon the humors: or after the fires, in turn, a shower overflows, the earth soon, more fertile with both heat and moisture, gives birth to most beautiful things, until, becoming more barren day by day due to dryness, it gives birth to less beautiful things, and at last, for the sake of remedy, a similar flood or conflagration returns. Remember, however, that the motions and positions of celestial bodies pertain not so much to the generation of forms itself, which properly occurs through seminal reasons, as to the matter to be disposed in one way or another. The third cause of degeneration pertains especially to human affairs: that in the very newness of the world, whether it becomes new through creation, or appears to be made new through prior destruction, humans are governed by the diligent providence of superior deities, as if by shepherds. For being weak and naked by nature, and unskilled in art, they utterly need the guidance of superiors. Providence, however, never abandons its own in necessary matters. Hence it happens that nature also does not fail in necessary things. Therefore, in the body of an animal, nature works harder for the greater necessity of any member. Therefore, human affairs once proceeded entirely correctly and divinely for a long time, indeed more divinely: but when human ingenuity, sufficiently cultivated by time, seemed to need less of the constant solicitude of daemons, it began to be governed more negligently by daemons, or rather angels: whence human affairs daily slide into worse conditions, until the human disease, incurable by itself, provokes the necessary care of the divine. By what reason, however, the world is continuously more beautiful even from various degrees of degeneration or from some deformity of its parts, we have sufficiently said elsewhere and will say.

The seminal reasons of nature are not notions, although they are made in nature by the mind. Likewise, they degenerate in nature first from the mind: then in matter they fail from nature.
Again, what the mundane animal will be like, if considered with reason removed.

XVII. The seminal reasons, however, just as in any soul, are not certain notions: otherwise, by knowing, they would continuously generate, and by generating, they would know: so neither in the soul of the universe, whose life is any more efficacious life, and therefore by the simple virtue of life it can generate without the aid of notion. Firstly, indeed, reasons of this kind do not exist for intelligence: for intelligence separates itself, and, if necessary, the thing to be understood, from matter. But an efficacious force, such as that of natural seed, since it is only to be generated in matter, first attacks matter and penetrates deeply into it. Secondly, they are not ratiocinations: for these are, as it were, accidental and imaginary, and therefore cannot make substantial and vital things. They are accustomed to making things in the manner of art, from outside and with the aid of external instruments, and certain imaginary things: but seminal reasons act intrinsically, and through themselves and through instruments joined in the manner of any nature, and they make substances. Furthermore, they are not imaginations: for these, as appears in us, effect nothing in the body without the efficacy of affection: moreover, affection is not sufficient for imagination to generate forms, but perhaps for local motion. For from imagination strengthened by affection, local motion immediately occurs in the spirit and heart. From this motion, subsequently, qualities which have long been in the body now

--- Page 179 ---
IN BOOK III. ENNEAD II. 135

...are now excited, whence they moreover produce either another quality or a passion. Similarly, in the soul of the world, imagination does not primarily generate the forms of things, since it itself seems to be something more imaginary even than ratiocination: but when joined with affection, it leads to the local motion of the world: before which motion, the forms of things already exist in the world, having been generated there long ago, namely, by the generative power of the world through seminal reasons. Therefore, from reasons of this kind infused into this nature, the primary forms of things are procreated in the world: but subsequently, from imaginations contemplating individual things to be generated, through motions, as it were, individual, daily motions, and individual ones occur, by which the forms of things are stirred to mutual alteration: by this perpetual alteration, matter everywhere is duly prepared daily to receive new forms from the reasons. Therefore, in the soul, imagination and nature are companions; similarly, in the universe, alteration and generation are always companions. Nor unjustly does nature, the generatrix of particulars, accompany imagination, and vice versa, which (imagination) disperses itself through particulars, yet not closely reason, which ultimately retreats to universals; nor intelligence, which always perseveres in universals. And if intelligence or reason perceives particulars, it consequently acts thus: but especially, it has in the meantime a zeal for universals. Therefore, generation or alteration and motion, which pertains only to particulars, seems to be immediately close to imagination after nature, concerning itself only and especially with particulars. But since generation is entirely concerned with matter, if we are to find the power that immediately generates, we are compelled to descend below any cognitive power. For any cognitive power has the form and action by which it knows separated from matter. Just as therefore that which is light at its highest, and splendor in its middle, becomes heat at its lowest, and generates as heat, not as splendor, nor as light: so in the soul, which exists as intellectual at its highest, but discursive in its middle, and finally merely vital and vivifying at its lowest, it generates and vivifies not as intellectual, nor as discursive, but as vital. And if it does things, and meanwhile knows them, it is not because it knows, but because it is so constituted and is naturally affected in such a way, that it therefore does such things. Indeed, I said not because it knows, I mean by some cognition beyond its essence: for in its very highest part, to understand is the same as to be; and therefore, by this essential and vital intelligence, through essential and ideal notions, it naturally produces forms, that is, seminal reasons, in nature, just as nature shapes forms in matter through them. Just as therefore from a circle, which is made by the throwing of a pebble into water, another circle immediately arises, and then similarly: so from a certain orb of the ideal divine mind, a nearly similar orb depends in the mind of the world-soul: and from here, soon into nature, and from nature similarly into matter. Therefore, for the formulae impressed by the soul's intelligence into the generative nature of the soul to be essential and efficacious, and to produce substantial things, it is necessary for the forms, both in the divine mind and also in the soul's mind, to exist in such an essential way that there, to understand is the same as to be: and also to understand that by understanding, nature is formed, just as in nature to be is the same as to live, and in a certain way, to vivify matter is the same as to live. But the question is asked, Does the animal intelligence form nature by some rational or imaginative discourse, as an artisan often forms matter? By no means: for even the most perfect art does not consult further, but now acts in the manner of nature which it already attains, having imitated it as far as it could. Moreover, if it were to decide to form nature by some discursive thought, it would already have referred the forms to be produced to others as a firm exemplar and spectacle, upon which the gaze of wandering reason might be fixed, around which a stable discourse might be conducted, and to which it might compare its findings. Therefore, the question is asked, Does it perceive certain external spectacles, or does it have such firm forms within itself? Not external and corporeal ones (for these do not yet exist, being, I mean, still to be generated by nature, by nature still to be formed by intellect); therefore, it possesses forms within itself. But that which is possessed intrinsically and naturally is not to be sought by wandering. Therefore, if nature continuously forms matter without any ministry of counsel, much more does the mind form nature joined to itself without counsel, and vice versa. Conclude that discourse itself, through momentary acts, is everywhere something beyond essence, and an accidental something like flashes of lightning: subsequently, while it appears in parts, it suddenly vanishes, and thus cannot by itself make firm and substantial things, but for the production of such things, the firm and essential efficacy of another nature is needed. Thus, not by solicitude, not by labor, but by tireless ease, both natural things will sprout from nature itself, and the seeds of nature will sprout from intelligence. Conclude again: just as in heaven, native light and most stable warmth remain, while configurations change daily by their circuit: so in the life of the world, intelligence and nature remain in their reasons, and effectively produce through them stably, even if any universal or particular discourse is conducted there.

But since the second soul of the world, that is, a certain life irrational in itself, attributed to the mundane body by the intellectual soul of the world, is the ultimate trace of divine things, and similarly possesses seeds as certain ultimate traces of ideas, it is clear that the world, composed of this life and body, degenerates far from divinity: and often its seeds seem to be impeded in their work, and such an animal, when compared to higher things, will appear imperfect. For although this mundane animal can be called gentle and blessed by a certain perpetual presence of its intellectual soul, nevertheless, since this animal is different from and posterior to the intellectual soul, it is permissible to conceive the soul itself as separated from the animal. which Plato considered in the *Statesman*, in the *Timaeus*, and in the *Laws*. Come now, tell me, what would this vast and most robust animal soon be like if the bridle of intelligence were removed? Indeed, iron, even if now fiery, and air, even if now luminous, we can nevertheless call naturally cold and dark: for iron soon clearly declares its coldness, and air its darkness. In such a condition, Plotinus seems to portray this mundane animal as if it were fierce. Imagine also, if you please, a wise man, with a body excessively choleric or melancholic; examine the disposition of the body, and you will see this animal, restrained as if by reins under a wise soul, acting calmly and appearing gentle, but meanwhile most ready for anger and sorrow: and if it were sanguine, prone to lust, which affection, though scarcely indicated while awake, it reveals more easily in dreams: imagine a mundane animal almost like this, from fire as if from bile, prone to wrath and pride; from earth as if from black bile, more inclined to sorrow; from air as if from blood, to wantonness and lust; from water as if from phlegm, more prone to sluggishness; from prime matter, which is like a certain dregs settling beneath natural things, it will appear to you bitter and sharp alike. For dregs are considered both bitter and acidic due to their dryness and coldness. Therefore, this animal will appear at times most fierce from its greater powers, and at times destitute from matter, and too pusillanimous, and envious, and querulous about its own utility and changeability. Finally, you will cease to wonder that from an animal so affected, in which not all things are as desired, many things also happen to others contrary to their desire.

Whence evils: whence all things: three artificers under the good of the whole: four of the world.

XVIII In the last chapter of the book, first, he briefly pursues the cause of evils arising from the preceding discussions. m 2

--- Page 180 ---
136 COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO.
then he comprehends the causes of the universe. The cause of evils, however, is considered in two ways: one by reason of consequence, the other by reason of end. For just as a lesser good follows a greater good, and again, the least good follows the lesser in a long order: so also evils happen to the least. Moreover, just as in a musical harmony the fourth voice, indeed even the second and seventh, which would not be consonant by themselves, together with the consonant voices create a more pleasing harmony: so in the order of things, lesser goods with greater ones, least goods with lesser ones, and evils with the least goods, render the common good of the whole more admirable. What then? That what seem evil in this or for this, you will find to be good in that or for that; finally, all things lead to the common good of the universe. After this, he posits three artificers of the world. The first, indeed, the divine intellect: but the second, the animal intellect and the intellectual soul: the third, the image of this soul, that is, life, thence dedicated to the body. In this matter, Proclus being witness, Porphyry agrees with Plotinus. But why does he not call the Good itself an artificer? Because in an artificer there are exemplars of works. But in the Good itself, since it is the most simple unity, he does not dare to place the exemplar of the world, which is manifold: but Plato and Plotinus name the Good itself both the father of the mundane artificer and the end of the mundane work: as if the son, pregnant with love for the paternal good, creates the world by the grace of the good, and conforms it to the good. Therefore, the Good itself generates the intellectual world: but this procreates the animal (world): this similarly (procreates) the natural (world): but the natural (world procreates) the corporeal. But one flows forth from another almost as a circle in water depends on a circle: and just as light comes from light, splendor from light, heat from splendor, generation from heat. Indeed, the Intellect, in procreating the intellectual soul, in no way departs from the father: nay, through its conjunction with the father, it has the power and act of creation. Similarly, the intellectual soul, insofar as it leans upon the supreme intellect, overflows from it and pours forth into another (soul). The other (soul) in turn, that is, corporeal life, insofar as it depends on the soul whose image it is, is filled with seeds, and at the same time fills the matter of this world with forms. Indeed, the Good itself transcends stability: for stability exists in the Good and by the grace of the Good: but the intellect itself exists as stability: the intellectual soul is judged to be the first stable (entity). But life, the image of this (soul), is indeed stable insofar as it exists from it, but accidentally mobile, insofar as it is coupled to the body, which is properly mobile. But Plotinus properly calls such life the seminal world: which the ancients called an image, which is always engaged in assimilation. For this is called not so much a soul, as an image of the soul. For as much as it approaches matter, alien from the intellectual source, so much does it degenerate from the intellectual soul. Also, the seeds in it are not so much reasons (rational principles) as images of reasons. For if reason properly consists according to form in the intellectual soul, then deservedly in the lower life it is only an image of reason. For who would call that true reason which, ignorant of itself, has no account of itself? This life, therefore, is a certain image, full only of images: this image has always attained the likeness of the exemplar, and always attains it. Again, it is always formed, and is perpetually being formed, by which reason, the very acts of the seeds seem to flourish differently at different times: yet they always correspond to the exemplar: by which, again, life is revolved, as it were, together with the body of the world: by which, finally, simultaneously with the celestial revolution, the mind is affected and imagines differently and differently, and externally is always clothed, as it were, in other figures. Perhaps Plotinus also, with these words, touches upon the opinion of Heraclitus and Timaeus, who say that this world, manifest to our eyes, never *is* in a fixed state, but is perpetually *becoming*. But entirely, just as water is shaped under a seal, and the shape does not remain when the seal is removed: and therefore the shape seems not so much to have been made once, as to be always being made, especially if the water continuously flows beneath: so almost does matter relate to nature, and nature in turn to the soul fertile with intellect. Plotinus wishes this world to be *made* or to *be* only insofar as the image of the soul flows from the soul, and the soul proceeds from the mind, and the mind is generated from the Good, and finally the Good, as long as it is that very thing which is the Good: and the intellect, as long as it is that very thing which is the intellect. With these (higher principles) thus remaining, the subsequent things naturally either always remain or flow forth from them, just as light from the sun, and thereafter light from light.

But we, concerning these matters, can say according to religion: If we consider eternity in divine things, then the procession of the world from there would rightly be seen as eternal: but if (we consider) will, the world proceeds to that limit which the divine will has decreed, by whose judgment, just as there is a limit of virtue and magnitude in the world, so also there is a beginning and an end.

Whether the stars have any agency.

**T**HE motion of the stars
around each thing does in-
deed signify future events,
but does not cause everything,
as many believe; we have elsewhere
stated this, bringing forward some arguments:
but it must now be discussed in the present with more exact and numerous arguments. For it is not of little importance to hold this or that opinion about these matters. Many astrologers relate that the planets, by their motions, cause not only other things such as poverty and riches, and health, whether prosperous or adverse, but also base and beautiful things, and, what is greatest, even vices and virtues. Likewise, individual actions arising from them in individual times, just as if they were angry against men, namely in those cases where men themselves inflict no injury: inasmuch as they are such as they have been constituted by the planets. They add, moreover, that the planets bring about what are called good things, not because they love those who are to receive them, but because they themselves, according to the diversity of their motion and place, either well or

A   FIRST, it must be considered whether the
    heavenly bodies are animate or the opposite. For if

    Therefore, they will only extend their actions and

    For those things do not happen to them which cause

Just as in one living being from one principle, who can infer different things from different members? For indeed, who can also infer character, or even dangers and the avoidance of dangers, by rightly considering either the eyes or other parts of the body? Indeed, these are parts of our body, and we are also parts of the world. Therefore, some things serve others. But all things are full of signs, and a wise person infers one thing from another. And many things, customary daily, are known to all. What then is the mutual order of all things? For thus it is consistent that presage is valid in auguries, and indeed also in other animals from which we presage individual things. Therefore, it is necessary that all things are ordered together and depend successively. For not only does one harmony prevail in any of those things which are best connected, but much more and primarily in the universe. Where it is necessary that from one principle the manifold animal itself becomes one, one, I say, constituted from all. And just as in each individual thing, every part has its own work, so also in the universe, individual things obtain individual works; and much more so because these are not only parts, but also wholes and greater things. Therefore, each thing proceeds from one principle, performing its own proper function, while other things everywhere contribute to others. For nothing anywhere is separated from the very form of the whole; and they act upon each other and are acted upon; and something comes to each thing, by which it is either helped or hindered. But they do not proceed randomly, nor as it happens; for something else is produced from these, and something else naturally follows in succession, and something else results.

Now indeed, the soul also, while beginning to perform its own proper function (for the soul does all things, having the nature of a principle), proceeds mostly rightly. But if, led by other things, it deviates, it follows by a certain judgment the course of those things which are produced in the world, unless perhaps it is released. For the judgment itself always remains, since the universe is ruled and directed by the order and power of the dominant (principle). The stars serve this and contribute to it, as not insignificant parts of the sky, both for the beautiful form of the whole and also for the function of signification. Therefore, they portend all things whatsoever that arise in the sensible world, but they clearly do whatever other things they do. But we perform the works of the soul according to nature, as long as we do not stray or err in the very multitude of the whole. But straying, we pay the penalty to judgment, namely, both the error itself and a certain worse fate that will come to us in the future. Therefore, how about riches, virtues, and vices? Virtues indeed are due to that which is older and more excellent in the soul; but vices arise from a certain interaction of the soul with external things. But concerning these things, it has been said elsewhere.

This (spindle) the Fates and Necessity, mother of the Fates, twist with him, and they revolve it in the generation of each individual.

--- Page 186 ---
142 PLOTINUS ENNEAD. II.

Whatever is born proceeds into generation through this circuit and revolution. In the Timaeus also, God, the craftsman of the world, hands over the principle of the soul itself: but the gods who are borne along apply grave and necessary passions, angers, desires, pleasures, pains, and another kind of soul, from which such disturbances arise. These words of Plato certainly seem to bind us to the stars, receiving souls, that is, from them: and likewise subject us, falling hither, to necessity.

He also says that we have morals from these same (stars), and according to these morals, actions and passions proceeding from a certain passive disposition. Therefore, it must be inquired what else we are besides this. Perhaps, indeed, what remains is what we truly are: to whom nature has also given the power to dominate passions. For besides the fact that we are surrounded by these evils due to the very nature of the body, God has bestowed virtue entirely free from servitude. For we do not need virtue when placed in a safe state, but when, in the absence of virtue, danger threatens in evils.

Therefore, it is necessary to flee from here, and to separate ourselves from those things which are joined to us in generation: and effort must be made, lest perhaps we are that very composite, namely the animated body: in which the nature of the body prevails more, having acquired a certain trace of the soul, so much so that the common life itself is primarily of the body. For whatever belongs to this are corporeal. But the ascent to the other soul, which exists externally, pertains to the sublime, namely to the beautiful and divine, over which nothing anywhere dominates: indeed, the mind uses its powers to escape that very thing: and lives according to this very thing when it withdraws into itself. But whoever is devoid of a soul thus constituted, now lives in fate. In this state of life, the stars not only signify to man, but he himself also becomes as a part of the universe, and not unjustly serves the whole of which he is a part.

For everyone is twofold: partly indeed comprehending both (the composite and the true self) within himself, partly indeed existing as what he is. The whole world also is partly indeed a composite something from body and a certain soul enslaved to the body, but partly indeed the very soul of the whole, which is not in the body, but impresses certain traces upon that which lies in the body. The Sun also and the other (heavenly bodies) are similarly twofold. And the one soul, which is pure, brings forth nothing evil or base: but those things which are made by them through the universe, insofar as they are parts of the universe, namely both because they are body, and because they are animated body, proceed as certain parts: meanwhile, with the choice of the star and its true soul looking towards what is best. But the other things follow from this very thing: indeed, not so much from this very thing as from those things which are around it, just as many things are made from fire by heat diffused everywhere from it: and if anything flows from one soul into another related to it. But troublesome or difficult and adverse things are born in the world because of a certain mixture: for the nature of this world is mixed: and if one somehow separates its separable soul from it, one will see that what remains is not great. For the world is only then truly a god, if that separable soul is counted in its substance. For what remains is a daemon, whom Plato called a great daemon: and the affections in it are also daemonic.

**A** If this is the case, then a significance must now also be granted: but effects seem to be conceded neither entirely, nor to their wholes, but only to the extent that something of them remains. Again, it must be admitted that the soul, even before it comes into generation, slips down, bringing something from itself; for it would not descend into a body unless it possessed something passive, and indeed something immense. It must be admitted that fortunes befall the soul entering the body, namely, this very thing, that it enters according to the course of the universe.
**B** Finally, it must be admitted that the course of the world thus brings it about that it contributes simultaneously in its operation, and fulfills from itself what must be accomplished by the universe; since those things which are in the very course of the universe obtain the order of parts.

**XI**
**C** Nor indeed should it escape us that what comes from celestial beings does not turn out to be entirely the same in those things which receive it, as that which proceeds from the higher beings. Just as if fire in us, degenerating far from the celestial fire, and an affection prone to love, having become weaker among us, produced a love that is not honorable; so spirit, when it happens to exceed the measure necessary for fortitude, creates rage and fury, or sluggishness. So the pursuit of true honor and honesty brings an appetite for those things which seem beautiful and honorable. So the decline of the mind generates cunning; for cunning emulates the mind, being unable to achieve what it desires.
**D** Therefore, these individual things, though not evil among the higher beings, become evil among us. For those things which proceed from there are neither the same as those, nor do they even remain as they proceeded, being mixed with bodies and matter and with each other.

**XII**
**E** Moreover, those things which come from there converge into one, and from this mixture, whatever is generated takes on something, from which its very being arises, and it turns out to be of a certain kind. For the celestial influx does not make a horse, but gives something to the horse; for both a horse is generated from a horse, and a man from a man. But the Sun comes as an aid to this formation. But man is made from the seminal principle of man, yet so that what is external either hinders or helps. For a son similarly comes forth congruent with the parent; but often for the better, and sometimes it happens for the worse, yet it is never drawn away from the subject itself. Sometimes matter prevails rather than nature, so much so that the effect does not come forth perfect, when, namely, the species is overcome by matter.

**XIII**
**F** Next, when some things indeed happen from the worldly motion, but others by no means, it is necessary now to distinguish and judge and explain whence each thing truly is. The principle therefore will be of this kind: The soul governs the whole by reason, just as in any animal the very principle of life, from which the individual members of the living being are formed, and are ordered to the whole of which they are parts: in the whole, all things are present; but in the parts, only what pertains to each individual part. But those things which come from outside, partly indeed oppose the natural appetite,
**G** but partly are in agreement: yet all things, like its members, harmonize with the whole from all sides, having obtained the nature they possess, and at the same time fulfilling the whole with their own impulse...
