MARSILIO FICINO'S
COMMENTARY ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD,
CONCERNING MATTER.

SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

Q SINCE Plotinus nowhere speaks more beautifully, nor more clearly, nor more distinctly, than where he discusses the formless, obscure, and indistinct subject of things: therefore, this book, discussing matter, seems not so much to demand commentaries from us, as to be content with certain admonitions. He will therefore prove that in both worlds, the intellectual as well as the corporeal, there is a certain matter of its own, and in both, one underlying all things: and that this differs from that only as much as the form of this world differs from that. He will refute false opinions about matter: he will most diligently confirm the true ones: he will conclude that matter, in both cases, is a certain infinity, that is, a nature or potential, enclosing no limit of form within its own depths, but terminable only from elsewhere, formable from elsewhere. That matter, again, in the divine world is indeed a being, but formable by intellectual act. But matter in the sensible world is not truly judged to be a being, but a shadow of that being, perpetually subjected to natural forms as images of that being to be grasped.

Diverse opinions of philosophers concerning matter, and that a certain matter also exists in incorporeal things.

I In the first chapter, he presents a very common description of matter, namely through its relation to forms: in which all agreed that matter is the receptacle of forms, but others explained what follows differently. The Stoics, Cynics, Cyrenaics, conceiving nothing beyond body, wished matter to be merely substance: and forms to be nothing other than certain affections of matter, and matter itself to be a body extended in three dimensions: whom we most extensively refute in the first books of the Theology. But the Pythagoreans and Platonists, and Peripatetics, conceiving something beyond body, were also able to conceive matter as non-corporeal: and therefore they understood a certain matter even in incorporeal things. For just as they posit something formal and divine in bodies, so in a certain way they concede something material in divine things, so that these may be more aptly accommodated to those, and from their order this order may exist. For we conceive corporeal nature as derived from animal nature, and animal nature as derived from intellectual nature, and composed in a similar proportion: and we have found that the most perfect composition in bodies is that which is made from matter and form. For in this alone is the greatest unity: since both matter is something of form, and form in turn is something of matter: indeed, matter is as it were form in potency, and form is as it were matter in act. Therefore, this unity is similar to the Diapason consonance arising from a double proportion: where the acute voice with the grave voice, as it were form with matter, unite into one. If therefore there is any composition in animal and intellectual nature, which certainly there is, since they exist after the One itself, certainly the composition is of such a kind, in which there is both form, and moreover something as it were matter. Concerning this matter, we discuss more extensively in the seventeenth book of the Theology, and in the commentaries on Philebus.

Which

--- Page 193 ---
IN LIBR. I III. ENNEAD. II. 149

That there are not many equally primary principles, and that matter is from God.

II. In the second chapter, he asks whether there is any matter in intellectual nature; and he adduces five reasons by which matter seems not to exist, which he will refute in the following [sections]. But you, among these things, will note that there cannot be many principles equally supreme of all things. This, as far as it commonly pertains to principles, we sufficiently demonstrate in Theology. But as far as it pertains to God and matter, that they cannot be equally principles, note this here. Atticus and his followers, and in a certain way even Plutarch, posited that matter existed from itself from eternity in no other way than God, the artificer of the world; and indeed that [matter] was living, but devoid of reason, and therefore by itself tossed about in disorder; but finally to have received reason divinely, from which it began to be formed and moved by reason, and the world thus to have been constituted at some point, which also existed before it was reduced to chaos, and in turn will at some point return to chaos, having been reformed by God once, and to be reformed by God again.

--- Page 194 ---
150 COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

Matter, because of extreme destitution and insatiable appetite among us, is the origin of mutability; deservedly, it is such here, where material forms emerge: but there it is not such, where matter is entirely formal. Nor indeed, because matter and form are there simultaneously, is there less order of origin (so to speak) there, by which matter is conceived to precede form. For order is something else than time, and prior to time: for time demands order in motion from prior to posterior. Therefore, in the heavens, there can be a certain original order of this to that, like that of a certain matter to form: just as in the sun, there is an order of substance to intimate light, with no temporal interval intervening. Nor again, because matter appears corporeal among us, should you dread the name of matter among the higher beings: for even in bodies, since it precedes both the forms of bodies and dimensions in origin, it is neither a body itself, nor is it truly judged corporeal.

That there is something similar to matter in the intelligible world, and concerning ideas.

IIII In the fourth chapter, he proves that in the intellectual world there is something in a certain way similar to matter. He indeed wishes it to be held as certain that ideas exist there, which we abundantly prove in Theology. Indeed, from the fact that there are many species in the mind, it is clear that the essence of the mind, which is one mind, exists as something other than ideas, and therefore underlies ideal forms as if it were matter. But that there are formal reasons differing among themselves there is clear, because from there, that is, from the first origin of forms, formal distinction in things arises, and not from unformed matter: not again by chance, nor by a partial order of everything; nor finally from diverse agents, unless they are directed to one by a certain single guiding principle. In that very guide, as a mind both uniform and omniform, there is both a destined unity and a described distinction of all things pertaining to the necessary order of the universe. But in what way? This has been said elsewhere, and is yet to be said. Now note that Plotinus does not ascribe ideas to the mind as pictures to a tablet, but applies them as species to a genus: otherwise, there would be not so much unity there, as a gathering and aggregation. Therefore, there is one intellectual nature there, which someone will call intellectuality (if I may use that term), in which all species, that is, ideas, converge as a general nature. But they differ among themselves through various modes of intellectuality or intelligence, not merely (so to speak) notional, but also effective, like a seminal power. And such formal modes and differences, like certain particular forms, accede to the general nature of intelligence itself for conceiving ideal species. Dialectic, however, which divides that genus (so to speak) into species, is not external but internal: not sought, but natural. For there, what is distributed is a vital essence, as it were an animal. Into which it is distributed, are ideas, like certain animals. And what distributes is the very power of intelligence strengthened by the good, as the power of conceiving in a man. But if the various properties there, because they distinguish and bring forth the most absolute act, are like forms, certainly the common nature itself relates to these as matter. Thus, the corporeal world is an image of the superior, referring to the incorporeal world as an exemplar: if the multiform refers to the multiform, if this matter refers to that. But in this world, parts are indeed in the whole, but the whole is not in the parts. There, however, that whole intellectual nature is contained in every idea, but in different ways, as will be explained elsewhere. Then indeed, if you cut that world into parts afterwards distinct from each other, it will have the same matter as ours. For section is a passion of this matter of ours. But note that matter properly admits section insofar as it is quantitative: and matter, if it is devoid of quantity, does not admit it: nor again will quantity suffer it, if it is far from matter, the primary patient. Thus, quantitative matter is cut rather than quantity or matter alone. But if anything conceived there embraces many other things within itself, so much so that the whole itself never appears to have been disjoined by section, you will indeed deny that this matter of ours is there: but you will find something there in the meantime as if it were matter, when having contemplated many things at first glance, you soon find one under the many. Indeed, it first presents itself to you as manifold and multiform. For the formal comes into knowledge first as moving, although there, in origin, something material itself is prior. And again, prior to this material is the very act of the good itself, by which this material becomes actual. Now indeed, since being simply precedes being this, and being such, deservedly being is considered there first, rather than being manifold and formal.

Confirmation of the foregoing concerning the penetrative and resolute power of the mind: what similarity there is between inferior and superior matter, and what dissimilarity, and how it is constituted from alterity and motion.

V In the fifth chapter, he resolves what could be objected to the foregoing, and at the same time confirms what has been said: admonishing you not to deny that there is some matter in the heavens on the grounds that essence there always has its forms and is at the same time one, when even among us matter is always formed and makes one with form. Nor is it surprising that matter lies hidden there, if matter always lies hidden here too. The intellect conceives this there, and the intellect finds this here by resolving. Indeed, the power of intelligence, being most efficacious, naturally penetrates and resolves all things like fire: and because it is likewise most simple, it never rests until it has arrived at the simplest by resolving. In resolving natural things, what it conjectures to lie hidden under the formal reasons of things as a minimal being, it calls matter, as it were, the deep: and formal reason, it calls sublimity: and what surrounds these, it places as it were between the sublime and the deep. But if you see formal reasons of things entirely separated from matter, and yet converting their efficacy to matter, you will see these very things in nature, and nature itself. If, moreover, you conceive of such formal reasons not only as separated, but as converting their efficacy to themselves, you will immediately contemplate the mind. For the divine mind is the exemplary reason of the universe, and efficacious by converting to itself, knowing all things simultaneously and making them. Then indeed, every mind born from it is full of formal reasons, and looks at forms in things, and formal reasons, as certain rays of divine intelligence, congruent with its own reasons. Just as therefore the eye, created by the sun and solar, in the solar light everywhere beholds solar colors, and is admonished to call what lies hidden beneath them dark: so any intellect, created by the divine mind, and thence imbued with the lights of ideas, always seeks out ideal similarities in the formal reasons of things, and gladly recognizes them: and under forms, as it were certain lights of divine intelligence, it divines that matter lies hidden as the lowest in things: and because it is by itself devoid of forms, as it were ideal rays, it is therefore dark. Remember that the matter of bodies does not agree in genus with that matter of the incorporeal world, but by a certain relation. For both seem to relate similarly both to their forms and to the One itself.

--- Page 195 ---
IN LIBR. IIII. ENNEAD. II. 151

seems. Both are almost similarly defined into act through their forms: both are referred to the One almost similarly:
since from it (the One) depends in the same way, namely, through the mere mode of procession, a trace upon nothing, through the mode of something indeterminate and determinable. Again, this matter and that matter interchange something between themselves. For just as this (matter) obtains certain gifts of incorporeal nature, so too that (matter) in turn has ideal reasons of bodies in the mind, and in the soul, besides such reasons, it undergoes motions and certain affections, like passions, towards this matter. Which again, both here and there, hold the place of forms, and almost similarly regard their matters and the One. For they depend on the One in a single mode of conversion, aspect, and limit, and seem to limit their matters in both places. But the forms of this world differ from those: because these are made proximately by the soul, those by the intellect, or God. And this matter differs from that: because this (matter) is indeed a depth of images, while that (matter) is a depth of forms, of which these (images) seem to be images. Therefore, just as form there is a true thing, so too matter is essence. Just as here form is an image of form, so too this matter is an image of essence. And it is so far from calling this matter essence, that it scarcely dares to call that (matter) essence either, namely, if it is compared to the subsequent perfection of essence.

After this you will observe, that the intelligible world is indeed always, but always exists from the Good, almost as that light joined to the sun is immovably from the sun: but the sensible world does not so much *be*, or *exist*, as it is always *becoming* from that (the Good), like the mobile light in the air from the sun, as they say. And what is below the moon sometimes *becomes*. Therefore, that world fills all eternity, this (world) fills all time: but what is subjected to the moon fills a part of time.

Let us consider in the intelligible world essence as formable, preceding itself as formed, in a certain order, I say, not in time, and its form to be the fullness and series of ideas: and we consider the father of that world as the One and as the Good: in unity, the most eminent simplicity: in goodness, a fruitfulness entirely communicable. From unity, wonderfully separated from all things, we think that which in the intelligible world is in the place of matter, solitary and still indefinite, and separated from subsequent forms, depends: but from goodness, that which is already formal and fruitful by its exuberant communication. With the father of that world, we distinguish unity and goodness by relation alone, but in the son-world of that (father), we distinguish formable essence from ideal form, and ideal forms among themselves by formal reason. In the sensible world, however, to the formal distinction coming from above, is added material, and local, and temporal distinction.

Matter in this (world) follows that (world's) matter, form follows form. But let us return again to that matter. After we have posited the One itself, we are accustomed to think that something depends from it which is not it. This, therefore, both because it depends from it, is not it, and because it is not the One itself, in turn depends from the One. To depend from it seems to be a certain motion: but not to be it seems to be otherness and diversity. Therefore, these two follow each other, although the reason is not the same for both. For not everywhere does whatever is not something immediately depend from it. But matter indeed has no formal or ideal reason, but only a material one. But this reason is especially thought of as namely depending from it, and not being it, and vice versa. For this reason, the Pythagoreans called matter the dyad. For just as the dyad is the first process from natural unity, so the matter of the superior world is the first procession from divine unity. It also consists in a way of twin elements, whatever they may be, namely dependence and negation simultaneously, as if by motion and primary otherness: but whatever you add to these is already formal, and matter seems to bring this back through an appetite converting it to where it had proceeded from: which appetite indeed now seems to complete the triad. Although matter by itself lacks the efficacy of form, it does not lack conversion, if indeed conversion itself is appetite: since appetite follows the proper indigence of matter. But what is acquired through this appetite now completes the tetrad, which properly pertains to form. After this, the pentad follows, pertaining especially to action: the hexad to the innermost end of action: the heptad to the external end superior to action. By these numbers, certainly, the superior world is completed: and it rests in the agent

But these things we indeed prove by a similar method in the fifth book of Theology, and by a new argument thus again confirm them. Just as a body among mathematicians is defined into quasi-external terms, namely into two surfaces, one of depth, the other of height, which are neither bodies and are certainly something other than nothing: so among physicists it is bounded into internal terms, which are neither bodies nor even nothing, namely from above into form, from below into matter. But this is not some act of beings: for beneath any act there underlies that which can be made and that which can suffer from an act. IN LIBR. IIII. ENNEAD. II. 153

(matter) has quantity. It is clear that it does not have its own quantity, because it relates indifferently to large and small, and because otherwise, how much would it be? But since quantity is one thing, and "quantified" (quantum) is another, and "quantified" is something twofold: if matter were quantified, it would be judged a composite thing. And thus it would be resolved into something prior. Therefore, it would not be prime matter. For prime matter, to be prime matter, and the first to be formed, and the first to suffer (receive), must be utterly empty of forms, just as it is necessary for the author of forms to be full. He who does not make forms in matter from absolutely no forms, but rather, in the manner of a seal-maker and by means of a seal, expresses and imprints into matter the forms which he himself possesses in a certain way. When I speak of forms, I also understand quantity, through which, as a formal something, matter exists and is said to be quantified, just as it is qualified through quality. Thus, the author of forms will perfectly form (as we have said) if he utterly dominates matter. He will dominate in this way if he himself possesses all forms, but matter possesses none. So that matter, being thus utterly destitute, may more vehemently desire and more eagerly appropriate whatever is offered to it. Likewise, so that he may be the artisan of all things, not just some, and be the common and primary artisan. Likewise, lest it (matter) ever oppose the artisan with its own quality, if it had any, when he is about to impart another quality. Nor, if it had its own quantity or figure, should it resist the artisan who is about to impress another, or at least compel him to bestow forms according to its own measure rather than according to his authority. Now, since he first gives what he bestows and delivers it to empty matter, he deservedly has no obstacle; nor does he necessarily bring quality in place of a past quality, nor again in place of quantity, since he himself bestows the first quantity. You, however, should consider these things to have been said primarily about the common artisan of things, and about common nature and the primary formation of things. Remember, moreover, that the will of the common artisan does not by some chance coincide with a certain magnitude of matter, and conversely, so that the mode of the form is compelled to follow the mode of quantity. For if that concurrence happens by chance, fortune will be the foundation of order. And that which is accidental in things will by that very fact be prior and superior to that which is per se. Nor again should you think that the first author, in his principal action, depends on a certain quantity of matter, much less on a certain figure, which would otherwise impede many actions. But know that since the artisan himself precedes matter in order and power, he dominates matter with the utmost freedom and labors minimally in forming it, so that no transgression ever occurs in the work. And therefore, he moves and forms matter primarily according to his own nature, reason, and will, rather than according to the mode of any quantity. For since he moves and creates not through quantity, but through an efficacious form, deservedly such a form first responds to his action in matter; and quantity subsequently accompanies the form, while, namely, at the impetus of the formal action and the ingress of the efficacious form, matter is moved and extended, "it is extended," he says, "properly to the extent that the impetus of the penetrating form agitates it, and the ideal reason itself prescribes, and finally, the formal or seminal reason demands." Nor undeservedly does a certain quantity or figure follow a certain species, rather than the converse. For these two, as less perfect, depend on species as on perfection; and as not efficacious, they serve the efficacious form, and are comprehended and made by the reason of the form itself. Nor should you doubt that quantity is contained within species. For quantity is a certain form, and as something less formal, it is contained within species as something more formal; and as if implicated there, it is soon unfolded into matter. Matter, however, through certain species of living things, has certain magnitudes and figures. That quantity pertains to form and is not matter is evident from this: that quantity, where it measures and numbers, has the nature of a determinant. Pure matter, however, is considered only determinable. I omit how forms of things are everywhere brought forth, either differing among themselves or often changing according to the mode and change of quantity and figure. Which pure matter would certainly never bring forth. I pass over now the hidden effects which often result from certain figures and numbers in our bodies or souls. Certainly, to be quantified is posited to be simply, before being quantified; for nothing would ever be quantified unless it simply existed. But it exists simply even if it is not quantified. Therefore, when the simply existing being itself, which precedes being quantified, is first thought to be extended, then quantity itself first arises, namely, the extension of being. This very portion of being which is extended is matter now made corporeal; extension, however, is quantity. Extension indeed needs a subject, since it is an accident and a certain passion necessarily following the formal act of being. Now, when something is extended, and yet extension itself is not extended, this very thing which is extended is matter, subject to extension, and necessarily prior to extension. For unless it exists in some way, it cannot be extended. Nor indeed is it permissible to suspect that the subject of quantity is form. For any other form, as incomparably more efficacious than quantity, does not submit to it, but rather subjugates quantity. Finally, that in the intelligible world there is an abundance of virtue and a power present through all things and an excess of the inferior: this is referred to in the sensible world through quantity as its image. But that which there (in the intelligible world) underlies as an abundance of virtue, seems to be referred to through this matter. Therefore, since quantity and matter do not refer to the same thing, they are certainly not judged to be the same. But who does not see that numbers exist even in things separated from matter, and points and lines, indeed even surfaces, are neither matter nor necessarily have matter? Conclude that quantity, since it is something formal, depends on the agent rather than on matter. And since it is the least among formal things, it is deservedly bestowed everywhere as the more excellent form demands.

Confirmation of the above.

IX. But lest you perhaps wonder that no quantity is contained in the very concept of matter, and that matter is not quantified by itself, remember that since there are many things besides quantity, such as substances and qualities, and similar things, the concept of being is deservedly different from the concept of quantity, and more common and prior; and therefore many things can both exist and be understood, even if they do not exist, nor are understood to be quantified. Thus, neither is the soul quantified, which generates quantity, nor is matter quantified, which precedes bodies; nor is quantity itself quantified, lest we proceed to infinity. Since that which is quantified becomes quantified by quantity, just as something qualified becomes qualified by quality. From this it is also confirmed that quantity is something formal. Thus, a living body is colored by natural color, yet color itself is not colored. Nor again is the seminal reason which creates natural color in an animal itself a color; similarly, neither is the quantity and figure appropriate to a living being itself quantified or figured; nor is the seminal virtue, the fabricator of such quantity and figure, itself a quantity or figure. Then, just as an incoming quality makes matter, which was not yet qualified, suddenly qualified, so too an incoming quantity simply makes matter, which was not yet quantified, quantified. Nor should you think that matter, at the first advent of quantity, is extended from a narrower to a wider state. For narrowness and wideness are certain modes of an already existing quantity. But before the first access of quantity, neither is quantity in matter, nor therefore are there modes of quantity there.

--- Page 198 ---
154 COMMENT. MARSIL. FICINI
And indeed the formal essence of quantity is neither great, otherwise it would not be congruent with small things; nor again small, otherwise it could not accommodate itself to great things. Similarly, matter is neither properly of a specific quantity, nor of such a quantity that it is equally indifferent to undergoing all modes of quantity; nor again simply quantitative, lest it possess anything formal in itself and be composite.

How matter is known, since it is formless.

X Therefore, it is doubted how matter can be known, since it lacks all forms, but it is necessary that both the thing to be known move the knowers through form, and that the knowers act concerning it through a form consonant with the thing to be known itself. Since, therefore, knowledge occurs through forms, we seem consequently to be thinking of formal things, not formless things, unless perhaps we endeavor in our mind, by separating all forms from the mind, to conjecture something in things that is similarly separated from all forms. But meanwhile, while we strive, we certainly strive with some form: and therefore we unwillingly strive for a form, even though we believe it to be formless: while, namely, we think of it as indefinite with all our might: and under such a form we suspect matter to be indefinite as well. Thus, therefore, by a certain indefiniteness of our conception, we think of the indefiniteness of matter. To the same end contributes a certain indefiniteness, as if material, naturally and actually hidden under the mind's form. If an infinite circle is imagined, the concept and definition of the circle will indeed be finite and certain: but the gaze of the eye, or a similar act of imagination through the infinite circle, will wander infinitely. Similarly, if someone, with all forms removed, like an observing eye, directs the keenness of the mind's gaze into matter with all its might, he will see absolutely nothing: just as the eye sees nothing when lights and colors are everywhere removed. But here the mind conjectures meanwhile that with light removed, a dark body underlies. Does it also conjecture there, with forms removed, that a formless thing underlies? It does indeed conjecture as best it can: But such a conjecture is neither by legitimate ratiocination, which is accustomed by the guidance of the mind and ideal reason to conceive forms from forms: nor again by legitimate imagination, which is accustomed to behold forms, either from the mind or from the senses: therefore, the conjecture about matter is compounded of spurious reason and again adulterated imagination. But such an indefiniteness of the mind regarding the suspected indefiniteness of matter, has meanwhile something definite, inasmuch as it acts through forms, and defines something about matter. Yet it does not properly understand. For intellection is the contemplation of ideas, or at least of ideal things. Nor again does it properly ratiocinate. For ratiocination is a kind of collection. Here, however, it does not so much collect as disperse, while it denies everything about matter. And if it affirms anything, it meanwhile confirms what is denied. For while it affirms matter to be the receptacle of all forms, it meanwhile confirms it to be utterly formless in itself. And since the soul, as it were...

**Matter is entirely the same as the privation of all forms, if privation signifies a certain infinity and formal power.**

**XIIII**
Up to this point it has been discussed how matter primarily relates to those things which are more remote from it, namely to quality and quantity. Next, in what way it is compared to those things which are closer, namely to privation and the infinite. But first concerning privation. Therefore he discusses that Peripatetic saying, 'matter and privation are indeed one in subject or in reality itself, but two in reason.' When the Peripatetic said that these two are in reason, that is, he must assign two definitions.

one: Or rather, is each placed in the definition of the other? Just as is usually said of a snub nose and the snubness itself. If so, there are still two things: namely, the nose and snubness. Or perhaps one of them is in the definition of the other, but not vice versa, like heat in the definition of fire, but not the other way around. If it is said this way, there are also two things: the subject and the quality. After this, it discusses whether matter and privation are called one thing, because privation adds nothing to matter, but denies other things of matter. Thus it will be ambiguous how there are two concepts/accounts: one indeed pertaining to the subject, that is, matter, and the other to the relation which is made by privation to other things. It is certainly probable that the concept/account not only of privation but also of the subject is rightly referred to other things. Those things which are above matter are not only referred to an end, but also have it that they are ends of some things. But since matter alone is the end of nothing, to which anything might serve in natural order, but it alone serves all things: and whatever is entirely empty of the function of an end: but everywhere naturally constituted towards an end and always lacking and desirous of an end: it is rightly said that its nature is referred to other things by its very concept/account. So that just as in the highest things the whole concept of end exists, but not *towards* an end: so conversely in the lowest there is indeed no concept of end, but everything is *towards* an end. Do not here, meanwhile, dream of dialectical relations. For we wish the relation of nature itself and of divine providence to be understood here. But nothing is more alien to matter than logical relation. For this is founded either in opinion, or in some thing, as a subject. But matter, on the contrary, is only a subject and a foundation. Furthermore, it is probable that here by the name of privation is signified a certain relation, that is, the indefiniteness of this subject, and its need for other things, naturally established and eagerly tending towards them. And therefore one cannot easily discern how there are two concepts/accounts: one indeed of privation, the other of matter. For they are one not only in reality, but also in concept/account. But no one would say that matter is privation in the way we usually speak of other privations, that is, as certain defects in subjects. For matter itself is the subject of all things. Again, let no one think of matter as privation like nothingness: for when bodies are either composed of matter or resolved into matter, it is far from the case that they are made from nothing or reduced to nothing.

Infinity does not happen to matter, but is matter itself.

XV. But this privation which is called infinity, or infinitude, that is, an aptitude only formable in itself, and possessing no formal ends in itself: this infinity, I say, does not indeed happen to matter, but is matter itself. Consider concepts/accounts and numbers. Concepts, I say, formal ones, dependent on seminal and ideal concepts. Numbers, I say, both of such concepts, and of the properties that are in them, and of the degrees of their power, and of the differences between them. Concepts indeed define/limit: and order by defining/limiting. Numbers, however, order, and define/limit by ordering. Likewise, concepts and powers of forms, both terminate genera as if they were matters into species, and terminate the vague appetite of matter towards an effect. Numbers also order and define/limit the series of things, matter subject to them: likewise they define/limit the powers and motions of qualities: and through these they also seem to terminate matter. Since therefore such concepts and numbers define/limit, certainly there is a subject which is defined/limited by them. And that first is matter itself. For composites through this have that they must be defined/limited from elsewhere: and nature, or soul, or mind through a certain matter of their own have that they need the limits of forms. Matter, therefore, since it is this very thing which is defined/limited from elsewhere, is by its very nature infinite. Just as that which is illuminated from elsewhere is in itself dark. Somewhere therefore, indeed everywhere, an infinite nature underlies, indeed infinity itself. For just as an infinite thing corresponds to a finite one: so also infinity corresponds to an end. To a substantial end, I say, a substantial, not fictitious, infinity. Infinity, I say, not in another: just as the first end and limit is not in another. But if anyone says that this infinity is not matter itself, but entirely happens to it, he will be forced to admit that infinity has something formal in itself: inasmuch as it is in a subject: and determines the subject under some such condition: which certainly seems to be against the nature of infinity. Now, infinity itself is not any formal concept/account. For it is the extreme of formability. In which if there is anything properly formal: at least from that part it is not formable. Nevertheless, so that it may look to the highest form-giver, to attribute all forms: the subject corresponding to this in proportion must have absolutely none. Furthermore, if matter is infinite in itself, infinity ought not to happen to it. But if it is said to be terminated, it is not prime matter. Finally, if matter is imagined as a certain formal limit, and infinity, that is, merely formable aptitude, happens to it, whatever formal is imagined in matter will suddenly be lost. For nothing actually formal remains under extreme formability. That the matter of the corporeal world is infinity is confirmed by the fact that the matter of the incorporeal world is also infinity. For infinity does not happen to that: for whatever is in it exists as an end. But from that, this depends through a similar mode of infinity. Think therefore there of the simply one, superior to one being. Consider in one being infinity, that is, a power formable by the one itself. Which, inasmuch as it extends into formal limits there, is named power and infinity. Inasmuch as it is led into perseverance outside the limits of duration, it is named eternity. That infinity, indeed, thus named in a certain way according to defect, follows the infinity of the One conceived according to supereminent excess. And inasmuch as one exceeds, so firmly does the other succeed, as if opposed to the first by relation. But then from the infinity which is formable there, the infinity of mundane matter itself begins: thus formable under nature, just as that is under the good. But the two infinities introduced here do not agree in genus, under which they might differ by specific differences. And yet both are most simple: and while this one depends on that, then by referring to that it seems to agree with it: and because it is not that, nor instituted for similar forms, it is judged to differ too much from it: not indeed by a difference added to it, but by itself, or moreover because it is not born for similar forms: but this also is to differ by itself. But since that formable power, although it is as matter to ideas, nevertheless in itself, and to us, is considered as form, therefore it is not indicated as indefinite as the matter of bodies. Especially because that formable nature is always and similarly reduced to the act of form. But this is reduced gradually: and disperses acts. There, too, is that formal matter. Here, however, in turn, form becomes material. Therefore, the indefinite condition is found more in this than in that. But the condition of the limit prevails there: here it necessarily fails. Therefore, if you consider a composite of matter and form, you will say that this is in a certain way infinite, namely by reason of matter. However, you will not say that this infinite is the very nature of infinity. Which is indeed said to be of the infinite itself, in the sense that it is infinite: for this pertains to matter. But when, considering this very matter as if separately, you say 'this infinite,' this infinite is certainly the same as infinity itself, which we just called the infinite itself.

**A** If there is form there, there is moreover also that which is formed, about which there is difference. Therefore, there underlies matter which receives that form, and is perpetually a subject. Furthermore, if an intelligible world exists there: but this world of ours is an imitation of that, and is composed of matter: there too it is necessary for there to be matter. Otherwise, by what reasoning will you call it a world and an ordered whole, unless you contemplate species or forms? But in what way will you behold a species, unless you also comprehend that in which the species is?

**B** Indeed, the superior world itself is entirely indivisible everywhere, and again, in a certain condition, divisible. And if its parts are dispersed among themselves: the section itself and dispersion is a certain affection of matter: for it is properly that which is said to suffer section. But if the many things that are there are one impartible being: then those many things existing in the one, are in that one as matter, and are its forms. For the one itself which is varied must be considered in

**C** the first place, as varied and multiform. It must be considered again as formless before it is varied. For if you remove from there by thought variety, forms, reasons, intelligences, without a doubt that which precedes these, formless and indefinite, appears: and nothing appears of those things which are with it and in it.

**D** But if, from the fact that an essence of this kind always has these things, and both are simultaneously one, it is said that there is no matter there: it will follow that neither is there matter of bodies here. For this matter is never without form, but always a whole body: and nevertheless it is composite. And the intellect finds a duality. For here it divides until it reaches that which is simple: which, namely, cannot be further resolved. But insofar as it can be referred to something else, it proceeds by penetrating into its depth. Finally, the depth of each thing is matter. Therefore, all matter is dark, because reason itself is light, and intellect itself is reason. Therefore, reason

**E** perceiving in each thing, conjectures that what is inferior is, as it were, dark beneath the light. Just as the eye, being luminous, looking into light and simultaneously into colors, which are certain lights, leads one to say that those things which lie hidden beneath the colors remain dark and as matter, covered by colors. Nevertheless, what we conjecture to underlie intelligible things as dark, or what underlies sensible things, differs greatly: and that matter differs from this matter as much as the species

**F** inherent in that differs from the species which inheres in this. For divine matter, receiving that which limits it, obtains a determined, intellectual life. But this (matter) indeed becomes something determined: yet neither living, nor anything intellectual, but something devoid of life, although adorned. Furthermore, this form is imaginary: and therefore the subject is imaginary. But there, both the form is a true thing: and consequently the subject is a true essence. **VI. Proves that there is primary matter in bodies.**
Now let us speak thus concerning the receptacle of bodies. First, that there must be something subject to bodies, which is something other than bodies, the mutual transformation of the elements shows us. For that which is transformed is not entirely corrupted: otherwise, a certain essence would utterly vanish into non-being: nor again is that which comes into being made from that which in no way is. But a certain transformation occurs from one species into another. But that which takes on the species of the generated thing remains, while it divests itself of the other. This is moreover evident from destruction. For this pertains to the composite. If this is so, each perishable thing is from matter and form. Induction also testifies that what is dissolved is composite. Resolution again shows us the same thing. As if a phial is resolved into gold: and gold is resolved into water: and water finally, when it perishes, by a similar reasoning, demands something proportional. Furthermore, it is necessary that elements are either species, or primary matter, or consist of matter and species simultaneously. Indeed, it is impossible for them to be species. For in what way, if they are without matter, will they have mass and magnitude? But neither are they primary matter: because they are dissolved. Therefore, they are composed of matter and species simultaneously. And species indeed pertains to quality and form, but matter pertains to the subject. And that indeed, because it does not become a species, is not defined.

**VII. Refutes false opinions about matter.**
Therefore, against Empedocles, who posits elements as matter, the corruption of the elements themselves cries out. But Anaxagoras, introducing a certain mixture, like water, and saying that this actually contains all things: indeed removes the intellect which he had introduced. Since he does not say that it bestows form and species: nor that it is prior to matter, but simultaneous with matter. Indeed, it is impossible for them to be simultaneous. For if the mixture itself partakes of being, certainly being itself is more ancient. But if being itself is also a certain mixture, then there is need of some third thing besides these. Wherefore, if it is necessary for the artificer of things to be prior, why then should species be in matter according to small parts: and then the intellect discern the confused things with inextricable difficulty? Since it is permissible for matter, if it is not qualified, to impress quality and form...

**XIII**
*Whether mat-

BUT now it must be asked, whether matter is privation itself, or rather privation is predicated of matter. He therefore who said that matter and privation are one in substratum, but two in concept, ought to have shown how it is most fitting to adduce the concept of each. Indeed, the concept of matter, which defines it, touches nothing of privation; and similarly for the concept of privation. For either neither is in the concept of the other, or both are in the concept of both, or one only is in the concept of the other, whatever that may be. If therefore both are defined separately, and neither requires the other, both will be two, and matter will be something other than privation, although privation may happen to it. But in the definition of one, the other ought not to be perceived even potentially. But if they are related as a nose and snub-nosed: so also is each twofold and two. But if it is related as fire and heat, namely, since heat is in fire, but fire is not necessarily found in heat, and matter is thus privation, as fire is hot, certainly privation will be a species of matter, but the subject will be something else, which indeed must be matter. And so, not even by this reasoning will it be one. But are they perhaps one in substratum, but two in concept, as if privation does not signify the presence of anything, but rather its absence? And thus privation would be the negation of beings, as if one were to say 'non-being'? For negation adds nothing, but says 'not to be': and thus privation will be as non-being. If therefore it is thus called non-being, because it is clearly not being, but something else: will there then be two concepts? One indeed regarding the subject, the other indeed privation, signifying a certain relation to other things? Or rather, the concept of matter looks to other things, and the concept of the subject entirely to other things. But if the concept of privation shows its indefiniteness, perhaps it will touch its nature: perhaps with this exception, that both are said to be one in substratum, but two in concept. But if from the fact that it is something indeterminate and indefinite and formless, it is the same as matter, how then will there still be two concepts?

*How matter

AGAIN it must be investigated, whether the infinite and indeterminate itself exists in another nature as an accident: and how it is an accident: and whether privation is an accident. Indeed, if all numbers and concepts are outside infinitude—since they are limits and orders, and order itself descends from these into other things, and they order what is indeed not ordered, nor [yet] ordered, while the limit and end and concept *do* order—then it is necessary that what is ordered and limited is infinite by its own nature. But matter is ordered, or also whatever is not matter, from the fact that it either participates in it, or obtains the condition of matter. Therefore it is necessary that infinitude itself is matter. However, it must not be called infinite as if by accident, and from the fact that infinitude is an accident of matter. For first, whatever is an accident to something, must be a certain concept: but infinitude is not a concept. Secondly, to what existing thing will infinitude be an accident? Surely to the limit and the limited?

A But indeed matter is neither something terminated, nor a limit. Likewise, the infinite approaching a terminated thing will destroy its nature; therefore, the infinite is not an accident of matter. Therefore, it itself is the infinite, since also in the intelligible world matter itself is the infinite. Which indeed perhaps is generated from the very infinity of the One, whether power or eternity, so that in the One itself there is not infinity, but it itself is the author of infinity. By what reason, therefore, is there the infinite both there and here? B Perhaps the infinite is twofold. But how do they differ? Namely, as archetype and image. Is that which is among us therefore less infinite? Perhaps indeed more. For insofar as an image falls short of existence and truth, to that extent it is more infinite. For infinity is more in that which is less terminated. But that which is less in good, is greater in evil. Therefore, that which is there, as that which exists more as being, is as it were imaginarily infi- C nite. Therefore, is the infinite the same as to be infinite? Perhaps where there is form and matter, each is distinct; but where there is only matter, either the same must be said, or altogether, which indeed is more correct, its very being is not to be assigned to the infinite there. For that which needs something, and obtains it, holds itself as a certain good between good and evil, if indeed it is equally disposed to both. But that which has nothing, being pressed by need, indeed, since it is need itself, it must be evil.

MARSILIO FICINO'S
COMMENTARY ON BOOK I CONCERNING THAT WHICH IS IN ACT,
AND THAT WHICH IS IN POTENTIAL.

SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

Also concerning act, and potential, Also concerning metals and stones.

[Large decorative initial L] HE BOOK concerning potential and act, summarily confirms those things which were said in the book concerning matter, and is more clearly understood through them. It is divided, moreover, into five chapters. In the first, you will note, after certain doubts, that whatever is said to be in potential, necessarily refers to something else, namely to that which comes from it, or is in act. Likewise, potential properly refers to act. Again, in that which is in potential for something, sometimes the substance remains, with something new arriving, sometimes it changes: whether the change occurs for the better or for the worse. You will consider, moreover, that there is no potential in the intelligible world for a new act, either to be produced or to be acquired: otherwise, if an act is never reached, it will be judged to be in potential in vain, or if it is sometimes reached, there will be temporal change in eternal things. Therefore, lest these absurdities follow, all potential there is from eternity reduced to its whole and complete act. Next, you will observe that the potential for doing should not be said to be in potential: but the potential for suffering can be said to be in potential. Finally, you will observe Plotinus here, as he has already revealed twice elsewhere, to believe that metal is congealed water, whether he thinks it is simply water in the manner of crystal, or mostly water. For it is the opinion of the natural philosophers that in composing mixtures, heat and cold act rather as agents than as matter, for they cannot easily be mixed due to their vehemence. But dry and humid are matter under these. Where indeed the dry prevails over the humid, rock solidifies; but where humidity exceeds dryness, metal is formed, which, due to the exuberance of humidity, melts at fire, which liquefaction dryness prevents in rock.

Concerning two kinds of matter, and act, and potential, both in bodies and in the soul.

II IN the second chapter you will observe a twofold matter. Firstly, indeed, composite and natural, accepted for the form of art, as when a statue is made from bronze. Secondly, matter also natural, but simple and immediately accepted for a similarly natural form, as when

--- Page 215 ---
IN LIBR. V. ENNEAD. II. 171

the power of form or habit is brought forth to the efficacy of action. Again, observe here that the act which is form, or in place of form, since it approaches the subject as yet unformed and powerless, needs the benefit of some external cause: but the act which is action, proceeds from the very power of form or habit.

How potency and act relate differently below the heavens and in the heavens, and again in the intelligible world.

III After this, he forbids anything in the intelligible world from being indicated as being in potency: in potency, I say, which both tends towards a new act, and is a thing of a different nature than the act. He says, however, that whatever potency is imagined there, the thing itself not only always exists in act, but the act also exists: firstly, because what is posited there as a quasi-material potency, is a certain form, and therefore also an act: secondly, because this potency and the act it looks towards, are not two natures, but one. Nor, however, should we say that because that matter always has the same form, it therefore absolutely exists as the same thing: for even if God were to eternally continue the form in corporeal matter, the form would still be something other than matter, as we believe happens in the celestial bodies. Again, just as in one who has already learned, the very potency of learning does not perish: for the docile potency is not removed by doctrine, but perfected: so too in the

--- Page 216 ---
172	**COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO**
	Confirms the foregoing.

V	He again raises a question in the fifth chapter: If matter is nothing in act, in what way can we speak of it? And he confirms what has been said by disputation. Now indeed, matter is therefore called the matter of beings, because it is in potency to receive images from them, or rather, it is itself the potency formable from them. Indeed, in any art, to name matter under the artisan is nothing other than to introduce something having nothing artificial, but capable of receiving all things. In nature, however, to subject matter to the architect of all things is not so much to bring forth something that is in potency to forms, as it is to bring forth a potency that is entirely formable. Such a potency, although it is considered in a certain order to precede the effect of form, nevertheless, because the very nature of this potency is nothing other than formability, it necessarily depends on the act of form. Where, even if while the form still seems future, the potency itself already seems present, awaiting, as it were, the effect of the form, nevertheless, what is called the presence of this potency is nothing other than possibility (if I may so speak) and the futurity of the form: and, as someone might imagine, a certain confused beginning of the form. Now indeed, if you compare form to the efficient cause, what is future for the form depends on the presence of the cause: but if you compare matter to the very nature of the form, whatever presence is imagined in matter depends on the future of the form itself: indeed, even on what is already present. Indeed, form seems to be included in the very concept of matter, while it is defined as formability. Likewise, if you refer this lowest thing to the highest of the universe, and say that just as that is pure act, the former of all things, so also this is pure potency, formable only under all things, then truly, if you attribute anything of formable potency to that highest, you immediately remove its nature; whatever act you again dedicate to this lowest as its own, you suddenly lose the nature of this also: since its being is judged to be in potency, the formability of this act. Its presence is nothing other than the futurity of the form. Moreover, matter is so separated from the nature of being that it neither adheres to being as its property or affection, nor represents being as an image, nor is it so impressed under its image as to be affected thereby, or to contract or preserve a trace: always naturally divesting itself of any acts, but preserving possibility: only coming to aid where the degree of true beings is the last; that is, nature itself, and there indeed subsiding into the images of beings, and bringing nothing familiar back from them to itself. Nothing, however, can be said of it as pertaining to beings, except that it is a shadow of nature. And since it is so much further removed from being than the image of being, it ought in no way to be considered either a being or to have being. Now indeed, we ought to judge concerning being contrary to non-being. Being in act certainly has more of being than being in potency: conversely therefore, what is called non-being in act has less of being, or more of non-being, than what is called non-being in potency. Since therefore matter is most remote from the first essence and truth, beyond what can be conceived, and is therefore falsity itself, and thus truly non-being, if you imagine this in its act, you will assert it to be even more non-being. And the more truly it will be to call matter possibility, the more falsely it will be to consider it act, and vice versa. Conclude the book with this sentence. Truth itself even gives force to falsehood, otherwise, unless it were true that something is false, it would not be false; and the more truly something is false, or the more truly it is that this is false, the more undoubtedly false it is: Thus therefore, the truer matter is matter, that is, the truer it is as a possibility for beings, the falser it is as act, and vice versa.

III
In the intelligible world there is nothing in potentiality relative to another, although there is a certain potentiality there, but it is always in act, so that the whole is said to exist as act.

But when he who is a grammarian in potentiality becomes a grammarian in actuality, why is that which is in potentiality not the same as that which exists in actuality? For Socrates is the same, both he who is wise in potentiality and he who is wise in actuality. Is it then the case that he who is ignorant is also knowing? For he was knowing in potentiality: Indeed, a man becomes knowing accidentally. For it is not by virtue of being unknowing that he is knowing in potentiality, but it happens to him to be unknowing. But the soul, existing as apt in itself, persists in potentiality even insofar as it is knowing, and still preserves what is called potentiality: so much so that he who is already a grammarian does not cease to be a grammarian in potentiality. Nor perhaps does anything prevent it from having different modes of being. For there (in the case of the bronze) it is said to be in potentiality *only*; but here (in the case of the grammarian) it is in potentiality *already having a form*. If therefore that which is said to be in potentiality is the subject, but that which is in actuality is the composite, like a statue, what will the form that is in the bronze be called? Perhaps it is not inappropriate to call "act" that according to which the subject is in act, and not merely in potentiality; to call, I say, the form and species not simply "act," but rather "the act of this." Because we can also name another act by a more specific reason: namely, the act opposed to that potentiality which brings forth into act. For that which is said to be in potentiality receives from another that it may become in act: but that potentiality through which something can be done, from itself brings forth an act in a certain way opposed to itself, like a habit, and that which is called an act according to that habit, namely fortitude, and to act bravely. But enough of these matters.

Now, for what reason these things have been said, must now be explained by us. To this, therefore, all things tended, that we might clearly consider in what manner in the intelligible world that which is in act is to be spoken of: and whether there is only that which is said to be in act, or also whether each thing is an act: and if all things there are acts, by what reason that which is named "being in potentiality" exists there. Indeed, if there is neither matter there, in which that which is said to be in potentiality consists, nor is anything of those things which are not yet, going to be, nor is it transformed into another, nor does it, remaining itself, generate another from itself, nor, departing from itself, does it hand over to another to be in its place: certainly there will not be there that which is said to be in potentiality: where is the kingdom of beings, not of temporal, but of eternal things. If, therefore, someone, positing matter in the intelligible world, should ask how matter can be there, if that which is judged to be in potentiality is not there according to that matter (for if matter exists there in another way, nevertheless in everything there will be one thing as matter, another as species, and another as composite) what will they answer? Perhaps that matter there is said to be species, when the soul itself is indeed a species in itself, but matter relative to another. Is it then in potentiality relative to that? By no means. For it is its species, and not a species in the future, nor is it distinguished otherwise than by reason, and thus it has matter as if considered twofold: but both are one nature, just as Aristotle asserted an immaterial body as a body. But what shall we say about the soul? For it is an animal in potentiality, when it is not yet born an animal, but is about to be born. Likewise, it is musical in potentiality, and similarly as many other things as are sometimes brought about, and are not always. Therefore

MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY ON BOOK VIII. CONCERNING SIGHT, AND WHY THINGS THAT ARE FAR AWAY APPEAR SMALL.

SUMM

--- Page 232 ---
188 COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO
if you turn your gaze, this wall will not appear as large to you as if it were marked with many colors. For you can scarcely distinguish the parts of a dimension from each other where the variety of forms does not distinguish them, but you suddenly slip from any part of the dimension, unless a difference in quality stops your gaze. By these things, the second question can be answered, namely, for what reason two buildings situated on an opposite and very distant hill from us, and distant from each other by a stadium, appear to be even less distant. Likewise, that if they are separated from us by a hundred stadia, they appear to be even a shorter distance from us. For where we perceive the variety of forms more confusedly, naturally we also do not distinguish the quantity of the interval.

That things which are more remote do not appear smaller because of smaller angles.

11 In the second chapter, he refutes the response of those who think that a pyramidal figure is extended from the visible object to the eye by lines of rays, and reaches the pupil with a certain cone; and that the more remote the object is, the more gradually acute the cone becomes. And so, while we perceive the thing with a gradually smaller angle, we also conjecture a smaller magnitude, especially when it has proceeded so far that the angle is now smaller than the pupil. What should be said about the rest, we will discuss elsewhere together with Plotinus. For now, however, this is especially rejected, that they say a body appears smaller for that reason, because the angle has now become smaller than the pupil. For this reasoning will concede there that some other things are seen by the pupil in addition, when one thing cannot fill the pupil with its angle; but indeed where the object is so immense that nothing further can be seen in one gaze, then it also appears smaller than it is, although the angle by which it is said to be seen has not become smaller than the pupil. For the entire hemisphere is seen with the whole vision, which so completely fills the pupil that it can see nothing else besides. Therefore, that it is thought to be smaller than it is, does not happen because it is seen through an angle shorter than the pupil. Among these things, you will notice an indication by which you may confirm, according to Plotinus, that the form of the object does not reach the eyes, but the ray of the eye (goes) to the object. For vision, like a certain action, is performed in the very manner of a visual form. If, therefore, the object were to conform itself to the narrowness of the pupil (as they say), it would never be judged larger than the pupil; but now it is judged much larger, because the visual ray, extended outwards, spreads itself through the very magnitude of the thing. But certainly we cannot deny that rays from luminous bodies arrive at the eyes in a certain pyramidal figure, and with this very figure, convey at least the spiritual quality of the thing, or its power, or its action, to us. Conversely, the radial nature of sight also testifies that rays are emitted from the eyes, especially in animals that see at night. And where some see nearby, others see far away; nor do we see very sparse things, nor very close mists, because they do not terminate the still powerful rays of the eyes. I omit what both humans and certain animals accomplish externally with the gaze of their eyes. Finally, more light is necessary near the object than near the eye; for where our ray is emitted, it is strong. Nor is it moreover expedient for more abundant light to be scattered here, but near the object, already weak, it is nourished by much light, to be immediately diffused through the object by the same (light). For it seems probable that the visual ray of the eye is extended through the pyramidal width of the incoming light, with the aid of the same light towards the width of the thing to be seen, as far as it is able to proceed; and when it is thus terminated, the effect of vision is accomplished. But that vision is accomplished by a certain interaction of both, namely, the visual ray and more abundant light, Plato in Timaeus, and Galen and Calcidius in the same place, teach and confirm with insight. But the said light is either innate to the visual ray, or applied from outside.

**MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY**
**ON BOOK IX OF THE SECOND ENNEAD**
**AGAINST THE GNOSTICS.**

**SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.**

The One and the Good are the same and the first of all. Likewise, there are three principles: The Good itself, Mind, Soul.

**P**LOTINUS's mind, we can infer, was not entirely alien from the Christian law, because since he was always a disciple of Ammonius, a Christian, and always a friend of the most Christian Origen, he is said to have agreed together with Origen and Herennius, that he would never depart from the teachings of Ammonius: and that he kept this promise. Moreover, he sometimes scorned the worship of pagan gods with a noble spirit: Porphyry, his own disciple, is a witness, with Amelius exhorting him to this. Finally, frequently irritated by many heretics partly corrupting, partly even despising his Plato, he indeed responded very broadly: yet in responding he brought nothing common against Christians: but only specific points against the heresy: although otherwise it was permitted at that time to attack Christians with impunity, and opportunity was offered. Porphyry recounts in his description of Plotinus's life who indeed were the authors of this heresy: and what the heretics, who were called Gnostics, similar to the Manicheans, professed. From their opinions it is certainly clear that their heresy, although they worshipped Christ, nevertheless dissented no less from the common opinion of Christians than from the Platonists. But as far as the present work's purpose is concerned: these are their principal errors. Concerning the One Good itself, they dreamed I know not what. Moreover, they most ineptly distinguished separate Intellects. They inserted something intermediate between Intellect and Soul. They thought that a corrupted Soul had made the world evil from an evil principle.

That there is nothing superior or prior to the Good itself or Goodness, likewise to the One itself or Unity, is shown thus. First, it is necessary to remember that what is not first, is not simple: and conversely, what is not simple, is not first. For if any thing is not the first of all, it will certainly depend on another: and therefore there will be two things in it, namely, something of a cause: and something moreover proper to it, differing from the cause. Therefore, while it is not first, it deservedly cannot be simple. Again, if any thing is not simple, it will necessarily have in itself both this and that. We will ask therefore, whether this is only from that, or both equally from both: or neither from neither: or both from some third thing. If you answer that this depends on that, that will certainly be the first, but this the second: nor will it be permissible to say that anything composite here is the first. Nor again will it be permissible to say that both are made equally from both: otherwise the same thing compared to the same thing, will be both cause and effect, and prior and posterior. But if you say that both are made from some third thing, then not this composite, but that third thing will be the first and principle. Moreover, it is impious to posit two things in the supernal realm: of which neither is from the other, nor are both from a third: otherwise they will combine without any determined cause or reason, but by chance. But rash chance cannot exist in the supernal realm: otherwise there would be no order in what follows. Wherefore, as we have said, what is not first, is not simple: so also we say that what is not simple, is not first. Therefore, the more prior something is, the simpler it is, and vice versa. Therefore, what is first, is most simple, and vice versa. Wherefore, (so to speak) primality itself is simplicity itself, and vice versa. Since therefore Unity and Goodness hold the highest place in simplicity, both are certainly the same, and the first of all and the principle. Goodness is indeed most simple: otherwise it would be composed of many things, and therefore would need parts and a composer, and thus would by no means be self-sufficient. It is necessary, however, for goodness itself not only to be most sufficient, but to be sufficiency itself. For this is desired as good. Therefore, the Good itself, since it is most sufficient, is also most simple. It is therefore first: especially because if it is not first, that which will be superior to the Good itself, will also be better than goodness: even though nothing better than goodness can be imagined: for it alone is better than whatever is better. Then indeed we ask, whether the Good itself desires that which is perhaps placed before it or not. If it does not desire, it is strange for an effect not to desire the cause by which it is perfected. If it does desire, again it is marvelous for the Good itself to covet something outside itself, since every desire terminates in the good. Moreover, concerning other things, we similarly inquire: whether it desires beyond the limits of the good that which is imagined to be superior to the good or not. Indeed, it is impious for all things not to desire the first principle. It is impious again to desire something beyond the good. From all these things it is concluded that the Good itself is the most simple of all, and the first. But no one doubts that Unity itself or the One itself is most simple. For in every essence, composition or number can exist or be imagined: In unity alone it cannot: otherwise it would not be unity itself, but something one and a multitude. Division moreover

--- Page 236 ---
Its power extends even to things not yet formed. Secondly, at the stage of commonality or origin, form is the formal order; and finally, at the third stage, vital motion itself is posited. But since the more common a function is, the more it pertains to a prior cause, rightly the first cause of all is the Good itself, or the One, from which and on which depend unity and the striving towards the good. But the second cause of things is the primal mind, to which formal order belongs. The third is the primal soul, by which every vital motion everywhere is brought about. Therefore, when we behold the universe, both most beautiful in its forms and order, and most effective everywhere with vital motions, we rightly think that mind rules everywhere and soul breathes everywhere. And since both the order of forms conspires into one for the sake of the good, and vital motion strives towards the good, not without reason do we wish both the mind, which thus orders all things, and the soul, which thus moves all things, to depend on the One and the Good itself. Thus therefore, this corporeal universe, and that which is moved by another, is first brought back to the soul, which is self-moving,

If he has said anywhere that the simple and first act of intelligence is distracted by perception: explain it thus, namely, when perception is an action differing in reality from intelligence, and when perception is by some ministry of imagination, too different from intellect, and meanwhile distracting to other things. He refutes next what they say: that between the mind itself and the soul there is a certain intermediate substance, which they indeed call intellectual reason itself; but they say the soul receives reason from this (substance). For in this way, the soul will have no true and perpetual intelligence. For true and perpetual intelligence is either in the mind itself, or in that which is most immediately participant of the mind. But the soul, according to their opinion, would receive something of intelligence not in the first degree, but in the second, and an image of it rather than its nature. And thus it will neither perceive itself, which is the function of intellectual nature; nor will it be able to conceive the substance of any intellect as independent of subsequent natures; nor comprehend the formal principle of anything, or embrace the definition of truth itself.

when the subject has preceded, just as finally nothing follows. Therefore, from the beginning, there existed a certain necessity of consequence from a superior and efficient cause. Therefore, by the same necessity of consequence, it will always be.

The Maker of the world made the world not by inclination, but by consistency.

IIII He refutes again what they say, that the first soul did not create the world because it remained in its dignity, but because it degenerated. But before I proceed with Plotinus' refutations, it is helpful to review Porphyry's words, to the same effect, from his book demonstrating the paths to the intelligible. Thus he says: None of the substances which are universal and perfect turn to their own generation. But all perfect substances are rather reduced to generating things, and indeed even to the mundane body: which certainly, since it is perfect, is reduced to the soul: the intellectual soul, I say, and therefore it revolves in a circle. But the soul of the world is raised to the intellect: and the intellect is raised to the principle. But a little later he adds: In particular substances, and in those capable of falling into many things, there is a proclivity to deviate towards generations, and therefore in these, a transgression is said to have occurred: in these, infidelity is condemned. Therefore, matter itself contaminates these, because they can be deflected to it, even though in the meantime they are capable of turning themselves to the divine: wherefore perfection, indeed, stood second to the prior things, preserving the same things turned to the prior. Defect also sometimes deflects certain prior things even to posterior things, and causes these very things to love, meanwhile diverging from the superior. Thus he [Porphyry]. In these, he confirms that certain demons, or souls of men, by degenerating from divine things, fabricate bodies. But the world was constructed by a certain divine soul, persevering in divine things. For to accomplish so great, so beautiful, so lasting a work, and to lead it without transgression, and to move it with such wonderful reason, is not the power of something sometimes inclining, but of something always existing in the best state, and making the creation, not so much that it may appear best, as because it is naturally itself the best. But if that power is the best, and as appears from its motion, indefatigable, never

--- Page 239 ---
**IN BOOK VIII, ENNEAD II. 195**

...whether into an earthly or airy [body], but not to have transferred the soul of man into beasts. For thus also the teachers of the Hebrews are said to have understood. Plotinus also judges that these [people] perverted the words concerning the creation of the world, since they take the three words of Timaeus as three substances; by which, however, three properties of the same substance are signified according to Plotinus, namely, that the same God, the maker of the world, conceived [it], that is, decreed [it], and by naturally decreeing, accomplished so many species of things in the world as his own intellect would contemplate ideas in that already living [being], that is, in its living essence. But the heretics said that the living being itself is the intelligible being itself, the first, superior to all intellect. But he who contemplates ideas in it, is the first intellect in a material sense; and he who conceived to create, is the first soul, and that this [soul] creates by some counsel, albeit a bad one, after it had degenerated from the higher [realms]. But Plotinus will prove that the first intelligible and the first intellect are the same in this way: Since the first intellect understands in a perfect manner, it intimately possesses the intelligible. Therefore, it is understood by itself, as if it itself were the intelligible itself, just as it is intellect. Likewise, that which is the first and perfect intelligible must be understood in a perfect manner. But it is understood by perfect reason if it is understood by itself. Therefore, whether you look at the intellect, the intimate intelligible immediately follows; or you perceive the intelligible, the intimate intellect immediately accompanies. And rightly so, because there is a far greater proportion of the intelligible to the intellect, and vice versa, than there is of the visible to sight. For the intellect penetrates the very thing to be understood, and divides, and defines; which no sense accomplishes concerning the sensible. Since therefore the proportion between the intelligible itself and the intellect is wonderful, rightly, by the same path by which something has arrived at being the supreme intelligible, it follows that it is also the supreme intellect, and vice versa. But Plotinus thinks this [being] is the first artificer of the world; nor does he wish the first soul to be excluded from the function of the artificer; but he denies that it makes the world by counsel and leads it with solicitude, otherwise neither could the substance of the mundane work subsist, nor could order persevere, if it were made and moved by some mobile action of the artificer, especially a laborious one. Moreover, he detests much more that they say the artificer soul is devoid of mind, and subject to perturbation, and worse than our souls; when in this creation nothing is done foolishly, nothing appears disturbed. Therefore, he distributes the order of principles in this manner. The most absolute unity or simplicity of God, since it so greatly surpasses all things that it has absolutely no similarity or relation to anything, and therefore does not look at anything before it; certainly it either accomplishes nothing, or all things at once. But indeed the supreme goodness is above all things.
