The maker of the world made the world not by changing itself, but by the abundance of its natural power, as a statue of God.

VIII. When heretics are asked for what reason the maker of the world constructed the world, they respond: because it fell from contemplation, and, as if ambitious, turned itself to acting and commanding. But it was better to assign natural fecundity than an iniquity of will, and thus to answer those asking: Just as heat, by virtue of being heat, naturally heats, and light, by virtue of being light, naturally illuminates and similarly vivifies, so that most powerful agent acts by the presence of its natural power. But it seems altogether contrary to all religion and philosophy, what the heretics were saying: that the maker of the world was formally changed in itself before it made the world, and that the creative faculty, which is eternal—indeed, it is the same there as eternity—had a beginning at some point, namely, when that maker became less powerful due to a fall from better things. It is also against religion to blame the world as evil. For also in Genesis Moses says that the artificer of the world made both individual things in the world good, and all things very good. To this also tends that [saying]: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of his hands. Thus, therefore, the magnitude and power and motion of the universe shows us the wonderful power of divinity, the marvelous order, wisdom, especially preserved amidst such a variety

that the world is evil by nature, and from an evil source. That our souls are better than the soul of the world, and even become better than angels. And this indeed without any effort or duty of purification, solely, namely, by the confession of that heresy. And by certain rites, and a certain pronunciation of words: nor is it permitted for anyone to become good otherwise. Finally, that God himself cares only for the human race. But that there is no providence on God's part for the whole world and worldly things. Which indeed are opposed to the Christian law no less than to the Platonic teachings. For whether you listen to Paul to the Romans, you will learn that God is not only of one nation, but of all nations: or the Gospel, you will know that God provides for the universe even to the smallest things. Likewise, that prophetic saying is confirmed, namely, that all can be called gods, and all sons of the Most High. And together with the Prophet, angels are preferred to souls. Not adoration, but virtue obtains a divine gift from God.

XVII The proper function of providence shines forth in the best disposition of the universe, and in the best state of the world's maker. The heretics foolishly and excessively took away all this, while blaming the Lord and author of providence for the blameworthy disposition of the world. Now indeed, so that they might prove there was nothing good in the world, they said that no laws, either of nature or of men, were good: and that what are called virtues are nothing: nor did they themselves speak anything about virtues: nor did they have any thought for purifying souls. For they preached that if anyone merely thought of God, and invoked Him with certain prayers among them, he would obtain absolutely everything: even if the disturbances of the senses were none.

but it was altogether beautiful once, when it chose and took to fashion a beautiful body, again under a beautiful star and daemon. Moreover, a soul can sometimes be beautiful in a body that is not handsome: either because that which was once not beautiful, eventually became beautiful: or because often, for a beautiful soul striving to fashion a handsome body, a certain impediment arises or has arisen from the things that surround it and that flow together. Our soul, because it is the sister of the soul of the world, can both overcome the Fates, and attain to its blessedness.

XX Where it says that our soul is the sister of the world's soul and of the celestial souls, remember that the intellectual soul is neither a part nor an offspring of the mundane soul or of the celestial souls: likewise, that it can sometimes attain to their blessedness, and in a certain way become their colleague in the governance of the world. Moreover, that we can never, when it withdraws into itself, lessen or even avoid fatal blows. Finally, that it is not permitted to depart from this mundane custody with bonds forcibly broken, and much less is it right to accuse the celestial spheres or souls.

**B** THEREFORE it is not fitting to place more things in the intelligible world for them, nor superfluous thoughts there, which they do not admit, but one intellect always behaving in the same way, entirely unchangeable, which also imitates its father as much as possible: but our soul, partly living with those things, partly inclining towards these things of ours, and finally, partly placed in the middle. **C** happens to the soul, because it did not consist in the best of the universe: in which indeed that soul consisting, which is not a part, and of which we ourselves are not parts, has bestowed gifts upon the universal body of the world according to its capacity to receive: and it (the soul) meanwhile lives far from all solicitude, governing no consultation, nor correcting anything curiously: but adorning the whole from its very intuition towards higher things with wonderful power. THEREFORE, always illuminated and possessing eternal light, it then leads to lower things: and these (lower things) are always contained and live by this light, and from it they receive life according to their respective capacity: just as if by some fire placed in the middle somewhere, whatever can be heated from it is heated: even if the fire is confined within a certain measure. But when powers of unconfined measure are not lacking to the universe,

But if anyone should say that it is to be resolved into matter, let him answer, why he does not similarly concede that matter is also resolvable? [Right Column - English Text]

they blame. And they reduce the architect of the world and the soul entirely to the same thing. To this, indeed, they attribute the same passions as to particular animals.

It has been said elsewhere that this world neither ever began nor will cease, but exists as long as divine things exist. Moreover, that the interaction of our soul with the body does not make the soul better, has also been said before them. But to take the soul of the whole from our own and judge it accordingly is as if someone in a well-ordered city, observing the class of potters or bronze-workers, were to blame the entire city. It is worthwhile, however, to consider how differently the soul of the world governs: namely, the mode is not the same, nor does it govern as if bound.

For besides the many other differences enumerated elsewhere, it was also fitting to consider this: that we are indeed bound by the body, as if by an already formed chain. But in the universe, the soul, already bound by the nature of the body, binds whatever it apprehends; yet the soul of the whole is by no means bound by those things which it binds itself. For it, as mistress, provides the beginning; therefore, it neither suffers from them nor with them.

But we are masters of these things. As much as it (the soul) is raised to the divine which is superior, it remains whole and simple and is not hindered; but as much as it imparts life to the body, it receives nothing back from it. For commonly, that which is in another necessarily receives a passion from that in which it is. But this (the soul) does not further impart anything of itself to that which possesses its own life. Just as if something is inserted into another, it suffers along with that in which it is, when the latter suffers; but if it (the inserted thing) ever dries up, it allows the other to have its own life.

Since neither, when this fire that is in you is extinguished, is the whole fire extinguished; nor, even if the whole fire is extinguished, does that soul suffer anything, but rather the constitution of the body itself. And even if some world could exist through the remaining parts, that soul would nevertheless have no care for it; because its constitution is not similar to the world, nor to any animal: but there, it (the soul) as it were, hangs over, commanding it to stand firm, while here (in the animal) the elements, as if slipping away underneath, are brought back into their former order by a certain secondary bond. But there (in the world), they have nowhere to flee. Therefore, it is not necessary to contain them within, nor to push them back inwards by external coercion; but wherever its

nature willed from the beginning, there each thing naturally remains; but if any of them are naturally moved, those things suffer in the meantime, to whose natures such movement is least congruent. But those things that are naturally moved are rightly carried along, inasmuch as they are members of the universe; some, however, are destroyed from this, since they cannot sustain or deviate from the order of the whole: just as if a great dance is performed in order, and in the middle of its course a tortoise, caught somewhere, is crushed, since it cannot escape the order of the dance; yet if it were to connect itself to the order of the dance, it would not suffer anything from these things.

**BOOK NINE.** **209**

From the fact that one professes to possess something, one already possesses it; indeed, many, knowing that they do not possess many things, boast that they do possess them, and even those who do not have them think they have them, and that they alone possess them, although they are the only ones who do not possess them.

Moreover, anyone discussing many other things, indeed all things, will abundantly and easily find how, in detail, their discourse is. Indeed, I cannot but be affected by shame on account of certain friends who, before they entered into familiarity with us, fell into such discourses, in which they still somehow persevere, although they are not ashamed, but rather strive more earnestly that their opinions may undoubtedly seem true, or even they themselves believe the matter to be so. But we speak only to those known to us, and certainly not to the many who listen to them; for we would achieve nothing by persuasion, trying to persuade them not to allow themselves to be perverted by those people, even if we bring forth demonstrations, for by what reason would they prevail? But they boast more stubbornly. Since there is another way in which one writing may refute those who do not hesitate to cavil about the most excellent and true mysteries of ancient and divine men, therefore, let us for now set aside that mode of discussion. For those who have perfectly understood what has just been said will clearly be able to judge what the rest are like.

I also omit for now that saying which surpasses all absurdity, if indeed it is proper to call this absurdity: for they say that the soul and a certain wisdom nodded to that which is inferior, whether the soul initiated this nod or wisdom was the cause of the nodding, or whether they wish both to be the same; elsewhere, they certainly report that souls have descended, and members of wisdom, and that these enter bodies as if human. But the soul for whose sake they say souls have fallen, they again report that it does not fall at all, as if it did not nod, but only illuminated the darkness. Thence, an image resulted in matter; then, forming here an image of the image through matter, or through materiality, or however they wish to name it, saying indeed that this is one thing, and that another, and inventing many other names for the sake of obscurity, when they thus make what is called the world-maker among them.

And imagining the world as having fallen away from its mother, they deduce it from itself to the furthest images.

Although it was fitting for those who now know, to proceed from here, but those who follow should correct these first principles of ours, approaching these things from divine nature. For it belongs only to that nature which neglects bodily pleasure, to understand what is good and honorable. But those who are entirely devoid of virtue will in no way be able to ascend to higher things. This also provides testimony against them, that they make no mention of virtue, and entirely dismiss all discourse concerning those things which pertain to virtue: nor do they strive to define what virtue and the good are, or how many there are: and altogether whatever things, both excellent and numerous, are contained in the disputations of the ancients: nor again from what sources good things are acquired and possessed: nor in what manner the soul is cultivated and purified. For what they are accustomed to say, 'look to God,' is of no use at all: unless they clearly teach in what manner one is to look. For one might say that nothing prevents someone from looking indeed, yet not abstaining from any pleasure, nor restraining anger: and merely invoking the name of God itself, meanwhile succumbing to all disturbances, and not striving to repel them. Virtue, indeed acquired through prudence, and having progressed to the highest degree, shows God to us: but if anyone pronounces God without true virtue, he has nothing but the name.
Let no one think that he will become good by this very fact, that he despises the world, and the gods who reign in the world, and the other good and excellent things of the world. For every evil person has this primarily, that he despises the gods: nor is anyone entirely evil before he despises the heavenly beings. And if he is not yet evil in all other respects, yet from this one thing alone he becomes evil in all. Therefore, what they say, that they worship intelligible gods, has nothing consistent or akin to it. For whoever loves something, pursues with affection whatever is akin to that which he loves. For you also love the children of him whose father you love. But every soul is a daughter of that father. And the souls in the spheres of the world are intellectual and good, and much more akin to the heavenly beings than ours. For in what way would this world be separated from that, and in what way also the gods who are in the world? But concerning these things we have also spoken in earlier [parts]. But now it must be affirmed that those who despise the kin of the higher divinities do not even know those divinities, but apprehend them only by words. Moreover, what they say, that providence does not reach [the world], how can that be pious? Likewise, how is it entirely consistent with themselves? For they assert that the care of God is only for humans. But whether of humans, only while they are there, or also on earth

XVII
Above the corporeal world is the animal (living) world, mobile in a certain way, and possessing the dimensions of bodies by the magnitude of its own power: and producing this world by the stability of its own power, and most beautiful itself (producing) the most beautiful....

--- Page 261 ---
**BOOK NINE. 217**

From a most beautiful appearance, what impediment could there be, that it should not also be beautiful within? Then indeed, for those to whom nature did not give perfection from the beginning, it perhaps happens that they least attain the end: and therefore they can become corrupt. But indeed it did not happen to the world, that it was ever as if a child, and not yet perfect: nor did anything new grow together for the world as it progressed further, and was added to its body. For whence could that have happened? Since it already possessed all things. But neither is it permissible to imagine anything added to its soul. And if perhaps one were to concede this to the Gnostics, it would still not be permissible to admit anything evil.

They will perhaps say that their discourses indeed cause the commerce of the body to be shunned and held in great hatred: but our discourses detain the soul in the body. This, however, is very similar to if two people inhabit the same beautiful house: and one indeed blames the construction and arrangement of the house and its builder: nevertheless, he remains there: but the other does not blame it at all, but says that the builder of the dwelling constructed it most skillfully: but he awaits the time, as long as he lives there, when he will depart from it: as one who will then no longer need the dwelling: but that one seems wiser and more prepared for departure because he knows how to say that the building is constructed from inanimate stones and wood: and is far removed from the true building: ignoring that there is a great difference between tolerating necessities and bearing them minimally: since he will not depart unhappily from the building which he considers beautiful, if he loves the beauty of the stones moderately.

Indeed, we must remain, while we have a body, in dwellings which have been fabricated by our good soul and sister, possessing very great power, through which it fabricates without labor. But do those men even deign to call the worst people brothers daily: but utterly disdain to call the Sun and other celestial bodies brothers? Moreover, with utterly insane mouth, they separate the soul of the entire world from fraternal fellowship, and indeed, as long as we are corrupt, it is impious to unite ourselves with the heavenly beings by kinship: but only then, when we are good, and are not bodies, but souls in bodies, and thus able to dwell in them, so that we approach as closely as possible that manner of dwelling by which the soul of the world inhabits the whole body.

This, however, is not to be cast down from one's own rank, nor to indulge in external allurements, nor to be broken by hardships. That soul is indeed not struck, for there is nothing from which it can be struck. But we, dwelling here, can repel blows by virtue, so much so that by greatness and strength of mind, some blows become lighter, while others do not touch us at all. But when we have approached most closely that which cannot be struck, then at last we shall imitate the soul of the world and the stars. Likewise, when we have attained the closest likeness, we shall finally conspire into the same.

Then indeed the same spectacles will be offered to us, which are present to the heavenly beings from the beginning, and are not lacking to us, namely, both to those well-constituted by nature, and to those prepared by study. But if some boast that they alone

MARSILIO FICINO'S
COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST BOOK
OF THE THIRD ENNEAD,
CONCERNING FATE.

SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

On eternal things and their action: On the causes of things that come to be: On four opinions concerning fate.

[Marginal note: 1 2 3 with symbols]
IN the order of things, some merely *are*: others, moreover, *come to be*. Likewise, those things that merely *are*, are either principles, or from principles. Again, those things that exist: either always occur, or sometimes. Indeed, things that are primary, insofar as they are primary, cannot be referred to other causes. For that which is simply primary, simply also has no cause. But that which is primary in some genus, has no cause in that genus. Therefore, in the genus of mobile things, that which is mobile in itself, insofar as it is primarily mobile, has no superior cause by which it is mobile: but by which it is intellectual, it has some [cause]. Similarly, the First Intellect is not properly intellect through a superior cause, but that it exists as something one and good, it possesses from a superior cause. But the Good itself has nothing from any cause. Therefore, those things that exist among the eternals from a cause, indeed have their essence from that [cause], which essence is perpetually accompanied by both being and action. Which action or act (to speak according to Plotinus's opinion) is the same there as being. Certainly, where action passes outside, it is undoubtedly other than being. Likewise, where action, even that which remains within, proceeds from an adventitious form, it is also other than being. But where it is both intimate and perpetual, and from an essential form alone, it is indeed the same as being, or at least what is called existing. For being is both from that same form and in that same form: that, namely, from which the act proceeds and in which it resides. Thus, heating, indeed, proceeding from fire into water, is undoubtedly other than the being of fire. Again, to be hot in ignited iron is other than the being of iron: because it is from an adventitious form. But in fire, to be hot is nothing other than to be fire. Since, therefore, in utterly eternal substances there is no adventitious form: and therefore, to act is from the same natural form and in the same natural form from which also is being, and so intimately, it is deservedly the same to act as to be. For we call being the act of essence and of the essential form. Which act is indeed intimate, and an action utterly intimate. For this reason, since life in the soul is not an adventitious form, to live is the being of the soul. Similarly, in intellect itself, to understand, naturally shining forth from the intellectual form, is the being of intellect itself: especially since intellection is the primary action. And therefore, since it is most perfect and intimate, it does not differ from being. This, indeed, the Platonists posit as primary: who do not properly place action in the Good itself: since all action is about the Good. Thus far let it be said concerning those things that properly *are*: which indeed we wish to be neither subject to fate, nor in fate. But those things that *come to be*, if they come to be at some time, we think are subject to fate. If they always *come to be*, that is, if they perpetually revolve, we place them not so much *under* fate as *in* fate. In summary, however, we ought to refer every action placed in motion in any way, as not entirely perfect, to a cause: and indeed, ultimately, to a permanent one. Concerning that which is moved by another, there is no doubt that its motion and action proceed from another. Moreover, that which is moved from itself, that is, by its own nature, has by its very nature that it acts movably: but that it acts simply, and that it *is*, it obtains from elsewhere. For mobile action, since it is more imperfect than stable action, signifies that the essence in which it is, proceeds from another. And such action is governed by a certain stable power of the same essence. Indeed, since motion is like an indeterminate and needy accident, and suffers admitted privation and dispersion, it deservedly depends most [on something else]. Wherefore, from the subject in which it is, and from the efficient power from which it is produced, and from the end for the sake of which it is made, and from a certain inciting occasion

--- Page 263 ---
IN LIBR. I ENNEAD. III. 219

depends on the inciting [occasion]. Let no one, therefore, imagine that a certain inclination and incursion of atoms, or a sudden motion of some body, or a similar inclination of the soul depending on no cause, gave a beginning to things, but rather let him consider every such action or passion to be produced by some higher cause, or even incited by surrounding circumstances. Since, therefore, whatever happens at some time, happens from a cause, we have proximate and manifest causes in most cases. But where proximate causes are not sufficiently evident, or are not sufficient for the effect, we deservedly investigate more remote causes: especially when, under the same impending proximate cause, the effect follows in one instance, but does not follow in another. And when from similar works of men, similar things do not happen to everyone. Likewise, where fortune and the concurrence of things favor beyond the merits of actions, and the opposite. Finally, the diversity of talents, customs, and fortunes, which cannot be so great from causes known to us, compels us to investigate more hidden and higher causes. But in the investigation of hidden causes, the opinion of fate arose among philosophers. Indeed, they define fate by a certain common notion, as a certain necessity imposed upon things from above. Since, therefore, there are especially four opinions concerning principles, namely, there are four opinions concerning fate. demons, executors of a life already chosen and powerfully fated. Indeed, Saturnian demons rule Saturnian souls and perform Saturnian duties; Jovian ones similarly rule Jovian souls and perform Jovian duties; and the rest likewise. And just as humans in any region are partly Saturnian, partly Jovian, so too are demons similarly varied, dwelling in every sphere of the world: the better ones among the Saturnians perform better Saturnian duties; but the worse ones among them are accustomed to performing worse events under the same influence; and in the same way, Martian ones and the rest likewise. But where Plotinus says that the daily motions of the celestial bodies, besides the common welfare of the world, are moreover useful, where they signify future events to those able to understand: he shows that what is signified can be avoided if it is bad; but if good, it can again be aided: much more than a physician can aid health based on the signs that are in us; otherwise, both in Astrology and in medicine, the observation of signs would be in vain, and God, who prescribed the signs, looking out for the welfare of those below from heaven, would have warned in vain.

**Those who introduce a necessary series of events, inevitably carrying out each thing, take away both contingency from the lowest things and freedom from deliberation.**

VII. The fourth opinion concerning fate, which we undertake to discuss, agrees with the second opinion in that it believes all things are generated through seminal reasons from a certain vital principle infused into all,

--- Page 266 ---
COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...The work therefore proceeds then by necessity, but the soul is not, as if compelled, moved to action, if neither an incitement creeping from the body follows by choosing, nor does it consider external advantage or disadvantage concerning bodily things. Nor does it look entirely to external things, nor is it deceived by false opinion, but has intelligence and certain reason, free from passion, as its guide, and directs all things to its own best state as to an end. From this, certainly, that the wise soul directs its actions to itself as to an end, it is clear that it possesses not an external, but an internal principle of action. To this extent, the soul is judged to act, because it operates through a form proper to itself, intimate, and principal, and for its own sake. But when it, either degenerating from itself first, or ignorant, or externally incited and instigated by the body, undertakes something, looking elsewhere than to the soul, it is considered not so much to act as to suffer. It acts most of all when it not only operates from itself and for its own sake, but also acts in itself by itself alone without instruments, that is, it exercises the function of contemplation. But when it lives a voluptuous life without moderation, or follows an active life without prudence, it serves and suffers most grievously. But as often as it pursues an active life with prudence, it partly acts itself, but partly is acted upon, inasmuch as it is also incited to motion by external things, and performs its duty according to the condition of circumstances. Remember, however, that Plotinus here considers the concurrence of things that closely surround us, which he calls fortune, not necessarily everywhere to be reduced to celestial fates, so that it is arranged perfectly, just as celestial things arrange themselves: for the order in these is not as exact as in those, nor is the firmness equal, nor the harmony similar. Hence that saying of Plotinus: "The effects of celestial things among us occur according to the condition of inferior causes"; likewise, "natural effects have a much greater similarity with proximate causes than with remote ones." Again, celestial influences are often not so much causes as signs, therefore he speaks with a certain condition when he says: "And if anything further from the motion of celestial bodies contributes to the work." Finally, he thinks that the order perhaps resulting from there to here can sometimes be changed by human diligence and strength of mind.

**Intellectual nature acts freely, but its effect is sometimes impeded in reason.**

X Therefore, he concludes that things are not agitated by chance, but that there is an order in things consequent through causes, whence things can be artificially made and signified: nor again are all things always driven by external necessity: since it is necessary that not only those things which are moved from without, but also those which are moved from within, exist. And those things which are moved from within, partly indeed by a certain determined instinct of nature, but partly by an absolute and ample and free principle, otherwise the order of movable things will either be null, or will not be reduced to the highest: and those things which are movable, through another to that which is movable by itself, which nevertheless must exist, will least of all be referred. For that which is carried only by the instinct of nature does not move itself, but is either propelled by that which impels nature, like an arrow, or is drawn by a kindred thing, like iron by a magnet. Therefore, the intellectual soul does all things with a certain best, that is, intellectual reason: by means of which reason, whatever it produces, being entirely universal and absolute, it acts from an intellectual principle, it does not suffer. For intellectual wisdom, according to Plotinus and most great philosophers, does not have an external cause, that is, one inciting by force from external occurrences, but shines from within from eternity, and gleams intrinsically, hitherto with absolutely nothing impeding it. It also shines forth into the reason closest to intelligence, and using intelligence whenever it is not impeded. But it is impeded sometimes commonly by a certain distraction of the soul concerning many things, and sometimes specifically in some who are either born insane or become so, and this indeed in three principal ways: for they are either dull, or forgetful, or stupid, or furious. The cause of this insanity is sometimes the ineptitude of the sensual instruments, sometimes the elevation of vapors, sometimes a more vehement intention of imagination by which the act of reason is diminished, sometimes an excessive occupation of nature around the cure of disease, and finally a certain demonic occupation. Perhaps, indeed, just as monstrous actions in morals usually proceed from us by the instigation of lower demons: so insanity often occurs by a certain wondrous contrivance of demons: who, just as they excite vapors of humors and sensible images to incite vices, so also they sometimes provoke vapors in the body and images in the phantasy to incite and thoroughly strengthen it, so that reason is either diminished or deluded thereby. Indeed, that insanity is caused by demons wonderfully irritating the humors, Serapio and Avicenna and greater authorities do not deny, and the Gospel everywhere testifies: where those possessed by demons are healed, the insane are cured. For it is not probable that a soul participating in divinity would either sin so wickedly or be so insane, unless a demonic nature moreover strives for it: therefore perhaps in the second chapter he said that the immense diversity of talents and morals is not only from manifest and proximate causes. Therefore, the Apostle Paul says that our struggle is not only against the body, but against demons destined for this dark air. Therefore, a favorable disposition of humors and limbs, or the position of the stars, does not produce wisdom, but signifies that the use of wisdom is not impeded by an opposite disposition or position. With this impediment removed for us, it sends forth the light of wisdom by itself. What we have said about demons is thus confirmed by Porphyry in the book 'On Oracles': "There are," he says, "bodies of men full of malignant demons, especially those who live on more delicate feasts. For when we eat, they come and adhere to the body: therefore fasting and chastity are especially praised: not because the good God is properly pleased in this way, but so that those who delight in blood and impurity may depart, who, so that they too may enjoy these things, enter the bodies of the voluptuous." For it is clear that a vehement desire for perishable things and the impulse of a lustful spirit do not grow excessively from anywhere else than from the presence of malignant demons: therefore, when appetite is more vehemently inflamed, and the ardor of pleasure so agitates the soul that all thought wanders to external things, then know that such demons are present, whose presence causes the naturally avid spirit in us to grow. These things there, which he also confirms in the book 'On Abstinence' with almost the same words.

MARSILIAN SUMMARY.

That not all things proceed from fatal necessity.
I.

[Decorative initial Q showing a seated figure]INCE indeed you desire, Lawrence, to understand separately what Marsilio Ficino thinks about these matters, I will repeat the matter itself from another beginning. It is established that the Good itself provides for all things, from the order of all things wonderfully instituted towards a certain end. In which order indeed both individual things everywhere are directed to their own good, and all things together lead to the common good. And if it may seem strange that the Good itself, in the order of its providence, permits evil, it is nevertheless sufficiently established that it often permits it, namely for the sake of good, while it permits the destruction of present things, so that infinite new forms may subsequently be generated: which indeed to exist simultaneously, neither the repugnance of forms allows, nor does space admit. Since indeed God is goodness itself simply, yet is not simply necessity itself, but as far as it pertains to good, evil seems more (if I may say so) to be opposed to God than contingency. Therefore if it permits evil, doubtless it also permits contingency. Nevertheless, just as evil everywhere leads back to good, so too the contingent everywhere reduces to the necessary. For whatever, while it was future, could happen and not happen, that whole, even while it now exists, is necessary to exist, and when it has passed, it was necessary to have passed: and with circumstances collected from all sides by condition, the contingent often seems to become necessary. Therefore, the opposite of necessity, according to its formal definition, should not be considered that which is called impossible: for in the very opposite of formal necessity, no necessity ought to be included, yet this is included in that which is impossible. For impossible is that which cannot be. But that which cannot be, is necessary not to be. Likewise, in the necessary itself, the impossible seems to be included: for that which is necessary to exist, it is impossible not to be. Therefore, the true opposite of the necessary is the contingent. For just as the very definition of the necessary is limited to being only, or not being only: so conversely the definition of the contingent tends towards being, as well as not being. But truly

--- Page 268 ---
224 COMMENTARY ON MARSILIO FICINO

(things that) would be judged from heaven, the same things among us happen contingently from this matter and region. Matter, I say, because it is always equally desirous of all forms. Region, I say, because innumerable and conflicting qualities converge here. Therefore, regarding the celestial influx, which by a certain proper order is sometimes destined to proceed to something certain, *both* this matter (which is also desirous of other things and easily capable) gets confused with others and loses its form, subsequently about to receive something else, *and* the region full of discordant qualities immediately mixes and transforms it, so that scarcely anything certain arises here from heaven, and you can scarcely guess what kind of thing is about to be born, unless perhaps you have surveyed the whole: so that you may be able to discern how many and what kind of causes and conditions flow together at any moment, both from above, and from the middle, and from below, and what again and of what kind arises from all of them.

Therefore, if corporeal nature, which is both more manifestly subject to the celestial body and seems to be determined especially to one thing, does not necessarily admit celestial influxes—I mean precisely such as are sent from heaven, much

also dissimilar, inasmuch as it proceeded outwards, and not only degenerated from it, but moreover became something else and different by a certain proper quality: just as a ray [of light] in the sky is caressing, but on earth devouring; likewise in the sky it is shining, but in a cloud it is red, so that it is not surprising that something here subsequently becomes such, which properly does not originate from there. Therefore, many such things are produced everywhere by causes inferior to heaven, and such things as are not produced by heaven. Other things are consumed by time: on the contrary, the same animals grow old, under whatever star they are said to be born. Similar things happen concerning the devastation of fruits and crops, at whatever time they may have grown, due to human custom and desire, not due to a fatal series, one may argue. Indeed, I daily observe the boundaries and influences of the planets, and diligently explore what they portend. I omit that on an (as it is called) unfortunate day, prosperous things happen to many: on a fortunate day, adversities befall many, and in any given moment, of those contending, some indeed overcome, others are overcome. Certainly, the astrologers' unlucky days are often most serene and peaceful, and lucky days often the contrary. I, for my part, have experienced that the qualities of both bodies and minds are affected differently by differences in the air, rather than by different aspects of the stars. Finally, I have found that the noted effects of the planets turn out to be vastly different according to the diversity of regions and people. If rain is promised, in one place it rains much, in another little, in another nothing, according to the differences of regions. And so, since philosophers never wished to rest in proximate causes, whoever posited corporeal principles, such as atoms, making individual things by their motion, impulses, and mutual entanglements, said that individual things come to be and exist in that condition, by which those principles come together, act, and suffer: and that our impulses and affections are such as those make them. These therefore introduce this necessity everywhere into principles, and into those things which are from them: and whoever says that other bodies are principles, and that all things are made from them, he indeed thinks that all things serve a certain necessity founded in these. But others, ascending to the very principle of the universe, deduce all things from it: and think that this first cause diffuses itself through all things, and not only moves, but also makes individual things. Which indeed they also call fate, considering fate to be the most powerful cause moving all things, not only all other things that happen, but also our thoughts to proceed from its motions: no otherwise than as individual parts in an animal are moved, not indeed by themselves, but by that which holds the chief place in any animal. Others moreover judge fate to be the circuit of the whole world embracing all things, and making individual things by its motion, and accomplishing them by the mutual positions and configurations of stars, both wandering and non-wandering. And relying on predictions made through celestial bodies, they think that individual things happen from there. Moreover, someone could describe fate in another way, saying that it is a mutual entanglement of causes, and a connected series emanating from above, by which later things always obey earlier things: and these very later things are reflected in the preceding ones, as if by which it is brought about, that subsequent things always follow the antecedents.

**ON BOOK II, ENNEAD III. 235**

**MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY**
**ON BOOK TWO OF THE THIRD ENNEAD,**
**CONCERNING PROVIDENCE.**

**SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.**

**Order in the world does not happen by chance.**

**C**HANCE we are accustomed to posit only in those things which can be otherwise. But the possibility of things being otherwise arises only from the indeterminate nature of matter, always flowing into one thing and another, and not from the nature of form, which always determines something certain. But in the order of the universe there is both prime matter, which is not from matter, and forms naturally subsisting in themselves, which also cannot be from matter. Therefore, neither these substances, nor their distinction in themselves, can come about by chance. For perhaps the distinction of certain individuals, distinguished from each other by the mere division of mass, can happen by some chance. But the distinction of species among themselves, which is formal, cannot possibly have happened by any fortune. But things must have been produced from the beginning along with a special distinction: since in the universe there are many things which are neither generated from each other, nor again from some common source, inasmuch as they do not agree in matter. Therefore, neither the formal distinction itself, nor the production of things, could have happened by any chance: especially since a cause existing per se is prior to that which is per accidens. Since therefore later things mostly proceed from a cause determined per se, it is impious to say that prior things arose from a fortuitous cause, and that the most mobile chance was the principle of stable things: when, however, the opposite must necessarily happen, that is, mobile things are always ruled and led by stable things and ordered in their motions. Moreover, since it has been proven elsewhere that the universe is made by the divine intellect, which is evident from the most artful order of things proper to intelligence, it is necessary that the common form of the universe be both conceived by the intelligence of God and constituted by His will, which no event frustrates. Since, therefore, the form of the world is not beyond the intention of the agent, it rightly does not happen by chance. But since the form of the whole consists in the distinction and order of its parts, neither could the distinction of things itself again have been fortuitous. Finally, what is best in a work should rightly be indicated as the end of the work: but the best of the whole world is placed in the mutual order of its parts. But order cannot exist without distinction: through such an order the world is constituted in its integrity, which is its best. Therefore, the order of the parts of the universe and their distinction, as the best end of its production, is why the order and distinction of things cannot have happened by chance.

**Worldly order does not arise from matter.**

If the distinction of species does not result from chance, it follows that neither does it result from matter. For since matter is naturally indeterminate towards very many things, if anything proceeds from it, it flows forth fortuitously: especially if no intention of a superior agent is introduced. If you say that matters are diverse, and therefore various forms proceed from them, you will be compelled to confess that matters, since they have the most imperfect condition of being, rightly depend not on themselves, but on a superior principle. And therefore, both that they exist and that they are distinct, they derive from elsewhere. And thus, that matters are not the primary cause of distinction in the world: especially since there are many things, distinct from each other, none of which consist of matter: and matter itself is not separated from immaterial things by other matter. To this is added that any agent, when it acts through form, intends form as an end. Therefore, forms were not introduced into the universe for the sake of matter, but both matter exists so that forms may be natural, and matters are thus affected everywhere, and thus so that forms may be such. But the distinction of things according to species is formal per se. This distinction, therefore, should not be referred to matter as the primary cause, but matter entirely to forms: which indeed is moved differently by a cause acting through form and intending form. And rightly so, since matter is viler than form, forms are not referred to matter as an end, but conversely matter is referred to forms, while indeed by the very form of the supreme agent, it is made, and moved, and affected in certain ways everywhere. Therefore, formal distinction in the universe proceeds not primarily from the condition of matter, but from the intention of the author. But whatever follows matter, inclines not so much to the formal as to the deformed, or the division of matter in quantity, does not vary the special form.

**Worldly order does not arise from a diversity of principles.**

If anyone, admiring the diversity of things, therefore introduces a diversity of primary agents as a cause, he ought to consider whether these diverse agents have that order among themselves or not. If they have some common order, they possess it from some one superior source. From which they are, and are distinct, and are united, to which the distinction of all things is finally reduced as to a cause. But if those agents are said to have no order, they will concur by chance, and no perpetual order will be preserved in things.

**The order of things does not arise merely from the succession of things: but from the intention of one.**

There are those who cannot derive the diversity of multiple things from one immediate cause, but believe that multitude gradually grows from one into two, from two again into three, and so on, or four. Namely, from the fact that the first cause is entirely simple and absolutely one, and makes one, which, not being able to completely equal the purity and act of the cause, lapses into potentiality and act. But this opinion indeed assigns determined causes to individual effects, but cannot assign one cause to the entire universe of things, but will believe the whole to result from the concurrence of all causes: and thus to happen by some chance. Therefore, what is best in the universe, namely the common whole...

u 4

--- Page 280 ---
236 COMMENT. MARSIL. FICINI
the good of the whole, consisting in the order and distinction of all parts, must be referred to the best cause of those that exist. Therefore, the distinction and disposition of things proceeds not merely from the successive degrees of causes, but from the providence of the first cause. But who does not see that it is impious to reduce this very thing which is best in all things to a certain defect of causes? inasmuch as, namely, a subsequent cause degenerates from the simplicity of a prior cause. Now indeed, if the complete disposition of the world, which is placed in the order of all parts, just as order consists in distinction; if, I say, such a disposition, as the ultimate form of the world, and the best and most formal gift, and the end of all things, rightly corresponds to the first cause, then deservedly do subsequent causes after God serve this disposition. Therefore, this does not result as if by chance from the gradual action of subsequent causes; but to establish or preserve this, subsequent causes do whatever they do, as if to an end prescribed to them by the mind of the first cause. In which mind, if the disposition of things is designated, certainly all things are necessarily described. And if there is the most efficacious intelligence there, very many things can proceed from it at once; especially because divine power can do very many things through one act, and, as if immense, is not limited to one; and the simpler it is, the more (so to speak) united and stronger, and more powerful for pro

--- Page 281 ---
IN BOOK II. ENNEAD III. 237

inasmuch as it is a formal order. But since there is no motion and time there, nothing of the present form has passed into the past: nor is anything lacking in the future. Again, since there is no dimension, by which one part usually differs from another part, all are in every part: And therefore every form is omniform, although in different ways. For the formal distinction itself is not removed, although dimension and time are removed. For even where there is dimension and motion, many very different qualities are simultaneously in the same thing, and all are in every part of it. Since therefore in the intellectual world all things are in each, and therefore nothing is lacking to anyone, deservedly there is no motion there, no impulse from one to another, no injury, or new generation. For the unity of the container does not allow some things there to be contrary to others. Indeed, even if they were contrary: yet this would not make an impulse into that, since nothing is lacking to anyone, and each thing is entirely in act, so that nothing can be made from it. But altogether because motion is proper to the body of the heaven, and status (rest) to the incorporeal, deservedly, just as the heaven moves more by this very fact, the more it acts and generates on earth: so also that (the incorporeal) the more truly it remains, the more truly it does this whole, and makes all things in this.

How this world is made from the supernal, and degenerates.

II. But in what way does this world proceed from that? Indeed, just as from any simpler seed a manifold sprout naturally springs forth everywhere: the fecundity of that (seed) truly turns into a very great progression in this (sprout). Its immense power in this becomes ample dimension: that vigorous act here passes into motion, and eternity into time. Therefore, from the distance, both of form and of position, discord arises: but from division, indigence occurs: from both, appetite, and motion, and impulse. For since all nature is from the good, and therefore none of its intention is towards evil, but towards good: doubtless natural things do not act out of hatred among themselves to destroy what is alien: but out of indigence and self-love, so that they may sustain and refresh themselves from elsewhere. But since the first nature in each genus, as most fertile, makes by itself in that genus what follows, much more does the first essence and life need no other aid than essential life, by which it may generate the essences and lives of things: but by that very fact, properly by which it is and lives, other things thence obtain essence and life. If it is said to effect also through intelligence and will, nothing is therefore added from there. For intelligence and will there is nature itself. Insofar therefore as nature acts, it acts by necessity: but insofar as nature there is intelligence, it acts also by will. But since it acts both through voluntary nature and through natural will, doubtless it does not need inquiry and counsel for acting. Therefore, if you distinguish essence and intelligence there by reason, you will see the matter of this world flowing from essence, and form from intelligence: and just as essence there is thought to precede intelligence in a certain order, so here you will think matter precedes form. But before that intelligence provides form to the world, it presents to itself an incorporeal (form) near to it, far distant from the corporeal: namely, from its own life, creating the soul of the world as if intermediate between essence and intelligence, a vegetative life capable of intelligence, also intermediate between corporeal matter and form: just as life there holds the middle ground between essence and intelligence. And this very reason is the seminal reason of the world, and as it were a certain word of divine intelligence, by which matter, being struck, received the mundane adornment. But where you read, "Intellect infuses reason into matter": explain it as not only intellect simply as intellect, but also animal intellect, namely formed by the first intellect. For from that (first intellect) through this (animal intellect), and from this (animal intellect) by the power of that (first intellect), the generative power springs forth into matter, depending on the essence of both. Similarly it is usually said: The Sun generates natural things, which however it does with light flowing from it. And there solar light and lumen together will effect these things through heat. But it compares both intellects to the male. For it generates as separated from what is generated. But the seminal nature of the world by the seminal power of the male, for both act intrinsically. But the world to the generated offspring. For everywhere the members are now distributed among themselves, and the parts are now repugnant, which were together in the seed and did not fight. Indeed, the world consists of necessity, that is, of matter and defect from contingent matter. Likewise, of intelligence, that is, of a formal order referring to intelligence. It is resolved into parts, as it were intimate, that is, into matter and seminal and formal reason. But the very essence of the intellectual soul is not an intimate part of the world, but presides over it.

Four worlds after the good: intellectual, animal, seminal, sensible: and how procession and judgment occur.

III. If anything in considering the world offends you, do not accuse God: as if he had not consulted well and chosen concerning the construction of the world. For he does not need counsel: but nature itself acts sufficiently. Nor again accuse nature in the first principle of things. For it is goodness itself, and by goodness it makes the simply best work most immediately, namely the intellectual world, and this indeed by its first purpose. For if it acts by goodness, it acts also by will. For will concurs with goodness in the first. Therefore it wills the intelligible world by a first (so to speak) will: but the animal world which subsequently follows from the intelligible, it wills in a certain way by necessity, by a necessity (so to speak) of consequence: for it is not hidden from it that the second follows from the first work, nor again does it reject it, but it does not approve it as the first. Similarly, that intellectual world generates the animal world not by counsel, but by nature. But since its nature is intelligence, and intelligence is will, while nature acts, intelligence acts also by will: first, I say, the animal world, and consequently also the seminal world in nature, which it knows necessarily follows the animal. By the same reason, the animal world, that is, the intellectual soul, generates life and generative nature by a certain natural intelligence and will: namely, the seminal world, the ultimate trace of divine things. But by necessity of consequence it generates the sensible (world) following the seminal: following, I say, from the seminal (world) using only life to effect this: not however by intelligence or will, which it lacks. For thus by living it acts just as the intellectual soul, and the first intellect acts by understanding, and conversely, thus naturally intellect by understanding acts, and in the manner of nature, just as nature by living generates, and by the order of intelligence fabricates. Therefore, do not entirely estimate and weigh the admirable dignity of the good itself, or of pure intellect, or of animal intellect, from the sensible world: but from the sensible (world) infer the dignity of the seminal, from this the nature of the soul, and from the soul the excellence of the mind, and finally from the mind the good. Then indeed, in contemplating the sensible world, do not fix your gaze on the parts, but behold the whole: nor refer the whole to the parts, but the parts to the whole: nor demand this work to be simply the best, but the best as far as

--- Page 282 ---
238 COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...but the best insofar as it takes degrees, and the nature of the fourth world already after the good. You will note meanwhile where the world is imagined to speak: sometimes there are many kinds of living beings in the lowest sphere of the world: and also many above, throughout, immense in dignity and amplitude of space, virtue, and magnitude: of which he names the first gods, the second demons, the third particular souls, which are transferred into demons: and where he places the peoples of demons, he shows that throughout the world above us there are distributed flocks of demons, and that they have their leaders who follow the stars as kings: for the bodies of demons above us everywhere follow the movements of the stars by their own motion, and everywhere perform a similar dance. They also imitate the stars in their powers, magnitude, figure, and mode of action: and as stars act by the gaze of their rays, producing an effective imagination in those who follow. You will note moreover that aether is ignited air: likewise that all things depend on the good, inasmuch as all things desire the good. Finally, that life itself, simply speaking, is mind itself, simply speaking: where he says that intellectual nature alone has all life. Thus, therefore, you will infer that every degree of things participates in life insofar as it possesses something intellectual. Porphyry thus confirms in Timaeus that the world is made by God not by counsel, but by nature: Arts indeed require instruments, because they neither preside over all matter, nor dominate entirely, and they labor externally. Natural powers, however, because they are perfections and intrinsic, act by their very being alone whatever they do: thus all things, and thus the soul always nourishes, increases, generates, breathes, feels, and the rest, by essential life. Even powerful imagination, by a certain act of its own, immediately affects the body with various qualities and motions. Furthermore (as theologians relate) demons, by their imaginations, without instrument or external act, widely perform wonders, suddenly as they wish, emitting most effective rays from thence, and often by the motions of their imagination showing extraordinary forms to those who are able to perceive such things: much more does the world's creator, by his very being, that is, by his very understanding, exhibit substance to the universe: an individual, namely, to a divided world. For to whom is it strange that the corporeal is propagated from the incorporeal? Indeed, from a tiny seed often sprouts a vast animal, composed of so many, so great, and so diverse members. Yet even in a small seed, the seminal reason itself is not small, while it produces great things: nor again great, while it thrives entirely in every particle of the seed, but seminal reason indeed needs matter: divine reason, however, needs nothing, but fabricates all things: and while it remains in its own nature, it produces and moves all things. Thus far Porphyry.

Whatever evils appear either concerning bodies or concerning souls, are reformed into good.
IV
While this element somewhere lends its parts to other elements, meanwhile it borrows parts from others elsewhere: and therefore the spheres of the elements seem to suffer no evil. Similarly, in the dissolution of composites, the world itself suffers no evil. For either the elements then return to their spheres, or another composite is generated, and generation itself, while it takes parts from the elements, adorns them with new forms: and this perpetual vicissitude of generation is necessary for the world. For since worldly matter both can and ought to receive innumerable forms of composites for its perfection, and cannot receive all at the same time: because neither does the matter, from which they are made, suffice for innumerable composites simultaneously, nor does space contain them, nor do such diverse things concur: it has come to pass that it receives by perpetual change, while the heavens likewise assume innumerable figures by motion and acquire new powers, which they can neither admit simultaneously nor while remaining fixed, as if they were conflicting: and meanwhile, by motion, it contributes to the natural transformation of lower matter. By this reason, therefore, both local and formal transmutation, both in heaven and under heaven, contributes to the best state of the universe, and is therefore considered good: especially because the order of the whole world is a certain rule, as it were, for the best of the universe, by which we ought to judge individual things as good, insofar as they appear to contribute to the order. Order, however, seems to require that what has been constructed by another, and then constructed from the destruction of others, should sometimes be destroyed by another, in turn, for the construction of other things. Whatever meanwhile is born or happens to be harmful and evil to some, is not permitted to occur otherwise than by contributing to other and more things, and to the good, and unless it duly completes the order of the universe. Moreover, the order of the whole requires that if, from the wonderfully overflowing power of the first principles, very many subsequent degrees arise, and from the unity of the first principles, stable things immediately originate: that thereafter, by a descending procession, as the state itself grows, it should be mixed with motion, and immediately self-moving essences should come into being, before descending to things moved by another. For since motion is derived from state, motion itself is rightly distinguished by the distinction of the state itself. Therefore, just as many things stable by another are reduced to other things stable in a certain way by themselves: so also those things which are moved by others are finally resolved into those which have motion from themselves. Then, indeed, in the very order of self-moving things, the higher ones must be constituted in a certain common power, and

**Rational souls are compelled neither by superiors nor by inferiors to base actions.**

[Symbol] Since he said in the preceding (discussion) that humans are free under providence, he then doubts how to understand what is often said by Plato: that humans do not become evil of their own accord. For if this is so, they seem to be compelled to sin, whether by heaven, or by some other fatal and inner instinct, or by a seminal principle. It is answered that when they sin, they are voluntarily moved to the action they chose, although they do not voluntarily fall into a perverse habit, which secretly and gradually grows from frequent actions. Thus they begin their movement from will; and insofar as they proceed thus for a long time, they necessarily slide into such a habit; and from such a habit they are necessarily transferred to such punishment. That humans are not everywhere drawn to action by inferior bodies is clear, when they choose and perform things which reason proves to be both beyond and contrary to the condition of inferiors. That again, neither by superiors, whether bodies or their ruler

from present things it wishes to form future things, so that it may achieve an infinite number of things in succession, which it cannot achieve all at once. Among these, you will note four things concerning the seminal reason, that is, concerning universal nature. First, that this is the efficient principle of all generable things. Second, that this embraces all these things, inasmuch as it comprises the seeds of all things. Third, that individual things which are generated are made individually through it, namely, according to its effective and exemplary power. Fourth, that the entire disposition of natural things among themselves and their vicissitude is prescribed in it, and is thus expressed outwardly just as it is impressed inwardly, so that nothing is left outside of providence. For even that which happens contingently in operation is not contingent to the reason itself, but is already pre-signed and wonderfully ordered. Among these, he touches upon the opinion of those who think that the souls of all living beings can be separated from their present bodies, and not be resolved into the soul of the universe, but subsist in their own individuality, and return again to bodies. By one power, indeed, you understand and dispute; by the other, meanwhile, you nourish the body, and generate and dispense individual things in the body: for this reason, you neither generate what you understand, nor, conversely, do you understand what you generate. But consider the divine mind to generate equally and conversely by the very same act by which it understands. Just as to shine and to be hot, which are in fire by two qualities, are in the sun by one: so to understand and to generate are in you two acts through twin powers, but in God they are a single act, to which is subject both a certain intelligence of the world-soul, like art, and the vegetative power of the mundane soul, in place of nature. To these, indeed, is subject the body of the world, so animated, so directed, like the body of an animal and a plant. For these three conspire with each other: the divine mind, the world-soul, nature, in which all mundane things are so present that the whole is comprehended in each part. The conspiracy of these, therefore, is called the root of the mundane tree, or the radical vigor diffused entirely everywhere through the tree. In the mundane tree, however, things are now so different that from the root comes the trunk, from this many branches, from these more shoots, from these very many leaves and fruits: in which, even in the outermost parts, the vigor of the root itself is preserved, apt for propagation. In these, therefore, it can first be considered that all mundane things, however much they may seem disconnected from each other, are nevertheless interconnected, and subject to the same principle; then, that they can easily communicate with each other in action and passion. Furthermore, that all things are most easily governed by the same [principle] remaining everywhere, and connecting all things thoroughly into one, articulately, like a nerve.

**English Translation:**

256 PLOTINUS ENNEAD. III

Therefore, Intellect, infusing something of itself into matter, itself remaining immobile and quiet, fashioned all things: and this is the Reason flowing from Intellect. Indeed, what flows from Intellect is Reason, and it flows always as long as Intellect itself remains in the order of things. But just as in the seminal reason, all things are simultaneously in the same place, and nothing fights with another, or disagrees, or hinders, and yet something happens in the mass, where indeed one part is elsewhere, and another is hindered and harmed by another: so certainly from the one Intellect and the Reason flowing from it, this universe has sprung forth, now distant from itself: and necessarily, some things are born friendly and salutary to each other, while others are hostile and pernicious: and partly willingly, partly unwillingly, they destroy each other: and by their very destruction, they bring about mutual generation. And at the same time, the maker established a single harmony in these things, suffering and acting in such ways, while each sounds its own peculiar note: but Reason constitutes in them a single consonance and tempering of order throughout the universe. For this universe is not like Intellect and Reason there (in the intelligible world), but a participant in Intellect itself and Reason. Therefore, it needed consonance, namely, with Intellect and necessity simultaneously concurring: and the latter indeed drawing it towards what is worse, and deflecting it into the privation of reason: since it itself lacks reason, while Intellect temporarily dominates necessity. For the intelligible world is solely Reason, nor can another such be made, that it might be solely Reason. But if anything else was made after it, it had to turn out less than it, neither more than Reason, nor again merely some matter, otherwise it would have lacked order. Therefore, a mixture emerged. And indeed, that in which the world is defined is matter and reason: but that from which it begins and is governed is soul perfected in the mixture: which indeed should not be thought to labor, since it governs the whole most easily as if by its mere presence.

III
The corporeal world proceeds from the intelligible divine nature, and is as optimal as it can be, if the whole of it is considered.

Nor can anyone rightly disparage this world as if it were not beautiful, or as if it were not the best of all that can exist with a body: nor again accuse the cause by which the world exists. Firstly, indeed, since the world exists out of necessity, and was not constructed by the counsel of reason, but by a more excellent nature generating a work similar to itself according to nature: then, even if counsel had been involved in its cause, the world is not a disgrace to its author. For he made a whole that is entirely beautiful and sufficient, and friendly to itself: moreover, equally fitting for its parts, both greater and lesser. Whoever therefore blames the whole in its parts, blames foolishly: since it is proper to consider whether the parts harmonize and are accommodated to the whole by comparing them to the whole: and when considering the whole itself, it is by no means proper to look at the smallest individual particles: otherwise, that would not be the act of a man blaming the world, but of one taking certain parts of the world separately from others. Just as if someone were to look only at a hair of an entire animal, or a small toe, neglecting to contemplate the wondrous spectacle of the whole human, and by Jove...

A just as if someone, having completely disregarded all other living beings, were to take the most abject, or, having dismissed an entire genus, like a human Thersites, were to bring him into the midst. But since what has been made is the entire world at once, if one wishes to turn the ears of the mind to it, perhaps you will hear it thus exclaiming: "God undoubtedly made me, and from that I was made perfect, constituted from all living beings, self-sufficient, completely satisfying to myself, lacking nothing: because all are in

IX
Besides the action of God, other things also act, especially men, who meanwhile are provoked in all ways by providence to God.

It is not right, however, that providence should be such that we are absolutely nothing; otherwise, if providence itself is everything, and it alone, there will no longer be providence. For whose providence would it be further? Indeed, it would be divinity alone. But now divinity indeed exists, and it applies itself to another, not, however, so as to remove that other itself; but approaching, for example, man, it preserves in him what it is to be man. And this is to preserve one living by the law of providence: which indeed is acting whatever the law prescribes for him. But it prescribes that men who have become good will thereafter maintain a good life, even after death, while bad men will have the opposite. But it is wrong to think that those who have turned out bad are guarded by other saviors, while they themselves, being lazy, rely only on vows. For this reason, it is neither right for the gods, having interrupted their own life, to dispense individual affairs to the wicked; nor is it fitting for good men, living a different life, better than the human condition, to apply themselves to governing worse things; since neither have these (good men) ever cared by what way they might become leaders of others' good, meditating on how that (goodness) might be present for themselves, but they also invite if anyone spontaneously arises good; since more would have already become good, if people had appointed these (good men) as leaders. The human race, therefore, made an animal indeed, yet not the most excellent of all things, but holding a middle and choosing order, at the same time, however, in the place where it is placed, by the benefit of providence, it is by no means allowed to perish, but is continually recalled to higher things, everywhere by all the devices which divinity uses, continuously making virtue powerfully dominant; by which indeed it has happened that the human race has never lost its rational faculty; indeed, it is a participant, even if not supremely, of wisdom, and of mind and art and justice, which individuals exercise among themselves, and where they inflict injury on some, they believe they are acting justly: for they judge them to be worthy who are affected by injury by them. **A** No wise person blames the earth for bringing forth its adornment. **C** But if humans are unwillingly evil, and are such unwillingly, no one will blame either those who inflict injury, or those who suffer, as if they suffer such things by themselves. Perhaps indeed they are said not to sin spontaneously, because sin itself is not voluntary. **X** Although evil habits are not voluntary, actions are voluntary.

**270 PLOTINUS ENNEAD. III.**

...having by nature their essence, which is supplied. For indeed in the whole, beauty and decorum flourish, if each thing is arranged where it is fitting, sounding forth evils in darkness and Tartarus: for in these it is beautiful to sound thus. Therefore, that whole is beautiful only if, not if anything whatsoever is like a stone, but rather if each one, contributing its own proper tone, rightly leads to one complete harmony, itself also resounding life, but a lesser and inferior one, and more removed from perfection. Just as in a flute, a single sound does not suffice, but a lesser and moreover weaker one is required to completely achieve the entire consonance of the flute: because the harmony is divided into unequal parts, and indeed the individual tones are unequal among themselves; but a perfect harmony is made up of all. For indeed the universal Reason is one, but it is distributed into things that are not equal: whence the places of the whole are diverse, partly better, partly worse; then unequal souls thus correspond to unequal places. From this it follows here that the places are dissimilar, and unequal souls obtain dissimilar places, as if according to certain dissimilarities of a flute or another instrument: and they also inhabit places differing among themselves according to the variety of souls, singing indeed their own songs in each place, but harmonious both with the individual places and with the universe. But what is sung badly by any soul to itself, is sung well to the whole. Likewise, what happens to them contrary to nature, happens to the universe according to nature. Neither does a lesser tone harmonize less with the whole than a greater one, nor does one singing more unsuitably to itself, on this account render the whole more unsuitable: Just as neither does some wicked commoner render a city established by just laws worse, if indeed it is expedient to use this other example now. For indeed the use of the wicked is also necessary in a city when circumstances sometimes demand it thus, and such a person is rightly placed.
