**MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD, CONCERNING DAEMONS.**

**SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.**

Summary of the book, also concerning daemons, and concerning one's own daemon.

[Large decorative initial S] UMMARY of this book concerning each person's daemon is of a daemonic rather than a divine nature. Since the soul is all things, and naturally possesses free motion, it can indeed form itself within itself into the proper likenesses of all things, and subsequently conform such bodies of animals and plants to itself. If, therefore, it has lived in the manner of a plant: after this life it forms the body of a plant, in which only the vegetative power acts: but sense presides over such a life as a daemon, not as an agent, but as an assisting observer. Similarly, if a soul living as a beast, finally becomes a beast exercising sense with only vegetative power, the rational power hangs over it idly, and as some observing daemon. But he who lives by reason together with sense, has the mind assisting like a daemon: he who finally lives by mind, seems to have God appointed as his daemon. In this matter, Plotinus partly followed Timaeus, who said that a superior power of the soul is the guide of man and a daemon. He also followed the Pythagorean verses: which implore God to show us what Daemon we should use: then they declare that in each person there is, as a daemon, a certain divinity of their own nature, which can reveal hidden things to us. Hence, Plotinus and Iamblichus, following the opinion of the Egyptians, assign to each person their own intellect, as a daemon of reason always contemplating all things. But to compose this book, he was led, as Porphyry narrates, by the magical works of an Egyptian priest: who both professed to demonstrate each person's daemon with his eyes, and demonstrated to Plotinus and many others present, not Plotinus's daemon, but God: since Plotinus not so much by reason A

--- Page 322 ---
288 COMMENTARY. MARSILIO FICINO.
...than by intelligence he lived, relying namely much more on intuition than on discourse, and not merely suppressing disturbances, but extirpating them. Wherefore, in this book he not only teaches what kind of daemon each person has, but also exhorts to obtain God instead of a daemon. So far, the summary of the book. But that there are, besides the parts of the soul, other external daemons in addition, both very many and leaders of men, Plato often declares, and all Platonists, and Plotinus himself elsewhere, and especially in the book on Love. In this book, however, he especially introduces daemons who are parts of the soul, because it had not yet been discussed by others, and corresponding to these degrees of daemons, we also have different degrees of external daemons. For where life is ordered according to imagination, our external daemon is more keenly in the lowest air, namely, and agitates us through our imagination with its own imagination; but where life is lived according to reason, the daemon from outside, from the middle air, turns human reason with its own reason; where finally life is intellectual, the daemon from the highest air inspires intelligence through intelligence; and they do this not so much by choice, as by the custom of nature. For also in us, the contemplation of intellectual light naturally moves the imagination to imagine sensible light, and imagination in sleep moves the senses, and in waking, frequently the affections in the manner of nature; and conversely, passion moves sense, sense moves imagination, and this naturally

--- Page 323 ---
IN BOOK IV. ENNEAD III. 279
however it can in us, and however we can, we accomplish. After, namely, that celestial influence vanished for many years, even if it will not return to the same state: from which it appears that it rather signified our actions than performed them. But now let us proceed to the words of Plotinus.

How intellect produces soul, soul nature, nature matter.
1 All bodies always do something, and by acting, they emit something outwards, simple ones indeed without any internal change of themselves. For since they are uniform, and part holds part, and they have nothing alien within, deservedly no substance flows out. Thus fire provides heat and light undiminished; similarly, water, by providing cold and its quality, generates substance in turn: but composite things, by contrast, emit vapors outwards with some detriment to themselves. Much more do intellect and soul always propagate something from themselves: intellect propagates soul, soul propagates sentient and vegetative life, which we can call nature. But intellect indeed creates soul, like a simple body, without being changed: while soul, like a composite body, produces nature by being changed. Altogether, however, intellect, soul, and nature first generate substance: then, within substance, quality. For this is characteristic of a more excellent agent, first to generate substance, then to affect it in wonderful ways, as if by beholding, when it is turned towards its generator. But in what way does the soul produce nature by being moved? Not indeed moved by discursive thought. For it does not generate its essential being from its accidental being: but rather, with an inner otherness reigning, it defines from its intellectual power a sensual and natural faculty far different from intellect. Just as in a composite body, its own vapor diffuses itself to its circumference by a certain alteration not harming the substance: but vapor flying further outwards, with a certain detriment to its substance, seems to represent that passion of the soul, by which it sometimes promotes the vegetative power beyond itself, beyond the spiritual body naturally most familiar to it, to composite bodies. For then it is not moved in a certain way, but truly changed, that is, with a certain loss of its dignity, it undertakes the work of the lowest generation: and as it is changed within itself, it creates such a body for itself from matter according to its powers. Remember among these things, that the soul of the world itself, if compared with the divine mind, generates in a certain moved way, as we have explained: if compared with our soul, it completes generation unchanged, that is, in no way distracted from its principal actions. But where it is said that matter is procreated by nature, understand it as by universal nature, which accompanies the mundane soul: although any intellectual soul (as Plotinus wishes), unless it finds matter already procreated, seems to be about to procreate it. Here he calls matter the ultimate of the universe, subject to nature itself, which is the ultimate of divine things, which from utterly indefinite matter forms bodies, applying forms from above. Just as it itself, and soul and mind, were previously as it were in some way infinite, before they came into their proper form, but never utterly indefinite: although they are conceived as such, insofar as they are referred to the most absolute act.

On the transmigration of the soul: and that it does not pass into beasts.
11 What Plotinus himself once thought about the transmigration of the soul, unless perhaps he is poetic like Plato, his writings declare to readers. But we wish that he, having meditated more diligently (as philosophers often do), if indeed he held that opinion, had at least changed his view in this way, which he seems to have adopted not so much from the necessity of reason as from the custom of his people and age. Although the human soul is changed in some way within itself, it is never transmuted beyond certain limits of the human species, which also seems to have pleased Iamblichus, who said that the soul preserves its species in any transmigration: since its movement has its origin from itself, and acts within itself. And indeed, where it is said to be all things, it must be understood to be all things not in any way whatsoever, but in its own way, that is, proper to its own species. Therefore, do not say: If the soul is all things by natural power, then it sometimes becomes all things: For the soul itself never becomes a corporeal form, or a body, because, namely, the soul is not such a form or body in any way whatsoever, but properly according to its very mode of life. Thus it also does not become a beast, because the soul is not simply an animal, but only in a human manner. Moreover, since we see certain effects arising not from any causes whatsoever, but from specific ones: hot things from hot things, grapes from a vine, a lion from a lion, and therefore conversely, certain species of things do not procreate any effects whatsoever, but their own: assuredly, we should not hope that a bull will ever be made from the generative nature of man, which is a certain and human species from the beginning, unless perhaps nature itself sometimes changes its species by itself, and from human becomes bovine, which indeed cannot be done. For since it is said to be mobile and eternal by itself, it is never transmuted by another, nor will it even voluntarily abandon its own species: since individual things always strive to preserve this for themselves. Now indeed, for this very reason, that the generative human nature itself cannot be bovine, it happens that neither can a man procreate a bull, nor a bull a man. For nature is further distant from nature than the effect of this nature is from that. Altogether, however, other species of things are not accustomed to degenerate into others, unless they both lose their internal qualities, and again admit external ones, and come into mixture: and so they gradually cease to be what they were, which a Platonist will not concede to happen to our soul: but he will concede that the generative property of man differs in species from the generative property of brutes no otherwise than the human species from the wild. Added to this is that since the soul is said to become such or such in Plotinus through its choices and actions, if they are its own, they are human: therefore, it will not pass beyond the human species through them. Furthermore, it is vain to say that a soul enslaved by wicked actions becomes a beast deprived of reason: since it uses no reason at all. For the sharpness of reason does not lie entirely idle in the wicked; on the contrary, it is constantly engaged, although it is very much occupied with the spectacles of sense, and objects of imagination, either to be acquired or to be avoided. What then is the cause that the wicked often appear sharper and more effective than the good in their works, if not the sharpness and effect of the rational power alike? Therefore, if a wicked soul is to be transferred again into an earthly body after this life, it will return not into a brute, but into a man similarly abusing the cleverness of reason. For the very necessity of similarity seems to lead to this. For Plotinus himself clearly confesses that man acts not only according to one, but according to all the powers of the soul. But it will be purified someday; for thus, with providence dispensing, it will sometimes fall into such calamities because of its crimes, that it will repent of a life shamefully lived, with common discipline and a daemon meanwhile exhorting it. Finally, no voluptuous person will ever become a plant devoid of senses. As if indeed a voluptuous person neglects sensory actions, and in this way becomes a tree deprived of senses: on the contrary, no one uses the senses more than the intemperate.
A 2

--- Page 324 ---
280
COMMENTARY ON MARSILIO FICINO
If, therefore, it is to be turned back again to earthly bodies, it will return not into a plant but into a human, whom the violent dominion of his senses so troubles, vexes, tortures, and destroys, that at last he becomes weary of a life of pleasure, while laws and divine powers recall him to a better life. I omit that the souls of the wicked and effeminate are sent hither and thither by God, so that those who have persisted perversely in pleasure may sometimes be punished by cares and pains. But he who, when to be punished, takes away every act of reason, takes away immense and innumerable cares; he who takes away sense, takes away pain with sense. But remember that souls are purified not only in earthly bodies, but also in aerial ones, which punishment we have more clearly explained in our Theology. Therefore, let not what Plato says move you: that every soul has care of all inanimate things; for it does not follow from this that any soul whatsoever is insinuated into any bodies whatsoever, which Plato himself would deny to be possible. Indeed, if a rational soul not only rules and moves an earthly body, but also an aerial and a celestial one; if it sometimes lives in higher abodes; if it performs various functions, similar also to the providence of celestial beings: thus it seems to have sufficient care of all inanimate things, and to introduce various species within itself, not by changing its own nature, but by claiming for itself the likenesses of others, if only its essence is eternal. Therefore, Timaeus Locrus rightly denies that human souls pass into beasts; he also denies that they immediately transmigrate from one human to another human, inasmuch as he thinks they live in aerial bodies in the meantime, and are thus purified by mental vexation. But he says that sensible torments, whether they occur in a living body, or in water, or in fire, are fabricated so that those who are not led to virtue by persuasion may be terrified. Indeed, men thus affected do not understand even spiritual punishments, namely, the sorrow of the soul recognizing itself deprived of the highest good, and the anguish of imagination accompanying then the very repentance of the soul, when the sins of this life are atoned for in an aerial body. Timaeus himself will certainly not deny that these punishments are reserved for sinners. For he thinks our souls are different from each other and immortal. For he is a Pythagorean, and highly esteemed by Plato. He also says that God released our souls from the same powers and reasons as the soul of the world, and sent some down from other stars below the moon; again, that the supreme nature of the soul consists of identity. Therefore, according to Timaeus's opinion, it must be said that the soul of man, which by sinning has fallen into perverse reason and a more vehement imagination, immediately after death in an aerial body, which it even now possesses, is tormented by that same perversity and vehemence of thought among the lowest demons, who prick the soul with similar goads, until, recognizing the cause of such anguish to have been its aversion from the intellect, it gradually returns to it—which it can then perceive more clearly than now, being distracted by fewer things—and thus is gradually elevated to the order of higher demons, and finally to the stars themselves, each with the celestial body it possesses from the beginning, to that star either whose order it obtained from the beginning, or to which it rendered itself similar by living, but everywhere it preserves its human property. For man is earthly, he is aerial, he is also celestial, he is moreover solar and Martian; but everywhere man is the rational soul itself, vivifying the body in a certain way: in heaven indeed only the celestial, in the air the aerial through the celestial, on earth the earthly through both. But perhaps Timaeus will finally think that after certain ages, through a certain relaxation of contemplation and an intention towards generation, the soul subsequently falls back through the same grades of demons and aerial men, finally descending to an earthly man; and that after a man's death, this soul, akin to the world-soul and partaking of celestial things, is not cast into beasts, nor immediately again into an equally earthly man. For it is more opportune to be purified in an aerial body, and more fittingly recalled to higher things; but always to return to a body and habit of life most similar, whether

Now, the demonic kind changes its order. For it passes from the Jovial into the Martial, from which the soul then first becomes unfortunate. But on the contrary, if it comes from military service to religion, it undergoes a change from the Martial to the Jovial, unless it continues to be contentious there also: whence it is not exceedingly fortunate. But however much many may sometimes seem to change their mode of life in this body, they nevertheless preserve something of their old condition: and therefore they have not yet entirely cast off the old demon. Hence, by what follows, it is evident that the soul's primary disposition, whether natural or elective, greatly affects the body, so that a bad soul ultimately brings back bad things, and a good soul good things, from any body given to it, and similarly reports from circumstances. Wherefore the demon is not changed, nor does it differ because of the differences of bodies and fortunes: inasmuch as the very habit of the soul preserves its ancient form. But when this is completely changed into its opposite, the demon also changes, and with the demon, truly, fortune. For he himself arranges chance events for us. Mind generates without alteration of itself: the soul in a certain way begets all things.

man is considered. The soul, finally migrating from the body, becomes that in which it abounded. Therefore, we must flee to higher things, lest we fall into a sensual form, obeying sensible images; nor should we plunge into a vegetative life, enslaved to the lust of generation and entangled by the sweetness of tastes; but to the intellectual, to the intellect, to that we must rise with all our strength. Whoever, therefore, have preserved human nature, are reborn as humans again; but whoever have used only sense, return as brute animals; yet, so that those who have used sense especially along with anger, arise as wild animals, and in these, difference also brings about a difference of such (animals). But those who have used sense through concupiscence and pleasure, return as deceitful and gluttonous animals; but if they have lived not so much by sense along with these, as by the degeneration of sense, they sprout again as plants along with them. For only, or especially, the vegetative flourished in these, and all their care was to be changed into plants. Therefore, those who have lived too much delighted by musical melodies, not depraved in other things, are reborn as musical animals. And those who have reigned without reason, become eagles, unless they are infected by some other depravity. Those who, without wisdom, more confidently handle sublime things, often looking up to heaven, are changed into birds, always seeking higher things by flight. He who has attained civil virtue, returns as a man; but he who has not sufficiently attained civil virtue, transforms himself into a civic animal, a bee or similar.

III
Our daemons are something presiding over the soul itself, namely, a power to the power of the soul by which we live: Therefore, according to the differences of life, there are different daemons in us.

WHO then among these shall be called a daemon? Who also a God? Is it he who especially operates in these? For what operates, leads each one as if it were the principal thing there. Is that then the daemon, which has obtained the living being? Perhaps not. Indeed, it is what is above it: which indeed presides as if quiet: but what is after it, acts, and we are especially that which acts. And if we act and live as sensual beings, reason itself is our daemon; but if we live by reason, the daemon is what is superior to reason, a daemon, I say, presiding, granting a busy office to another. Therefore, it is rightly said in Plato: "You will choose a daemon." For we choose a prefect for ourselves according to our kind of life. Why then does he himself lead? Perhaps it is not given to lead one who has finished life: but before, indeed, he could when he was living. But one who has finished life must grant action to another: inasmuch as he has already laid down his actual life. Therefore, he now wishes to lead, and what has overcome, lives itself, having another daemon itself; but if it becomes heavy, namely, with a worse custom prevailing, it pays penalties. By this reason also, the wicked slides into worse, namely, that which acts in man declines through the likeness of life into a bestial life; but if he could obey his superior daemon, he would become superior, living that daemon's life, and prescribing to himself a president, that more excellent part of himself, by which he is led; and beyond that, moreover, another, until he progresses to the supreme. For the soul is many, indeed all things, both higher and again lower, down to every degree of life. Namely, each one of us is an intelligible world, and through our lower parts we are joined to this world, through

A
From the higher things, however, which pertain to the intelligible world, we attain the intelligible world, and we remain in the sublime through that which in us is entirely intelligible. But through that which is its ultimate part, we are bound to the lower: as if sending down a certain emanation from itself to the lower, or rather, its act, with itself in no way diminished.

B

Perhaps what is called election there, obscurely indicates the election and affection of the soul generally and everywhere. But if the choice of the soul is dominant, and that part prevails which it has made more ready by the acts of a previous life, then the body should no longer be called the cause of any evil for the soul. For if the very character of the soul, by a certain prerogative, precedes the body, and it has what it has chosen, and does not change the daemon (as Plato says), then surely it is neither good nor bad here. Perhaps each is such by potentiality, but becomes so in act.
F
What then is to be said, if someone who has good character sometimes falls into a bad body? And conversely, someone imbued with bad character sometimes obtains a good body? Perhaps those things which pertain to both souls can affect both bodies in one way or another, since other external fortunes do not entirely transgress the whole election. But when it is said that first lots are cast, then examples of lives are proposed, after these fortunes follow: again, lives are chosen from those present and proposed according to character: all these things, I say, rather attribute authority to souls in composing their own characters which have been given.
G

VI
A living soul, through intelligence, has God as its daemon: the daemon does not compel the soul. Likewise, it can be changed according to the soul's change, likewise concerning the judgment of souls. Likewise, how the stars repeat, and in turn fall back into fate, in which they not only suffer, but also do something.

WHO then is the good person, or what does he do? Perhaps the good person is one in whom that which is better operates: otherwise, he would not be good, if he had a daemon cooperating with him. For the intellect acts in this, either therefore it is the daemon itself, or according to the daemon: and the daemon for this person is God. Is it then also above the intellect? since that which is above the intellect exists as the daemon itself. But why does one not enjoy this gift immediately from the beginning? Perhaps because of the disturbance vehemently brought about by generation itself. Nevertheless, even before the discourse of reason, there is a certain inner movement, desiring those things which are consistent with itself. Does it correct and direct entirely to the best? Perhaps not entirely: since the soul is so affected, that existing as such in these very things, it has this life, and this choice and purpose. Moreover, this daemon of whom we speak, is said to lead the soul to the underworld: nor does it remain entirely the same, unless perhaps the soul again chooses the same things. But how does it behave before that? It is said indeed to lead to judgment, to arrive in the same form after a certain end of generation, which it had sometimes before generation: then, as if from some other beginning, for that intermediate space of time which flows between the preceding and following generation, the daemon threatens souls paying penalty, and perhaps then it is not so much life for them, as judgment and punishment. But for souls entering brute bodies, is there less of a daemon present, or something else? Perhaps a bad daemon or a foolish and lazy one. But for souls advanced to higher things, what divinity is present? Indeed, among them, some still lead a life in the sensible world, while others are already outside the world. And those in the sensible world, some near the sun, or any other of the planets, others indeed in the firmament: each according to how they had directed their actions here by reason. For it must be thought that in our soul there is not only an intelligible world, but also a certain disposition conformable to the soul of the world itself. Since therefore that [soul of the world] is distributed in the inerratic sphere and also in the erratic spheres according to different powers, it is clear that powers conformable to its powers are also in us, and that proper actions emanate from individual powers: Then indeed, souls which have departed from here to there approach a star most suitable to the character and power which we have most used in acting and living, and congruent to such a god and daemon: where the soul will either use this very same [power], or one presiding over this power. But it must be considered what that better thing is. Regarding souls that have departed outside the sensible world, it must be believed that they have transcended the daemonic nature, and all fate of generation, and all necessity of this world, as long as it dwells in the intelligible world: Moreover, that it has drawn back with itself that essence also which is in it, desirous of generating. MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY
ON THE FIFTH BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD,
CONCERNING THE DAIMON.

SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

Every power, both of knowing and of generating, rejects the base, and strives towards the beautiful: because all proceeds from and is moved by the first beauty.

I NDEED, I believe, Magnanimous Lorenzo, that you will not now demand a long discussion on love from your Marsilio: both because we have discussed much about this in the Symposium, and especially

--- Page 332 ---
288          COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO
beauty in the soul/mind: natural beauty, however, gives birth to beauty in matter, and each naturally desires, according to its powers, to generate beauty in a subject, so that finally the beauty of the creature is more apt.

          The Double Soul of the World. Two Venuses. Two Loves: which are not passions,
                    but certain existences.

II  SINCE we see intelligence perfected in us to the extent that both the act of understanding and the thing to be understood are separated from matter and the conditions of matter, it is permissible to conjecture that the first intellect itself, simply, is most alien from matter. Moreover, the intellectual soul, immediately generated from there, and therefore supremely intellectual, cannot unite with matter into the common form of a single composite. For this is both a certain intellect and simply soul; but life, born from this subsequently, as a certain soul and simply nature, can now unite with matter. Therefore, we call that intellectual soul in the world the first Venus; but life, entirely infused into the world from there, we call the second Venus. In both, a perpetual love thrives, incited by the beauty of the divine mind, both in the first, to generate similar beauty within itself, and in the second, to express beauty in matter according to its powers. Plotinus, however, thinks, following Plato's mind, that the intellectual soul of the world, while acting intrinsically around God, by understanding Him and willing to conceive within itself not something imaginary, but something natural and subsistent (as I believe) imitating the mystery of the Christian Trinity in this. He believes, moreover, that just as shining and heating are two things in fire, but ultimately one in the sun, so knowing and loving are indeed diverse in rational power, but exist as one act in intellectual substance. But since such an act in the soul of the world is intimate and about the intimate, and from this, it most effectively produces within itself offspring congruent to this act: this offspring, because it is born from intelligence, is something intelligible; because it proceeds from love, it is something amatory; indeed, it is love itself, subsistent, produced from a certain act of loving. For since there, to exist and to act are entirely the same, doubtless, by thus acting internally, a certain existence is produced internally; in this produced existence, the essence is the same as that of the producer, differing in this very respect, that in the former it is propagating, but in the latter it is propagated from it. It differs moreover by a certain relation, inasmuch as this amatory existence is both of the lover and of the beloved, in its very being. It differs furthermore in that in the propagating existence, the vision of beauty itself is rather placed; in the propagated existence, rather the pleasure itself concerning beauty.

                    Confirmation of the foregoing.

III  IF a pregnant woman often, due to the wondrous vehemence of imagination and affection, affects the fetus with a certain natural quality, for this very reason, because it is connected to the mother; if again a similar movement of the soul expresses sudden qualities in its own body: what wonder if something substantial is born in the soul itself from a similar vehemence? Especially in the intellectual soul itself, where action is vehement, and affection is not adventitious, not mutable, but entirely natural and firm. And he who sees, rejoices, and desires is most effective, and its object is most powerful, and it flows powerfully. These things are confirmed by the fact that if everywhere accidental things are reduced to certain substantial things, congruent to them by a certain proportion, it is necessary that loves, which are certain adventitious passions, be rightly referred to substantial loves. Here you might note again that the world must have two souls: one, in a certain way, separate, which presides over the body like an artisan; and the other, conjoined, which is inherent in the body from there, like a form. Indeed, it is necessary for a separate soul to be present, both because such a soul immediately shines forth from pure intellect, and because a mixed artisan does not absolutely command its art. Moreover, it is necessary for a conjoined soul to be in the world, both because the first soul is fertile for generating this one from itself, and because the world must be a most perfect composite. Therefore, it must have the most perfect form for its matter, that is, living and sensual. However, one does not properly arise in the world from the intellectual soul and matter (as Plotinus wishes), because intelligence, through action and affection, tends towards the opposite of matter, just as he does not think one is formed in us, inasmuch as the intellectual soul in us does not communicate with the body in passions proper to the body, nor does the body communicate with such a soul in actions properly pertaining to such a soul. It is permissible, however, to say that the intellectual soul is both mundane in the world and human in us; and that from it and the animal soul, one is therefore formed, because from its influx, together with matter, a single sensual animal is formed, to which it always inspires life, which would perish without its continuous spirit. Remember, indeed, that these twin souls in the world are again twin Venuses, which similar twin loves accompany. Remember also that love in this second soul of the world not only generates all beauty in the matter of the world through generative power, but also through the effective power of imagining, both to look up to the divine form, and to challenge both the world and what is in the world, according to their powers, towards it.

          Two loves naturally inherent in each soul, as if they are two daemons.

IIII  He has lightly touched upon loves which, as certain new movements of souls, are daily incited in us by things brought forth from outside, as if they were known; but he more diligently pursues substantial loves, that is, essential and perpetual instincts towards beauty, naturally inherent in the soul and continuously drawing it towards beauty, even if you neither choose nor notice them. Of these, one is naturally inserted into the power of knowing, the other into the power of generating. And because, like a prefect, it leads the soul and governs it in the manner of providence, it is called a daemon; although the more excellent love is also called a god. It is said, however, that the soul generates these, not daily, but from the beginning, when, according to its nature, partly handed down to it from eternity, partly contracted by the choice of life at some point, it conceives such instincts to rule for an age; by whose certain hidden nod, more affections and concepts are daily aroused in us, which indeed neither external spectacles alone, nor present bodily affection, nor new deliberation provides. And indeed, a certain perpetual tenor of life, largely directed towards one thing—especially as regards the kind of life, sciences and arts, and natural faculties proper to each individual—is governed by such a daemon, being guided meanwhile by a certain external daemon congruent to it. And all rational souls, through their loves of this kind, are congruent with the loves of the mundane soul, inasmuch as they themselves are sisters of the mundane soul; and these, together with their loves, thus depend on the soul of the world and its love.

--- Page 333 ---
IN BOOK V. OF ENNEAD III. 289

love, not because they derive their essence from it, but because the beginnings of that impulse, as if harmonizing, initiate their own movements, and through their own ends, they finally move towards its end.

Concerning Demons.

[Decorative initial O] But that demons must be intermediaries between stars and humans, we have sufficiently demonstrated in our Theology, namely, that every sphere above us, superior and far larger than ours, had rational inhabitants conformable to its sphere, just as ours has. For Apuleius also proves that there are certain fiery animals with this testimony of Aristotle: "In burning furnaces, certain peculiar animals were seen to fly, fitted with tiny wings, which spend their entire life in fire: they are born with it, and with it they likewise perish." Indeed, that which first receives life from the life-giving substance itself, that is, the soul, is fire alone. For fire among bodies is closest to the soul, because it is most excellent, most effective, most mobile. Hence it follows that all things live when heat sustains them, and do not live when it does not sustain them. Secondly, through fire, air, which is closest to fire, seems to receive life,

--- Page 334 ---
290 COMMENTARY ON MARSILIO FICINO

...neither does it overcome otherness, nor does state overcome motion, nor common nature particular [nature], nor the faculty of acting the power of suffering, through which disposition such an essence indeed seems to be accommodated both to a perishable body and to a disturbance of the soul. For this reason, which Iamblichus also asserts, demons do not have providence in common like the Gods, but individually for their own actions and provinces.

**On the origin of demons.**

VI. As for what Plotinus says in the sixth chapter, that demons are generated from the whole soul itself, and what Porphyry says in the book *On Abstinence*, that demons sprang from the whole soul, you should not understand this to mean that the very substances of the souls that are in demons are created from the soul of the world. But rather, understand here the whole soul as that mixing bowl, or goddess, and common idea, from which Timaeus asserts that, besides the soul of the world, the souls of the spheres, and again the souls of demons and humans, were produced separately. For Proclus also says in *Alcibiades* that demons are generated from the life-giving goddess, from whom souls are also generated. Plotinus also holds that from the world itself, and from every rational soul, a certain irrational soul emanates, which he calls a demon. But demons of this kind, even if they follow their own souls, are nevertheless generated by them under a certain common influence of the mundane soul; for it is

since it is utterly absurd to say that beautiful nature, wishing to create, would wish to generate in something ugly. But indeed, for those who are incited to generate here, it is sufficient to attain what is beautiful here. This, however, is lacking in images and bodies; for the principal exemplar is by no means present in them, which is indeed the cause for them of loving even this [earthly] beauty. Therefore, among those who are recalled from this beauty to the remembrance of supernal beauty, this beauty is cherished as an image; but among those who by no means remember due to ignorance of the passion, this our [earthly] beauty is considered true beauty: and if they are temperate, the familiarity entered into with this beauty is without fault. But the fall of the intemperate into venereal mixture is a sin.

Therefore, he who is affected by a pure love of beauty is content with beauty alone, whether he remembers [the supernal beauty] or not. But he who moreover has another concupiscence mixed in, that of immortality in a mortal thing itself, seeks beauty with all his might for the sake of achieving here in perpetual generation and eternal perseverance: and while he proceeds according to nature, he strikes and generates in beauty, sowing indeed for eternity, and in beauty, because of a certain kinship of beauty itself. For the eternal itself is also akin to beauty, and eternal nature is the first beauty, and all things that are made by it are made beautiful. Therefore, he who does not desire generation seems to be more self-sufficient and content with beauty itself: but he who desires to generate strives indeed to beget beauty due to a certain need: whence it appears that he is by no means self-sufficient: but he believes that in creating, he will then at last make something beautiful, if he has generated in beauty: but indeed, those who strive to generate contrary to law and contrary to nature, begin their course from a certain natural impulse, but having transgressed the natural path, they slip through slippery places, and having fallen, lie prostrate, ignorant of where love was leading them, and to what end their appetite for generation tends. Likewise, ignorant of how the image of beauty should be used, and finally, ignorant of beauty itself.

Indeed, those who cherish beautiful bodies not for the sake of mixture, love them for the very reason that they are beautiful. Again, those who follow a mixed love, towards women I mean, by which perpetuation is preserved through generation, and do not deviate from this in any way, these desire beauty and perpetuation simultaneously, and both are temperate, although some are more excellent than others: and those who are more excellent, some indeed cultivate this earthly beauty of ours as if it were sufficient for them, but others also cultivate beauty itself, those who indeed remember [the supernal], and yet do not disdain this [earthly] beauty, inasmuch as they consider it to be a certain effect and play of that [supernal beauty]. These therefore dwell in beauty without turpitude: but others fall into turpitude through beauty: for the appetite for good often slips also into evil: and these indeed are the passions of the soul.

We say therefore that Venus is twofold, asserting one indeed to be celestial, a scion of heaven; but the other born from Jupiter and Dione, the leader of human marriages, herself less attaining [the celestial]. But that one [the celestial] is without a mother, and before marriages, since weddings do not occur in heaven. That celestial one indeed, which they say was born from Saturn, that is, from intellect, it is necessary

**C** that she be a most divine soul, born inviolable immediately from the inviolable intellect itself, and permanently supernal, inasmuch as she neither wishes nor is able to descend to these mundane things, because she is endowed with a nature that is absolutely not inclined to lower things. It is necessary, I say, that she be a certain separate substance and an essence in no way partaking of matter. For this reason, they obscurely said she is without matter, when they said she is without a mother. Which indeed, a God

**D** rather than a Daemon, we ought rightly to name her: since she is sincere and pure, and subsisting in herself. For that which is born immediately from the mind is also pure, inasmuch as it is most powerful in itself by the proximity of the intellect itself, and has an innate appetite to establish itself in its generator, in a generator, I say, powerful enough to sufficiently retain it among

**E** the higher beings: whereby it happens that that soul never falls, which immediately hangs from the mind, and has this function much more than the light diffused around the sun, to perpetually proceed from it and be referred back to it. Following therefore Saturn continuously, and if you wish, even the heaven, father of Saturn, she reflected her action back to him, and reconciled herself to him, and by loving, begot love. And with this very love, she looks up to him, and produces the substance and essence of this soul's action. Then indeed, both look there, both the genetrix herself and the beautiful love begotten, a substance indeed always intent on another beautiful thing,

**F** and having its being in this very middle, namely between the one desiring and the one desired. And indeed, the eye of the one desiring is that which offers to the lover, so that through it he may discern the beloved, but itself running ahead, and before it offers him the faculty of seeing through an instrument, it is already full of the spectacle, or vision. Prior indeed, I say, yet not contemplated in the same way, from the fact that it presents the vision to him, but itself, as it were, feeds on the fruit of the vision of beauty wonderfully diffused around it.

# MARSILIO FICINO'S
### COMMENTARY ON BOOK SIX OF THE THIRD ENNEAD, "THAT INCORPOREAL BEINGS DO NOT SUFFER."

#### SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

[S]UMMARY of this book is to assert that an incorporeal thing cannot suffer. He calls an incorporeal thing that which either includes no quantity in its nature, although it may be able to receive it externally. This, however, is matter. Or it entirely excludes quantity. This, however, is mind and soul. Furthermore, he wants passion to be a change that can destroy substance, whether it occurs by division: such as happens to quantity and necessary things having quantity; or whether it occurs by alteration: such as happens to qualities contrary to each other, and moreover to forms which such qualities necessarily accompany. Therefore, both prime matter and the soul are incorporeal things, claiming neither quantity nor such a quality as their own, and are therefore separated from passion: and the soul much more so than matter. For the soul not only does not admit pernicious forms, but also does not seem to receive new forms of any kind whatsoever at any time. Therefore, in the following sections, many things are discussed concerning the immutable essence of the rational soul and its parts, some things moreover concerning the first essence, and very many things concerning its opposite, that is, prime matter, inasmuch as it is finally confirmed that an incorporeal thing is free from passion.

The Soul neither suffers, nor receives forms or qualities. Also, concerning twofold imagination.

Therefore, in the first part of the book, which contains five chapters, he shows that the soul is not subject to passion: in the second part, he will then show something similar concerning matter. As for the first part, observing that no impulse or quality from bodies falls upon the cognitive faculty of the soul. For if it were to occur in some natural way, and, so to speak, materially, cognition and discrimination would immediately be confused: and judgment; or if it were to happen at least by some imaginal condition, that bodies form the soul, which is unspeakable: for it pertains to the soul, as superior, to form bodies, not to be formed by them. But altogether, all cognition and affection of the soul, even that tending towards corporeal things, is a certain action of the soul concerning such things, and in the meantime, it does not suffer from them. For it does not agree with bodies in matter, such a communion usually brings about some reciprocal passion in the agent. What then is to sense? It is indeed in the soul this very thing, namely, to apply itself, and to deploy its power around those things to which its essence is congruent and naturally apt: to remember likewise, is to accomplish this very thing most readily. Therefore, no cognitive faculty is formed by new images, but the intellect itself is always actually that which it cognizes: reason and phantasy, however, from that state in which they are potentially those things which are to be conceived by them, sometimes actually become those things which are always actually in the intellect. The exterior sense perceives sensible things, it does not receive them. The vegetative [faculty] nourishes and moves, and is not nourished or moved in the meantime. Porphyry confirms all these things, showing that when the soul is said to suffer, this very passion is not any alteration in nature or any quality, but a certain accommodation and affection of the soul to this or that thing, and that it is a certain action of the soul concerning external things, but a limited one, namely, when it itself contracts the amplitude of its power and affections to a narrow scope. And Porphyry concludes that all movements of the soul, as they are called, are not properly movements in the soul, but in the body: and that in the soul they are actions, but in the body, these same movements become passions. He adds that the acts of vegetation and sense and memory are not imaginal, but are in some way natural, like heating, being hot, illuminating, shining; Plotinus holds the same view. You will note, moreover, a twofold virtue commonly in the soul: one, as it were, private, namely, proper to any of the parts of the soul: this is, that each rightly performs its own office; the other, as it were, public, namely, that all parts rightly harmonize with each other, that reason be governed by the mind, and that the irrational powers then obey it, among which concupiscence should be subject to audacity. Neither virtue is like a quality impressed upon the soul as a subject, nor similarly is vice, but rather it is like movement and act, and the cessation of these. If, however, there is any quality in us, either impressed from elsewhere by way of nature or image, or acquired by actions, such a quality is indeed not in the soul, but rather in the body, properly so, or thus affected, in which both formations and passions occur, while the soul vegetates, senses, is affected, and judges. Finally, no change occurs in the soul except a certain progression from potentiality to actuality: and this indeed not by another mover, but by the soul itself: nor again into an act that arrives as a quality, but one that proceeds as an action. If, however, any part of the soul is called passive, it is not understood as something subject to corporeal passions, but as the principle of passions. You will again note a twofold imagination in us: the first indeed in the rational soul, capable of discourse and judgment, similar in some way to reason: the second, however, impressed by this in the soul or life in us lacking reason, which imagination certainly does not so much use discourse as it is carried by instinct, however intimate: but concerning the passions of the body, which as a common

--- Page 345 ---
IN LIBR. VI. ENNEAD. III. 501

common sense is the principle of the other senses. Plotinus sometimes, by a certain transference, places imagination even in the vegetative part, which is neither a discourse through forms, like the first, nor an intuition of form, like the second: but an expression of the form vigorously existing within itself, and through this, an impression on matter, where natural action is like a certain substantial imagination acting, by no means imagining. Here you will also note that the faculty of desiring and being angry springs from the vegetative faculty of the soul: just as reason naturally flows from the intellect, and then the first imagination, from which the second also flows.

**That in true essence are contained life and intellect: Also concerning the one that is above**
**essence, and the one that is below it.**

*In the sixth chapter, you will note that true being is that which is entirely being, that is, to which nothing necessary for the perfection of essence is lacking: and perfect essence includes an intimate and perennial act of itself, that is, life, and indeed demands this most intimate act. Such indeed it is, if it be intelligence: for this is the reflection of life into essence. From the first essence, therefore, as from a root, life and intellect simultaneously spring forth into itself: but such a sprout is born from it only insofar as it has fecundity from the Good itself, a common one, I mean, like a vine from the sun. But that this fecundity may be properly distinguished into life and intellect, it proceeds from the essence itself, just as it happens with a vine that the power of the sun is determined towards the grape. Therefore, the gifts of living, understanding, and the like, flow indeed from the Good itself, as the most common principle and end, but from the first essence itself, as from its own root, and a certain formal power. Therefore, Plotinus here understands true being and true essence not only as being itself, the head of all beings, but also as every form having its own being, and existing in its own essence, and therefore separable from matter, in which consequently there is no potentiality and inclination towards non-being, no foreign nature is mixed: nothing necessary for its existence is lacking, the potentiality of the species is always reduced to act: in which again, together with essence, life and intellect are equally included. Of this kind are all intellects and intellectual souls, enumerated in the genus of true being. For sensible forms inseparable from matter are called not true beings on account of reasons contrary to those we have stated here. But since matter is much further removed from the first form of things than sensible forms, and these are not truly called beings, it is customary for Plotinus and Porphyry to call matter itself truly non-being: because it includes nothing formal in itself, but utterly excludes it. But to be is the function of form: since the first essence is the same as the first naturally omniform form. To this point must be brought what is both denied and again affirmed concerning the One itself in Parmenides: and what is similarly said in the Sophist concerning being and non-being. You will therefore understand the One in three principal ways: either that which seems to be equal to being: or that which is superior to being, or that which is inferior. Concerning the One which is equal to being, especially concerning the first being itself, all species and properties of things are equally affirmed. For it is the fount of all beings, and their exemplar. Concerning this, therefore, it is usually said: it is the same and other, stable, mobile, equal, unequal, great, small, and similar things. For here are the ideal reasons of all things. But concerning the supreme One, all these things are similarly denied: for there it is not the form of these things, but the cause. Finally, concerning the lowest One, that is, matter, all these things are equally denied: for it has nothing formal in itself.*

**That natural things are not true beings, and that matter is called non-being, and seems to have forms like a mirror, which it does not truly possess.**

*Among these things, where he says that natural things are not so much truly being as seeming to be, he introduces a certain Epicurean objection, by which it is contended that only corporeal things possess true essence, and that this is especially evident from two points: first, because by their solidity they resist division, and second, because they vehemently strike objects. To the first, it is answered that such hard bodies, while they seem to resist, are exposed longer to the striker, and await the blow, because they are most inept for flight, and because of the same ineptitude for motion and an ineffectual nature, after they have been divided into parts, they cannot return to their former shape: but more subtle bodies, where they seem to yield to the striker, due to their marvelous efficacy, most swiftly evade the passion, and for the same efficacy, similarly return to themselves suddenly. Finally, since motion in things is a certain action, and a very strong indication of inner life, and everywhere there is a trace of life, and those things that are least corporeal are most prompt to motion, it follows that insofar as things approach incorporeal nature, they approach a life capable of motion and efficacy, and therefore true essence, while corporeal things fall away from essence: in which part, a similar answer is given to the second point, namely, that corporeal things, when they fall upon something and cause more serious harm, do so not because they are firmer, but because they are utterly weak, so much so that they cannot sustain themselves, and therefore by their own ruin and fall, they harm whatever is nearest. For even those who are most inept at riding especially press down on and tire out horses: and languid bodies are usually most burdensome to those who carry them. After this, remember that matter is indeed an empty shadow of the first essence, and material forms are various images of ideas contained in the first essence, having no similarity with them in nature, although in the effect of representation they seem to have some similarity. And therefore, matter, like a mirror, while it receives only images, or perhaps does not even receive these but only seems to receive them, truly suffers nothing, especially since matter, being the ultimate, cannot be resolved into anything else, and therefore cannot suffer. Certainly, no form is contrary to it, since it is equally naturally exposed to all. Therefore, it can suffer from nothing: since not just anything that happens in matter suffers from just anything, but from contraries. Likewise, matter contracts no quality or virtue proper to itself from the presence of form, and therefore does not suffer: otherwise, it would long ago have become familiarly multiform, and therefore would no longer be the most common subject, equally formable by all. Now, if in any alteration the substance of the subject itself must remain, while the qualities are changed, much more in worldly transmutation is it necessary for matter to remain. Finally, since the very goodness of nature in no way allows anything substantial to be resolved into nothing, and simple substances cannot sometimes be resolved into anything else: deservedly neither simple forms subsisting in themselves, nor simple matter can ever perish or suffer. Matter, indeed, since it is evil, that is, most distant from the Good itself, does not desire the good in such a way as to claim something natural from it for itself, but rather to put on a certain imaginary garment from it, and deceive: and the more it remains in its formlessness, the more it is evil, or the evil itself: nor does matter itself become hot, but the composite: it merely sustains heat, soon to lay aside the heat as a garment, its nature being minimally changed. Again, when something is divided, quantity and what follows it are divided, not matter, which precedes quantity by nature.*

--- Page 346 ---
302          COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO
But just as in the procession of colors, the last, that is, blackness, has nothing of the first, that is, whiteness: so matter, being the ultimate in the descent of beings, possesses nothing within itself similar to the first, nor does it receive anything of the nature of the first on its surface, but merely certain empty imitations. And because of its extreme dissimilarity to the first, it claims no taste or odor of being for itself from the presence of its images, so that it is equally prepared to receive any forms that may come in the future, however much they may contradict previous ones. But among these things, you will especially observe what he says, that natural things, if compared with divine things, have no greater substance than the images of bodies appearing in mirrors. Nor do these depend on divine things any differently than images depend on objects. To this tends that saying of Solomon: All is vanity. To this tends that saying of Paul: For now we see through a glass, darkly. But since we now see both bodies and the mirror, on which the images entirely depend, we therefore perceive the vanity of the images themselves; otherwise, if we did not see those things, we could not refute this, but we would consider what are images to be true things: just as now we believe that what are called natural things are true substances, because we can see neither divine things nor matter, from which (divine things) into which (matter) they leap forth and recoil like images from objects into a mirror. Indeed, either, as physicists believe, the images of things are themselves in mirrors, or, as optical theorists teach, there are no images in mirrors, but rays of things fall into the mirror, and thence, if they are reflected to the eye. Which happens when they are reflected at equal angles, then the things themselves render their rays to the eyes in such a way that the sense is nevertheless deceived, thinking it sees things elsewhere than where it sees them; but however the matter stands, Plotinus and Porphyry want the comparison of matter to divine things and sense to be like that of a mirror to visible things and sight: indeed, they consider this matter, as if entirely opposed to self-being, not to admit the rays and acts of the first being and mind within itself, but rather, like something dense and impenetrable to beings due to its dissimilarity, to immediately repel their acts, and by this very quasi-reverberation, to appear to the senses as if sensible, what are in themselves intelligible, so much so that we think we are inspecting in matter what are in the first being and intellect, and from there they move the soul to know. Finally, since beings themselves or ideas, while acting upon matter, neither lose anything of their nature, nor are moved from their state, nor agree with matter in proportion or affection: therefore, what seems to be given from it, as if empty and most weak, always needs this material seat. And meanwhile, this matter, because it never truly receives anything, nor does it truly receive whatever it seems to receive due to its natural falsity, therefore it is never filled, but always offers an occasion for perpetual mutation to those things that affect it.

      How much the soul surpasses matter, and how a certain quantity of matter follows
                        the mode of any species entering into matter.

When this wood is said to be outside that wood, these two are not much separated from each other, because they are separated only by external boundaries, but are joined to each other in species. Fire is therefore more outside water: for they are separated not only by external boundaries, but also by contrary qualities: but since they agree in genus, they can sometimes be mixed in matter. But the soul is separated from matter by its entire genus, and therefore, although it penetrates matter, it is nevertheless further outside matter. And therefore, the forms which the soul of the world, having obtained from the divine intellect, strives to transmit everywhere into matter through its seminal virtue, matter cannot reconcile with itself, nor mix with itself, although those forms may mix with each other. Then indeed, matter, just as it is by its very nature devoid of all forms, so too is it devoid of quantity: for this is a certain form. And since quantity is the last of the forms, therefore a certain quantity and figure is destined for things, especially according to the mode of the species and form, by the mind and soul. Therefore, in the formal reasons of species existing in the mind and soul, a certain quantity and figure is included and defined, which accompanies each species. Indeed, in the formal reason of man or horse, the quantity of man or horse is decreed. This quantity is brought into effect due to the efficacy of the universally formal reason, and a certain motion of it in action, and because of the procession of the natural form emanating from it. Therefore, by this efficacy, motion, and procession, matter itself is produced into a mass upon the face of matter, namely, as much as the form itself requires, whether mundane for the world, human for man, or leonine for a lion. And just as a quantity proper to each species comes into matter, so it also departs with the species, and at the advent of a new species thereafter, a new quantity comes into being, just like the quality proper to the species. Quantity is produced in matter according to the distance from the quantity of the acting virtue and formal motion. Indeed, matter, due to its weakness, cannot avoid such motion, or receive forms without some such distraction. But the soul, since it is itself a certain form, and a subsisting species, therefore embraces all species of things in the same quasi-center. For this form receives those forms in the manner of a form: and the manner of forms is that each, as if simple, is wholly collected in any part of itself, and all are most easily contained in any part. Hence it again follows that our reason can comprehend forms both without numerical multitude in the very unity of the species, and separate them from the dimension of quantity. But matter always receives forms with a certain extension, because it is drawn everywhere by the motion of the form divinely proceeding upon it, its nature meanwhile willingly yielding to the drawing, prepared for any mass everywhere: because it possesses no mass of its own. And while it is extended into dimension throughout the entire space of the world, it is not divided into multiple matters, but remains one and continuous, both because it is not subject to passion, and because it does not resist, but willingly follows the extending power, and is extended by

On the impassibility of incorporeal things.

The soul, sensing and

about passions, which passions indeed
occur concerning something else,
perhaps concerning such a body, but the
judgment itself is in the soul: nor is
the judgment itself a passion, otherwise there would have to be another

B If, I say, we speak thus, nevertheless even here there is doubt in the judgment,
whether it has nothing of that about which it judges in itself, or a certain form
of it, which if it has, it will seem to have already suffered. However, it is permissible
to say that those things which are called formations of the senses or of intelligence
itself, happen in a way far different from what most people believe: which appears
especially in intelligences themselves, which are also actions, capable of knowing
something without passion.
C But entirely, our reason and our will desire that the soul not be subjected to such
conversions and changes as are the heatings and coolings of bodies. Moreover, it is
necessary to diligently consider concerning that part of the soul which is called
passive, whether we also declare this to be immutable, or whether we concede some
passion to this alone: but of this in what follows. Now, however, let us discuss the
doubts of the former (points). Indeed, it is doubted in what way that which is
D before the passive and sensation, and whatever else belongs to the soul, can also be
immutable, since depravity occurs in it, and false opinion and ignorance often happen.
Again, conformity and disconformity, while it rejoices, grieves, is angry, envies,
emulates, affects: it never rests at any incident, it is moved and changed. But if the
soul is a body, and has magnitude, it is difficult, nay, even impossible, to show it to be
impassible and immutable in any of those things which are said to happen concerning
it.
E But if it is an essence devoid of magnitude, and it is necessary that the endowment

304 PLOTINUS ENNEAD. III.

[Latin Column]

A that its incorruptibility is not lacking, one must be careful to grant such passions to it, lest perhaps unknowingly we grant that it is corruptible. But then, if either number or reason (as we are accustomed to say) is its essence, in what way will any passion happen to number or reason? But rather it must be thought that irrational and impassible principles become passions in it, and that these things, transferred from bodies into it, must each be understood by opposition, and as if translated according to an analogical proportion, so that the soul, having these, does not have them, and suffering, does not suffer, and what the manner of such things is, must be considered.

LIBER SEXTVS. 307

[Right Column]

A They say perturbation and agitation are in the estimation and expectation of evil. It is certainly agreed that phantasy is in the soul, both what we call the primary opinion, and that which is born from this. Nor does opinion extend further, but concerning that which is lower, it is a kind of faint and obscure opinion, and a certain indistinct imagination, such as is inherent in nature, like a certain action insofar as each thing acts, as is usually said, without the function of phantasy. But the sensible perturba-

B -tion following from this is clearly produced in the body, such as trembling, shaking, pallor, impediment of voice. For such things do not occur in any part of the soul, otherwise we would call it corporeal. For if any part of the soul suffered such things, such things would not even reach the body, since that very thing whose function it is to initiate these no longer performs its mission, because it is already oppressed by passions and distracted from itself. Therefore, this passive part of the soul is not indeed a body,

C but a certain species, yet in matter: both the faculty of desiring, and the power of nourishing, increasing, generating, which indeed is the root and principle of the concupiscible and passible species. But no perturbation or passion ought to happen to the root of any species, but it itself ought to remain. But its matter undergoes passion whenever passion creeps in due to the presence of that mover. For that which is vegetative, when

--- Page 353 ---
LIBER SEXTVS. 390

A
to exist as absolute Being. Therefore, it must be constituted as possessing all things within itself, and at the same time all things as one; all things, if indeed we define being by these things: but it must be so, otherwise intellect and life would not emanate from Being itself, but these would be adventitious to Being, nor could they, however, come from non-being, and Being itself would indeed be devoid of life and mind. But that which is not truly Being will have these things as they ought to be in inferior things, and in things posterior to Being itself.

B
For that which exists above Being indeed bestows these things upon Being, yet does not itself need them. If, therefore, Being is such, it is necessary that it is neither body, nor that which is subject to bodies; but that which is subject to bodies must dwell in non-being. But in what way is the nature of bodies, and in what way is matter, not being: in which these mountains and stones, and the whole solid earth, and whatever else can resist others? Indeed, those things which are struck, compelled by impacts, reveal their very essence.

C
If therefore someone should say, in what way then are those things which neither collide, nor inflict or suffer force, nor resist, nor are seen at all, namely soul and intellect, beings, and truly beings? We, on the contrary, will say: among those things which are more corpulent, earth rests, but that which is less ponderous is more mobile, and of that which is higher, that too is more mobile. Now indeed fire is most mobile, and now escapes corporeal nature.

D
But (as I think) those things which are more self-sufficient, disturb others less, and cause less trouble. But those things which are more ponderous and earthly, the more they fail and fall, and cannot lift themselves, these indeed, falling due to weakness, seem to inflict collision upon others by their very ruin and as if by inertia: inasmuch as bodies that lack life fall more troublesomely upon whatever is nearest, and strike more violently, and harm.

E
But animated things, inasmuch as they participate more in Being: the more they possess being, the more they tend to be harmless to their neighbors. Therefore, motion, which is a kind of life in bodies, or an imitation of life, is more present in those things in which there is less corpulence, as if a greater defect of being in that to which it happens, makes it more a body. Again, from what are called passions, it can be more clearly known, that what is more corpulent is more passible, namely earth more than other things, and the rest by similar reasoning.

F
For when other things are divided, they suddenly return to unity, with nothing preventing it. But when that which is earthly is split, the divided portions always remain separate from each other, as if lacking natural power, which from a small impulse remain as they were impelled, and are lost: so also that which has become most a body, as if having most slipped into non-being, is least able to recall itself into unity.

G
Therefore, ponderous and violent concussions are a kind of ruin, by which things, falling, in turn act upon other things. But when the weak encounters the weak, it is strong against it, as non-being encountering non-being. These things, therefore, have been said against those who place beings only in the category of bodies,

--- Page 354 ---
210 PLOTINUS ENNEAD. III.

evidently led by the testimony of impulses and concussions: likewise, testifying to the truth of imaginations made through sense, who are affected similarly to dreamers, while they think what they see is real, when they are dreams. For sense is the function of the sleeping soul: for as much of the soul as is in the body, so much indeed sleeps: but true awakening and vigilance is true separation from the body, not a resurrection together with the body. For the transmigration that occurs with the body is a kind of transition from sleep to sleep, as if one passes from bed to bed: but truly complete is that which rises entirely from bodies. And these things, since they have a nature repugnant to the soul, also have the opposite for their essence. Moreover, their generation, flux, and destruction testify to this, which are indeed most alien to the very nature of being.

BUT again, we must return first to the underlying matter: and then to those things which are said to be in matter, from which it may be clearly understood, both that matter is devoid of passion, and that neither matter nor those things truly exist. It is therefore incorporeal, since body is posterior and composite, and it itself, together with something else, completes the body. For thus it has obtained the same appellation according to the incorporeal genus, because both, namely being and matter, are diverse from bodies. But since matter is neither soul, nor mind, nor life, nor species, nor reason, nor even a limit: for it is a certain indefiniteness. Again, neither power. For what could it do? But since it escapes all these things, it certainly ought not to obtain the appellation of being, but is deservedly called non-being, nor yet is it called non-being in the way that motion or state is usually called non-being, but truly non-being, a phantom and imagination of mass, and an appetite for substance or subsistence, standing indeed not in a state: invisible in itself, and fleeing him who wishes to see it: and when one does not see, then it is in a way present: but when one looks more intently, it is not perceived. Again, always appearing contrary in itself, small, large, less, more, deficient, exceeding, a phantom, neither remaining nor again able to flee: for it will not even be able to do this one thing, since it has received no value from the intellect, but has been made in the defect of all being, wherefore in any of its denominations it lies and deceives, namely if it is conceived as large, it is meanwhile small, and if more, it is also less: and the being that occurs in its imagination is non-being, like some fleeting plaything, so much so that what seem to happen in it are playthings, phantoms in a phantom, indeed as in a mirror, where something is situated elsewhere, but appears elsewhere: and what seems to be filled, having nothing, but appearing to have everything. And what enter and exit are imitations of beings and phantoms around an unformed phantom: and because it is unformed, therefore seen there. They seem indeed to effect something in the underlying matter: but they effect nothing, inasmuch as they are weak and fluid, and have no solidity, nor any power of repercussion, and

**VIII**
What that is to which passion belongs, and what does not belong to matter.

**C** But in general, that which suffers must be such that it is in contrary powers and qualities to those which approach and inflict suffering: for to that which is hot, alteration occurs from that which cools. Again, to the present moist, alteration happens from that which dries, and we say the subject is altered when it becomes cold from hot, or moist from dry.

**D** ...cold from hot, or moist from dry. This is also attested by what is called the corruption of fire, when a change into another element occurs. For we do not say that matter is corrupted, but fire; therefore, passions are about the same thing as destruction. For the way to destruction is the reception of passions, and that which can perish is also that which can suffer. But for matter to be corrupted is impossible: for into what and how it might be resolved, we cannot conceive.

**Dubitatio.**

**E** But indeed, since matter itself receives very many heats and colds, and qualities altogether innumerable, and is distinguished by them, and has them as if kindred, and mixed with each other (for they are not each separate above): but matter itself, left as if in the middle, how is it that when qualities in mutual mixture suffer from each other, it does not also suffer along with them? unless perhaps someone has placed it entirely outside of them. Nevertheless, whatever is in a subject is present to the subject in such a way that it imparts something of itself to the subject.

**IX**
Answer: That matter neither truly receives, nor receives true things, nor suffers; or what that which suffers can be.

**F** It must be observed that what is said, that one thing is present to another, and one thing is in another, is not to be understood by us in only one way, but sometimes it is such that something, along with its presence, affects that thing for better or worse by a certain change; which is indeed manifest in bodies, especially living ones.

**G** But sometimes something becomes better or worse by the presence of something else without reception, apart from suffering, as was said concerning the soul; sometimes also it is such, as if someone applies a figure to wax, where there is no suffering by which the wax becomes something else, when it is present
