A to it a figure. Nor again does any defect befall the wax when the figure is removed; then indeed, light does not even change the figure of what it illuminates. A stone, moreover, when made cold, receives something from that which makes it cold, the stone nevertheless remaining itself in the meantime, yet having acquired nothing beyond coldness. Therefore, what does a line suffer under color? Or a plane? Perhaps indeed the underlying body will be said to suffer, although what it suffers from color will be most difficult to define.
B For it must not be said that suffering is merely something being present, or being adorned with a form. If anyone, however, should say that mirrors and all transparent things suffer nothing from the images that appear in them, he will certainly offer an opportune example: for what is in matter are also images, and matter itself is even more alien to passions than mirrors. Therefore, heats and colds come to be in it, yet heats do not make matter hot: for to be heated and to be cooled consists in this, that a quality transfers the subject from one quality to another.
C Among these things, however, it would be worthy of consideration whether perhaps cold is nothing other than a certain absence and privation of heat: but qualities concurring in matter, many of them indeed act upon each other, namely those which are contrary to each other. For what does some odor do to sweetness? Or color to figure? Or what is in one genus, act upon another genus? From which one might most believe that one thing can be in the same place as another, or one thing in another, its very presence doing no harm to that to which it is present or in which it is present.
D Just as, therefore, that which is harmed is not harmed by just anything, so neither is it changed and suffers by just anything. But contraries only suffer from contraries, while other things are not changed by other things, namely, those for which there is no contrariety, these suffer from no contrary.
E Wherefore it is necessary, if anything suffers, that it is not matter, but something composite, or altogether many things existing simultaneously. But that which is alone, and by nature separated from others, and altogether simple, can suffer from nothing, but can underlie all things acting upon each other as a medium: just as in the same dwelling, when some strike each other, the dwelling itself suffers nothing, and perhaps not even the air that is in it.
F Therefore, let those things which are in matter, coming together among themselves, do whatever they can naturally do to each other: but matter itself is much more remote from suffering than any qualities in it which, because they are not contrary, suffer not at all from each other.

X Furthermore, if matter suffers, it must carry away something from the suffering, either the suffering itself or be affected differently than it was before the suffering occurred in it. Therefore, if another quality enters after that one, matter will no longer be what receives it, but matter *of a certain kind*. But if the quality itself also ceases, leaving something of itself behind because it had already affected matter, then still much more will another subject be made, and proceeding on this condition, the subject will be something other than mere matter, namely something varied and multiform:

--- Page 357 ---
LIBER SEXTVS. 313

A Therefore it will no longer be a common receptacle for all things, since it has already conceived within itself an impediment to many things that will sometimes come; nor will matter itself remain any longer, nor therefore will it be incorruptible. Wherefore, if matter must be as it was from the beginning, so it must always be the same; namely, to say that it has been changed is not to preserve it as matter.

B Moreover, if that which is altered must remain in the same species, being altered in its accidents, yet not changed in its substance—if, I say, that which is altered must remain, and that which suffers in it is not that which remains—it is necessary that one of two things happen: either the altered matter departs from itself, or, not departing, it is not altered at all. But if someone says that it is indeed altered, but not in the way that matter is altered, first, he will not be able to explain in what respect it is altered; then he will be forced to confess that in this way also matter itself is not altered.

C For just as in other things which are species, it cannot happen that they are altered according to their essence, since their essence consists in this very thing; so, since the being of matter is to be in the way that matter is, it is not permissible for it to be altered insofar as it is matter, but it is necessary for it to remain. And just as there the species itself is immutable, so here too it is necessary for matter to be immutable.

D Hence I think Plato, thinking thus, spoke correctly when he said, "the imitations of beings entering and leaving matter." For it should not be thought that he expressed "entering and leaving" without reason, but that he wished to make us cautious in explaining how species can participate in matter. From this it also appears that the Platonic doubt which is inquired into, namely how matter becomes a participant in species, does not tend towards what many earlier thinkers supposed, that is, how species come into matter, but rather how they are in it. For it truly seems wonderful,

E how, with these species of matter present, it itself remains the same, receiving no affection from them, especially since those things which enter into it suffer from one another. But indeed, according to Plato's opinion, it must be thought that those things which enter into matter expel the former ones from it, and that there is affection in the composite; not in every composite, but in that which needs a preceding form or a receding one, and which suffers a defect in its own constitution through the absence of something, but is perfected by its presence. Matter

F neither has anything more in its nature with anything approaching it, for then, with that approaching, that which is, is not produced. Nor again does it have anything less with anything receding: for it perseveres in what it was from the beginning. Embellishment is certainly useful and necessary for those things which need adornment and order, and adornment can occur without transmutation, just as when we place an ornament around something. But if something is so adorned that it has a distinctive ornament,

G it will be necessary for that which is adorned to be changed from what was previously ugly, and to become different, and thus to emerge beautiful from being ugly. If, therefore, matter, being ugly, has become beautiful, it is no longer that same ugly thing that it was before.

WHAT then? If matter did not exist, would nothing at all subsist? Absolutely nothing except entities: just as an image does not subsist when the mirror is removed, or anything of that kind. For that which is so constituted by nature as to exist in another, will never come to be if that other does not exist: for this is the very nature of an image, to be **B** in another. For if indeed it were to depart from the causes themselves, it could certainly exist, even if it were not in another. But since the causes themselves remain, if anything from them appears elsewhere, there must be something else, suggesting a seat to that which is not truly coming: which indeed, by its presence and boldness, and as it were, impudence and need, is as it were, pressed, and presses to be seized: yet it is deceived by not truly grasping, so that its persistent need always compels it to demand. For after it once **C** stood still (as the fable relates) it always desires: in which very thing its nature is shown to be devoid of good. But it does not desire to receive those things which the giver has, but it seems to be content if, whatever it may be, it receives something, so much so that from this it is shown that what appears to us in matter is different: the very name Penia, that is, "lack," declares that matter is not filled. But that Penia is said to meet with Poros, does not mean that she met with Being itself or with fullness, **D** but with something artificial and wonderful. And this is with a certain cunning of an image displaying itself. For since it is impossible for anything, whatever and however it may be outside of Being itself, to be entirely devoid of being—for this is the nature of Being, to make beings—and since non-being cannot be mixed with being at all, certainly something marvelous arises: namely, it participates without participating, and by its very proximity it obtains something, although by its own nature it cannot be truly joined. Therefore, what it has received slips away as if from an alien nature, **E** just like an echo from smooth and flat places: and what does not remain there, that also appears there, and seems to come from there. But if matter were to participate and receive in such a way, as some perhaps might think, certainly what approaches it would penetrate as if absorbed. But now it appears that it was not absorbed, but that it remained entirely the same, having gained nothing, but like a certain rebounding seat, it inhibited the process, and is a receptacle for things converging into it **F** and there mixed with each other: nor does it happen otherwise here than when some, wishing to kindle fire from the sun, place certain smooth and solid objects, which they also fill with water, so that the flame, restrained by what is contrary within, does not pass through, but remains outside. Therefore, in this way, matter becomes the cause of generation, and what is composed in it, is constituted in this manner.

Indeed, in those things which gather fire around themselves under the sun, inasmuch as they receive flame from sensible fire, they also have the property of being **G** perceived. Therefore, they appear, because what is produced there is external, and placed next and very near, and they touch each other, and their two boundaries are undoubtedly there. If therefore someone possesses the intelligence of the great, which indeed has the power by which it can not only be in itself, but also as it were go forth outside, and acquires a certain nature not existing in the intelligent principle, nor having a species, nor any trace of the great, nor of anything at all, what will it do by such a power? Not a horse, not an ox: for other causes will make these. Perhaps because it proceeds from the great as from a father, it cannot grasp anything else as great; but this will possess an imaginary (greatness). Therefore, for this [matter], which has by no means thus attained the great, so that the great itself might become in its own nature, what now remains is that it can appear great. But this is not to fail, and if it is propagated everywhere, not to proceed as if distinctly divided into many parts; but to have kindred parts within itself, and to be nowhere entirely absent. For it could not happen that in a small mass, there would be an equal likeness of the great, since it is an image of the great; but insofar as it desired it with hope, it approached: and running as far as it could, together with its concurring element which could not be abandoned, it produced the great—that which is not great, nor indeed so as to appear great, and which seems great in mass. Matter, however, meanwhile preserves its own nature, using this great as a garment, with which it was indeed clothed, when it concurred with it, while that running (element) was leading it. If indeed it ever casts this off, it remains again the same as it was before in itself, namely, as great as the present species renders it. Therefore the soul, possessing the species of beings, since it is itself also a species, simultaneously possesses all of them. Since also every species is whole at once with itself, and moreover seeing the species of sensible things as if reflected into itself and approaching, it does not endure to grasp them along with their multitude, but discerns them by subtracting the mass from them. For it cannot become other than what it is.

IN LIBR. VII. ENNEAD. III. 323

Essence or intelligence is life. It is therefore life: but how much? Certainly infinite: so that it is distinct from any part of time. Again, of what kind? Certainly whole at once, so that it is distinct from all time. Therefore, eternity is infinite life, whole at once, and to put it more briefly, simply infinite life: but time is life proceeding through the infinite. Indeed, the very present existence of eternity is entirely fixed like a center, and therefore one suffices. For since it never passes away, there is no need for any successor. But that which is called present in time, since it suddenly passes away, needs another present successor, lest the whole nature of time be lost, which is gradually accumulated from infinite moments succeeding each other, and therefore if it has any essence, it is mixed from being and non-being, while the present intervenes between the past and the future, which are not, and in whatever way it can, it emulates the very present of eternity through some constantly present aspect of itself, applying itself to the stable presence of eternity, and yet it is not stabilized: and therefore what it cannot achieve by remaining, by a leap...

--- Page 368 ---
324          COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO.
But duration itself, intimate to motions, is not everywhere, but is preserved in this motion and that. However, we think time is everywhere, and we are accustomed to measure any duration and perseverance of motion by time. Hence, time seems to be some measurable interval, and beyond the proper interval of motion, yet not an interval pertaining to place. Therefore, let us inquire about such an external interval without guidance, what it is naturally in itself, before this effect of measurement. For that which it is must exist in itself first, before it measures anything. We will also ask whether it measures rest, and in what way. For something rests, insofar as it is moved and [in relation to] another. Three things have been proposed about time by those who say time is something of motion: First, that it is the space and duration of motion, about which enough has been said; Second, that it is a certain measure of such duration; Third, that it is something accompanying or consequent. But let us now return to the measure, to which we have just gradually descended, and compelled [it] to answer what it is in itself before it measures, and whether it is an external or internal measure, and whatever it may be, how it measures motion similarly and rest. We add moreover how it is said to be a numerical measure, as if it were gathered from units. It is more probable, however, to simply call time a certain measure rather than a number, because of its very continuity. But if it is a certain measure, then it is a certain quantity, whatever its nature, or a certain quantum measuring motion, insofar as it runs together with motion. Here then it will be asked under what condition it runs together with motion, and why it measures motion rather than being measured by motion. For we are accustomed to measure so much time from so much motion, and to perceive time from action no less than vice versa. In summary, it is again doubted whether time is motion itself measured by a certain magnitude, or rather a certain magnitude measuring motion, or a third something. That it uses magnitude to measure motion, and altogether about this very measurable magnitude, it can be doubted. For it is so great in itself, just as motion is so great. Therefore, just as motion is judged to be so great by it, does it also exist so great by something superior? Finally, what it is before it measures (as we said) will be permissible to investigate. Similar doubts arise if the third opinion about motion is admitted, saying that time is something that accompanies motion. But we are compelled to posit that time itself is something: even if no mind using choice measures motion by time. For the soul of the world generates time by a certain natural and intimate motion of its own, using no choice for this.

Eternity is in the divine mind, Time in the soul of the world, by which the motion of the world is acted upon and measured.

Indeed, in the divine mind, time is not properly present, but a certain idea of time, as an exemplar conceived there for a certain likeness of eternity, imitating eternity indeed, but meanwhile degenerating by diversity: time, however, is properly in the soul of the world, in its very vegetative nature, and again in a certain natural imagination, constantly accompanying nature. In this twofold faculty of the soul, I say, the action for generating and imagining worldly things, due to weakness, is not performed entirely at once, but gradually now one thing arises, now another, ordered indeed, but dissimilar, and now it turns to these: now to those, proceeding according to prior and posterior. Indeed, the procession successively according to such degrees is motion: but the continuity and length of the procession is time. Now, if in any way the length of a body differs from the body itself, in the same way time differs from motion. The length, I say, of motion from motion. But this very length also relates to eternity as a line relates to a point: especially if it is permissible to imagine a line proceeding from a certain motion of a point, and the point being produced. Plotinus, however, believes that just as from the virtue of any soul, sometimes implanted in its seed, its own body sprouts: so from the natural power of the world soul, inwardly inspiring matter, the worldly body sprouts, and this is contained and ruled in the soul as in a certain place of the world, and is moved by the very motion of the soul, and is moved temporally, and at certain intervals of time, to the very time of motion which occurs in the soul, and to certain intervals of that time: since that soul, through its intimate motion, created time within itself, and together with this motion and time, produced the world mobile in time. But there is one place of the world, the soul of the world: one and everywhere time: since this soul also exercises vital motion everywhere, but meanwhile the worldly motion is ruled by its own motion of the soul: this [motion of the soul] however by its own and eternal intellect: that [eternal intellect] finally by the divine intellect and its first eternity.

P H I L O S O P H E R, B O O K V I I.
ON ETERNITY AND TIME.
On Eternity and Time.
Proem to Eternity and to Time.

When we say that eternity and time are different from each other, and that the former indeed concerns eternal nature, while the latter concerns that which comes into being: and when we consider this whole matter, we believe that we, as if spontaneously, from natural talent and a sudden intuition of understanding, have a certain manifest instinct concerning these things deeply implanted in our souls, always saying the same things about them, and naming them everywhere. But indeed, when we try to approach these things more closely and explain them more fully, we fall into doubts, and, taking the opinions of the ancients on these matters, some one way, others another, and perhaps even the same opinions differently, we finally dwell on these, thinking it sufficient if, when asked, we can report the opinion of the ancients, and thus we cease to investigate these matters further. Certainly, it must be supposed that some of the ancient and fortunate philosophers discovered the truth. It is worthwhile, however, to inquire next who in particular attained the truth, and by what method especially we too may come to know the same things. But first, we must inquire about eternity, what those who judge it to be different from time consider it to be. For once that which is held as an exemplar is known, perhaps its image, which they call time, will be more clearly understood. But if someone, before contemplating eternity, imagines what time is: it will perhaps happen to this person, progressing from here to there through a kind of reminiscence, to recognize that to which time is likened, if indeed this has a likeness to eternity.

What then should eternity be said to be? Is it perhaps intelligible essence itself: just as if someone were to say that time is the whole heaven and the world? For it is reported that some have thought this about time. For since we imagine and understand eternity to be something most venerable: and we judge intelligible nature to be most venerable, and cannot discern which of these is more venerable

...we may be able to distinguish: And since what is superior to these ought not to be described by such appellations, one might perhaps rightly take the intelligible nature and eternity for the same thing. Again, both the intelligible world and eternity embrace the same things in themselves. But indeed, when we speak of one in the other, and we place intelligibles in eternity, and when we declare any intelligible thing to be eternal—just as in Timaeus, where it is written: 'if the nature of the exemplar is eternal'—in these cases, I say, we affirm eternity to be something other than the intelligible nature; yet we confess it to be around it, or in it, or present to it. But the fact that both are judged venerable does not necessarily demonstrate them to be the same. For perhaps one of these has its venerability from the other; and as for what is again added, that the same things are contained by both, it must be explained that the intelligible nature indeed contains its own particulars, as parts, but eternity embraces the whole simultaneously, not as a part, but because all such things are called eternal through it. But should we judge eternity according to the state existing there, just as here they are accustomed to conceive of time according to motion? But rightly one will inquire first concerning eternity, whether we say it is the same as state, nor perhaps simply, but with the state that is considered to be around essence. For if it is the same as state, first indeed we will not call state eternal, just as we do not call eternity eternal. For that is eternal which is a participant of eternity. Then in what way will motion be eternal? For thus it would also be stable. Furthermore, how will the notion of state itself always have itself within it? But I mean not 'always' in time, but rather what we understand when we say 'everlasting'. But if 'always' itself is contained in the state of essence, then indeed we will again separate the other kinds of being from eternity. To these things is added that eternity must be understood not only in state, but also in unity; and moreover the function of indistancy must be preserved for eternity, lest perhaps it be entirely the same as time. But state, in so far as it is state, contains neither the understanding of unity nor of indistancy in itself. Therefore, we predicate of eternity that it remains in unity. Therefore it participates in state, but it will not be state itself.

For applying its own activity, one after another, and again another, it generated, along with the activity, that which follows in succession, and at the same time it proceeds with the thought of one thing after another, which was not before, for it had not produced anything by such a thought. But now the present life is not entirely similar to the previous one; therefore, it is another life, and insofar as it is another,
B it also has another time. Therefore, the extension and protraction of life received time, and the perpetual protraction of life has everlasting time, and past life has past time. If, then, someone should say that time is an activity of the soul in a transitional motion, always proceeding from one life to another, perhaps he would not speak beside the mark. For if eternity is life remaining in a state of rest and in the same and similar condition, and already infinite, and time must be an image of eternity,
C just as this world is an image of that world, it is clear that instead of the life there, one must place another here, in the power of the cosmic soul, as it were, homonymous with that, and instead of the intellectual motion, the motion of some part of the soul. And instead of identity and the similar and abiding form, that which does not remain in the same, but always accomplishes one thing after another. Again, instead of the indivisible property and the one of the one, already an imitation in
D continuous succession, possessing one. Furthermore, instead of the infinite and already whole, that which always extends itself to infinity according to what follows. Finally, instead of that which is whole at once, that which is future in parts, and always future as a whole. For thus it will imitate that which is already a whole being, and gathered at once, and already boundless, if it wishes to receive its being in the continuity of substance. For thus it will most of all imitate its being. But one must by no means take
E time outside the soul, just as eternity there is not outside that which is called being. Nor again is there succession, nor anything later, just as not there, but something intelligible within and existing at once, just as eternity there.

**A** or longer? Under what condition, again, would the soul further apply itself to something else? Unless perhaps into that in which it is. Indeed, not even into this itself: otherwise, it would have been necessary for it to have departed first, so that it might be able to apply itself to it: since not even the sphere itself would exist, which does not exist before time. For this also is in time, and moves: And even if it stands still while that operates, we shall measure how great its state is, as long as that external state of eternity perseveres. If therefore, with that ceasing from here and being completely united, time is immediately removed, it is clear that the beginning of this motion towards these things, and this life, constitutes time.

**B** it is clear that the beginning of this motion towards these things, and this life, constitutes time. For this reason, it was said in the Timaeus that time was made simultaneously with this universe: because the soul brought forth time together with this universe. For in such an action, this universe also was generated: and this indeed is time, but that (the universe) is in time. But if anyone should say that the movements of the stars are also called times by Plato, he must remember

**C** that Plato said these things were made for the manifestation and distinction of time, and so that the measure might be clearer to us. For since it was not permitted for the soul to determine time itself, or to measure by itself the individual parts of invisible and incomprehensible time, especially among men utterly ignorant of numbering, it (the soul) made day and night, through which it was possible to perceive two distinct things from this diversity: from which he (Plato) says the concept of number arose. Then perceiving how much

**D** is accomplished from sunrise again to sunrise, we were able to have a certain amount of time-space, with the kind of motion remaining equal: inasmuch as we fix our gaze upon this very thing as if relying on it, and use it as a kind of measure, a measure of time, I say. For time itself is not the measure. For in what way would it measure, and what would it say when measuring? Would it say of something, "this is as much as I am"? Who then is it that is called, or says "I"? Or according to whom is the

**E** measurement made? Does not something therefore exist in itself, so that it can be measured, and yet is not the measure itself? Therefore, the motion of the universe will be measured according to time: and time will not be the measure of motion according to what it (time) is, but accidentally, namely, by existing as something else first, it will reveal how great the motion is. Then indeed, a single motion, taken over such a period of time and frequently counted, will bring to knowledge how much time has passed. Therefore,

**F** if anyone should say that motion and revolution somehow measure time as much as they can, as if showing in their own quantity how much time there is: since it cannot be understood or taken otherwise, he will certainly not deviate from a proper explanation. What is therefore measured by the circuit, that is, declared, will be time, not indeed generated by the circuit itself, but demonstrated. And so, that which is measured by a determined motion seems to be the measure of motion, and measured

**G** by it (the motion) as if distinct from it: since if both the measurer were one thing, and the measured certainly another, the measured would be so accidentally. And so it would have been said just as if someone said that what is measured by a cubit is magnitude, yet not saying what it itself is...

Perhaps in every such soul, and it is uniformly in all, and all are in a certain way one. Therefore, time will not be dispersed: since neither is eternity, which exists in all uniform things according to a different principle.

MARSILIUS FICINUS ON
BOOK EIGHT OF THE THIRD ENNEAD,
CONCERNING NATURE, AND
contemplation, AND THE ONE.

COMMENTARY.
SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.
Natural things are made by a certain active life through quasi-contemplative reasons, implanted in it by the divine intellect.

[Large decorative initial P] HILOSOPHERS of old, some simply natural ones, used to think that all natural things are generated from a certain elemental quality and motion: and that such things arise or such things (happen) according to the virtue of the quality which was active in the agent, and according to the efficacy of the motion thence ceasing in matter, nor that any reason of intimate art was presiding over these. Plotinus, however, wants corporeal qualities and motions to be led by an incorporeal form not subject to motions, but presiding: which he calls universal and primary nature. I speak of a substantial and vital form, which is neither any quality of bodies, so that it can equally procreate all, nor acts by the mere impulse of motion, so that it can dispose all things with a certain moderation: but acts by a certain formal reason of its own, and by a certain natural art: just as if the artificial reason, which is an accident in the artisan, were something subsisting by itself. F 2

--- Page 384 ---
340 COMMENT. MARSIL. FICINI

although within matter: and thus by its own nature acts artfully, as an artisan acts artfully by choice: indeed, it acts artfully by natural art, just as fire naturally heats by natural warmth. Therefore, qualities and motions obey this living and natural reason, as instruments: although without corporeal motion, it produces corporeal motion, and without the quality of fire, it generates fire: and without manifest seed, it everywhere generates living things: inasmuch as it possesses in itself the essential and living reasons of all things: which we sufficiently prove in our theology, and thus briefly confirm here. Beyond nutrition and growth, which are certain kinds of generation, is generation itself, simply speaking, which is also preserved in all these. Since therefore these certain generations are the works of certain lives or certain living things, indeed, generation itself, simply speaking, and the first and common generation, is the work of life simply speaking, and of the common life ruling the whole world. And since in the mass of the world there are not everywhere certain manifest seeds of corporeal things, certainly in life itself, as a whole, are the seeds, and the proper reasons of seeds and of things appearing to the senses. For nature, which acts without choice, acts by an indwelling form, and everywhere necessarily forms certain forms with certain forms, that is, with seminal reasons: by which, indeed, as principles and rules, it defines all motions, which are indeterminate in themselves, with a certain tenor, and leads qualities, which act with full impetus whatever they do, and are naturally confined in a narrow space, by a certain balanced moderation to their work: and that indeed, though multiform, with a uniform order. Nor does it look to a certain end everywhere, in those things which themselves do not see the end, otherwise than art and counsel are accustomed to do. This living and natural art contains in itself all natural forms according to their act, no differently than human art possesses its artifices. For matter, which is always in a potential state of being formed for all things, is brought to the act of all things in no other way than through a life indeed presiding over matter, but related to it, comprehending all things in itself in act. Indeed, this nature, the artisan of all things, needs neither some such or such matter, nor matter itself simply, for its existence. For it daily renders matter such and such, and moves matter with swift command. Now indeed, it does not need this or that quality of matter for its simple action. For it can generate qualities without qualities, inasmuch as it is the common principle for generating all things equally. And if it everywhere generates living things without manifest seeds, it can all the more procreate elemental qualities through its own seeds alone, without the ministry of such elements. But if it uses matter affected by certain qualities, it does not indeed use such qualities out of necessity, but by accident. Which is certainly confirmed by those who believe that in generation, resolution occurs all the way to prime matter. Therefore remember that nature is such a true principle of generation everywhere. For material form, because it is the last of forms, properly generates nothing formal. For that which is last in any genus, generates nothing in it. Therefore, material form is not so much a principle of generation, as a certain affection of matter induced from above by an occult principle generating species. That it generates nothing, is confirmed by this, that generation pertains to life: but this lacks life: and that it lacks life is clear from this, because essence must proceed further than life: yet essence does not proceed all the way to matter: indeed, neither does form. Therefore, essence defines into quality, and indeed defines intrinsically, therefore life into nature, similarly above the quality of matter. Indeed, this nature is incorporeal. For that which is corporeal, if it moves anything, is meanwhile also moved, I say, it is moved even in substance. But the first mover is that which remains in substance, so that it can perpetually continue its tenor in motion. If however it is an intimate and familiar mover, like a certain form, such as nature itself is, it is necessary that while it moves, it is also moved in a certain way, rather by a certain mode of itself, one after another.

--- Page 385 ---
IN LIB. VIII. ENNEAD. III. 341

while the intellect contemplates and beholds itself. But second forms are naturally expressed from the contemplating intellect into the intellectual soul: and here too are certain contemplations. Third (forms) are imprinted thence into nature. Which, since they are expressed precisely from contemplations, are themselves also certain contemplations, lest I should so often say 'contemplamina'. Finally, fourth (forms) are conceived from the very contemplative concepts of nature in the matter of the world. And since they follow the aforesaid contemplations in a certain order and imitate them perfectly, they can be called certain contemplations. Indeed, artworks pertaining to sight are usually said to be certain intelligences and ingenuity of the artist; much more so musical sounds; even more so songs, because they carry with them a more expressed thought and a living emotion, especially words, whether spoken or written. Therefore, natural forms primarily have this, that they are both called and are certain intelligences, and expressed concepts of intellectual nature itself, or of natural intelligence. For nature itself, the artisan of things, is a certain living power.

they understand, and what they do not understand. Therefore, intellect and intelligible are distinguished from each other by a certain formal reason, and such a distinction is very close to what is called a real distinction. This very real distinction is the ultimate one: therefore, that first form, in which intellect is coupled with the intelligible, is not the most simple unity: therefore, it is not the first principle of the universe, which is simply one and most simple: just as whatever is first in any genus is necessarily simple in that same genus. But that intellect is necessarily manifold, and therefore not first, is also confirmed thus: If intellect is the highest knowledge, it has the intelligible conjoined with it, namely, the same in reality, although not the same in concept: Likewise, that which is intelligible primarily and in itself, also consequently has this, that it is also intellect. For such an intelligible is a subsistent separate form, and therefore, reflected in itself, it brings forth intelligence. But if a material thing is called intelligible, it becomes such insofar as it is transformed into something else, or is consequently understood through something else. Therefore, since intellect and intelligible accompany each other, so much so that what is one is also the other: and these differ by formal reason, necessarily the first intellect is manifold, and not the supreme principle of the universe. It is then doubted in this manner: the principle itself, insofar as it is outside the genus of intelligence, seems to be unknown to itself: and insofar as it exists above the intelligible genus, it can in no way be known. To these things it is answered: that it enjoys itself by a more excellent reason than by knowing; and that the soul enjoys it perhaps by a more excellent knowledge than intellectual, or rather by a more eminent way than by knowing. For intellect simply and knowledge is not the highest in us, but a good-like unity, through which we first enjoy unity and goodness simultaneously: just as through luminous sense we enjoy luminous sensible things. Therefore, just as he who strives vehemently to imagine ceases from movement and sense: and he who wishes to understand deeply calms imagination: so he who desires to attain that which exists above intellectual and intelligible nature, must entirely pass beyond everything intelligible, and set aside his own intellect, and impose complete silence on intelligence, being reduced, namely, to something first of himself, through which he may enjoy the first principle of the universe. Conclude that one thing and another enjoy themselves differently. The body of an animal indeed enjoys itself through sense, but reason enjoys itself not through sense, but through something better: and intellect also becomes master of itself not through any discursive reasoning, but through something more eminent in itself: similarly, the one itself and the good enjoy themselves through something higher than intelligence and cognition. Therefore, if one must ascend gradually from imperfect to perfect, certainly above imagination, which is accustomed to traverse only through some kinds of things, and moreover for a long time, reason must be placed, traversing through all things, and needing shorter time for this, and where it is most perfect, the shortest possible time. Above this is intellect, always perfected without time: which, if it perfectly has and sees all things in itself, does not have them confused, but distinct and pure, it does not behold obscure things, but discerns clear and distinct ones. Therefore, above this necessarily manifold intellect is the first principle of the universe, which is neither merely one thing of all: otherwise, it would not have power over all things, nor could it be the principle of all things: nor is it so much all things that it is not one and simple, for this is the first. But everywhere unity is prior to multitude, and the simple to the composite: nor again is it both one and all things equally. For if this is granted by anyone, we distinguish thus: either it is all things collectively, or rather individually: if collectively, that is, that there is one certain form with a multitude: either this one form is before the multitude, and thus this alone is the principle, nor is it necessary, for it to be the principle, to add multitude to it: or this one form is with the multitude simultaneously: and thus it is not the principle of all, since it does not exist before all things: or this one form is placed after all things, than which nothing seems more absurd to say. But if the other member of that disjunction is accepted, namely that that principle of all things is so all things, that concerning each thing demonstrated by sight, by running through individuals, it is true to say, "this is the principle," it will follow that anything whatsoever is the principle. But since the principle is necessarily unique, there will be only one thing in the universe: or conversely, there will be as many principles as things are posited to exist.

The Good itself is above essence, life, intellect, nor can it be attained by intellect.
Since in the grades of living beings we see that the most perfect degree of life is ultimately intellectual life, we can conjecture that the first life in the whole order of things is simply intellect itself. Therefore, whether you consider it as life, it is a certain movement towards an end, and therefore towards something else, as towards the good: or if you take it as intellect, it is a certain movement towards the true, as towards the good: in both ways, therefore, it is something dependent, nor is it content with its own essence, whose life and intellect exist, but it seeks something better than essence, that is, the good itself, which neither needs life according to form, nor intellect by which it strives towards the good: since it is the good itself, which needs no action at all: since every action is towards the good, about which it is concerned. And since this entirely exists above intellect and intelligible, and names are usually imposed from the conception of the intellect, it has no proper name. But it is called good, because from it all things are made, and things made are perfected. It is also called one, because meanwhile it surpasses all things, nor does it move while these proceed from it, otherwise nothing would remain anywhere: nor is it divided into parts, otherwise the one itself would cease: which being removed, all things would immediately perish: nor is it multiplied into forms at all, otherwise, suffering admission or addition, it would no longer be true unity and immense simplicity. If you proceed through trees, through animals, through soul, through mind, you will find that in each of these, that which is most simple and most one, is the most powerful of all, and the principle of the rest. Similarly, you will reduce the universe to the most powerful unity, concerning which you will predicate nothing further, once you have first conceived unity itself or goodness: otherwise, if you predicate anything besides, you will compose, and diminish by composing, and render it needy, and posterior. Therefore, do not add intellection to this. For the reason of intelligence is one thing, that of the good another. For not both equally suit everyone. Therefore, intelligence joined to the good makes a collection, nor therefore will you apply ideas there, which are conceived by intelligence, and differ absolutely from each other by formal reason, especially ideas of contrary and opposite things, which is clear from the order of the universe generated from it according to essence and form. For what differs in reality and subject in this work, these differ in the intellect of the maker of all things by absolute formal reason: otherwise, this order of forms would consist either in some disordered chance, or would proceed from utterly unformed matter. But the Platonists first forbid applying formal and absolute distinctions, and also forbid applying life or essence after unity or goodness, whose striving does not rest in itself, but contends towards the good. They command to place that first principle above essence and being, just as they judge matter, which is the ultimate opposite, to be placed under essence and being: and therefore, just as in attaining matter one must descend below all things

--- Page 387 ---
IN BOOK VIII, ENNEAD III. 349

...all concepts of intelligence that are formal: so, to reach that [the Good] above all such concepts, one must ascend: nor should it be thought that it can be reached by a mobile, or multiple, or formal act of intelligence, because it wonderfully exists above motion, multiplicity, and form.

The Good itself is the father, whose son is the intellect, always full from the father, and of this intellect, the world is the image.

Just as sight is one thing, and light is another, for grasping which the eye is made, even if an eye were imagined to be full of eternal light: so intellect is one thing, and truth itself and the good is another, towards which the intellect naturally strives: and the intellect itself differs from that [the Good], which, because of its proximity to the Good, always most fully enjoys the Good: Therefore, the Good itself, like light, has no need of sight. Now, if someone could behold the entire ornament of the visible world all at once with a single gaze, they would admire it beyond measure, and as if from a certain image, they would more easily suspect the intelligible world to be its maker, but much more beautiful. [Marginal note: I. Nature remaining in itself, through seminal reasons, forms matter without choice and instrument.]
Therefore, since here there are neither hands, nor feet, nor any instrument, either adventitious or innate: but matter is necessary in which it may make or place in form, it is clear to almost everyone. Nor indeed is it to be thought that nature thus accomplishes its work, as if by pushing and pressing. For what kind of impulse or pressure can produce various and multiform colors and figures? since neither wax sculptors and similar formers, whom they call doll-makers, or observing whom, some have thought nature's own handiwork to be very similar, can make colors, unless they apply these from elsewhere to their works. It was worthwhile to consider, just as in such practitioners of arts, something must remain within, according to which, remaining, they fabricate works by hand; similarly, there must be something of that kind in nature, which is indeed a certain permanent power and fabricates without the ministry of hands: remaining, I mean, entirely: for it does not need some things as remaining, and others as if moved. For matter is that which is moved there, but in the power itself nothing is moved: otherwise, what is moved will not be the primary mover, nor will it be nature itself, but that which is immobile in its entirety. Someone might object that reason indeed remains immobile, but nature is different from reason and is moved. But if they say it is entirely [immobile], reason will similarly be so: but if something of it is immobile, this very thing will also be reason. For it must be this form, and not composed of matter and form. For what need would it have of hot or cold matter? since the matter subjected to fabrication brings that with it: whether it is of this kind, or rather even before it assumes quality, it is touched by reason. For fire does not need to approach for matter to become fire, but reason does. Which indeed is a clear argument in animals and plants, that seminal reasons are the effective producers, and that nature exists as reason, which, as if its own offspring, generates another reason, while indeed it transmits something to the subject, yet meanwhile remains in itself. Reason, therefore, brought forth externally according to visible form, is now the ultimate, and lacking life: and therefore cannot make another reason further. But reason having life, with the maker of form, and as if a sister, and itself possessing the same power, generates the ultimate reason in effect.

[Marginal note: II. Seminal reasons in nature are as if certain contemplations impressed from above by intellectual contemplation, and therefore what are made by nature are also made by contemplation, and are certain contemplations.]
In what manner, therefore, does it make? And in making, how does it attain some contemplation, and what contemplation? Indeed, if it acts while remaining, and remaining in itself, and is reason, it is certainly contemplation. For action is accustomed to occur according to reason, being indeed different from reason: but reason assisting and presiding over action is not action. Therefore, if it is not action, but reason, it is undoubtedly a certain contemplation. Now indeed, in universal reason, the ultimate reason proceeds from contemplation, and thus is called contemplation, as if conceived by contemplation itself and

A perceived. But every reason superior to this one behaves differently. And one is not like nature, but like soul: but the other is in nature, and is nature itself. But does this also arise from contemplation? Entirely from contemplation: but if it has also in some way contemplated itself. For it is the effect of contemplation, and of a certain contemplated thing.
B But how does it have speculation? Indeed, it does not have speculation proceeding from reason: I mean, proceeding from reason: namely, the consideration of those things that are in itself. But why does it not at all consider its own things, since it is a certain life and reason and efficient power? Or perhaps because to consider is not yet to have? But if it has these things, it certainly acts from what it has and effects. Therefore, for it to be what it is, that is certainly for it also to make: and whatever it is, that very thing is also making. And it is a certain contemplation, and (as I might say) a beholding, for it is reason.
C Therefore, insofar as it is contemplation and beholding and reason, to that extent it makes, namely by that reason by which this exists. Therefore, it has now become clear to us that making is a certain contemplation: namely, it is the effect of contemplation, with speculation remaining, and not acting in any other way, but making precisely because it is contemplation itself.

IF ANYONE, however, should ask this (nature), for whose

Indeed, the affection of my mother and my generators is preserved in me: for they draw their origin from contemplation. My generation also is derived from speculation.

**A** that the other is, and all contemplation is: so much so that even what seems to be action according to contemplation is nothing other than a certain very weak contemplation. For it is always necessary that what is begotten should in some way indeed agree in kind, yet turn out weaker: since it gradually becomes diminished by the descent itself. Indeed, all things proceed smoothly and quietly, because they do not need contemplation or action appearing from outside. The soul itself indeed from the highest

**B** contemplates the ages, and what it thus contemplates, as something that arises externally, neither in the same way with that which is before it, certainly produces that which is after it: contemplation certainly begets contemplation. For contemplation itself, or even the object of contemplation, has no end: for this reason, it both proceeds and advances through all things. For what prevents it from spreading through all things? since the object of contemplation is the same in every soul. For it is not

**C** circumscribed by magnitude, yet not in all things in the same way: therefore, not in the same way in every part of the soul. Hence, certainly, in Plato, the charioteer of the soul imparts what he has seen to the horses: but these receive it from there, as those who desire what they have seen: for they have not received the whole. But if, desiring, they act, they will act for the sake of what they desire. And this is the object of contemplation itself and contemplation.

**D** ACTION, therefore, occurs for the sake of contemplation and the object of contemplation: therefore, the end of those who act is contemplation. Namely, what they could not achieve by a direct path, they strive to grasp, as it were, by circuitous routes. The same also happens when they attain what they desire: which indeed they wanted to be present. Not indeed so that they do not know, but so that they recognize what has already been acquired, and behold it present in the soul, as if placed there for the sake of viewing: because they always act for the sake of good.

**E** always act for the sake of good: But this is not so that it is placed outside them, and they have it minimally in themselves, but so that they themselves possess what becomes good from action. But where is this? Certainly in the soul. Therefore, action again falls back into contemplation itself. For what one grasps with the soul, which is a certain reason, what else is it but silent reason? And the more reason there is, the more silent it is, and vice versa. For then it also brings about quiet, and being full, it requires nothing further: and contemplation in such a

**F** state, established because of the very confidence of possessing, rests inwardly. And the surer the faith, the quieter the contemplation: which indeed rather reduces the soul to unity. And by this very reason you will know that it, insofar as it knows (for now we must proceed seriously), comes into unity with the known thing. For if there are two, this one will indeed be one thing, and that one another. Therefore, it will seem to be something adjacent: and that very dual thing has not yet contracted true familiarity,

**G** as when reasons existing in the soul do nothing. Therefore, reason must not be something external, but united with the mind of the learner, until it finds its own. The soul, therefore, when it becomes familiar with reason and is affected by it, simultaneously brings forth, and, being ready, now proceeds into action. For what it had before, it perceives, and by its own ready expedition, as if

But when it has left its former state and passed into another, then having returned, it again contemplates, a part of it having been left behind thus far; but the other part, remaining in itself, achieves less. Therefore, the virtuous soul is now itself the effect of reason, and what is within itself, it also demonstrates to others; but to itself, it is a vision. For now here it is brought to unity and to quietude, not only as far as external things are concerned, but as far as itself, and finally, all things within.

THEREFORE, as reason has partly indicated through all things: all things are from contemplation and are contemplations, both truly existing things and those generated from them. Namely, these contemplating, the things themselves having become contemplations, offering themselves everywhere to sense, or to cognition, or to opinion. Furthermore, actions are directed towards cognition as their end; appetite also strives for cognition. Moreover, generations, drawing their beginning from contemplation, culminate in a species, and another pattern to be fabricated. And altogether, individual imitations of efficient causes everywhere produce spectacles and species: and also, created substances, as imitations of beings, declare that efficient causes look to the work itself as their end, not to effects, not to actions, but to the work itself, for this very purpose, that it may be a spectacle to those who behold it.

Indeed, even thoughts desire to see this very thing; and even before them, the senses themselves, whose end is cognition. Again, before these things, nature itself, possessing a pattern and reason within itself, moreover generates another reason. Therefore, it is clear that since the very first things of all consist in contemplation, all other things necessarily desire contemplation itself; since the end proposed to all is that which is also the beginning. Now indeed, even when animals generate, the seminal reasons within stimulate them to procreate, and all of this is an action of contemplation, and a stimulus affecting the fabrication of many species, and various spectacles, and to fill all things with reasons, and as it were, to behold perpetually. For to make something exist is to bring forth a certain species, and this is to completely fill all things with contemplation. Furthermore, errors, both in things that are generated and in things that are acted upon, seem to be nothing other than the failures of contemplators and a certain deviation from the object of contemplation itself. Indeed, even an inept artisan is judged similar to one who makes deformed shapes.

[Middle section]
MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY
ON BOOK IX OF THE THIRD ENNEAD,
CONCERNING EIGHT CONSIDERATIONS.
SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

First Proposition, that the author of the world is the first intellect,
son of the Good itself.

[Main body text]
NINE principal considerations appear in this book. The first is concerning the author of the world: where, if one follows the path of Iamblichus and Proclus, he will explain that saying of Timaeus about the demiurge of the world, namely, that the demiurge of the world conceived of arranging as many species in the world as the intellect understands ideas in the living being itself. He will explain it, I say, thus: that there are at least three divine substances between the first principle, that is, the Good itself, and the world. Of these, the first, according to its form, is essence, partaker of the Good, and moreover, the cause of life and intellect. The second, indeed, according to its form, is life, partaker of essence: but the formal cause of intellect. And finally, the third, through its form, is intellect, partaker of life, and cause of the world. He will name the first Caelus, the second Saturn, and finally the third Jupiter: And he will consider Caelus to be as much superior to Saturn, and Saturn to Jupiter, as essence is superior and prior to life, and life to intellect. And that essence is superior to life, inasmuch as it diffuses itself more widely, and that life, on account of a similar amplitude, is superior to mind. Therefore, he will say that the formal intellect, Jupiter, is the proximate maker of the world, having in itself the intellectual ideas of worldly things: which ideas he indeed received from the vital intellect, namely from Saturn, in whom the ideas are equally intellectual and intelligible, which Saturn has from the essential intellect, namely from Caelus himself, in whom the ideas are only intelligible. Thus, therefore, he will interpret Timaeus: The providence of Jupiter conceived of fabricating as many species in the world as he observed the Saturnian intellect contemplating ideas, in the living being itself, that is, in Caelus: who by essence is the cause of life. But with Plotinus, there are not three substances, but only one substance, which is named first essence and life and first intellect. For first life is nothing other than the innermost and perpetual vigor and act of essence, and of the first form, most efficacious of all for action. The first intellect is also a certain reflection into itself of the first life, especially that which is consistent with itself. Plotinus therefore calls that substance the first intelligible, inasmuch as it is living and fruitful, and can conceive intellect within itself, and move the concept, and thoroughly form it. He also calls this substance intellect, as far as it pertains to its vital action, arisen from itself and reflected into itself. Again, he calls it something cogitative in a certain way: because it resolves to distribute outwardly what it has seen inwardly. Therefore, he thinks that in the order of things, motion arises before division, and that God, the intellect, being utterly immobile, cannot, I say, by a flowing motion, be propagated into multiple unparticipable intellects: but the genus of soul, being mobile by its very nature, is multiplied into many souls. And since this genus [of soul] is a partaker of intelligence: therefore, in this, intellect is propagated into many participable intellects, inasmuch as the genus of soul is propagated into many species of soul. He also considers that the intellect, the demiurge of the world, generates soul, both the soul of the world itself, and the remaining common souls of the spheres and stars, and finally, particular souls, namely of daemons and humans. And since distribution especially pertains to the genus of soul as mobile and multiplicable, therefore he wills that intellect...
G 3

--- Page 398 ---
354          COMMENT. MARSIL. FICINI
the builder of the world, through the world soul itself first created, and through the common souls, its colleagues, to have carried out distributions
through its own degrees of worldly animals.

Second Proposition: How the soul can gather itself into its own intellect, and through this intellect be formed by the divine. There are also in this
chapter three other propositions: two about the soul, and one about God.

Up to this point, the first consideration, which declared the intellect to be the world-maker. The second consideration, however, treats
how the soul can transfer itself into this universal intellect, namely, if the soul, just as it gathers multiple senses into one sense of imagination, so too gathers imaginations, widely diverse among themselves, into one common rule of reason: then reduces the various discourses of our reason to a stable norm of intelligence: let it be entirely formed by its own intellect as much as possible, through which it will be universally formed by the intellect of the whole world-maker. This can
happen in the degrees of life, since it is the same in the degrees of knowledge themselves. Geometry consists of a thousand propositions, and the posterior is deduced from the prior by necessity, and therefore the subsequent ones are comprehended by the antecedents, and all are contained in the first. Our soul, indeed, through its rational faculty, transferring itself from potentiality to act, and vice versa, if it possesses the whole of geometry, can indeed have all its propositions by a certain potentiality and habit, while it has some of them in act. Meanwhile, our intellect also, in anything considered according to act, considers through the same act, and possesses all. Therefore, we must strive for our rational faculty to conform itself to the intellect as much as possible. In which state, it may contemplate all subsequent notions in the first, by the same act by which it contemplates the first. In
the third consideration, Plotinus believes that the world soul, because it once and most powerfully embraced the entire animal form of life within itself, and from there completely occupied the whole body and space, cannot change the form of life within itself, nor exchange bodies outside itself: and similarly, he thinks the souls of the spheres and stars, and all celestial souls, behave, because they firmly obtained universal providence from the beginning. But particular souls, having obtained a particular mode of providence, such as those of most demons and humans, in a certain alternation, somehow fulfill that perpetual providence of the superiors: and insofar as they themselves change from this form of life into another, to that extent they change bodies and abodes: whence they seem to approach a body and place, namely, by a change first made within themselves. But
the body of the world seems to approach the world soul itself. For that [soul] remaining firmly in its habit, this body, thus affected from the beginning, is thence vivified, just as the transparent region of the ether is always illuminated by the Sun. But particular souls are also said to descend sometimes from the soul of the world, namely: because from the universal providence and form of life, which they sometimes possess together with the world soul, they slip into their own. For they did not firmly possess it. In
the fourth consideration, he divides our soul into three forms, namely, intellectual, rational, and lacking reason: and he thinks that the soul sometimes transfers itself entirely to its intellectual form, and then dwells with the divine intellect, sometimes descends from there into itself, that is, into the rational form proper to this soul: sometimes, however, from here into a form inferior to reason: whence it produces an image of itself, namely, life communicated to the body: to which life, indeed, is subject, and the ultimate image of all, that is, matter, which the soul, through its vegetative power, by its first proximity, forms with corporeal quality and a certain figure: then soon, through this affection, as if by bait, it is naturally attracted to vivify this body, now disposed in a certain way. In the fifth consideration, you will note thus: Just as in a circle there is a point within itself which is the center, and a point in the entire circumference and every part of it, proceeding from that which is within itself, indeed, as if it were itself or its propagation. Likewise, just as there is unity in every number and its part, flowing from a certain unity outside the number, simply conceived in itself: so in the entire essence of things there is a certain unity, the foundation of essence, and the preservation of everything, proceeding from divine unity, remaining super-essential in itself, and thus filling all things, inasmuch as its omnipresent presence creates from itself a certain super-essential unity in every created thing, the producer and preserver of every essence.
Now, because this unity is more excellent than essence, we infer that wherever it is, it is made and preserved by the presence of divine unity.

Concerning our intellect also, how it is always in act.

The sixth consideration is about the soul and mind together, in this manner: The diaphanous nature of the eye, that is, translucent, comes primarily from the solar nature, and therefore naturally desires light, and is easily filled with the light of the sun: similarly, the diaphanous nature in heaven proceeds from a certain celestial light, preceding the diaphanous according to the order of the universe, and emanating from intellectual light. And immediately, while it emanates, producing the diaphanous, and filling what is produced, whence heaven becomes as it were the eye of the celestial soul, providing for all things with this diaphanous nature and light: in the same way, the divine mind generates the rational soul with its light, as if a diaphanous matter beneath that light, and fills it with perpetual light: by which the soul always understands itself as illuminated by the mind, and the mind as always illuminating. Our intellect, the head of the soul,

--- Page 399 ---
IN BOOK IX. ENNEAD. III. 355

and these, knowing their proper objects, similarly differ among themselves: imagination indeed judges the particular, but reason collects and discerns the common species in particulars, while intellect recognizes the Idea. But since the Idea differs more remotely from the species outside of which it exists, than the species from the individual in which it is preserved, therefore intellect is more distant from reason than reason from imagination. Nevertheless, intellect is inherent in the soul: otherwise the mind could not infer that ideas exist through reason, unless reason acted through a virtue implanted in us by the intellect. And because reason resolves particulars to the universal, and the corporeal to the incorporeal, without the aid of our imagination, indeed, even against its will, as it draws back to the opposite: therefore the intellect, without movement or reasoning, always contemplates ideas, always, I say. For if it does not arrive at them by new imagination and argumentation, either it never arrives, or it always possesses them. Rightly, since the soul is a medium between eternity and time (for its essence is fixed, and it precedes the motion dependent on it), it is fitting that in its fixed essence, by that very sign by which it precedes motion, there should be a power and action utterly immobile and stably contemplating: inasmuch as this intuition, tending from a stable essence and power to an entirely stable Idea, claims stability for itself on both sides. Just as, therefore, in the soul, from that which is under eternity, mobile imagination is fitting, so from that which is above time, the intellect acting immovably is appropriate. The act of the intellect is indeed entirely immobile: the act of imagination, however, is entirely mobile: finally, the act of reason is mixed: nor could the soul be a fitting medium of the universe, unless it possessed these three within itself.

How God is above motion, and state, and cognition. Also
concerning that which is in act, and that which is in potency.

The seventh consideration proves that in the first principle of all things there is no motion, let alone a flowing one, nor even a metaphorical one, which is an act tending towards something else. For that which is absolutely first and last does not tend towards something else. It also proves that there is no state there, namely, the rest towards which motion tends, opposed to motion. And absolutely, it neither rests in something else, as it is not moved towards something else, nor does it properly rest in itself, as it is simplicity itself. For in it no such distinction falls, by which that which rests is accustomed to be distinguished, both from rest and from the seat in which it rests. Now, motion derives its power from a state, while it maintains its course from the stability of a motive power; but a state derives from unity. For to stand is nothing other than to preserve one's own unity. Therefore, unity itself precedes both motion and state. Therefore, it also precedes the act of intelligence, which is a kind of motion from the potency of understanding to the intelligible truth as a good. In every intelligent being, therefore, even if it understands itself, such a distinction is considered; but in the first, there is no absolute distinction. Finally, one is the nature of existence, and entirely another is that of intelligence: for not everything that exists, understands. To the first principle, existence will indeed be granted: if intelligence is added, then a composition will occur, and it will be clear that existence itself was by no means sufficient for its own perfection: inasmuch as it would have needed intelligence, through which it would tend towards progress.

In the eighth consideration, you will note that the condition of formal act and formable potency are opposed to each other: so much so that potency receives act, but act, insofar as it is act, does not receive potency. Where, therefore, there is only act, as in the first principle, the thing is eternal: because no potency for another form lies hidden there. Likewise, where the entire formable potency has been transferred into the nature of the form, so that the form there is in no way drawn back to the nature of potency, the thing is also eternal: especially because the potency there possesses the whole act as much as it can, and desires to have it: such are intellectual essences, and celestial fire. Fire, however, beneath the sky, among lower things, is more perfect, inasmuch as it is most in act: which is apparent from the efficacy of its form, and from its perpetual motion, and because it does not tolerate mixture. But since it has matter under act, and is not content with it, it is not eternal. In the ninth consideration, remember that intelligence itself is not the good itself simply, the first and last, otherwise it would be simply desirable: but now it is chosen under a certain condition. For you choose to know, if only you know well and happily, and what will be beneficial to you as a good. Likewise, the good itself does not have self-cognition: both because this (cognition) is one thing, and the good itself is another: and because if it suffices for itself before cognition, it should not be added; if not, it was not the good itself. However, in what manner God is neither blind nor ignorant, even if cognition is not added to Him (above which Dionysius the Areopagite also places Him), we will explain more opportunely in the fifth or sixth Ennead.

THE MIND (as it is written in the Timaeus) beholds the ideas implanted in that which is living. Hence the craftsman of the world is said to have thought to include in this world what the mind contemplates in that which is living or animal. Is it then, he asks, that species already exist above the mind, and that the mind inspects them, already existing? Therefore, in the first place, that which is called living or animal itself must be investigated, whether perhaps it is not intellect, but different from intellect. Wh-

A That which deliberated, having inspected the spectacles placed in the living being itself by the intellect, to operate, to make, to distribute.
