MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST AND SECOND BOOKS OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD, CONCERNING THE SOUL.
SUMMARY OF THE BOOKS.
The first intellect is the first essence, from which and in which other intellects always exist. Likewise, how the soul is indivisible and at the same time divisible.

SINCE we have discussed more extensively elsewhere what Plotinus here discourses concerning the soul, especially in the first, third, and seventh books of theology, we will therefore touch upon it briefly here. Generation always strives towards being: first indeed towards bare being, then towards living being, after these towards being which is called sensual, and finally towards intellectual being as the highest, where the intellectual soul descends to commerce with the body. Such indeed is the order of essence or of coming into being acquired in the degrees of generation. Above this order exists the order of essence in the eternal degrees of the universe, in which the intellect itself simply holds the highest place as a principle: from which the animal intellect, descending in generation, holds the highest place in the entire order of generation as an end, not indeed simply made by generation, but accommodated to the body to fulfill the providence of the whole. Moreover, the intellect itself is simply whole everywhere: and in it are not only through ideas, but also through their own (so to speak) intellectual existences, souls, according to their own proper intellectual faculty, even while they are in the body. Just as lines drawn from the center all the way to the circumference do not depart from the center while they reach the circumference, and rays not leaving the sun meanwhile touch earthly things: and just as lines and rays projecting outwards are distant from each other in space, yet in the very principle they are in the same place simultaneously: So souls among us, distant according to the position of the body, are all there according to the intellect in the divine mind: according to their own intellects, I say, differing among themselves there, just as the ends of lines and rays are different from each other, even where they touch the center and the sun. From this Plotinus wishes to show that the intellect of a prophet and of an abstract man, even if it only seems to be in the East, nevertheless foresees what happens in the West, and from one place performs something miraculous in another, and by its thought and affection secretly moves others: because, namely, all intellects are in each other, and everywhere: since they are always in the simple divine mind, which is always present whole everywhere. By this presence, indeed, God perceives prayers, and men converse most intimately with God. He also wishes intellects to be such familiar daemons of men, and constant guides attributed to each individual. For external daemons perhaps cannot be applied to individual men individually to such an extent. He believes that Plato, when he says in Timaeus that the soul is composed of a certain indivisible essence, and likewise a divisible one around bodies, understood the first essence to be the intellectual power of the soul, never declining towards bodies: but the second to be that nature of the soul which entirely accommodates itself to the body, which nevertheless is called indivisible in the meantime: because even the soul united to the body, however much the members of the body may be distant from each other, does not distance itself from itself: since it is entirely the same in any given member: and that both faculties of the soul (as we have said) are thus present, both in our soul and also in the soul of the world. But since he says that the intellect of both the world and man is present in all the members of its body: and likewise that the divine intellect is present to all parts of the world, why is it not said from this at least to be divided through the body in the same way as the soul? Because, namely, any intellect by its presence contributes nothing to the body, except through the soul: so that it seems to be present rather than inherent. Furthermore, the intellect behaves equally in any portion of the body, so that it seems entirely undivided: but the soul exercises one power and action in this member, another in another, and accommodates life and sense and motion through different degrees to the members of its body, and thus seems in a certain way divided in the body. In the second book here concerning the soul, you will note that Aristotelian Entelechy, by which the soul is called the act and perfection of the body, can be understood even in Aristotle not only as a form, and a soul inseparable from the body, but also as that which is separable from the body. Therefore you will consider that what is properly divided, is divided in substance: but what is moved, can indeed be properly moved, according to its accidents and qualities and modes, yet in the meantime the substance remains: and therefore substance is affected and harmed by division rather than by motion. But since in the very descent of things, the good indeed begins from the highest, or evil from the lowest, we rightly find, in descending, that which is properly mobile before that which is properly divisible. Therefore, beneath the divine intellect, which is entirely indivisible and immobile, we find the soul indeed indivisible, although properly mobile: then the corporeal form and quality, mobile and divided everywhere. Finally, the body, which is also the origin of this division, and as if inert, is moved from elsewhere.

When

--- Page 404 ---
360          PLOTINUS'S ENNEAD. IV.
But when we call the soul divisible, we speak not properly, as of a body and even a quality, but improperly, understanding that it is not indeed cut according to the sections of the body like a quality, but adapted to a mobile and divided body, and distributing its powers, and actions, and gifts differently to different members. You will note meanwhile that corporeal mass and form, by its nature entirely dissolvable, both in us and in the world, cannot be bound together otherwise than by the soul, which is not equally divided, but is whole in every part. Likewise, the soul of the world, insofar as it has a multitude of powers and forms within itself, is in a certain way mobile, adapted to vivify the body of the world: adapted, I say, by the divine mind itself, which is indeed entirely immobile, yet having a multitude of forms within itself, although not differing there down to the smallest details as they differ in the soul. Likewise, insofar as unity reigns first in the divine mind, and then in the soul of the world, and eminent simplicity flourishes, from this, all things are wisely governed by a certain intellectual reason. Conclude here five grades of things: The Good itself is only one in itself, the divine mind, one, many, the soul, both of the world and our own, is one in itself, and many. Any corporeal quality and form is many in itself and one: the mass of the body itself is no longer considered one according to itself, but many. The remaining things are explained in Theology (as we have said).

A whole is more than matter, and more than its parts: therefore if a material whole is given, a formal whole is also given. Likewise, if a whole is from parts, then also a whole is from wholes. For since the universe is optimally constructed by supreme reason, whatever true reason concludes to be in the best state, already exists in the universe by right: for from this, reason also infers it. A material whole is called such as wood: for even if it is multiplied into parts by material division, it is not multiplied into forms. A formal whole is a tree: for it is divided into many forms clearly differing from each other. In this formal whole, a true material whole also exists: for from the fact that it is distinguished into different particular forms, it is also distinguished into materials that are in some way different, namely by their own differing forms. Since therefore the world is the most absolute whole, it is certainly also a formal whole, and a whole from wholes. But it will not be a whole from wholes unless there are many things in it not only differing in forms, as in a tree, but also disjoined according to existence, and separated by actions: like singers in a choir, where each one agrees with the others in a common office for the same purpose, and meanwhile is proper to himself, and exists by his own right. But the judge of sensible passions is ultimately one, exhibiting a single judgment by comparing different things, both through imagination and also through reason. Thus, I say, it is in us. But it cannot happen in exactly the same way in the world, in which, if a single soul for individuals is imagined to exist, different people will indeed be able to suffer different things (just as now in any of us there are different instruments), but ultimately a single judgment will be applied, the same opinion, the same understanding. For these things pertain to the judge, who is free from passion, if indeed he is a true judge of passions and things; and therefore he exists in himself somehow separated from those who suffer, and therefore is unique, and not diverse because of various instruments. But indeed, since there are contrary judgments among people, these are properly, of course, understandings, and also proper substances of souls; since the rational function is performed not through instruments, but through the intimate faculty of the substance.

There are many intellectual souls besides the soul of the world, which are distinguished from one another not by external boundaries, but by internal ones.

In the third chapter and thereafter, which again

--- Page 411 ---
IN BOOK III. ENNEAD. IIII. 367

*Intellectual souls are distinguished from each other not by accidental, but by essential properties:*
*and how many souls*
*are said to be one, and from one.*

For since the first intellect and the first essence are the same, all intellects are deservedly true essences, and therefore distributed by true differences among themselves: that is, not by accident, nor by terms taken from outside, like divided parts of a continuum, and masses themselves among themselves, and mostly material forms, but according to the dignity of their essences subsisting in themselves, they are distinguished by their own intimate differences and terms. For this is more truly distinguished from that, if it differs by a formal property, than if by a material division, or an accident, or a place. Therefore, every intellect possesses its essence and being in a certain intimate identity of its own, and (if I may so speak) otherness. Identity, I say, inasmuch as it is the simplest form, never falling from its simplicity: otherness, again, inasmuch as such a form is distinguished by itself, as if by its own property, from any other thing, and from any other intellect. But if it is distinguished primarily and by itself, it always remains discrete, far from confusion. Conceive in the divine mind a great soul, that is, a general idea of intellectual souls, in which the species of souls are conceived: and that idea is a certain intellect there, and these species there are certain intellects. Such ideal intellects are distinguished there among themselves, not indeed by different existences (for there is hitherto a single substance), but by a certain reason and formal property. But if such essential properties are thought to proceed outwards, they are suddenly distinguished more, they are therefore distinguished by existences. For they are so effective within, that they bring forth not something accidental but substance, and diverse substances according to the diversity of formal reasons. Such substances, proceeding immediately from the first intellect, exist primarily as intellectual. But since they themselves are also very effective for intimate conception, each one expresses in itself a certain property, now animal from the intellectual, and more distinctly in many. Just as a ray shines forth from a spark, or from the beginning of imagination, with a simpler word, a word is produced in utterance, now more manifold and mobile. Therefore, from one ideal soul, many souls come forth, both of the world and of others. And although these are different substances, they are nevertheless in some way one among themselves for three principal reasons: first, because all are under the same idea; second, because they are least separated by places and times; and third, because each of their intellectual peaks are formed by one and the same divine intellect in act, and all perpetually contemplate the same: I omit that all naturally contribute to the same end of universal providence.

*How every rational soul is all things, and how the species of rational souls differ among themselves.*

The highest principle of all, by virtue of its supreme simplicity, is above all things, and by virtue of its power, it immediately effects all things. Therefore, its son, the Intellect, is the first all, and thus is perfectly all, and for that reason, every idea of it is all ideas. Therefore, the soul, naturally and immediately flowing from its own idea, draws all things to itself: thus, every intellectual soul is the universe. I confirm this whole point again: the first in any genus and the simplest is there, and contains all things within itself. Therefore, since the Intellect itself is the first form, it is deservedly both uniform and omniform. Thus, every rational soul, inasmuch as it is intellectual, is not only the simplest form, but is also omniform, and all things: all things, I say, in act, just as the Intellect itself is all things in act. But inasmuch as the soul now becomes not so much intellectual as animal, it retains indeed the same function by which it is still all things: but retaining it less perfectly, it is now the universe in potentiality, and deservedly so, since God placed it in the middle of things, and tempered it from all things. He tempered the diverse species of souls in such a way that the soul which would be the life of the universal world would always turn to the universal intellect, and moreover universally, and moreover most attentively. Hence it came about that it would always bear the universal providence of the whole, and this with wonderful power, and therefore with marvelous ease: since all power comes from above. The remaining celestial souls after this one would indeed turn to the universal intellect: yet not so universally, nor with equal attention: therefore, they neither exercise such universal providence, nor such powerful providence. Finally, the lower souls are constituted in such a way that they sometimes turn themselves to the universal intellect: and then either more or less universally or attentively: and therefore sometimes they would concur more with universal providence, other times less, and also less powerfully. Likewise, that sometimes they would turn themselves not so much to the universal, as to their own intellect, and would be less perfect: sometimes to reason, where also perfectly less: sometimes they would often lapse into imagination, and become most debased. Finally, when the rational soul unfolds the universe within itself, it is admitted to the universal providence of the soul of the world: but when, gradually falling from its universal function, it directs itself to a part of that function, it gradually undertakes particular care, and more fully assumes its own body, and labors more.

*Doubts are answered, and it is proven that rational souls are not from the soul of the world.*

Plato, intending to prove in Philebus that the world is animated, says: "From where would our body, which is composed of parts of the elements, have a soul, unless the world, which is composed of whole elements, possessed a soul?" That is, the intellect, maker of the world, was not so imprudent as to give us a soul, but not give one to the world: especially since the soul of the world was to prepare, through a universal influx, the seminal materials of animals for receiving their own souls from wherever. Therefore, our body has an intellectual soul from no other source than the world, that is, from the same maker of the world, and a sensual soul mostly from our intellectual soul, with the soul of the world contributing to this primarily. Timaeus also asserts that rational souls are constituted not from the soul of the world, but from the same author from whom that soul is, and from similar kinds: and that these are neither that soul, nor parts, nor powers of it, but that they are disposed by God in diverse species and degrees: whence he introduces these souls as falling into bodies and wandering, and exiting, which cannot happen to the soul of the world. But he says in Phaedrus, that whenever a particular soul, which is also the universe in potentiality outside this body, turns itself to the universal form by actively thinking and loving, this soul also is to be admitted to the universal providence of the world, endowed namely with a celestial body from the beginning: since even in a perishable body, the contemplative philosopher, and likewise the civil man, experiences the same according to their abilities. Therefore, wherever Plato seems to imply that souls follow celestial motion, there and elsewhere he also adds that they can choose not to follow. It has also been proven,

H 4

--- Page 412 ---
368 COMMENT. MARSIL. FICINI

that they can resist celestial influences by prudence, art, and morals. From which it appears that if there is any life in us that is a follower of the body, and through this serves fate, this life can depend even on the soul of the mundane body; but that soul in us which resists bodily incitements and worldly impulses descends from a higher source than the world. And indeed, even if we are born within the world, we nevertheless have a superior soul from elsewhere, which measures even the world. For even a fetus in the womb receives a soul other than the mother's soul, and has a soul from elsewhere than from the mother.

How souls differ, and how they are immortal, remaining in their own form, and how the soul of the world, present everywhere, contributes to the life of all.

In the eighth chapter, you will primarily consider these things, to the end that our souls, both among themselves and also with the soul of the world, so greatly agree, that they are often affected by a similar instinct, and some impulse easily flows from some into others, and particular souls are secretly moved by the universal: it is certainly not necessary that our souls are begotten from the soul of the world. For a common participation in the mundane soul, as well as in other souls from the same divine mind, and the same general idea of souls, and a similar procession, is sufficient for this agreement and, as it were, compassion. Therefore, there are four principal differences among human souls: they differ in some way according to the differences of bodies, when they seem to have motions more or less agitated according to the difference of blood, bile, and spirit. They are said to differ by a preceding life: if it is true that this soul is now more inclined to actions, that one to contemplation; because the former indeed led a very active life before birth, while the latter was entirely contemplative. Platonists also think that they differ in some way by species naturally from the beginning: inasmuch as human souls are under the same proximate genus, but differ among themselves by certain species, and by the smallest possible differences, by which they are distributed from the highest degree through the second, third, and fourth. Finally, they think that they differ because, although every rational soul is a universe, it can nevertheless affect itself in different ways by a certain free motion, as one turns itself to a contemplative life, another to an active one, another to a voluptuous one. And those who devote themselves to contemplation, some choose this form of contemplation, others that one above the rest; and what they have chosen, they soon assume as if it were their nature. Although every soul is all things, such a seeming equality does not, however, make souls equal among themselves without any distinction. For in the first mind there is a common reason for ideal souls, not merely individual, but very general, possessing various degrees of ideal souls among themselves, whose number is followed by an equal number of souls, and a similar order. And just as in the divine mind this idea is all things in one way, and that idea in another: so this soul is all things in a different way than that one, and uses its universe differently. Furthermore, it is consistent with reason that compounds made of four elements can be resolved into pure elements: and if the inferior elements cannot be entirely separate from the superior ones, at least the superior ones can exist somewhere separate from the inferior ones in their purity. Similarly, a compound of matter and form, as if twin elements, can in some way be resolved into pure matter, and entirely reduced to some form pure in itself, which exists by itself and in itself without matter, although matter cannot exist far from all form. Just as the formal element (as I said) exists far from the material, although the converse does not happen, intellectual souls are numbered among this kind of forms. Indeed, such a form is a simple essence, possessing its being by itself in itself, in which its being is the same as its essential unity. On the contrary, the essence of compounds behaves differently: namely, in these, essence and being, which consist in multitude, are different from unity, which, as unity, does not admit multitude; and being there follows union, which unity precedes. To what end are these things? So that you may understand that the very form of the soul, whose being is the same as its essential unity, is utterly indissoluble, just as unity is indissoluble: especially because if being everywhere in things is through form, it follows that a simple form subsisting in itself always continues its being in itself. Furthermore, if a simple form not mixed with matter were to be destroyed, it would be reduced to nothing; if it were to be generated, it would be generated from nothing. But physical reason by itself does not concede this. Therefore, the soul is eternal: especially because if it is to be conceived from something, and yet cannot be from any material, God, its author, would be compelled to create it from His own substance; whence He would be compelled to be mutable: especially if He sometimes does what He had not done before. Plotinus therefore means these things, to assert the soul as eternal: how much of which is to be affirmed has been sufficiently stated in our Theology. Among these things, note that each such form is in itself one thing numerically distinct from others, not accidentally, but essentially, essentially I say: because souls do not receive number from the number of bodies, or bodily qualities: as if one soul of the world were propagated into many through diverse affections of bodies. But now, every soul thus subsists by itself always one in number, just as in its essence it has its being, and its being is the same as its unity. Therefore, just as the simple essence of the soul, as simple and subsisting in itself, is eternal, so also is every singular being of it: since its being is only in its essence. Likewise, just as being is eternal, so also is every numerical unity: since there, to be is the same as to be one thing. For a simple essence remaining in itself is distinguished not by external, but by internal means, so that no one may dream that our souls, having sometimes abandoned personal properties, are to be confused into some general soul. Indeed, corporeal things composed of matter and form preserve a perpetual unity of species through succession: but by no means a proper numerical unity. And yet they would not preserve a specific unity in themselves, unless they perpetually drew it from the soul, the fount of generation. Therefore, the soul, as far more excellent, always retains in itself its own numerical unity, not only specific, but indeed, just as through it compounds that dissolve return, with similar times recurring, precisely similar and the same in species: so the soul, changing its form in some way within itself, as if more excellent than the body, sometimes returns to the same number, and to the same body, and the same person. Hereafter, when it is asked how a simple and intellectual form, whether of the world or our own soul, is sometimes said to be infinite? The answer is, not because it can be divided infinitely, but because it flourishes without end, and can act everywhere and always. Thus, therefore, neither is the soul of the world divided into infinite souls, nor is it extended in the manner of a corporeal quality, insofar as the mass of the world is extended, but it remains one: and whatever portion of the body can receive anything from it, it itself, whole, animates everywhere. Our souls also, just as they do not become so many in number, from so many bodies—

--- Page 413 ---
IN LIB. III. ENNEAD. IIII. 369

...bodily portions and qualities, thus neither are they stretched into a mass, nor are they extended like whiteness over extended matter: but they are as many as there are intimate properties, and as much mass as is prepared for their influx, so much they form in a certain individual and everywhere whole and perpetual vigor. Nor is our soul cut into multiple souls, whether because of diverse limbs, or if any limb is amputated: just as the soul of the world itself is neither divided in itself, nor becomes multiple souls, when the parts of the world are divided among themselves. For this one remaining (soul), however much a living part of the world may be separated, it is nevertheless whole at the same time in each. It is also in the middle because of the continuity of prime matter, indeed, and of the fifth essence, which is the proper receptacle of the soul. Among these things, if Plotinus seems to anyone to posit no other soul than the world soul in plants and animals generated from putrefaction, you beware lest you easily concede this: for he himself seems to refute it in the book on the immortality of the soul. You will say therefore that the world soul itself is indeed present to all such (beings) pr

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

For since the entire mass of the world and its form depend on it, nothing anywhere can resist it; especially because from it all things in a subsequent series so depend, that agents, moved by even the slightest initial impulse, are soon all set in motion, and lead to the action and end of the first mover. Therefore, those things which do not live act only externally and upon foreign matter, but in themselves they are inert; but those things which live act also within themselves, and act perpetually. The soul, therefore, the principle of life, especially the world soul, acts always and most powerfully within itself, inasmuch as its intelligence on the one hand forms its own reason, and on the other hand its own nature. And indeed, reason naturally discourses with itself, and swells with all things, and yearns for the seeds of all things, even of divine bodies: From this indeed intimate and rational motion, through the seminal reasons of things, is born the rational form of the world, similarly all-forming, a form, I say, most similar to the soul. For if the generating things that follow strive to generate things similar to themselves: assuredly this universal and proximate generator of the world generates a world most similar to itself.

ON THE SOUL I

Moreover, since we strive to investigate and discover all other things, we shall deservedly investigate first of all what this investigator in us is, especially since we desire to attain that very thing which is lovely and delightful in the very spectacles of contemplation. For in the universal intellect itself there is a twofold aspect: Therefore, reasonably, in particular intellects, this one indeed holds itself more in this way, but that one rather differently.

Moreover, it will be necessary to consider how the receptacles of the Gods are made; but we shall investigate that more opportunely after we have inquired how the soul is in the body. But now let us return again to those who say that our souls too are from the very soul of the universe.

For perhaps they will object to us that it is not a sufficient argument against our souls being parts of that (universal soul), that it is said our souls proceed as far as the soul of the world extends itself, or that it is handed down that they have very similar intellectual gifts, even if they concede this to them. For they will say that parts are often conformable to the whole. Moreover, they will bring Plato himself into the midst, as if holding this opinion, where, proving the world to be animated, he says: "Just as our body is a part of the universal body, so too our soul is a part of the whole soul."

Likewise, what is said and evidently shown, that we follow the circuit of the whole world, and from it have our customs and fortunes; again, that we, born within the world, deservedly receive our containing soul from it. Moreover, just as each part of us receives from our soul, so too we, by similar reasoning, since we are parts of the whole, receive from the soul of the whole as parts. Finally, what is written, "every soul has care of the whole inanimate," means precisely the same thing, as if, besides the soul of the world itself, no soul whatsoever is left. For this is the one that cares for the whole inanimate.

**Marginal Note:**
II. The soul, being one, cannot be divided into many parts, like bodies or dimensions and numbers, and qualities of bodies.

Therefore, to these points, it must first be said that those who posit souls to be conformable, because they are granted to attain the same things, meanwhile, by admitting the same common genus, secretly bring it about that other souls are not parts of one (soul), but would more probably infer that it is one and the same, and that any soul exists universally. But by making it one, they would reduce it to something else. This (soul), indeed, existing no longer as belonging to this or that, but to no one, whether of the world or of another, itself indeed does whatever the life of the world and of any animated being is judged to do.

For it seems correct that not every soul belongs to someone, since it is an essence; but that some exist which belong to absolutely no one; but those which are said to belong to someone, come to be sometimes accidentally, that is, become someone's.

Perhaps, however, in these matters, it must be understood more clearly how a part is spoken of; it is proper to dismiss the mode of parts appearing in bodies, whether the body is uniform or non-uniform, signifying only this: when in bodies of similar parts a part is named, it is a part according to quantity, not according to species, as we can judge in whiteness. For the whiteness which is in a part of milk is not a part of the whiteness which is in the whole.

--- Page 417 ---
**BOOK THREE. 373**

A But the whiteness of a part is indeed whiteness, yet it is not a part of whiteness (as a quality): clearly, whiteness is not a quantity, but is altogether lacking in magnitude by itself. And let that indeed be so. But when we speak of a part in things that are not bodies, either as we understand a part in numbers, just as two is said to be a part of ten (let this be said only of pure numbers), or as a part of a circle and a line is usually spoken of, or as a proposition or notion is accustomed to be called a part of knowledge.

B Indeed, in units and figures, it is necessary, just as in bodies, that the whole itself be diminished by division into parts, and that the individual parts be smaller than the whole. For since these are quantities, and possess their being in quantity itself, not existing as the same quantity, they necessarily become greater and smaller. Certainly, under this condition, a part cannot be spoken of in the soul. For it is not a quantity in such a way in the soul, that the whole is, for example, a ten, and a part is a unit.

How human intellects flow from the divine intellect, distinct from each other, and thus remain, and finally in themselves, and as it were beneath themselves, conceive animal natures.

It has certainly already been said, as far as concerns the sum of the discussion, that all souls are derived from one, from one, I say, many in the same tenor with intellect, divided in the same order, and also not divided.

F But the one reason of the mind is that soul which remains, and from it partial and immaterial reasons, just as there.

VI
On the differences of souls, inasmuch as they are more or less converted to the universal intellect rather than the particular, and inasmuch as to the whole or to a part of the whole.

BUT why indeed did the soul of the world, which is said to be conformable with others, make the world, but the soul of each individual by no means? especially since each also embraces all things in itself? For that it can be in many simultaneously, and already exists, has been said: but now that must be declared. For perhaps also how the same in one and another, partly indeed

G this, but partly that, either acts, or suffers, or relates to both, will be known from these things. But perhaps it is better to consider according to this very thing, in what manner and for what reason that one (the world-soul) made the world. But other (souls) a certain part...

--- Page 420 ---
370 PLOTINUS, ENNEAD. IV.

[Left Column]

govern the world. Perhaps it should seem nothing strange, that men endowed with the same knowledge, some indeed rule over more, others over fewer. Perhaps someone will ask, for what reason the matter stands thus. And someone will answer, that there is also a greater difference of souls, inasmuch as this one indeed did not depart from the universal, but resting there, contained a body around itself: while others, the body already made, and already having begun, and their sister soul dominating, gradually obtained their lots, as if that one had already prepared dwellings for these. Nor is there lacking another difference, by which this one indeed looks up to the universal intellect, while others rather look up to particular intellects, namely each its own. Perhaps indeed these too could make the whole: but since that one has already made it; no further faculty is given to these, after that one first laid the foundations: but in the same way anyone would doubt, if perchance any other had first built it. But it is better to say that the principal power and making belong to the principal soul for this reason, because it adheres more to the higher things. For to souls more intently applying themselves there, greater power arises. For preserving themselves on that secure foundation, they make most easily: for it is of greater power not to suffer in those things which it makes, but power from above remains. Remaining therefore in itself, it now consequently makes for others approaching: but other souls which have approached or proceeded, seem to have descended into the deep. Perhaps because in them very much has been drawn downwards, it has drawn them too with it, so much so that they now seem to have descended even through thoughts. For what is said in the Timaeus about the second and third order of souls, must be explained as some indeed adhering more closely to the higher things, while others depart further, just as it happens among us. For not all souls relate similarly to the higher things, but some indeed are united with the higher, others approach closely with desire, others finally achieve it less, inasmuch as they do not use the same powers. But these use the first power, those the second, and those finally the third, although each possesses all powers.

[Marginal Note:]
VII.
Responses to doubts proving that our souls are not from the soul of the world.

Let this much have been said concerning these things. But what is said in the Philebus induces the suspicion, lest perhaps all souls are parts of the World Soul, it does not indeed mean what someone supposes, but what was then most conducive to it, namely that the world is animated. For striving to prove this, he says, that it is absurd to say that heaven is inanimate, since we who have a body as part of the mundane body, have a soul. For in what way would a part have had a soul, if the whole were inanimate? But the opinion of Plato is clearest especially in the Timaeus: where the soul of the world already made, thereafter others arise in the same bowl: mixed with it, and conformed to it: but he assigns the difference of these through second and third degrees. But what is said in the Phaedrus, that every soul has care of the whole inanimate: what is strange? For what else governs, forms, orders, makes the nature of the body, if not the soul? Nor must it be said, that this one indeed can do it naturally: but that one by no means. Hence he adds: The soul itself therefore existing perfect, namely that of the universe, elevated higher, and not immersed, but (as I might say)

--- Page 421 ---
LIBER TERTIVS. 377

A soul floating above acts in the world, and whatever soul is perfect, will similarly administer. Furthermore, where it introduces a soul with broken wings, as if falling, it clearly asserts such a soul to be different from the soul of the world. Therefore, what was brought forward, that souls follow the circuit of the universe, and derive customs from it, and suffer from it, in no way signifies that our souls are parts. For the soul can, by the nature of places, waters, and air, ward off many things threatening from heaven: and also habitation and urban custom, and bodily constitutions resist celestial influxes. And if we have said that we, enclosed in the universe, have something of life from the soul of the world, and suffer from the celestial circuit, we have nevertheless introduced, on the contrary, another soul also resisting all these things, and by its very resistance clearly showing itself to be different. But to that which is said, that we are born within the world, we respond similarly, that in the mother's womb the fetus—

since, even if there is anything that it itself makes, it certainly A will not make it from matter. But if this is so, it is necessary to add something essential even from itself. Therefore, this very thing will be a change concerning that, if it now makes more or less. Moreover, it can be asked why it acts now, and not always in the same way. And yet what has been made will not be eternal, if indeed it admits more and less. But the soul is constituted as such a thing. How then will it be infinite, if it is fixed? Perhaps it is infinite in potential, because power itself is infinite, not B as something which is to be divided to infinity, since even God is not limited. Thus therefore souls also are: for no soul is what it is, as if by an external limit, as if of such a size, but it exists as much as it wills, nor is it ever led to depart beyond itself, but it flows indeed through the whole, which by its nature is so constituted from itself, that it runs through bodies into bodies; nor yet is it drawn away from itself, when it is present in both the finger of the hand and the foot simultaneously. So indeed also in the universe, C into whatever it runs through, it is like one part and another of a plant. And if some part is cut, it remains in the former plant, and in that which has been separated from it. For the whole body is one, and its presence is everywhere as if in one. But in a putrefied animal, if several animals arise from it, that (the soul) indeed is no longer the soul of the whole animal in the body: for it does not then have a proper receptacle for itself, nor has it perished. But those things which are apt for the generation of animals from putrefaction D receive soul partly from these, partly also from those, since the soul itself is never absent; although one thing can receive it, another cannot; and those living things which are thus made do not necessitate there being multiple souls: for they depend on one, insofar as that one remains one. Just as also in us, when some parts are amputated, for which others sprout, the soul is indeed absent from those, but it applies itself to these, insofar as it remains one. But in the universe, it always remains one. But those things which are in the universe, E some indeed retain life, others indeed not at all, while nevertheless in the meantime the very same powers of the soul persist.

IX
Second question: In how many ways the soul is introduced into the body, and what the soul of the world is like, and how it makes the world and its dimension, and in what way it is everywhere.

Moreover, it must be asked how the soul is introduced into the body: for this does not seem worthy of less admiration and investigation. But there are two ways by which the soul enters the body: one indeed occurs when the soul is already joined to a body, and either changing solid bodies, or coming from an airy or fiery body into an earthly one, which many do not call a "commutation of bodies," F because it is hidden whence the insinuation comes. But the other way is that by which the soul slips from the incorporeal into any body: which indeed is the soul's first commerce with a body. It is worthwhile first to consider this slipping, what passion then occurs when the soul, still living entirely pure from the body, first takes on the nature of a body for itself. Perhaps indeed it is fitting G to begin from the soul of the whole, and indeed necessary to derive the truth about this very thing; so that we may undertake to begin to describe its ingress and the animation of the body for the sake of clearer doctrine, since there was never any time, in which not

--- Page 423 ---
LIBER TERTIVS. 379

A that this universe might be animated: nor could a body ever subsist without a soul, nor could matter ever exist formless. It is permitted, however, to distinguish these things from each other by a certain thought and words: for it is permitted to resolve every composition by thought and words. Now indeed, the truth is thus. Unless there is a body, the soul will by no means proceed: for there is no other place where it can naturally propagate itself. But if it is to proceed, it will build a place for itself, therefore it will generate a body. B But when its state is strengthened in that very state, like a great light shining forth in the highest places, meanwhile, as it were, at the very extremities of the fire, a shadow results, and indeed, the soul, looking upon this, after it stood still, formed it. For it was impious for anything close to the soul to be devoid of reason: and therefore in that which was subsequently made, something too meager and obscure was also taken up, which is also called shadowy. The world, therefore, having been made like a certain beautiful and very varied edifice, C was not separated from its maker, nor did it again mix itself with it, but everywhere it was considered worthy of care and diligence, so much so that it indeed contributes to its own being, and to being beautiful, insofar as it could participate in being itself: but to the unmixed author, this same thing is harmless. For remaining in the highest, it presides. Indeed, the world is animated in such a way that it does not so much *have* a soul of its own, as it *has* a soul *imparted to it*: overcome, not overcoming; also possessed, not possessing. D For it lies in the soul sustaining it, nor is anything in it devoid of the soul itself. Just as a net in the waters, as it were, soaked with life, yet not able to escape the nature of that in which it is, but the net, indeed, as the sea is extended, is extended along with it, as far as it can. For no single part can be elsewhere than where it is placed. But the soul is naturally so great and so immense, because it is not limited to such a quantity: and therefore it can embrace every body in one and the same way, and E wherever that (body) extends, there too is the soul. And unless that (body) were, the soul would have no care to occupy magnitude: for it is in itself whatever it is. For the universe is only as great as the soul occupies it: and the world is determined in quantity, insofar as, proceeding, it has the soul as its preserver. Then the shadow is as great as the reason depending on the soul. But reason was such that it would produce as much magnitude as its species wished magnitude to be produced.

F When we have considered these things, it is necessary, returning again to that which always is so, to take all beings together, such as air, light, the sun, or the moon. But it is adorned according to reason, by the power of the soul itself, having, namely, through its entire self, a force, by which, through reasons...

But the souls of men, as images of themselves, like Dionysus looking into a mirror, existed there, hastening from above, yet not separated from their beginning and the intellect. For they did not descend together with the intellect, but indeed reached as far as the earth: but meanwhile their head also exists above heaven. It happened, however,

**D** to them to depart further for this reason, because their middle power is compelled to care more diligently: since that very thing into which they descend, utterly needs cultivation. But Father Jupiter, pitying the toiling souls, fashioned their bonds, by which they toil, to be soluble: and so he instituted intermissions of labors at certain intervals of time, in which they might live free from bodies: so that they too might sometimes be there, where the soul of the world always is, never solicitous about these things.

**E** For what the world already has, this suffices for itself and will suffice according to reasons perpetually subsisting, rightly accomplished in times, and perpetually restored to the same through certain courses of times, namely through the measures of defined lives, in which these things, together with those, according to those, are brought into their consonance. While all these things are carried out under one certain reason, mutually ordered, as far as the descents and ascents of souls and all other things are concerned.

**F** But that there is consonance in souls with the order of the universe, yet in such a way that they do not so much depend, as accommodate themselves in descending, and achieve one harmony with the mundane revolution, this can be an argument for us, because their fortunes and choices of life are signified by the figures of the stars: or because it has been said that the universe produces one harmonious concert, and that the whole of it, rather than by other means, was designated by the ancients, albeit more obscurely, through musical consonances.

**G** This, however, would by no means be so, unless the world, according to those things, did and suffered each thing in the established revolutions and orders, and courses of lives, through the kinds of discursions by which souls wander, sometimes indeed there, sometimes...

**Therefore, what is said about the inevitable law and divine**
judgment, thus exists in nature, containing and commanding, so that each proceeds in the C
order for which each image of primary choice and affection was made. And that universal species of soul is congruent and akin to that towards which it conceived affection within itself, and it looks to that which then sends and introduces it where it ought, not indeed that it should then go into a body, or into such a body, but when the prescribed term is already at hand, souls as if spontaneously descend where they ought, and enter. For its own day stands for each. Finally, with that day imminent, D
they glide down as if summoned by a herald, and enter a body suitable for them: and they behave almost as if they are moved and carried by the powerful forces and attractions of Magi. Moreover, they behave as the dispensation is perfected in any living whole, moving at a certain time, and producing, like hairs, and beard, and horns similarly: and at a certain time, certain impulses and strengths towards such things: likewise, flowers in plants never germinating before, E
and other things distributed in them similarly by certain ordered rules. But souls proceed neither entirely voluntarily, nor compelled. For to proceed voluntarily is not attributed to them as if they are said to choose deliberately, but as if they spring forth by nature, just as we are accustomed to be provoked to venereal desires, or to some honorable actions, by a certain instinct rather than by the counsel of reason. But always to such a one, such a thing is fated: likewise, to such a one, F
this moment, and to such a one, that moment comes decreed by fate. Therefore, the intellect superior to the world has it fated to remain there continually, inasmuch as it also sends something down from there to here: then indeed, individual things subject to the common law are gradually sent from there. For a common norm is inherent in each, and the law itself by no means receives the power to fulfill its function from outside, but is transmitted precisely on the condition that it is inherent in those who use it, carrying it everywhere: G
then indeed, when the time is imminent, which the law itself has decreed to happen, it is then acted upon by those who have the law within them, so much so that they themselves fulfill the law: as if it drives them around, and because it is founded in them, it performs its decrees more powerfully, as if weighing them down with its own burden, while also stimulating their zeal-

--- Page 427 ---
**BOOK THREE. 383**

...and an inner stimulus strikes, that it should proceed thither, where the innermost law dictates it should most of all proceed.

**SINCE** these things are so, this world, possessing many lights and illuminated by souls, is adorned differently for former worlds by other former worlds, or receives a different adornment from another, both from those gods and from other minds transmitting souls. Something of this kind is likely indicated by the fable which says: After Prometheus had fashioned the woman, other gods also adorned her. To this points what is related there, that earth had been mixed with water; likewise, that a human voice was given to that figure. Moreover, that goddesses representing beauty, then Venus and the Graces, imparted something, and that one gave one gift, another another, and that she received the name Pandora from the gift and all the givers. For all endowed this figure with some gift: a figure, I say, already formed by a certain providence. But that Epimetheus gave her no gift, what else does it signify than that the reception and choice of an intelligible gift is more excellent? But that fashioner is bound, because he seems in a way to touch his own work; but such a bond is external, and is loosed by Hercules: because he possesses a faculty by which he is also in a way loosed. But let anyone accept this according to their own judgment. But let this be established, that through these things, namely, gifts coming down into the world from above, are shown. Therefore, these things seem to be in harmony with what was said above.

**SOULS**, however, descending from the intelligible world, proceed first into heaven, and there receiving a body, they then through it slip into more earthly bodies, inasmuch as they advance further. And some indeed pass from heaven into lower bodies and vice versa, while others pass from some bodies into others: since for these, the faculty to lift themselves from here is not sufficient, due to weight and oblivion, dragging much with them, by which burden they are precipitated through lower regions. Souls, however, become different from each other either due to the diversity of the bodies into which they are insinuated, or also due to fortunes, or again due to educations, or moreover they themselves carry a difference from within themselves, and altogether they differ either through all these things or through some of them. Consequently, some entirely succumb to the fate dominating here, while others both yield to fate and live by their own will. There are also those who concede that whatever is necessary must be endured; yet they can reserve for themselves whatever belongs to their own proper function, living, that is, according to another constitution of laws embracing all beings simultaneously, and committing themselves to another rule. This (constitution of laws/rule) is woven from all the reasons and causes that are here, likewise from the movements of souls and the laws dependent thereon, being in harmony with them, and receiving its beginnings from them, and weaving together all consequences for them: then truly preserving all those things unshaken, whatever can preserve themselves in their state. But as for the rest, nature leads them around according to its own properties, so much so that in those descending, there is a reason for why they are as they are, namely, that some things are placed here and in this manner, while others are placed there and differently.

XVI.
THEREFORE, the punishments which are justly inflicted A
upon the wicked are to be attributed to the order that, as is fitting,
leads all things. But whatever things happen to the good beyond what is
just, such as penalties, poverty, diseases, perhaps occur because of the
misdeeds of a previous life. For these things are interwoven and even
portended, so that they themselves also seem to happen according to
reason. Do these things not happen according to natural reasons, nor
are they to be placed among those things which are principally
intended, but rather as consequences B
of them? As if, when a house falls, whoever was under it is killed,
no matter what kind of person he is; or if, when two things are moved
in a certain order, or even one, that which is struck is broken or
destroyed. But perhaps this very thing which is called unjust is neither
evil for the sufferer, and is conducive to the whole series of events,
and perhaps it is not even unjust, since individual things are justly
dispensed from preceding causes. For it must not be thought that some
things indeed have order among themselves, while others here completely
deviate into arbitrariness and license. C
For if all things must happen according to natural causes and
consequences, and one reason and one order, then surely even lesser
things are to be considered coordinated and interwoven. Therefore, what
is inflicted by one upon another as if unjust, is indeed unjust to the
agent, nor is it outside of cause and crime; but being coordinated in
the universe, it is certainly not unjust in this respect, nor is it
unjustly inflicted upon the sufferer, but it was fitting. But if he who
suffers is good, then whatever he suffers ultimately results in good. D
It must certainly be believed that this common order of the universe is
not devoid of divinity and justice, but renders to each what is fitting
by a most exact reason, yet has hidden causes within itself, and
therefore provides occasion for the ignorant to complain.

**XX**
**The soul is not in the body as in a place or a vessel, nor as a part in a whole, or a whole in parts, nor as a quality in a subject, nor as a form in matter: but the body is in the soul, as in that which vivifies, comprehends, and stably moves.**

XX IT REMAINS for us to explain whether these and other parts of the soul are in a place, or whether these are not in a place at all, while others are in a place, and where, and how, or whether no part at all is in a place. For if we do not assign a certain place to each part of the soul, placing nothing anywhere: then we will certainly consider it no more inside the body than outside, and therefore we will leave the body in the soul: nor will we be able to assign by what reason those works are done which are performed through bodily instruments: or if we describe a position for some parts of the soul, but by no means for others, then certainly those for which we have not described a position, we will seem to place them nowhere in ourselves, so much so that we will seem to believe that not our whole soul is in us. But we should by no means place any of the soul's parts, nor again the whole soul, in the body as in a place. For place is that which comprehends, and contains bodies. And where each divided thing lies, it lies there in such a way that it cannot be whole in any part, but the soul is not a body, nor is it comprehended rather than comprehending. Nor is it in the body as in a vessel, for in that case the body would be left inanimate, whether it contained the soul as a vessel or as a place, unless perhaps the soul is said to be gathered into itself, and by a certain transmission to transmit something of itself from itself into a vessel: and thus, as much as the vessel has participated, so much will already have been subtracted from the soul: But place, which is principally accustomed to be called place, is something incorporeal, not a body.

BUT should it be said that the soul is in the body, as fire, that is, light, is in the air? For while this is present to the air, it is not present [in the sense of being mixed]: and being present throughout, it is mixed with nothing, and indeed remains itself, while the air flows through. And when it is outside that in which the light is, it immediately departs, retaining nothing: but as long as it is under the light, it is illuminated. Therefore, it is rightly said here that the air is in the light rather than the light in the air: and for this reason Plato, in the very generation of the world, did not want it to be said that the soul was placed in the body, but the body placed in the soul. And he says that there is something of the soul itself in which the body is, and again something in which there is no body, as much, namely, as pertains to those powers of the soul which the body least needs. The same reasoning also applies to other souls. Indeed, it must be thought that the remaining powers of the soul are not present to the body, but those which it needs are present, and are present in such a way that they are neither located in parts nor in the whole body: and for sensation, the very power of sensing is present to the whole sentient being: but for performing actions, different powers to different [parts]. But I speak in this manner.

*Every power of the soul is in every part of the body as a whole, just like the soul. But it is said to act there where the instrument serves it: and principally there where the instrument has its origin. Thus, the act of sensing and moving is attributed to the head, from which, namely, the nerves, instruments of sense and motion, are derived: thus the act of anger around the heart, where its instrument is, namely fiery blood: thus nutrition around the liver, where airy blood is its instrument. But the act of reason, even if it has no communion with the body, is attributed in a certain way to the head, because the act of imagination is close to reason and participates in it.*

396          PLOTINI ENNEAD. IIII.

[Left column, Latin text translated]
...[they] exist, insofar as it had commerce with the other.
It is fitting, however, for the inferior soul to desire and to retain in memory the duties of the superior, especially when it is also modest: for it can become better from the beginning, and, educated under a superior, it can make progress. This [inferior soul], however, ought to willingly consign to oblivion the trifles of the inferior soul. It can also happen, when one [soul] is good, that the other, which is inferior by nature, is restrained by force by the better [soul]: and indeed, insofar as it strives upwards, unless perhaps its whole life here also has been such that it has commended only the best things to memory: since even here it is excellent to separate oneself from human pursuits, and that is the office of absolute virtue: wherefore it is necessarily right to disregard the memory of such things. Therefore, if anyone says that a good soul is forgetful, he will certainly speak correctly by this reasoning: for it flees from many things, and reduces the multitude to one, entirely dismissing the infinite and uncertain. For thus it does not live with many, but, considering these things as trivial, it dwells with itself, retaining only a few things, and these barely. Since even while dwelling here, whenever it strives to ascend to higher things, it entirely omits the rest. When, therefore, it has reached that highest point, it recalls few things from these; but when it is in heaven, it retains more. Now, indeed, that Hercules will boast of his manly strength in the heavens: but that superior [soul] will even disdain such things, having already proceeded to a more august place, and received into the intelligible world itself: and indeed, superior to Hercules, inasmuch as it has strenuously exercised and abundantly completed the more sacred contests of the wise.

[Right column, Latin text translated]

PLOTINUS
ENNEAD FOUR,
BOOK IIII.
On the Soul's Doubts, Second [Treatise].
MARSILIUS [FICINUS].

THE SOUL, having at some point cast off every body, even the celestial, and then formed by the divine mind, most intently contemplates all divine things simultaneously without discursive thought: therefore it is said not to remember human affairs, not because it is ignorant of lower things, while it beholds all the causes of lower things and possesses itself most perfectly; but because it most negligently recalls the smallest things when it is most attentive to the greatest things; and also because it does not recall in a discursive and mutable manner, as human recollection usually occurs. It contemplates, moreover, both through intellect and through reason whatever it knows, in a single intuition without motion, because it contemplates through one form of God. Nevertheless, through the very series of ideas having degrees distinct from each other not by time but by order, it discerns that some things are prior to others in order there. That someone among us, thinking something most intently, cannot meanwhile clearly think of something else, happens both from the weakness of power and also from the fact that one does not think of the principle of others. But there, power is most strong, and it contemplates the principles of all things: therefore, it contemplates all things simultaneously in those principles, especially because it is now entirely separated from motion and time. Finally, the Soul, after it has been formed by the divine mind and ideas, attains the One itself, which is superior to mind and ideas, and yet from there it still contemplates all things: for the power of the One itself, when first perceived in another, that is, in mind or soul, is derived into many things. Chapter I.

Is it then like a simultaneous intuition of something?

the power itself which is one, was one in such a way that it was also
many in another: nor all things according to one understanding.

For understandings there do not relate according to one, yet through all perpetually permanent power there, so that in other things they become many: for that, as it were, not being the One itself, can receive the nature of many things not previously existing in itself.

398 PLOTINUS' ENNEAD. IV.

The soul, indeed, in this body, while more attentive to something else, does not recognize itself in the meantime, because its power here is weak; and what is thought by it is not the principle of the soul: but when it contemplates the divine world, as it were, being both strengthened and perceiving its own principles, it thoroughly recognizes itself, its own state, and its actions. The soul in this body is mostly turned towards imagination, and through this, to sensible things, but after death, if it lives in an aerial body, it is finally entirely turned to reason, and through this to its own intellect, which always contemplates all things, and in the meantime, it is engaged in temporal discourse. But in a celestial body, reason is, as it were, made into intellect, both its own and common, and it has almost reduced past discourse to intuition. Here, therefore, insofar as it recalls the forms innate to itself, it recognizes itself: and insofar as it is in turn the forms themselves, for it is the forms themselves. Finally, the soul outside the heavens is thus formed by the divine mind and its ideas, just as the body is formed by the soul and the soul's powers, and just as heated iron is by fire.

**BOOK FOUR. 399**

...[just as fiery iron is formed by] the formations and images [of fire]. But it matters greatly what kind of things the soul thinks with emotion: for when it thinks by bringing its own latent forms within itself into actuality, it undoubtedly becomes those very things it thinks, and subsequently obtains a place and condition suitable for them. Chapter III.

A But having gone forth from there as if one step further, not at all stopping, but loving its own nature and desiring to be another, as if shining forth and now inclining more readily, it assumes, as it seems, memory of itself. But if memory is of higher things, it still restrains the soul lest it fall further: but if it is a recollection of our earthly things, it precipitates towards our things, but the remembrance of heavenly things stops its step in heaven. Indeed, whatever it remembers, it is and becomes that very thing: B for to remember is either to understand or to imagine. But this imagination itself does not consist in having something, but in seeing and being disposed, and in being such itself...

--- Page 444 ---
400          PLOTINUS' ENNEAD. IV.

When therefore that act, accustomed to thrive concerning intelligible things, ceases, the soul already recognizes what it had known before it was there.

The soul in this life can know divine things, not through imagination, nor even through reason taking its principles from imagination, but through intellect and reason taking its principles from intellect. When the soul through reason rises into the mind as if into a watchtower, although memory, commonly so called, is concerned with all imagination, nevertheless a certain memory also consists in reason and intellect. In the soul above the heavens, the act of intelligence occupies the usual use of reason and imagination, but in heaven, a use of this kind re-emerges, through which it remembers, as it were, in a human way, a former human life and human things: for it looked upon these things above the heavens in a certain more eminent way. Therefore, in heaven, souls recognize each other, especially friends and former acquaintances, both through the vivid movements and affections of their souls, and through bodies which they can have there, similar in form, in a liquid matter, yielding much more to the soul, which shapes it in whatever way, than earthly matter now yields to the affections of the soul. But then, if bodies there are spherical, differences will nevertheless be signs and indications of different souls to those who are indifferent, whether in figure, as we said, or in magnitude, quality, motion, gesture, nod, light, just as it happens in the eyes from the affections of souls, and in various clouds different figures and colors. There are some who wish the inhabitants of heaven to utter voices among themselves, for the heavens can also sound, but at least they converse with each other by mutual nods: but in the heavens they remember divine things more than human. But those fallen into the air, conversely: they can, both when in heaven and when in the air, because of their naturally free movement, halt their progress there for many ages, and retreat higher from there. Finally, what prevents one from always being in the higher realms by some optimal choice? Nothing, according to Porphyry and Iamblichus and Julian.

Chapter V.

WHAT then? Does not the very same     A

back into act for us now? Perhaps if the same

we have not seen by memory. But if the same

whenever we are incited to those things, and
this very thing is what sees in these things

from elsewhere by reasoning: but it is permissible
to say the same about intelligibles (as it is said)     B

For it is necessary to contemplate the things
that are there by arousing the same (power)

someone ascending a very high watchtower,
with eyes intently fixed from there, should look

it appears from reason that memory takes its
beginning from heaven, where the soul has     C

if, having departed from there and residing in

that happen among us, of the kind, namely,
that has been said: and it recognizes many souls

to have bodies around them in similar figures.

through the very manners and ways proper to

again awaken memory, but less than that

LIBER QVARTVS. 401

to emerge, and then again to retreat before they are precipitated to the lowest place of generation.

*The service of preservative memory is necessary where something can pass away and in turn return, destined to pass away again. Therefore, memory does not seem necessary for celestial souls, for they do not wander about to find or acquire anything new. Chapter VI.*

A Therefore, anyone can easily assert that wandering souls, variously changing themselves, use memory: for memory is of those things which have happened, or which have passed away. But souls which rest entirely in the same state, of what things will they be reminiscent? But if human reason indeed requires memory in the souls of all stars, but especially of the Sun and Moon, from this, it will transfer itself by a similar condition to the soul of the universe, and finally will dare to place a busy memory in Jupiter itself.
B But inquiring into these things, it will moreover consider their thoughts and reasonings, how fixed they are, and what their main characteristics are. Now, if they neither require anything, nor are uncertain (for they lack nothing), nor learn what they previously ignored, what reasonings or conjunctions of arguments or cogitations will be in them? Nor will they anxiously consult about devices by which they might arrange human and entirely earthly matters:
C for there is another reason by which the higher beings generously dispense all things.

*For the souls governing celestial bodies, the service of recollection is not necessary, neither in cognition, nor in life, nor in motion. Indeed, divine things suffice with an uninterrupted intuition: where they can indeed perceive that they see, but it is not necessary to repeat that they have seen, since there is not "having seen" itself, but "seeing" never interrupted: therefore, never to be resumed. Their life is also always the same, and their perpetual and continuous motion in their bodies is similar, and therefore, for each of them, it is always one, although it may appear or happen to us as manifold. They also foresee mutable things with an unchanging intuition, just as someone, with the same continuous gaze for some part of an hour, sees a person walking straight, changing in different ways, yet with an unchanging view. If indeed by this he judges that the person is here, was there, and will be there: such changes do not therefore occur in the vision itself, because they are judged to occur in the spectacle. Chapter VII.*

A What then? Do they not remember having seen God? Or rather, do they always see? As long as they do not see, it is not permitted for them to say they have seen, otherwise this would be the condition of those who have ceased to see at some point. What then? Do they not even remember having circled the earth yesterday or last year: nor that they lived yesterday and for a long time, and from what time they live? On the contrary, they always live. But that which is always the same, is always also one.
B But what is said in motion as "yesterday" and "last year," is as if someone experiences an impulse and motion made with one foot into many, and one motion, and he himself invents it to be different and different and many. For here, the motion is one, but for us it is measured as many, and days are different because nights also intervene. But there, since the day is one, how can there be many? Therefore, neither a previous year. But someone will object that there is not one, but another and yet another interval: and that there is one portion of the zodiac and another.
C Why then should the celestial soul not say, "I have already passed this part: but now I occupy another?" Moreover, if they foresee human things, how do they not also see human changes, and that there are now other men: and if so, that others existed before, and other affairs, from which it follows that they seem to have memory.
