402          PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

*The soul of any star, contemplating the ideas and principles of all things, always has within itself a certain knowledge of the universe, whether you wish to call this intellectual or rational, and meanwhile, through its celestial body, it perceives corporeal things: but what it perceives of the smallest things, it does not meanwhile notice through imagination, and therefore does not place in memory, both because it already comprehends all these things more deeply, and because they are of no moment to it, and also because it has already perceived all things for so long that nothing beyond its perception moves it as new. Nevertheless, through imagination, it does notice that it perceives those particulars which are especially necessary to the universe, such as stars, celestial bodies, and elements. Indeed, since the purpose of celestial souls is not merely to move through this part alone, or only up to this point, or only for so long, but to contemplate, and simply and always to move, and since their motion is perfect at every moment, and those souls are certain that the prescribed order of the universe will undoubtedly unfold within themselves: no care, therefore, touches them concerning any part of place, or time, or motion, or of a thing, or of any mutable thing. And so, neither while they perceive such things are they compelled to apply imagination and attention to them. Note that the circular motion of the heavens is neither an alteration, because it does not change form; nor is it local, because it does not change place; but it is vital, that is, an act proper to inner life, and likewise an indication: for to act within oneself and to move from within is proper to living beings. The motion of celestial bodies, however, is of such a kind as the pulse and heart's motion in animals, and nutrition in plants. Chapter VIII.*

Perhaps indeed it is not necessary either A
to commit to memory whatever one observes, or
to gather by imagination those things which follow entirely by chance. Likewise, for those in whose mind a surer understanding and knowledge of things resides, if ever things of this kind are offered to the senses, it is not necessary for them, neglecting intellectual knowledge, to gaze at that which is particular and sensible, unless one by the very act dispenses something: which, although it be particular, is nevertheless especially included in the very notion of the whole. But I speak B
concerning anything in this manner: In the first place, it is not necessary that what one sees, one places within oneself. For when it makes no difference, or is of no moment to oneself, then the sense, without our choice of the differing movements of what is seen, itself alone suffers this: but the soul meanwhile does not receive it within itself; since those very differences of visible things are neither a concern to us, nor will they contribute to any necessity or other utility. Now indeed, when one acts entirely for oneself, C
or for certain other things, then the memory of such past things is retained minimally, when one does not even perceive the sense of present things. Moreover, it is not necessary that those things which arise entirely by chance be placed in the imagination; and if they are placed, they are not placed in such a way that they are kept and observed: but anyone will be able to perceive that the figure of such a thing does not bring assent, if only one has understood what is said in this way: But I speak in this manner: If it were never D
our principal purpose to divide this part of the air presently and then that part, while we move from place to place, or even more, to pass through it: certainly, we would never be thought to observe this very thing while walking. Since, unless it were especially decreed for us to accomplish only a completely certain path: and it were permitted for us to traverse through the air, it would never be a concern to us in which particular stage of the earth we are, or how much space we have already traversed. Then indeed, if E
we were obliged to move, yet not properly only for a time, but only to move. Likewise, if we were accustomed to refer no other action whatsoever to time, certainly we would never conceive of one time after another in memory. This indeed is most evident from the fact that when thought holds within itself the whole of what is being done, and trusts that it will be accomplished precisely as it has it, it no longer applies itself to the individual things that happen.

--- Page 447 ---
LIBER QVARTVS. 461

A Furthermore, when someone always does the same thing, they will certainly observe the individual details of their work to no purpose. If therefore the stars, while they move, perform certain of their own duties, and are not moved so that they might pass through these very things which they pass by; and their work is neither to look at what they pass through, nor even to pass by, and the transit itself is accidental to them, being meanwhile occupied with greater things; finally, they always move through the same things and with a similar course, certainly among them time is measured by a certain discrete measure least of all (or: not at all).
B ...least of all computed, and even if it is distinguished, it is not necessary to retain the memory either of the places they pass by, or of the times; especially since they always have entirely the same life, when they also perpetually revolve around the same place, so much so that their motion seems to be not so much local as vital; since a single animal acts upon itself, indeed in a state as far as external things are concerned, but in motion through the life proper to itself urging it on.
C Therefore if anyone says that the motion of celestial bodies is similar to a dance, if only to a dance that sometimes ends, the entire progression of motion will indeed be perfect, continued from beginning to end; but each individual part will be imperfect when counted. But if it is compared to such a dance as is eternal, it will always be perfect. But if it is always perfect, it will not have a time in which it will ever be perfect in the future, nor even a place. Therefore neither will it thus have appetite, and consequently it will not be measured by temporal nor
D local condition; and so no memory of these things will occur. Furthermore, by this reasoning, our argument will be even more confirmed, namely, that they lead a blessed life, contemplating life in their own souls; and by the very harmony of their souls towards the One, and by their illumination from themselves throughout the whole heaven, just as strings moved on a lyre harmoniously sing a melody in a certain natural harmony wonderfully; and thus the whole heaven revolves, and its parts towards it,
E indeed it itself is moved in one way, and other things in another, although towards the same; since their position is also different, and the life of all is even more one and very similar.

*Jupiter, Ruler of the world, through one simple and all-encompassing form of himself, sees infinite things and effects infinite things with infinite power: not indeed by two acts, but by the same act by which he sees, by that same act he effects, and vice versa. But it would be absurd to say that he gathers knowledge of things from the things themselves: for through antecedent knowledge he effects things, nor could he comprehend infinite things, if he were to hunt for knowledge from infinite things: but now he perceives infinite things through one form of himself no differently than if the sun, through its one light, were to perceive innumerable rays shining forth from it. Chapter IX.*

A But Jupiter, adorning all things, and moderating, and arranging, always possessing a royal soul and a royal mind, and the providence by which each thing comes to be, and dominion over what comes to be; likewise certainly arranging individual things in order. Furthermore, unfolding many circuits, and bringing many already begun to their end, why should he not have memory in all these things, remembering namely how many and what kind of revolutions have already occurred; and again, how it may happen in the
B future, devising and conjecturing and pondering, and thus he will be most mindful of all, and the more so, the wiser the architect. Therefore, as far as the memory of the revolutions themselves is concerned, L 4

--- Page 448 ---
404 PLOTINI ENNEAD. IIII.

also brings about very great doubt through itself,
namely, how great the number is, and whether it is comprehended. For if it is finite, it will give a temporal beginning to the universe: but if indeed it is infinite, that ruler does not comprehend how many his works are, unless perhaps it is said that he always exists in one knowledge and life, and thus the infinite is there, and one thing consists there, not indeed through knowledge coming from outside, but consisting in the thing itself: since the infinite itself thus always remains whole at the same time, but rather accompanies and is perceived not by an adventitious notion: for just as he knows the infinite of his own life, so also he knows that the action diffused through the universe is infinite, especially since it is one, and yet not on account of this very fact that it applies itself to the universe.

*The order of the universe, which gradually unfolds in matter, is at the same time whole and immutable in both Jupiters, both in the first who is pure intellect, the segregated artificer of the world: and in the second Jupiter, who is the intellectual soul, the conjoined leader of the world. Neither Jupiter therefore deliberates in an ambiguous manner about things to be done: especially because the soul, with an eternal certain intuition, looks up to the order of the universe in the first Jupiter, and holds it firm, and has all the matter of the world subjected to it, and inwardly agitates it, turning all things most easily from its one life as if from one hinge, so that deservedly nothing resists its action, and no ambiguity arises. Chapter X.*

The Adorner, however, is twofold: for we call one indeed as an artificer, but the other as the soul of the universe: and when we name Jupiter, sometimes we understand the artificer of the world, but sometimes the leader of the whole world. Indeed, from the architect of the whole itself, whatever is said to be prior and posterior, we must separate far away, attributing to him a unique and immutable life, devoid of time. But the life of the world, which naturally has this very thing, that it leads, still seems to demand inquiry and reason: whether it also does not have its life in ratiocination, nor in seeking out what is most to be done? For it has already been found and ordered what is to be done, not indeed through these very things which are ordered: for those things which are ordered, these are the very things which are generated: but that which acts upon these, is order. This, however, is the action of a soul dependent on permanent wisdom, of which indeed the image is the order that thrives in the soul. But since that [wisdom] is not changed, it is necessary that this [soul] also not be changed: for it does not sometimes look up to it, and sometimes not look up to it: otherwise, if it were to intermit, it would immediately be in doubt. But indeed, the soul is one, and its work is one. For that which holds the dignity of a single leader, always prevails: nor does it sometimes prevail, and sometimes be overcome: for whence would there be many things there, so that conflict or ambiguity might arise there? But indeed, a single governor always desires the same thing: for what would be the cause for him to desire one thing and then another, so that, distracted into many things, he would be compelled to doubt? Moreover, even if the one soul of the world, existing, changes in some way, it will nevertheless not doubt: for it will not doubt how it is to be disposed merely because the world has many things, and parts, and oppositions of parts: for it does not begin from the last things, nor from the parts, but starting from the first things, and from the first by a certain way entirely removed from impediments, it diffuses itself through all things and adorns them, and on account of this very fact it dominates and prevails, because it itself remains the same in the same work and for the same purpose: but if it desires one thing and another, whence indeed would it desire another?

**A** But perhaps someone will admit that something of this kind is a work of nature; but since wisdom is in the universe, he will necessarily think that there are also discursive reasoning and memory. But this indeed is characteristic of men, of those who place wisdom in not-yet-being-wise, and who think that to seek wisdom and to be wise is this (process). For what else is discursive reasoning than to desire to find wisdom, and true reason truly master of the mind?
**B** For he who reasons is like one striking the lyre purely for the sake of striking, and one practicing to acquire a habit, and altogether one learning for the sake of knowing. For the reasoner seeks to learn that which he who already possesses it is wise; therefore, wisdom is in a certain stable state. The reasoner himself testifies to this: for when he first finds what he desired, he ceases to reason, and, placed in wisdom itself, he rests. If, therefore, we consider the very leader of the world to have the role of learners, we will certainly attribute to him discursive reasoning, doubts, and memory, comparing, namely, past things with present and future things.
**C** But if we rather think that he is constituted as one who knows, possessing his own completion in a certain state, we will rightly judge that wisdom rather befits him. Furthermore, if he knows future things—for it would be absurd to deny this—why should he not also grasp how future things will be? But if he knows how future things will also be, what further need is there to investigate by reason, and to compare past things with present ones?
**D** Again, the knowledge of future things, if only it is granted to him to possess it, will certainly not be such as it is accustomed to be in prophets, but such as in the makers themselves, certainly knowing that it will be so. This indeed belongs to those who have all authority, for whom nothing hesitant, nothing ambiguous occurs, and whose judgment, once assented to, perpetually rests. Therefore, the same wisdom concerning future things is there, which is also concerning present things according to a state. But this is removed from the investigation of reason;
**E** and unless he knows the future things which he himself is about to do, he will neither know how to do them, nor will he accomplish anything with a view to something, but he will do what happens by chance; but this is nothing other than to act by chance. Therefore, the reason by which he will act remains. And if the reason by which he will act remains, he will certainly not act otherwise than he intends, because the exemplar exists in him. Therefore, he will always act with one tenor and the same reason. For he will not act differently now, or differently in the future; otherwise, what will prevent him
**F** from straying far from his purpose? But if the work itself will be different, it will not indeed possess this difference from itself, but insofar as it serves seminal reasons; but these depend on the maker. Therefore, the work itself follows the series of reasons. Therefore, the maker is in no way compelled to err, or to doubt, or to toil in affairs, just as some have thought, believing the governance of all things to be laborious.
**G** Indeed, to labor in arranging a work seems to be nothing other than to handle foreign materials, that is, materials over which he least dominates. *Just as from the Sun shines light inseparable from it, which is not a proper quality of the air, but from the light is generated heat, now a proper quality of the air: so from our soul shines forth a vivifying act, which is not indeed a proper quality of the body, but generates something vital in the body, now made proper to the body. The soul indeed is substance and life; that inseparable act of hers is something substantial and vivifying. The quality hence attributed to the body is something accidental, and as it were vital: that act we call the idol of the soul, in which is sensation and vegetative nature. But that quality we name the image of the soul and its shadow: from this and the body is made a composite, in which are bodily pleasures and pains, of which passions the sensations reach the idol and the soul, but the passions themselves by no means. The previous comparison would have been more proper if we had compared the idol of the soul, not separated from the soul, to a visual ray not separated from the eye. Which if it ever proceeds from a reddened eye, will create redness in the eye of the beholder, to which you might say the shadow of the soul resulting in the body is similar.*

*To sense is not simply to know sensible things, but through certain passions or impressions made either by sensible things near the soul, or by the soul concerning them. The soul separated from every body, as it lives in itself, so, turned towards itself, through forms inherent in it, it knows divine things from divine things: and through those as principles it comprehends even sensible things, yet this is not sensing: for it cannot sense corporeal things, because it has no proportion with them, through which any impression or expression between it and them might occur: but when it is conjoined to the body, it uses spirit as a certain instrument mediating between it and external things, creating a proportion between both, in which qualities or passions coming from outside, emerge into a spiritual and pure species, and close to the soul, so much so that through this the soul excites the forms of sensible things lying hidden within itself: which excitation is sensing. All this, however, we declare more diligently in Theophrastus' book on the soul, together with Priscian and Iamblichus.*
Cap. XXIII.

**A** It must therefore be asserted that sensation concerning sensible things is a perception in the soul or in an animal: a perception, I say, in a power adhering to bodies, perceiving quality, and in some way forming their species for itself. *The spheres of the world and the stars have senses, and they hear our prayers. They are also said to have hearing, but of a kind far different from our hearing, because, like those who hear and grant, they often fulfill the prayers of those who vow. Among all parts of the world, as if members of a single animal, there is said to be a certain communion or contiguity, or continuity, or unity, of which there appear to be five foundations: The first is one matter everywhere for all things. Second, the harmony of qualities: for just as the elements, though discordant, are nevertheless harmonious in certain proximate qualities among themselves, so too all degrees of things, whether composed of elements or not, though differing among themselves, nevertheless touch each other in harmonious reciprocal limits. Third, one spirit everywhere: for just as heaven is one spirit in the heights, so within heaven, one spirit, either entirely celestial or most similar to heaven, is infused into all things, by which all things are governed from heaven, and the souls of the lower world are also joined to bodies through this spirit, and all living things coalesce through it: understand this spirit as similar to our spirit. Fourth is one generative nature nourishing all things, bound by the spirit to those that follow. Fifth, the soul of the world, one everywhere, connected by nature to the spirit and other things. Therefore, through this unity, consisting of five foundations, every most vehement motion, whether of those vowing reaches the celestial beings, or of the celestial beings reaches those vowing: especially if not only the soul of the world, but also all divine souls are present everywhere: although they sometimes manifest their actions more in certain places. Which Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus seem to desire. But the first God himself, most powerful of all, and most expansive in dominion, is most present to each individual: he exercises all the senses of the soul of the earth through the spirit there, as if celestial and illuminated by the rays of celestial beings, subject to its own nature, and governing earthly things: moreover, he hears prayers.*

Just as in an animal teeth, nails, hairs, so in plants adhering to the earth the effect of generative power appears: but this power itself does not seem to be proper to them, otherwise even when torn out they would likewise grow together by their own power. Therefore, this vegetative power is not so much proper as common, namely, in the soul of the earth: likewise, masculine and feminine power, that is, of generating and conceiving, which are discrete in animals, are conjoined in plants, in the same body of the plant. This is solely because the nature of the plant is thus inserted into the common nature, just as the body of the plant into the common body. Stars have sight and hearing, but they do not need memory: moreover, they hear prayers. Just as one who opportunely exposes his body to the light of the Sun is naturally nourished thereby, so he who applies his soul and spirit through prayer to the influences of the superiors, everywhere present, naturally receives benefits flowing therefrom. Some ancients adored stars besides the Sun, but many, especially Platonists and philosophers of that kind, adored only the Sun among celestial bodies. Julian and Iamblichus composed prayers to the Sun. Plato called the Sun the visible son and image of the highest God: Socrates, greeting the rising Sun, often experienced ecstasy: Pythagoreans sang hymns to the rising Sun with the lyre. As for the worship of the Sun, let them see to it: God certainly placed his tabernacle in the Sun. Chapter XXX.

*Some actions are natural, others artificial. Natural actions are either of the whole world towards its parts, or of the parts towards the whole, or of the parts towards each other in turn. Artificial actions either terminate in a work constructed by art, like sculpture in a statue; or they serve the work of nature, like medicine, agriculture, magic, with which oratorical persuasion and poetic and musical allurements have a certain similarity. The actions of celestial beings on lower things occur not only through heat and other qualities similar to elements, but through certain forces far different from known qualities. For the fact that differences in our morals, talents, professions, and fortunes are either caused or portended by celestial things, cannot be referred to differences in celestial qualities similar to elements. Nor do celestial things act upon us individually by counsel and choice, otherwise their minds would always be anxious, and they would daily be ministers of evils. Chapter XXXI.*

IT IS WORTHWHILE to consider A

*The heavens act upon all these lower things, not by some counsel choosing to act in such or such a way: nor only by bodily qualities, namely by heating, moistening, rarefying, or the opposite: but by certain natural powers of the vegetative soul, similar to certain powers, as it were, mediating between counsel and bodily qualities, by which our soul daily restores the humors and members of the body, and their shapes and qualities. Since the world is one animal, all corporeal things are parts of the world in two ways: first, because individual bodies are certain portions of the universal body: second, because in every body there is both the soul of the world itself, and a certain proper power of this soul, an effective endowment distributed to this body. Insofar, therefore, as individual corporeal things are members of the mundane animal, they easily suffer both from the whole and from each other: indeed, since even those things which seem to be distant from each other in space are close, due to the wonderful communion of one nature.*

From the very nature of life, they ought not to possess perpetually the same thing among themselves, nor their own distinct property; nor could it happen that anything should remain entirely in the same way always, if indeed the whole was to remain, having its stability in motion.

The whole world is one animal dancing by musical reason, and by dancing consequently varying all things along with itself. The soul of the world has described in its intelligence, thought, imagination, and nature, as if present, all future revolutions of the world according to their musical proportions; likewise, it has designated all events which either necessarily accompany the revolutions in the heavens, or in whatever way follow them under the sky. To such a musical designation, as if to a song and harmony of sounds, the revolutions in the world follow by affection, like certain gestures of an artful dancer. The dancer himself indeed first regards the music inherent in him by intention; then through this, the revolutions of the mundane members; thirdly, through these, he brings about whatever follows from them, or at least is signified. And some wise person, as if a musician, can foresee what kind of revolutions of the world follow where and how, just as what gestures of members follow what parts of sounds, except where either unsuitable matter does not entirely yield to the higher powers, or being too weak, suffers beyond measure; just as the will of man can fail to follow the tenor of the heavens, and conversely, human weakness can suffer beyond measure from it. Finally, just as in a dance certain affections of the members or other things occur beyond the artistic gestures, so too certain similar things occur from the world's dance. Cap. XXXIII.

**A** Since indeed the revolution of the world has nothing fortuitous in itself, but is carried out by a certain reason looking to the animal, it was necessary that there be a certain harmony of agent to patient, and a certain order within itself and ordering itself mutually; so that according to every relation of the revolution, again for those subject to this revolution, a different disposition must occur, as if they make one dance in a very varied choreography. In our dances, who can explain the manifest things that occur externally, consonant with the dance, as in each motion, those elements contributing to the dance—namely, flutes, songs, and other accompanying parts—change individually in different ways? **B** But not everyone can similarly grasp and declare the parts of him who performs the dance necessarily according to each figure, while the body accompanies and bends by a certain reason in following; in which indeed one part is pressed and restrained, another is relaxed, one part labors, **C** while another receives a certain respiration in a different figuration. The intention of the dancer indeed regards something else in the meantime, while the other parts consequently undergo the dance, and minister to the dance, and together perfectly complete the whole. Therefore, an expert in dancing will be able to assign how, in such a configuration, one member of the body is raised higher, another is contracted, that one is hidden, another meanwhile is pressed to the ground, while the dancer himself does not deliberately **D** act otherwise, but holds this necessary disposition in the very dance of the universal body, for this part performing the choreography. By the same reason, it must be thought that the celestial bodies do whatever they do, and signify many things; indeed, that the whole world acts out its entire life, moving immense parts within itself, and always transfiguring them. And the relations of the parts, both to each other and to the whole, and their different positions, provide other things consequent to themselves, as if **E** one animal is moved, having itself indeed according to such relations and positions and figures; but so indeed according to such, just as if those who are figured are not the authors of things, but the figurer; nor again does the figurer himself, doing one thing, do another. For he does not act *into* another, but it must be thought that he himself is all those things that are done:

Our body, as a part of the world, follows the world's fateful circuit. The soul also, insofar as it obeys the body, can nevertheless, by magnanimity, make light of the body's passions, and by art, avoid or alleviate them. In the various spheres of the world and their parts, and in the stars, there are naturally various powers. There are also various powers in the different figures there, firmly constituted by the stars in relation to each other: firm powers, I say. And different powers subsequently arise in different figures, which occur among the stars by perpetual diversity of motion. To these powers, both of natures and of figures, follow what happens beneath the Moon, partly indeed as if necessarily made from thence, like those who are seized by a dancing captor, but partly truly as more freely consonant, like those who eagerly respond to sound and dance, and sing, and dance willingly. The celestial figures indeed signify these lower things: but natures, together with the figures, effect things according to the disposition of the matter. But figures also signify many things which are not made by such, but from elsewhere. CAP. XXXIIII.

A Moreover, it must be judged that when we concede only that part of what is in us which is a part of the universal body as subject to suffering from it, and do not deem the whole of what is in us to belong to it, then we suffer moderately from it: just as the most prudent of servants, partly indeed yielding to their masters, but partly wishing to be their own masters, receive more moderate commands from their masters for this very reason: inasmuch as they are neither slaves nor entirely under another's jurisdiction.
B But the difference in configurations was necessary to occur, as it now does, because they both run and do not run with equal speed. Therefore, since they are carried along rationally, and different states of the animal emerge, and then what happens among us sympathizes with them, it is reasonable to inquire whether it should be asserted that these things follow those in consonance with them, or whether the figures have the power to effect things: and whether figures simply, or rather the figures of these things (i.e., the celestial bodies themselves). For the same C configuration does not bring forth the same signification or effect in one thing and again in others: because each thing also seems to have a different nature in itself. Perhaps it will be rightly said that the configuration of these things (the celestial bodies) is such a disposition, and of this kind: but for other things, the same configuration existing in a different way. But if this is so, we will no longer give authority to the figures, but rather to the things figured themselves, or simultaneously to both, namely, to the same natures having acquired a different state: but D also to the same thing differing only by place, we will concede other things. But what indeed shall we concede? Effects, or significations? Perhaps to the conjunction itself, that is, properly to the configuration of these things, both effects and significations in many cases, but elsewhere only significations. This reasoning therefore grants powers to the figures, and powers to the things figured: since both those dancing and playing in a chorus indeed have a certain power, and both hands, E and the other members also have very much of the figure. And in the third place are those things which follow, both the parts of those taken up in the dance, and those things from which they are made, or which arise from them, such as those that are rubbed by touching, and the sympathetic nerves and veins.

The Soul of the world, having contemplated this whole universe from eternity in the very series of Ideas, once and for all chose the entire course of the world by a common choice, thus approving that it should be so: meanwhile, the vegetative nature, its image subject to it, thus passes through the entire course of the world without choice: And the individual souls of the spheres and stars likewise relate themselves to God and the world: and they agree so much with the Soul of the world, both by will and by nature, that all their actions in the world can rightly be called the action of the mundane soul. All corporeal things, therefore, are parts of the mundane animal: All things

actions of natural things are movements of this animal: All mundane revolutions are gestures and, as it were, discourses of the same. Nothing either in it or from it is, or happens by chance: for all things are referred to the seminal reasons inherent in it, or, more profoundly, to the exemplary ones. Therefore, individual things either proceed in order, or are immediately brought back into order. The sun, the heart of the world, has and brings much more natural life than the other parts of the world. From here they are soon transferred into the spheres of the world, and their figures, both mobile and firm. From here into the species of natural things, in which thence lie wonderful powers over the elements, and from the very figures of the sky into lower figures, powers also wonderfully. And the figures of our countenances have certain specific virtues of attracting or deterring, whence it may appear that a proper power can reside in figures no less than in colors. Cap. XXXV.

Every member of an animal has the power to attract its proper portion of nourishment, and the heart to aromas, the liver to sweet things, the veins to blood, the arteries to spirit, and the testicles to semen. There are also medicines which attract certain humors, and seem to seek out certain members. The condition of the World Animal is the same: in which are scattered everywhere things which can draw this or that thing to themselves, if gathered into one and applied. For by their own nets or snares, men, by their own, horses, and similarly by their own, men, these or those can be secretly ensnared: just as they are openly captivated by the delights of forms and music. Finally, just as it is known concerning iron and straws that the magnet attracts, and indeed amber: so a diligent and fortunate investigator will find bait for attracting all things. For in each member of the World Animal, an inherent coagulating force exists, connecting all living things into one, temperately indeed by its own nature: but intemperately whenever, gathered from all sides, it is transferred into something, the world neither suffering nor sinning in the meantime. There are also different forces in this animal, separated from each other by nature, which, frequently joined by the Magus and cast into this or that member, act more violently, and destroy in these instances, (as I said) the world not sinning. Plotinus names four things in which a marvelous power resides, namely, the occult qualities of species, and figures, and harmonies, and vows: since those qualities are certain offshoots of forces latent in the life of the world, and lower figures and harmonies often refer to celestial figures and harmonies. A vow, however, is a vehement movement of our soul towards the divinity we implore: If you throw its very fine powder towards fire, when sulfur is crushed, the flame of the fire, extended far, will immediately apply itself to this powder. Similarly, he who implores a star, being opportunely prepared for the star, projects his spirit into the manifest and hidden rays of the star, diffused everywhere and vivifying, through which he claims for himself the vital gifts of the star. Finally, just as all fixed stars are connected to the firmament, so the lives of all stars and mundane divinities are connected to the mundane life, to which our life is also connected: so that it is not surprising that the vehement movements of our soul, poured forth through the common life everywhere active, extend even to the mundane divinities, and conversely, the movements of these divinities are led back to us through the same life. CHAPTER XL.

But how shall we say magical attractions occur?
Certainly, from a certain consent of things in suffering, and from a certain law of nature causing there to be harmony among similar things, but discord among dissimilar things: likewise, from the variety of many forces converging into one animal. For without any other contriver, many things are attracted by a certain magical rite: and the true power of magic is friendship in the universe, and conversely, discord. And the first poisoner (if I may so speak), enchanter, is of this kind: observing which, men use his philters and poisons among themselves: namely, from the fact that many things can naturally love each other easily, and they induce reciprocal love between things, the efficacy of the amatory art is born, using certain philters and fascinations: while they apply natures that are to be touched, reconciling some to others and having an inherent love: and they thus couple one soul to another, just as those who join together plants distant from each other. Moreover, they use figures having certain powers: and they themselves, shaping themselves in a certain proper manner, secretly draw forces to themselves, and the more easily because they are in one, and draw into one: for if someone, thus shaped, were imagined to be outside the world, he would neither attract anything, nor lead it away with allurements or measures, nor entangle it with bonds. But now, since it does not snatch as if to an alien place, it gains power to snatch: it certainly knows under what condition one thing in the same living being is drawn to another. For an inherent power of transmitting is in incantations and songs, and in a certain sound and figure;

For whatever has some kinship with another is sometimes ensnared by another. For that to which it is so related, as if by a magical rite, it captures and draws away; but only that which regards itself alone cannot be ensnared or snatched away. Therefore, every action of life, every active thing is ensnared and drawn; for it is carried towards those things which B provoke and entice. Hence that poetic saying: *For the people of great-souled Erechtheus are most beautiful in countenance.* But what does someone who has suffered something consider himself to be certainly related to another? Indeed, as if drawn not by the arts of magicians, but by the art of nature wonderfully seducing, and strongly reconciling and joining one thing with another, not indeed by place, but by love-charms applied from the beginning.

*The contemplative life is free: the active life is a servant of actions and things and fortune: the voluptuous life is a slave of the body. Chapter XLIIII.*

Since the mind possesses innate forms of things to be contemplated, and is itself these very forms, deservedly, inasmuch as it occupies itself in contemplating these with native pleasure, to that extent it dwells freely with itself. But he who carefully cultivates the body and external things serves the body, men, and fortune. Action and passion are opposed to each other. Therefore, every movement of ours which has had its incitement from corporeal and human passion is a certain passion and servitude. Finally, the very nature of life, as if a sorceress of the world, everywhere fashions images of the good, the true, the beautiful, like baits, by which it deceives souls devoted to this world through pleasure, avarice, empty glory, and detains and draws them as if slaves.

Therefore, only contemplation remains, which A cannot be drawn away by magical rite: for no one is drawn to himself. For it exists as one, and is itself the very spectacle which it contemplates, and reason is not seduced; but what must be done rightly, it does, and it performs its own life and work. But there, the soul does not do what is its own, nor does reason provide the beginning, but the beginning there is handed over by the irrational part, and the rules of action are proposed by passion. In the appetite for procreation and the care of children, a clear attraction appears; B and similarly in all things which attract those desiring with a certain sweetness. Also, actions, both those which are moved by anger without reason, and those which are incited by desire, as well as the eagerness for civil governance and the zeal for commanding, signify that the desire for domination, already incited in us, now incites. But then, the zeal for commanding, tending especially to this, lest injuries be inflicted upon us by others, draw their origin from fear; but those which aim that we ourselves may gain more than others C are led by desire. Finally, those things which serve necessity and utility, trying to fulfill the deficiency of nature, clearly show the very force of nature completely reconciling us to the desire for living. But if someone objects that actions concerned with honorable things are not drawn away by magical rite, otherwise, the contemplation of beautiful things would also be drawn away by such a condition, it must be answered that if someone follows honorable actions as necessary, looking, that is, at something else truly beautiful, D this person is by no means ensnared by magical means. For he knows necessity, and does not look to that which is in our actions, nor is this life directed to other things: unless perhaps through its irratio-

CONCERNING THE SOUL'S DIFFICULTIES, THIRD, OR CONCERNING SIGHT.
Concerning the doubts of the soul, or concerning vision.

[Large decorative initial S] TO SENSE is to perceive corporeal things individually through corporeal instruments. In sensual perception we find that the qualities or actions of external bodies reach the soul, or in some way arrive around the soul, and sometimes the power and action of the soul extend to corporeal things. This indeed could in no way happen unless the soul had a certain proportion to these things: but it does not have this unless it itself, through its vegetative power, in its own way forms a manifest body and especially a spirit: and so conforms it to itself, that its power and action sometimes extend to external things through this body of its own as an instrument, and the movements of external things, by coming to this, seem in some way to have reached the soul. Finally, for sight to perceive the thing to be seen, there is no need for an external mediating body necessarily assisting, as it were, for seeing: for sight itself and the eye are by nature sufficiently prepared to be occupied with the luminous, and the luminous in turn with sight. But if the mediating body is opaque, it hinders: but if it is diaphanous, it only has this, that it does not obstruct vision as an opaque body usually does; therefore, perhaps it will be seen without this.

*Between sight and the visible, light is necessary as a medium in itself, either common and external, or proper, whether of the eye or of the nature of a very luminous object: but a body is not so necessary as a medium between these. Vision occurs primarily because either a visual ray proceeds from the eye to the visible object, or something proceeds from the already luminous visible object to sight, or in both ways simultaneously, and entirely because both the eye and the visible object are so disposed in the living nature of the world that they have a property very much in conformity with each other, by which they are easily moved by each other, and act mutually, or suffer. For it would be sufficient for the eye to be touched by the part of the air contiguous to us, already formed. Between the sight and the visible, air is not necessary as a medium specifically for this purpose: that the form of the object be imprinted successively through parts of the air, from which it is finally imprinted on the eye. The first reason for this was assigned a little earlier. Two follow, one of which is of this kind: When in deep night we discern a tiny fire very far away, it should not be thought that a form is gradually imprinted from the tiny fire onto continuous parts of the air. For it cannot thus paint this, unless it also illuminates those same parts, and yet it does not illuminate them: otherwise, we would also see many other things in this straight space. The other reason is this: If air is painted in some way of its own, that is, corporeally, by the person to be seen, it will follow that that small part of the air closest to and equal to the pupil would show the eye only that minimum of the whole person which it presents: but now we see the whole object in any small portion of the air. Finally, the air suffers nothing from that species (form/image), if any is sent from the object, just as it suffers nothing from the light itself, through which it is sent: from the light itself, I say, insofar as it is light. For thus it is present and absent in a moment, nor does it remain when the illuminator is removed, and it is whole everywhere. From which it appears that light neither becomes a proper quality of the air, nor is it truly corporeal. Therefore, this incorporeal thing proceeds not so much from a body as from the life of the world. For when you see a spark at a very long distance, you hear the tiny sound of a locust: and certain animals hear the smallest things: likewise bees and ants smell honeyed things from very far away: even shellfish taste distant things: and the torpedo fish often stuns you through a long rod as if touching, it should not be thought: especially in higher things, that the longest space is broken by any minimal object, and materially affected: but that something spiritual, in a certain way, intervenes, which acts upon the sense through such a long space, that is, a certain special act proceeding from the very species of the thing to be sensed. From the species, I say, not so much because it is in matter, as because it depends on a spiritual and living idea. A special and spiritual act, I say, whether it occurs here within us in the instrument of sense, as in touch and taste, or also outside us in the air, as concerning sight, hearing, smell: or even proceeds from sight into the object: which act, indeed, in all things to be sensed, is everywhere between even the material passion made by the object in the air concerning the lower senses. It happens opportunely then by a certain power of common life, by the benefit of which, binding all things, the sense is so easily moved by distant things, and a conforming body suffers from a conforming one at a distance. Which also appears in magic: and celestial things and many others impart their powers to the most distant things: finally, the common life of the world so tempers this sense with this sensible thing, that when the sensible acts, the sense is moved and acts, just as in a lyre, when this string is moved, immediately the attuned one is also moved: and when you shout, the exposed wall echoes. We treat these higher matters more diligently in the commentaries of Theophrastus.

And this is so akin to sense, that when it first vigorously acts around the sense, the sense itself also awakens simultaneously to its own act concerning it: Just as for some people, a particular harmony is especially pleasing, and one [harmony] excites others to song and dance. And that this sense acts immediately upon the act of this sensible object, the same ubiquitous life of the world accomplishes, especially by tempering this with that and moving them simultaneously: just as at the movement of such a humor, such an imagination is moved, and vice versa. Likewise, at the various movements and phases of the Moon, humors are variously moved and affected: At the movement of sulfur, the flame is also moved: Whither you direct your right eye, the left is also directed.*

Perhaps this too has not perished: for this too is a certain image of illumination: but it must only be said that it is not there.

*Since the world is a universal and sensible body, truly nothing sensible can be placed outside the world. But if you imagine some body outside, communicating in no way with the world, it will not be perceived by worldly sense: but if communicating in any way, it will no longer be outside, but inside. That when the toe suffers, the groin immediately sympathizes, and this indeed rather than the knees, although more remote, happens because they are both in the same animal, and especially conformable to each other. Similarly, the stomach suffers at the suffering of the brain, and vice versa. By a similar reason, that even widely distant senses respond to the slightest movements of their sensibles, even without the medium suffering, is brought about by the one continuous nature of the world among these things: Just as the continuity of a very long and taut nerve causes that if even the lowest part is vibrated, the highest part is immediately vibrated. Hence it also happens that we imagine series of things impending from heaven and still future, or often imitate them by some more hidden instinct, and sometimes anticipate a friend approaching us before he arrives, by some hidden sense. Chap. VIII.*

Perhaps if sympathy concerning sensible things, sense is considered to be within the nature of the one animal, thus this world would certainly not perceive that body, unless perhaps that external body is said to be a member of this animal of

Therefore, such a supposition must be rejected, because it is not permissible to seek a consequence from it: for the very thing that is supposed in itself is destroyed and perishes by it.

A how great the external thing is, nor indeed at all how great it is, as how large the sky is; since a form received within cannot be so great. But what is greatest of all, if we were to receive the figures of those things we see within, it would not be permitted to discern those very things we gaze upon, but their images and shadows. But indeed what is said, that we cannot discern a thing placed upon the pupil, but can discern it when re-B moved, the same also, and much more, must be transferred to the soul. For if we were to place the figure of the thing to be seen in the soul, it would by no means discern that spectacle by which it would be marked. For it is necessary that there be these two things, that which sees, and that which is seen: therefore it is necessary that that which sees the figure placed elsewhere and not placed in itself be something else. Therefore it is necessary that vision is not indeed of a thing imposed, but rather of a thing not imposed, if vision is to exist at all.

*To sense is not to suffer from sensible things, but to act concerning them. Chapter 11.*
*Since the soul is incomparably superior to sensible things, and does not communicate with them in matter or nature, it never receives forms from them: and since in sensing it is to judge correctly, but passion confuses judgment, it suffers nothing from objects. But if any passion occurs from them, it reaches the body and the spirit: and by this spirit, thus struck or affected by external things, the soul immediately perceives such affections. But to perceive this is not to suffer, but rather to act, that is, then to vitalize the spirit differently, and to bring forth innate forms of sensible things (as Iamblichus says). Intelligence is much more removed from passion than sense: for it has internal forms, and is not turned outward.*

A IF therefore it is not sense, it remains to inquire how it happens. Does the soul perhaps speak of things it does not have? Indeed, of these. For this is proper to its power, not indeed to suffer anything, but to be strong, and to execute its own proper work. Thus, I believe, the visible and the audible will be discerned by something: not indeed if both are certain figures, nay, if they are not figures, nor any passions, but actions concerning that for which they are naturally instituted. But we, distrusting that any power B can know its object unless it is struck by it, meanwhile by moving it closer, cause it to suffer proximity, not to know: which indeed the soul ought to overcome by nature's gift, not be overcome. By the same reasoning, judgment must also be made concerning hearing: namely, that a figure is made in the air, like a certain distinct pulsation, articulated, as if of letters written there by him who uttered the voice. But the power and essence of the soul, as if reading figures written in the air, approaching most closely to that place, C where finally, having naturally proceeded, they can be perceived. Likewise concerning taste and smell, some things are indeed passions, while others are cognitions of passions, namely the senses and judgments of passions, which indeed differ from the passions: but the cognition of intelligibles is much more devoid of passion and formation. For these (intelligibles) conversely proceed as if from within, while sensibles are touched from without, and therefore the former are more actions, and indeed principal actions. D For they belong to the soul itself, and the soul itself performs each of these. But whether the soul sees itself as two things, and as if another: but the intellect as one, and both, two as one, must be discussed elsewhere.

*To remember and to recollect is not to preserve and repeat the forms of things once impressed upon the soul. Chapter III.*

*When they say that the soul, as a medium between incorporeal and corporeal things, has the forms of both within itself, we do not understand these forms to lie in the soul as certain accidents, like letters on a tablet, whether they were inscribed at some point, or innate. For the divine nature of the soul neither undergoes new impressions, nor does it have the principles of things which it possesses from the beginning so diverse from its own nature that they might be considered accidents: but as we have said elsewhere, just as in the soul there are natural powers of substance: intellect, reason, imagination, sense, and vegetative potencies, so too it has the principles of things to be known as if they were essential powers, just as it possesses the seminal principles of the limbs. Therefore, when the soul meditates on something, it brings itself forth from its natural power into a natural act concerning that very thing. But if it meditates on the same thing more attentively and and for a longer time, it conforms itself more powerfully to this very thing, and that [e...]*

--- Page 499 ---
LIBER SEXTVS. 455

A then after a long time you now grasp it. For this does not happen because you previously received parts of the figure, for you would also remember these, but rather it is suddenly brought about, as it were, by some final hearing or meditation accomplishing it. These things certainly testify that the power of the soul is stirred, by which we remember, and by which it is, as it were, strengthened either simply or for something. Then indeed, when memory supplies us not only with those things we have meditated upon, but also suggests or renders many others, accustomed, you see, to certain signs,
B from which, by the resumption of one thing, many other things are also more easily resumed, what other cause of such memory can anyone adduce than the very power of the soul, now strengthened? Indeed, forms of things settling in the soul would indicate weakness rather than power. For that which is marked by very many forms has become such by yielding; and since the impression of a figure is a kind of passivity, it follows that what has been most passive would also be most
C mindful, but the opposite of this clearly happens. For nowhere does exercise for a certain work render that which is exercised more subject to passivity; because even in the senses, it is not what is weak that discerns, like the eye, but that in which there is a more abundant power for acting. Therefore, old people are weaker both in their senses and similarly in memory. Therefore, sense and memory are a certain vigor and strength. Hence, since senses are not certain impressions of
D figures in the soul, in what way can memory be the preservation of those things which were not even deposited with it from the beginning? But if memory is a certain faculty and preparation for readiness, why do we not resume the same things simultaneously and suddenly, but rather successively? Because, you see, it is necessary to apply and exert the power itself. For we see this happen also in other powers, which are indeed prepared to accomplish what they can:
E and partly indeed suddenly, but partly, if they have gathered themselves beforehand, they perform their function. Moreover, very often the same people do not seem sharp and good at remembering, because the power of both is not the same: just as a boxer and a runner are not the same. For different ideas dominate in different individuals. Although nothing prevents a person possessing certain excesses of the soul, as it were, from rereading certain established things, nor does it prevent a person excelling in this respect from *not* being exposed to passivity:
F finally, because it is established that the soul is not subject to magnitude, it shows that whatever is in the soul is absolutely not passivity, but efficacy: and absolutely whatever pertains to the soul, in a certain wonderful way, holds itself differently than men suspect, who have never diligently investigated such things: and differently than the manifest impressions passing from things sensed to them signify, deceiving by a certain similitude. Hence, as letters are inscribed on certain tablets or notebooks, similarly they think about senses and memory.
G And indeed, those who are thus affected, whether they posit the soul as a body or as incorporeal, are utterly ignorant of how many absurdities follow from that supposition.

ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL.
On the immortality of the soul.

Each of us is wholly immortal, if indeed the soul itself is immortal. Chapter I.

[Decorative initial A in a rectangular frame] THE SOUL relates to the body in two ways: partly indeed as a substantial form to matter,
since through its presence a certain temperament of humors and vital spirit is born in the body;
but partly also as a user to an instrument, insofar as it moves the body at will; and it is separable
from the body, and indeed already in a way separated.

[Decorative initial V in a square frame depicting a figure] BUT whether each of us is immortal, or A [Marginal note]

partly perpetual—that is, in which part he
himself consists—one can learn in this way
by contemplating the order of nature. Man is
certainly not something entirely simple, but
has a soul, and has a body, whether as an
instrument, or joined to us under some other B [Marginal note]
condition. Indeed, it must be proposed and
granted that the nature and essence of each
are distinguished in this particular way. The
body, therefore, since it is itself also composite,
is shown by reason to be unable to remain
perpetually, and is perceived by sense to be
entirely dissolved and dispersed, when each of
the things that are in it returns to its own,
and one destroys another, and changes it into
another, and scatters it: especially when the C [Marginal note]
soul, which is accustomed to reconcile, is no
longer present to the masses. But if any body
is left alone, it is not yet entirely one, since it
can still be dissolved into form and matter,
from which it is necessary that even simple
bodies are composed. Furthermore, all bodies,
since they necessarily have quantity, consequently
perish when reduced to their smallest parts.
Therefore, if the body is a part of us, we are
not immortal in every respect; but if it is our D [Marginal note]
instrument, it must by nature be such as is
granted to us for a time: But the principal part
itself, and man himself, will certainly be either
such in relation to the body as form is to matter,
if indeed this (the soul) is as form to the body
as matter; or it will be like one using the body
as a kind of instrument. In either way, finally,
the soul is pre-eminently man himself.

**BOOK SEVEN.** **457**

*No body, insofar as it is a body, has its own inherent life: but the soul does. Therefore the soul is not*
*a body, nor therefore can it be from a body or bodies, since it is of a more excellent nature. Chapter II.*

*The body is dissolvable by its own nature: The soul by its nature connects the body, and reconciles contraries, while it mixes them in a certain rational way. Therefore it is neither dissolvable, nor a body, nor conceived from a certain mixture of bodies: but rather, conversely, the ordered principle of mixture in bodies proceeds from the soul. We will be very brief in this book: for on the same topics we are very extensive in Theology.*

**A** **THIS** very thing, therefore, which we call by the name of soul, what nature should we say it most especially has? Certainly, if it is a body, it is entirely dissolvable. For every body is composite: but if it is not a body, but of a different nature, it is necessary to investigate this nature either in the same way or in another. First, it must be asked into what body we ought to resolve this body which they call the soul. For since life is necessarily inherent everywhere in the soul, it is necessary,
**B** if that body which is imagined to be the soul is composed of two or more bodies, that either both or all together, or even somehow individually, possess inherent life, or that this one indeed has life, but that one by no means, or that neither has it. If, therefore, life is inherent only in one, this one alone will be the soul. But what body is this that possesses life from itself? Indeed, fire, air, water, earth by their very nature lack soul, and to whichever of these the soul is present, this
**C** uses a foreign life: but there are no other bodies besides these. Furthermore, whoever introduced other bodies besides some of these elements, they did not, however, say that these were souls, nor did they attribute life to them. But if anyone should say that none of them having life, yet the coming together of all constituted life, he would speak absurdities. Likewise, if each one has life, one is already sufficient. But it is entirely impossible for a confluence of bodies to create life, and for things that lack intellect
**D** to create intellect. And yet, however these are mixed, they will not be said to produce either intellect or at least a soul. Therefore, there must be something that orders and is the cause of the mixture. This, therefore, will rather obtain the authority and rank of the soul. Now, indeed, not only a composite body, but not even a simple body will exist in the order of things, unless the soul is in the universe: since the seminal principle approaching matter makes a body, but the principle itself cannot proceed from anywhere other than the soul.

*Every body, by the distance of its parts, ensures that when one part suffers, others do not immediately suffer with it: But through the soul itself, a living body has it that at the motion and passion of one part, all parts are immediately moved together: therefore the soul is neither a body, nor a form extended throughout the body. Chapter III.*

*It is not a dense body, otherwise it would not easily penetrate the whole: It is not a perishable body, otherwise it would not contain a most perishable body: It is not a form impressed upon the body, otherwise it would neither easily dominate the body for vivifying, and moving, and containing it, and it would depend on a more excellent form remaining in itself, and pouring life through the body. And this more excellent form itself would rather be the soul: which, being individual and whole everywhere, and outside the genus of contrary qualities, easily reconciles contraries among themselves, and connects the extended and dissolvable into one.*

**A** **BUT IF** anyone should not say so, but that atoms or certain individual bodies coming together by union make up the soul, he will certainly be refuted by the very consensus of suffering and the bond of nature: since it does not happen in this way through a whole that is one or sympathetic from non-suffering bodies, nor admitting any union: but the soul itself

**A** If someone, however, does not say this, but that atoms or certain indivisible bodies coming together make the soul by their union, he will be refuted by the concord of sympathy and the unity of nature. For it does not thus become one throughout and sympathetic from bodies that do not suffer nor admit any union. But the soul itself

**B** how could it sympathize with itself? For neither body nor magnitude is produced from atoms. Furthermore, if someone proposes a simple body, he will not say that the material part within it has life from itself (for matter is devoid of quality), but that which in it possesses the form of life. If, then, he calls this form a substance, then not both, but one of them will be the soul, which is no longer a body. For this too is not from matter; otherwise, we shall again be compelled to resolve it. But if he says that such a form is not a substance, but a certain affection of matter, it remains for us to say whence this affection and life came into matter. For matter itself does not form itself nor prepare a soul for itself; therefore, there must be something that provides life to it, whether life is provided to matter itself or to the body; and it is provided from outside and above all corporeal nature.

A it can, and naturally requires a certain place where it may be established, when it would be more fitting to seek a place where bodies might be placed: since these things truly are to be placed by the very powers of the soul. Therefore, if they say that life and soul are nothing other than spirit, like wind, it must be asked of them what they mean by that common saying among them, when they indeed say: the soul is a spirit having itself in a certain way. For they are accustomed to resort to this whenever they are compelled to introduce another effective nature besides bodies.
B If, therefore, not every spirit is soul, since innumerable spirits are inanimate, but a certain spirit having itself in a certain way, we will ask whether what is said "having itself in a certain way," and such a habit, is something real or nothing. For if it is nothing real, certainly only spirit will remain. And what is added, "having itself," will be merely a name. From which it will follow that they concede nothing else exists besides matter: but they will confess that soul and God and all similar things are merely names, but in reality only body exists.
C But if that habit is something real, and something else besides the subject and matter, which indeed is in matter, yet is immaterial, because it is not composed again from matter, certainly it will not be body, but an entirely different nature and a certain reason. Furthermore, it will appear no less from these things that the soul cannot be a body: for then it would be either hot or cold, or hard or soft,
D or compact or fluid and loose: likewise either black or white, and similarly it will be proposed concerning the other qualities of bodies. And indeed, if it is only hot, it only heats; if cold, it only cools: if light, it only lifts and makes things light wherever it is present: and if heavy, it weighs down and and makes things ponderous. Similarly, black properly produces black things; and white, white things. For it is not for fire to cool, nor for cold to heat. But the soul, in other animals, does one thing and another, and in the same animal, it produces contrary effects: partly indeed compressing,
E partly indeed melting and liquefying: Likewise it produces some things dense, others rare, white, black, light, heavy equally: although it ought not to produce one thing by another, but only one according to one quality of the body, and similarly one color. But now it brings forth many things equally.

_The soul, producer of motion, brings forth all forms, both by vegetative power through seminal reasons and by choice. And_
_it increases the body in a certain order to a certain limit, and meanwhile remains itself the same. Likewise, the whole soul is in any imagined portion of the soul, or any true portion of the body. And the whole power of the soul is preserved in any drop of semen._

These functions cannot pertain to bodily mass or quality, therefore the soul is incorporeal. Chapter V.

A But how will they be able to assert not only one motion, but different ones, when the motion of each body is one? If, however, they refer the causes of motions partly to choices, and partly to seminal reasons, they will indeed assert this correctly. But neither is choice proper to the body, nor are reasons, especially since they are different, and the body here is one and simple, nor can the body be entirely capable of such reason,
B except insofar as it is granted to it by that which makes it hot or cold. But by what power will it be fitting for the body to grow at certain times and to a certain limit? To which it naturally belongs to be increased, but not at all to increase, unless perhaps as much as in mass...

460 PLOTINUS ENNEAD. IIII.

...is simultaneously taken up by matter, as if ministering to that which it perfects through itself for growth. For if the soul, being a body, increases, it is necessary that it too be increased in like manner, by a certain addition similar to a body: if indeed it is to become entirely as great as that which is increased by it: then indeed that which is added will either be soul, or an inanimate body. And if it is soul, it will have to be asked, from where and how it enters, and under what condition it is applied. But if that which is added is inanimate, how will this be animated, and agree with the preceding, and come into one, and be consistent with the prior soul in its opinions. And will not this soul, as if foreign, rather be ignorant of those things which the other knows. And just as our other masses suffer, partly indeed it will flow away from it, partly also it will flow in, and nothing will remain entirely the same in us. In what way then will there be memory in us, and recognition of our own things, if we never use the same soul?

Furthermore, if the soul is a body, as the nature of a body is accustomed, it is distributed into many parts, none of which is the same as the whole. If therefore the soul were a certain magnitude such that if it were somewhat smaller, it would no longer be soul, certainly, like every quantity, it would be changed from its prior essence by a certain subtraction of parts. But if anything of those things which are extended in magnitude, though sometimes diminished in mass, can meanwhile remain the same in quality, then certainly, insofar as it is a body and has already become something else in quantity, it can nevertheless preserve its identity in quality, which differs from quantity. What then will those say, who think the soul is a body? Will they perhaps confess that any part of the soul in the same living body is soul just as much as the whole is? And again, a part of each part? But if they confess this, certainly magnitude contributed nothing to the essence of the soul: although it ought to have contributed, where the soul is a certain quantity: nevertheless the whole of the soul itself will be everywhere here, which cannot be fitting for a body, namely that the same whole can be simultaneously in many places, and that a part can be entirely the same as the whole. But if they deny that any part is soul, certainly it will be composed of inanimate things among them. Furthermore, if the magnitude of each soul is defined in this way, and consequently, if drawn to either side, whether to the greater or to the lesser, it will no longer be soul. When therefore from one coitus and one seed twin fetuses are procreated: or just as in other animals even more are conceived, the seed being distributed into many particles, where each is a whole, why should not such an event admonish those who wish to learn? where a part is the same as the whole, that this itself in its essence exceeds the condition of a certain mass, and that it ought to be entirely separated from quantity. For only in this way can it remain the same, with any quantity subtracted, as something which has no need of quantity or mass: since its essence is entirely something else. Therefore the soul is devoid of quantity, and similarly the principles.

Certainly, every divine and blessed thing must consist in this state, living and existing from itself, existing primarily, and living primarily, devoid of change according to its essence, neither rising nor setting. For from where it might be born, or into what it might be resolved, and if it is necessary for the true appellation of being itself to be inherent in this, it ought not sometimes to be, and sometimes not to be: just as the color white itself, by itself, is not white at one time, and then
non-white. But if white itself were being itself, then surely it would be, along with that which is white, and always. But now it only has this, that it is white. But that to which being itself is present from itself, and which is primarily being, undoubtedly always exists. Therefore, this primary being and always-being ought not to lack life like a stone or wood: but it must be living, and enjoy pure life: as much, that is, as remains of it. But that which is mixed from it with something inferior, indeed undergoes an impediment to the best things, yet does not lose its nature, but sometimes resumes its ancient state when it returns to its own.

There are two endowments of divine minds. One is the clarity of intellect discerning all things: the other is the best disposition of life. The soul especially attains such endowments when, separating itself from every bodily stain, it returns into itself. From this it appears that it is by nature akin to divine minds. Chapter X.

There are two arguments for divinity among us. One is prophecy: the other is the demonstration of miraculous works. Whoever, indeed, has brought forth these divine gifts, seems to have claimed them for themselves by this one office alone, namely, that they recalled the soul from the body to itself. From which it is evident that the very nature of the soul is connected with divinity by itself.

But that the soul is akin to a more divine and eternal nature is evident from this, that it is not a body, as has been demonstrated to us: nor does it have figure, nor color, nor mass, nor any quality that can be handled. The same thing, moreover, can be shown by these arguments. Indeed, since it is clear to us that every divine and truly existing being enjoys a good and wise life: we must next consider what the nature of our soul particularly is. Let us consider the soul, however, not yet in the body, conceiving irrational desires and angers, and admitting other disturbances: but one that has expelled all these: and has no commerce with the body, except as much as the utmost necessity compels. Such a soul will undoubtedly reveal to us that vices and evils are certain additions to the soul itself, and are cast upon us from outside: namely, that in a soul already purified, the best things are found to be inherent, namely wisdom and the rest of virtue, as if they were familiar. If, therefore, the soul is something of this kind, as often as it returns into itself, what then prevents it from being in the rank of that nature which we confess to be entirely divine and eternal? For wisdom and true virtue, since they are divine things, cannot ever be inherent in any vile and mortal nature, but it is necessary that such a thing be divine: inasmuch as it is capable of divine things on account of a certain kinship and communion of substance. Therefore, whoever among us is thus affected, seems to differ from the celestial by a certain small degree according to the soul: yielding, that is, only in this, that it is in the body. Therefore, if either all men, or most men, were endowed with such souls, no one would be so incredulous as to ever doubt that the nature of our soul is entirely immortal. But now, since men find the soul stained with many vices, they easily judge it to be neither a divine nor an immortal thing. But one must consider the nature of each thing by looking at its pure essence. For that which is added usually always impedes the knowledge of that to which it is added. Therefore, consider by removing: nay, truly, let he who removes, look into himself, and he will easily believe himself to be immortal:

Our same Bernard also desired this, when he, the orator of the Venetian senate here, heard us disputing most broadly on the matter. Bernard Bembus, I say, a man most learned, and a patron of the learned, and my brother in fate and genius. Therefore, for you and for him equally, this summary will be divided into four chapters: first, indeed, that the soul can dominate perishable things and resist bodily incitements; secondly, that, separated from bodies, it frequently devises many things, whether it reaches things themselves separated by themselves, or separates them itself; thirdly, that it naturally desires eternal things, and often, trusting in eternal things, neglects temporal ones; fourthly, that it worships the eternal God for the sake of eternal life. Finally, all natural religion is the firmest foundation of immortality for man.*
