But the body of the world, since it is perfect, full, self-sufficient, never suffering anything contrary to nature, is governed as if by a certain brief and easy command: and as the soul is naturally instituted to will, so it always conducts itself, neither is it incited by desires, nor affected by any disturbances: for nothing departs, nothing again approaches. Wherefore Plato also says that our soul, if it ever lives with that perfect one, will also be perfect, and will raise itself through sublime things, [D] and will govern the whole world. For when it is not absent from there, nor completely immerses itself in bodies, nor belongs to anything (particular), then it too, as a colleague of the world-soul, will govern the universe with equal ease: as if it were not an evil for the soul in any way to provide the power of being and of well-being to the body. For not all providence in administering inferior things prevents the provident one from persevering in the best state in the meantime. Indeed, there is a twofold providence [E] in the universe, common and proper: and the common one indeed arranges all things by a certain command free from anxiety, and by royal authority: but the proper one, by individually handling certain works, as I might say, manual craftsmanship, fills and contaminates the craftsman himself with the condition of the work. But since the divine soul is said to always govern the whole heaven in the way I have said, indeed surpassing what is inferior, but infusing the ultimate power into it from within, no one will be able to accuse God, as if He had placed the soul of the whole [F] in the inferior itself. Indeed, this very soul is never deprived of its natural function, possessing it from eternity, and always destined to have it similarly. Which indeed cannot be contrary to its own nature: since it is always assiduously present to it, and never began. He also says that the souls of the stars relate to the body in the same way as the soul of the whole: for the soul also moves the bodies of these (stars) by its movements: where it certainly preserves a fitting happiness for the stars as well. For [G] since there are two things, on account of which the commerce of the soul with bodies is especially blamed

--- Page 515 ---
LIBER OCTAVVS. 471

A. (It is blamed) both because it hinders intelligence, and because it overwhelms the mind with pleasures, lusts, and sorrows. Neither disadvantage truly happens to the soul which has neither completely immersed itself in the inner parts of the body, nor is subject to any [particular body], nor has withdrawn from the body, but conversely, the body [is subject] to the soul – a body, indeed, of such a kind that it neither needs anything, nor suffers any defect anywhere. Therefore, it does not infect the soul with desires and fears. For no disadvantage, no danger (B) occurs to such a body that the mind should fear; nor does any occupation whatsoever, inclining towards lower things, divert it from sublime and blessed contemplation. Indeed, such a soul always applies itself to divine matters, its faculty meanwhile not at all anxious, nor laboriously governing the universe.

But indeed, already turning to that which is inferior, it adorns it, and governs, and rules: for it could not possibly happen that all things would rest in the intelligible world; since one thing after another could be produced, which would indeed continually become less, yet would necessarily arise, as long as that which is superior exists.

*The divine intellect imprinted upon our intellect the all-encompassing form of the universe, which easily shines forth from there into an unoccupied rational faculty. Therefore, when reason turns itself entirely to it, and draws imagination along with it, it remains in the same state as the soul of the world. Chapter IV.*

*That is, it enjoys a similar contemplation of divine things, and meanwhile, dwelling in heaven, it turns its gaze and affection similarly to the universal governance of the world. But when reason, together with imagination, neglecting the universal form of the world, more diligently contemplates some particular thing, and loves it more ardently, and now even the vegetative nature itself entirely desires the same thing, then the soul, having become narrower, takes on a narrow body, subject to passions. Hence, therefore, troubled by innumerable cares, it is vexed.*

A IT IS therefore necessary that individual souls, using intellectual appetite in their very conversion to their author, and also having the faculty to dispense what follows—just as light, indeed suspended from the Sun above, but meanwhile extending itself to inferior things without envy—I say, it is necessary that they be preserved unharmed and uninjured, inasmuch as they live their life together with the whole soul in the intelligible world. Moreover, in heaven, together with the whole, they govern as colleagues, just as other kings, gathered together with the king of all,
B as colleagues arrange all things with him, nor indeed do they themselves descend from their royal seats, for then they are in the same state with the king himself. But when souls come from the whole to this, that they become a certain part and their own masters, as if the matter of acting together with another returns, then each one recalls itself to its own affairs. Therefore, when such a soul acts thus for too long, fleeing the whole, and already separated by some divergence from it, and no longer
C looks up to the intelligible, having become some part, it is indeed left alone, and as if abandoned, becomes powerless, and is distracted by affairs. For it is addicted to a certain part, while, separated from the whole, it enslaves itself to some one thing, fleeing all the rest: and having advanced and turned to that one thing, shaken from all wholes, it thus degenerates from the whole, and distracted, cares for its own particular concerns regarding those things that happen on all sides, handling and cultivating external things:
D not only assisting the body, but having progressed very far within it. Hence, therefore, as it is said, the soul, with its wings cast off or broken, is bound in the body, after it has strayed too far from the sound and harmless state of governing the better province: such a state indeed prevailed before in the soul of the whole itself. But what is before this, happened entirely better for the soul taking refuge in it. Wherefore the soul is bound, namely having fallen from on high, and thence bound with fetters, and acting by using the senses,
E because it is prevented from the beginning from using the mind: it is also said to be buried and hidden in a cave. Souls therefore necessarily experience both lives in turn, leading sometimes that higher one, and then again the lower one alternately: and for a long time—

Plato, secretly signifying these things, when he divides the beginnings of souls from the second bowl and now makes them parts, then also says that it will be necessary for them to fall into generation, after such parts have been made. But where he says that God sows souls, it is to be understood by us in this way, just as when he introduces God himself speaking and, as it were, preaching. For those things which are in the common nature of things, this very condition of treating them generates, and makes them, declaring by a certain succeeding order, how they always come to be, and how they subsist.

On the descent of the soul, the sayings of Empedocles, Heraclitus, and Plato agree. Chapter V.

*Since the soul is divine, in this perishable region it often turns to divine things: and since it is the last of divine things, through natural instinct and affection it comes into the body, therefore it comes by natural will, moreover it comes by a certain choice and by necessity, because by divine law it is necessary for souls that are thus affected, thus choose to immediately descend. They come spontaneously, as if to good, but not spontaneously do they fall into evil. For souls to come here pertains to the order of the universe, to the exercise of the soul's lower powers, to the experience of evil. Souls sinning more lightly are punished by a change from a happier person to a less happy or unhappy person. But those sinning more gravely are also vexed by demons, which Mercury, Orpheus, and Iamblichus confirm. A man easily frightens a boy with the ferocity of his face and masked terrors. The influences of Saturn and Mars vex imaginations with movements of black or yellow bile: certain Saturnian and Martian demons miserably agitate the imaginations of sinners with their horrendous imaginations, as if with masked faces: they can even afflict them with movements of humors.*

A Therefore, they do not disagree among themselves, that souls are carried into generation, and that they descend for the perfection of the universe: likewise under judgment, punishment, and the cave. Again, necessity and spontaneous motion: since necessity also carries with it the voluntary. Moreover, what is said, that the soul is in evil while it is in the body, neither does Empedocles' flight and error from God contradict it, nor that the soul has sinned, from which judicial punishment follows: nor again Heraclitus' rest in flight: B nor entirely the voluntary condition of descending, and again the involuntary. For whatever descends to a worse state does not spontaneously arrive at this very state, yet going by its own motion and meanwhile suffering worse things, it is said to bear the merits for what it has done: since indeed to suffer and to do these things is necessary by the law of perpetual and eternal nature. But if someone says that it happens for the use of another, descending namely from the superior itself, and sends that very thing from God, C he will be considered to disagree neither with truth nor with himself. For from what principle individual things are led, to the same, or to the extremes, even if there are many intermediates, they are referred. But since sin is twofold, and one indeed is in the very cause of descending, and the other while one transgresses in this state of life, that one certainly is this very thing, which the descending soul has suffered. In this, however, it is less, namely, to enter other bodies, and that indeed more quickly from a judgment assessing according to worth: D which, certainly made by divine institution, is signified by the name of judgment. But a more immoderate kind of wickedness is judged worthy of greater punishment, namely, by a certain prefecture of punishing demons. Thus, therefore, although the soul is something divine, and originating from superior regions, it is nevertheless immersed in the body. And since God is posterior by a certain voluntary inclination and cause of power, and of the posterior R 3

474 PLOTINUS ENNEAD. IV.

for the sake of its own manifestation, it thus descended here: and if it quickly fled from here, it is judged to have suffered no detriment from this, especially because it came to the knowledge of evil, and knew the nature of evil itself: likewise it brought forth its powers into light, and declared its works and effects: all of which, if they were to rest always in an incorporeal state, and were in vain, never indeed coming forth into their own act, and would lie hidden from the soul itself which possesses them, never indeed shining forth nor proceeding into effect: since everywhere action reveals potential, otherwise entirely hidden and obscure, and not even existing, not truly existing as such. Now indeed everyone marvels at the intrinsic things because of the variety of external things, while conjecturing what those things are like, through these very varied and beautiful things which proceed from them.

*The soul comes into the body not only by a certain weakness, being unable to remain further in divine things, but also by the power of a fertile nature sprouting into a germ: for corporeal form is the offspring of the fertile soul. Chapter VI.*
*By a similar fertility the first good overflows into the all-form mind: this into the similar soul of the world: this into the world likewise all-form. Likewise all causes everywhere into their effects. Finally, the mind, imitating the providence of superior things, transfers itself to inferior things with a certain zeal for providing.*

IF therefore it is necessary not only for the One to exist, otherwise all things not having their own form from it would be hidden, nor would any being at all exist, that is, if it were to remain in itself: nor would there be a multitude of these beings born from the One, unless subsequent things were to proceed from it, which indeed are endowed with the order of souls. It is also similarly necessary for souls not only to exist themselves, but also for their effects to appear clearly: since this is inherent in every nature, that it should make something subsequent, and unfold it into light, as if from a certain indivisible seed, and proceeding from a beginning to a sensible end, while indeed that which is prior always remains in its own seat: but that which follows is procreated from an ineffable power, inasmuch as it is present in superior things, which it was not fitting to remain sterile as if restrained by envy from generating, but to proceed always, until all things, as far as possible, advance to the ultimate, being indeed the cause of inexhaustible virtue diffusing its gifts through all things, nor allowing anything to be found anywhere devoid of itself. For there is nothing that prevents each thing from being a participant of the good, inasmuch as its own nature can be capable. Therefore, whether the nature of matter always existed, it was impossible for it, when it was, not to participate at all, because the good abundantly supplies to all, as much as each can receive: or if the origin of matter necessarily followed from preceding causes: not even so was it fitting for it to be devoid of gifts because of its very weakness, by which it is judged before a gift is thought to descend into it from above: when indeed that which bestows being, as it were, freely, would remain only in itself. The demonstration therefore of those things which are best in the intelligible world, is especially that which is most beautiful in the sensible world, a declaration, I say, both of their power and also of their goodness. Indeed, thus all things are always connected, both those which are judged intelligible and those which are sensible: and the former indeed existing by themselves, but the latter always receiving being by their participation, and imitating the intelligible nature according to their powers.

**PLOTINUS**
**ENNEAD IV,**
**TREATISE IX.**

Whether all souls are one soul.

*Plotinus' opinion is that the world has one soul proper to itself, and all animals have their own proper souls. Chapter I.*
*Unless the world had one soul, it would not be a perfect and truly unified composite, nor would the other souls in the world easily agree among themselves in order; likewise, unless we had our own souls, affection, passion, and animal action in one would soon pertain to all and to the universe. Plotinus, exercising his intellect around the opinion that posits a single soul in all things, plays back and forth, meanwhile contriving something else.*

Is it then that just as we say each individual soul is one, because it is entirely present everywhere in the body, and in this way it is truly one, with no part of it here and another part there in the body, so too in sentient beings is the sentient soul, and in plants one, and in the universe, that which is one in all things, not as if distributed by bulk, but having the same presence everywhere?

For why is my soul one, but the soul in the universe not one? For there is no bulk there, nor body, just as there is none in my soul. Indeed, if both my soul and yours are from the soul of the whole universe, and that soul is one, then these too must be one; but if both the soul of the universe and my soul are from one, then again all are one.

It must be investigated then what this one soul especially is. But first, we must examine whether it is rightly said that all souls are one, just as each individual's soul is one; for it is absurd that my soul and the soul of any random person should be one. For if it were one, then when I perceive, another would also have to perceive, and when I live well, another would live well, and when I desire, another would desire; and in general, we would all agree in passions everywhere, both among ourselves and with the whole, so much so that when I suffer, the whole universe would suffer with me.

But how, if there is absolutely one soul, is one part rational, and another irrational? And one in animals, and another in plants? But again, if we do not posit one soul, neither will the whole be one, nor will a single principle of souls be found.

--- Page 522 ---
478          PLOTINUS ENNEAD. IIII.

*Plotinus, though truly about to concede that souls are distinct, does not easily yield to the reason already stated, namely, the passage of the passion of one animal soon into another and into the universe. Chapter II.*
*He would prefer to say that the bodies of animals, neither continuous with each other nor with the whole, demand distinct souls. Likewise, where the entire animal virtue is completely gathered in one, this very soul, possessing the highest rank in the animal kingdom, would deservedly suffer least the passions and defects appearing in animals.*

A     FIRST of all, if my soul and another's
       soul are one, it does not immediately follow that both are the same with each other. For the same thing existing in one and in another will not have the same affections in both;
       just as the same human being is in me when I am moving, and in you when you are not moving: in me, indeed, when I am moving, it moves, but in you, when you are not moving, it rests; nor is it absurd or contrary to expectation that what is in me and in you is the same; nor is it necessary that when I feel, another also has precisely the same af-
B     fection: since not even in the same body does one hand feel the affection of the other, but the soul which is in the whole. But it is fitting to remember that many things sometimes lie hidden from the whole, even those that occur in one and the same body, and all the more so the greater the mass the body has, as is said to happen in larger whales and similar beasts: in
C     which, when a part suffers, no sensation occurs to the whole due to the smallness of the motion. But just as an affection that happens to a part in me does not necessarily occupy the whole, but that which happens to the principal part is diffused in a certain way even to the
E     part: so those things which come from the universe to each individual happen more manifestly, since individuals sympathize with the whole. But whether what happens to us immediately pertains to the whole, is hidden from us.

*Our Plotinus is still playing. Chapter III.*
*But just as mutual love among humans signifies a union of souls, so too perpetual and dire hatreds among them signify diversity. For a human does not differ less from a human, and any animal from an animal, than fire from water, and therefore is not less distinguished. Magical rapture, however, is largely fabricated, and we have declared its causes in previous sections. Elsewhere we have said that the formal reason of a certain thing is multiplicable into several essences, except for the first cause: therefore, just as the formal reason of body, quality, nature is distinct in several bodies, natures, qualities, so too are souls and intellects, and several souls and intellects. Then, if the soul is more excellent and more formal than quality, it is certainly established by divine providence that there are many grades of souls, just as qualities are formally distinct from each other, not like this heat from that due to the subject, but like heat from cold, dryness from moisture. Plotinus also hints at this at the end of the chapter, where he says that intellects are many, and that the judicial senses themselves are simultaneously with the intellects, that is, with intellectual souls. This discussion, however, signifies an assent that there is one soul in all bodies, not indeed rational, but vegetative, participating in a certain confused sense: nevertheless, any rational soul can form its own body with an irrational life, if it is not formed by the soul of the world.*

For we are not to seek a place where we should put it, but such a power is to be established outside all place. But when in the Phaedo and especially in the Theaetetus he commands to separate the soul from the body, E. he does not command to separate it by place. This Trinity of principles, especially Platonic and Zoroastrian, is confirmed by the Trinity of Christians. For paternal fecundity includes the Good itself; the intellectual emanation of the Son includes the Intellect; and the procession of the Spirit through the mode of will, and as it were a vital motion, includes the Soul. Furthermore, the firmament refers to the Good itself through the fecundity of the stars; Saturn, removed and alien from generation, refers to the Intellect; Jupiter, favoring generation, refers to the Soul; and Mars, already discordant and warlike, refers to the world. Again, the Sun is the Good; Mercury, closest to the Sun in its course, is the Intellect; Venus, desirous of generation, is the Soul; and the Moon, already varied and mutable in itself, is this world. Again, fire is the Good; clear and serene air is the Intellect; water, supplying moisture for generation, is the Soul; and earth, now mixed from all things, is the world. Finally, individually, the fertile essence of each thing is the Good; firm essence, virtue, is the Intellect; inclination, motion, action, is the Soul. In summary, regarding the soul: fertile memory is the Good; discursive reason is the Intellect; imagination and affection are the Soul. Therefore, nothing is more certain than this trinity of principles, because nothing is confirmed by greater and more numerous testimonies, and it rightly represents the sacred image of the universe of principles.

BOOK II.

CONCERNING the generation and order of those things after the First.
De generatione & ordine eorum quæ sunt post primum.

Just as unity, the principle of numbers, is not a number; and a point, the principle of the continuous, is not continuous; and light, the principle of heat and colors, is not heat and colors: so the Good itself, the principle of beings, is not some being, or beings: therefore, neither life nor intellect. Chapter I.

For it does not, by containing all these things within itself, as if pregnant, subsequently give birth to them, like intellect, soul, or nature: but it creates simply by supereminence, like unity, a point, or center, or light. But that which is proximately begotten from the Good itself, insofar as it immediately exists from that which remains, becomes being; insofar as it suddenly and naturally inclines, and as it were moves towards it, it becomes living; insofar as it is soon strengthened from there, and as it were turns back into itself in a certain circle, it becomes intellect. Similarly, from the remaining intellect, the intellectual soul exists; but from this soul, not remaining, but distracted by its discursive power from the intellect and intelligible things towards the imaginable and sensible, its image flows into act, namely a certain life devoid of reason, endowed with sense and vegetative power. Among these, what follows persists as long as what is superior exists. Our soul in the same body and at the same time acts as a plant, in which members it merely vegetates; it acts as a brute, in which instruments it only senses; it acts as a human, meanwhile reasoning; it acts as a demon, or God simultaneously, by understanding. The same human, again at different times, though under a human persona, exercises various such behaviors. Also, in the human species, some live a life as if plants, others as brutes, others as humans, some as if gods or demons. Whoever, therefore, shall have said that our souls, which have already assumed the habit of this or that life, will soon return into an aerial or terrestrial human, as if to live similarly, will hold a more probable opinion than if they had more freely transformed the human species into brutes or plants. For such a great transformation is both impossible according to nature and superfluous according to justice.

**Concerning the cognitive hypostases, and that which is beyond.**

**Concerning the knowing substances, and concerning that which is higher.**

*That which is to know itself is not therefore compelled to be so simple that there is absolutely no difference in it, as is the One itself: but it must be so simple that in any part of itself the whole is entirely contained, and its action is completed entirely in a moment. Of this kind is the Intellect. Chapter I.*

*When we say that the Intellect knows itself, we do not divide it into two, of which one part only knows, the other only is known, otherwise not the same thing would know itself, but one thing would know another: but we want the knowing itself, together with the known, to also embrace itself. The rational power, according to which we exist, uses the intellect in two ways: namely, through participation and through form: and in both ways it knows itself. Chapter.

Through participation indeed, insofar as it daily receives forms, notions, rules from the intellect, where, as if from an effect, through its own actions, it knows its own powers: through its powers it recognizes its essence, and that this [essence] always depends on and is illuminated by the mind: but through form, when after frequent use of such reception, it completely puts on the mind, just as matter puts on form, and acts under the very act of the mind, just as matter, after it has often received heat from fire, finally takes on flame. ...and we, in turn, of it, will we thus finally perceive the intellect and ourselves? Perhaps it is rather necessary thus: if indeed we are to perceive what is most important in the intellect, it is to know oneself. Then therefore someone himself becomes intellect, when, letting go of his other things, by this very act he gazes upon this very thing, and by this very act also himself: just as the intellect itself contemplates itself.

*In that which is superior to rational power, that is, to mobile intelligence, the same thing in reality is intellect, intelligence, intelligible; therefore it always understands itself. Chapter V.*

Above sense, which only looks outwards, is imagination looking inwards; above this, which only looks at external things: stands reason, which moreover observes internal things; above this again, which from other known things finally returns to itself to be known, is the intellect, in turn beginning from itself, and while it gazes upon itself, it contemplates all things—I do not mean the figures of things, but the things themselves—so that the knowledge may be most true. If, by touching itself, it touches all things, it is indeed both itself and all things; and by the very same act by which it gazes upon itself, it contemplates all things, and by the same act it simultaneously recognizes that it knows itself and all things. Especially the first and divine intellect, it is not turned to understanding anything other than itself, nor does it have accidental intelligence; but rather its essence, absolutely living and intelligent, by this very essential and vital intelligence, enjoys itself in act, comprehending meanwhile that it is existing, living, intelligent, entirely uniform, and omniform.

DOES the intellect then gaze upon one part of itself with another? But in this way, one will be the seer, and the other the seen. But this is not to know oneself as one thing. What then? If the whole is such that it is composed of similar parts, so that the seer does not differ from the seen: then indeed the seer, seeing that part of itself which is identical to itself, also sees itself. For the seer differs in no way from the seen there. But first, it would indeed be absurd to divide the intellect in this way: for how will the division be made? For it is not to be divided by some chance and rashly. Then indeed, who is it that divides? Is it perhaps he who places himself in the order of seeing, or rather he who places himself in that of being seen? Moreover, how will that seer know himself, while according to the act of seeing itself, he places himself in the rank of what is seen? For seeing is not present in the seen itself. Or will the knower thus consider himself rather as seen, than as seeing? And therefore he will perceive neither all, nor his whole self. For he knows this one indeed as seen, but he does not know the seer, and thus he will gaze upon not himself, but rather another. But will he by himself also add the seer, so that he may perfectly comprehend himself? But if he embraces the seer, he simultaneously embraces the things seen. If therefore in the perception itself the perceived things are contained, it is asked whether the figures of things, or the things themselves, are contained. If only figures, the things themselves are not possessed: but if these are possessed, certainly he who perceives them does not have them because he has divided himself: but he was both contemplator and possessor even before he divided himself. If the matter stands thus, it is necessary for contemplation to be identical with the contemplable itself (so to speak), and the intellect similarly identical with the intelligible: otherwise, if it is not identical, the contemplation will not be true. For he who is said to possess beings will rather have their figure, undoubtedly differing from them, which indeed is not truth. For truth must not be of another, but what it says, this must also exist. Thus therefore, intellect, intelligible, being are one, and this is the first being, and the first intellect possessing beings: but rather itself and beings...

--- Page 545 ---
LIBER TERTIVS. 501

A. But if intelligence and the intelligible are one, how then will the intelligent being understand itself because of this? For intelligence will, as it were, embrace the intelligible, or be the same together with it, yet it will not yet be clear that the intellect distinctly knows itself. Moreover, if intelligence and the intelligible are the same, for the intelligible itself is a certain act: since the intelligible itself is not merely a certain potentiality, nor is it devoid of life, nor again is living there adventitious B, or understanding in a different subject, like a stone or anything lacking life, and the first essence is the intelligible itself. If therefore, I say, there is act there, and first act, indeed the best act is intelligence, and intelligence (so to speak) is essential. For the truest intelligence is of this kind, and first, and existing first: and therefore this will be the first intellect. For this intellect is neither in potentiality, nor is it itself one thing and intelligence another: otherwise, C its essential nature would again be in a certain potentiality. Wherefore if it is act and its essence is act, it will be considered one and the same as the act. But since the being itself and the intelligible are one for the act, all things will be one simultaneously: intellect, intelligence, intelligible. If therefore its intelligence is the intelligible itself, and it itself is the intelligible itself, indeed it will understand itself. For it will understand through intelligence itself, that which it itself is, and it will understand the intelligible, D that which it itself is similarly. Therefore, it will understand itself completely from both sides, both insofar as it itself is intelligence, and insofar as it itself is again intelligible, which indeed it understands through this intelligence which it itself is.

*The intellect itself, since it remains in itself, and is inclined neither by action nor by affection towards other things, rightly acts concerning itself by understanding itself. But the soul, since it is affected contrarily, is disposed contrarily for knowing. Chapter VI.*

*In the whole order of cognition, sense holds the lowest rank, but intellect the highest. Therefore, since sense holds a straight line in knowing, merely touching other things, the intellect rightly acts entirely in a circular manner, contemplating itself and its own things deeply: but reason is very much oblique. The forms of things which are in the mind, are entirely essential. But those which are impressed from there upon reason from eternity, are quasi-essential: but those which daily arise in reason from the mind, are still less essential: finally, those which overflow into reason from imagination, are least essential. Therefore, the soul finally knows itself, when it adapts lower forms to higher forms.*

Therefore, reason has demonstrated that there must be something which properly and principally understands itself, but that which is in the soul understands itself in one way, and that which is in the mind understands itself in another and more principal way. The soul indeed knows itself as being of another: but the mind knows itself as what it is, and what kind it is, and what it is, and this indeed by its very nature, as you may see, turned in on itself. For seeing beings, it sees itself: and seeing is in act, and it itself is act. For intellect and intelligence are the same, and it B contemplates the whole with its whole self, it does not distinguish part by part. Has reason therefore demonstrated such a thing, as would have a credulous action? Indeed, it thus has necessity, but it does not have credulity derived from persuasion. For necessity indeed is in the mind, but persuasion is found in the soul. We seek indeed, as it seems, rather to obtain persuasion, than to perceive truth with a pure mind. But as long as we existed in the supernal region, in the very nature of the mind, we sufficiently had ourselves from there, and content with that state, we then understood,

This, I say, it is fitting to know, that it also knows whatever it sees, and knows what it says. And if it were that which it says, it would certainly thus know itself. But since they are present, or at least it comes to it from above, from where it itself depends, it is fitting, C of course, for this [soul] also, since it is a certain reason of itself, and receives kindred things, that by adapting these to the impressions within itself, it may finally perceive itself. Let it therefore transfer the image to the true Intellect, which is indeed the same as those things which are truly understood, and are truly and primarily existent: since it is clear that it cannot be that such an intellect exists outside itself. Therefore, if it is in itself and with itself, and that very thing which it is, entirely exists as intellect. For the Mind can never be D mindless, it is deservedly necessary that knowledge of itself be in it: especially since it remains in itself, and its work and essence is nothing other than to be solely intellect. For the intellect here is not engaged in an action by which, looking outwards from its function and distracted from itself by those things, it would have a knowledge proper to external things. Nor indeed is it necessary, if perchance it is constituted in action, to perceive itself: but for that to which no action E impends, nor indeed is there any affection in the pure mind, with every impediment entirely absent, a conversion entirely directed to itself not only shows its self-knowledge to be probable, but also necessary. Otherwise, what would its life be, when it is entirely free from action, and wholly placed in the mind?

*Since the Intellect does not turn itself to lower things, and is a form entirely in act, and therefore cannot be free from action, it deservedly*
*always acts about itself and God. Chapter VII.*

A cognizing, by this very reason it will know itself: for it is itself one of the things that are given, indeed it exists as all the things that are given. If therefore it knows Him, perceiving also His powers, it will also recognize itself as having been made from Him, and receiving from Him what He can do: but if it cannot clearly perceive Him, because perhaps that which is said to see, is itself that which is seen, by this very reason there will remain for it the vision and knowledge of itself: since to see this very thing is, namely, to exist as that which is seen.
B For what else shall we attribute to this? By Jove, rest. But the rest of the mind is not an alienation from the mind, indeed the rest of the mind is its own action, free from others on all sides: inasmuch as for all other things, to which rest and freedom from others is given, there remains their own action: especially for those whose being itself is not in some potentiality, but in act. Where therefore being is act, and nothing remains to which such an act might be directed, it certainly
C rests upon itself. Therefore, understanding itself, it thus certainly dwells with itself, and directs its action to itself. And if anything else depends on it, it depends because it tends towards itself, and rests in itself. For it must first consist in itself, then moreover act upon another, or something similar proceed from it: just as it is fitting for fire, that it first be fire in itself and have the action of fire, and only then can it impress its trace upon another.
D Now indeed the intellect is an act in itself: but the soul, insofar as it tends towards the intellect, as it were, dwells within: but insofar as it departs from the mind, it extends to external things. Therefore it emerges similar to that from which it came: from elsewhere again, although it may proceed somewhat dissimilarly, nevertheless even there it seems to retain a certain similarity, whether it acts or makes: namely, even while it acts, it contemplates in the meantime: and when it makes, then it produces species, like certain intelligences drawn in a long order from the first intelligences: so that all
E traces of intelligence and intellect are according to the first exemplar, proceeding in degrees, and imitating it according to their powers, the nearer ones more so, but the last ones presenting a certain faint image.

*Since the soul extends itself outwards through vegetation, sense, and imagination, but only through certain intellectual sparks does it become capable of reflecting upon itself, it is clear that the intellect itself is light perpetually reflected upon itself by itself. Chapter VIII.*

If you lightly press the corner of your eye with a finger, the inner light will immediately flash forth to itself: It would do this much more easily and abundantly, if you had as much light in your eye as animals that see at night. The intellect itself relates to itself similarly. Forms in matter are indeed so united with matter, that one work produces one action; much more so the seminal reasons of forms in nature: much more still are the intelligible reasons in the intellect united to the intellect: just as rays to light, through which the intellect and soul perceive sensibles more clearly than through sense. Now indeed both Avicenna, and Henry the Great, teacher of Scotus, Platonists by nature, believe that intellectual forms are present in the intellect or innate to its soul, or acquired by it, not so much in the manner of characters, as of a certain natural habit: by which habit the mind easily turns itself to this or that.

A It is clear again that if anyone wishes to know what especially that perfect and all-encompassing intellect is, and which first comprehends itself, it is necessary first to bring the soul back into the mind, or at least to yield its action to the mind—the action, I say, busying itself around those things of which it retains memory within itself. *If, with the motions of the lower faculties separated from the soul, you take its rational faculty itself, shining with all intellectual notions under the intellect, suddenly in this, as if in an image, you will contemplate the intellect as the sun in a full moon.*
Chapter IX.
*Moreover, the rational soul is also naturally an image of the mind, existing as light proximate to the inherent light of the sun, depending solely on the intellect. Timaeus names five worlds, and Plutarch introduces them. World signifies an all-formed ornament. Therefore, the lowest world is that which is seen in matter; far superior, that which thrives in nature; somewhat more sublime, that which is in the imagination, sometimes most full of forms; much more excellent, that which is in reason, as if a rival mirror of the intellect; the exalted one which shines in the mind. In the succeeding world, you will gradually behold the preceding one as if in a mirror, and conversely, from the higher, you will contemplate the lower as if from a watchtower.*

Therefore, the soul, as it seems, and that which is most divine in the soul, ought to consider what the intellect is about to know. Perhaps indeed you will attain it also by this condition: if first you separate the body from man, especially from yourself: Then the soul forming it

faltem let it assume the opinion-forming faculty, and from there ascend to higher things. But if it cannot even do that, let it at least take sense as bringing certain broader forms into itself: sense, I say, even in itself along with those things it is capable of, and already endowed with forms. Then, if anyone wishes to descend to inner things, let him turn his path to the generative power, and finally arrive at those things which it generates: but conversely, from here let him ascend from the ultimate forms back to the ultimate, nay, indeed, approaching the primary ones.

*In the first intellect are the forms of all things: then, according to essence, they are the same, but distinct by formal reason. Chapter X.*

*Since the forms of things are primary there, they are therefore perfect, and in a perfect manner. Therefore, they exist essentially: yet they differ from the intellect by a certain reason. For that (intellect) is one intellect: but these forms are many. Therefore, they differ among themselves by formal reason: especially since the intellect only inspects them: and by inspecting, it understands distinctly, and makes all things even more different from each other, that is, in reality, place, and time. Intelligence, like vision, is a kind of striving and apprehension and distinction: which three are also proper to light and fire. Therefore, the intellect, insofar as it turns back upon itself by understanding, exercises these three towards itself, and declares itself to be altogether manifold: otherwise, if there is absolutely no difference in it, or could be, there will be nothing there to strive for and towards: nor any need for application or striving. There will be nothing to apprehend, or to be apprehended, nor any need for apprehension, or any quasi-union of parts, or self-embrace: there will be no place for distinction. Thus far the Platonists. Christians, however, prove that the first intellect does not have such a multitude of forms, because by understanding all things through one form of itself and by one act, insofar as it refers itself as variously participable to all things, it disposes the multitude not in itself, but externally.*

Let this much be said about these matters. But if forms are not only made in the mind (otherwise these of ours would not be ultimate, but there [in the Intellect] are the primary forms, that is, the efficient ones, and therefore primary), then it is certainly necessary that both the forms made there and the maker exist equally, and both be one: otherwise, that intellect will again need something else. What then? Will not that which is superior again be in need? Certainly not: for that very thing which is in need, is the intellect. But does that superior [being] see itself? By no means. For it does not need vision. But this will be discussed in what follows. For the present, however, let us again discuss the same matter. For what is now being discussed is not to be made light of. Therefore, it must again be affirmed that this intellect needs to see itself, nay, indeed, it constantly possesses this very thing. Therefore, first, from this it has that it is manifold: then that it is of another: then necessarily that it is capable of seeing, of that seeing, I say, of which it is also said to be: moreover, that its very essence is vision. For if it is something else, vision must exist: but if it is not something else, vision will be empty. Therefore, there must be more than one thing there, so that there may be vision, and that vision itself may encounter the visible: and that which is seen by itself must be a certain multitude, and not entirely one. For that which is absolutely one has nothing to operate upon, but existing alone and singular, it rests entirely. For in what way does it operate, if one thing results and another? Indeed, if there is not one thing and another there, what will it do? And to what will it proceed? Therefore, whatever acts, must either act concerning something else, or itself be manifold: if indeed it is to act within itself. But if it does not proceed into another, it will rest. And when it rests entirely, it will understand nothing at all. Therefore, it is necessary that the intelligent being, while it understands, is entirely engaged in at least two things: and either one of the two is external, or both are in the same, and intellection always moves in a certain (so to speak) otherness, and again in a certain identity. Likewise

A Likewise, what are properly and especially understood are related to the mind as being both the same and different at the same time. And again, each of the things understood brings with it a certain identity and otherness at the same time; otherwise, what will it understand, unless it contains one thing in itself and another? For if it applies itself to something entirely one and impartible, it will be devoid of dis- B course and reason. For what will it be able to say or ponder about this very thing? It is therefore necessary for the intelligent being to receive one thing and another; and for that which is understood, as if distinguished by intelligence itself, to be diverse within itself; otherwise, there will be no intelligence of it, but only a touch and a kind of impact D such that it can neither be spoken nor speak, and without intellect (so to speak) it pre-understands; since intellect is not yet born, and that which reaches there does not yet understand. But the intelligent being must not remain simple itself, especially when it entirely understands itself. For it divides itself, even if someone should say that intelligence is silence. Moreover, that which is entirely simple does not need varied care by which it apprehends itself. E For what will it apprehend, if it should ever understand itself? For before it uses its mind to understand itself, that which it is exists entirely within itself. Finally, knowledge itself seems to be a certain desire, and a kind of discovery accompanying inquiry. Therefore, that which has no difference within itself regarding itself, rests everywhere, and investigates nothing about itself; but that which unfolds and develops itself, is certainly multiplex in itself.

Cum in intellectu primo sit numerus multorum absolutè inter se differentium, necesse est super hunc esse prin- cipium aliud simpliciter vnum, id est penitus simplicissimum. Cap. XI.

*Unless in the first essence, life, intelligence, to be, to live, to understand differ from each other in some way, these three, so diverse, will not easily hold their place in the order of things, so that to be is indeed the most common of all, but to understand the least, and to live moderately. Intellect itself is nothing other than a certain sight directed to its first light, as corporeal sight is to its own: by whatever perfection corporeal sight may be increased, it will always be inferior to light. Similarly, intellect, even when most perfect, from its light, that is, from truth and goodness itself, still seems to be secondary. Essence, as the most common of all, and therefore, after simplicity itself, proceeds first immediately from unity, and besides the very nature of essence, it presents an image of that unity, differing in some way from essence. Also, by the help of this image, it is converted to the One itself and the Good, not by an intellectual instinct first, but rather by a natural and vital one. Before this act of conversion, there was already essence and image alike; in the very act of conversion, the living appears; after this, the intelligent appears, while thus converted it receives a gift from the Good itself. And since the Good itself is above all things, relating equally to all, it does not receive from there something of all things, but equally all things, especially since it is the nearest receptacle. Therefore, from this, an all-form form comes into being, having ideal forms of things absolutely distinct from each other; whence a far greater distinction proceeds after it. In the same moment, it becomes multiform and intellect. Finally, since intellect carries with it a multitude of things absolutely different, it rightly depends on some most simple higher principle.*

To the Good itself, intelligence must not be added, which, namely, can be understood by any created intellect, however supreme. Chapter XIII.
The nature of the Good itself and of intelligence is so diverse, as we have said, that the former is indeed most common, the latter least so: the former desires nothing, the latter desires the Good. Likewise, to intelligence is opposed madness, to the Good, evil. Madness and evil are not entirely the same, therefore intelligence and the Good are not the same. Therefore, when you add intelligence to the Good itself, you seem to have judged it as another and different thing, and the Good as hitherto lacking, and as if composed. This paradox, namely that the first principle is above essence, life, and intelligence, is frequently asserted by Dionysius the Areopagite: who moreover adds that it enjoys itself in a certain more-than-intellectual way, which he calls super-intellectual. Likewise, to pre-understand by a certain ineffable reason beyond and above intellect, as if it enjoys itself by way of touch rather than vision. For intelligence is a kind of vision, and not by way of saying something about itself, but rather by way of simply being that which it is. But if by any condition, proceeding through the degrees of intelligence, the Good itself can be conceived, let it not be conceived as some intellect that needs intelligence, nor as intelligence, which is the act of intellect itself concerning the Good, but rather the Good itself towards which intelligence tends, or perhaps the light itself which intelligence seeks, in which perfected intelligence finds its end, a light indeed not in this (intelligence), but subsisting in itself. This very clarity is neither properly seeing, nor deprived of the good of vision as if blind: just as vision itself neither properly sees, nor is blind. Indeed, clarity itself, being the cause of all vision, is much more remote from the privation of sight than sight itself: nor is clarity determined to the genus of intellection. For that which is the cause of all things, above all things, is defined by none of the number of all things. Therefore, not by essence, life, intelligence, not by intellectual or intelligible clarity, but by clarity itself simply existing by itself in itself, the cause of the act of all power of clarity: it is conceived, however, according to the efficacious power of the act of powers, the producer of acts. And if the soul does not have hands and feet, yet because it does not need them, and has a generative and more eminent power of these, it is neither called maimed nor lame. By similar reasoning, neither is reason blind, even if it does not have eyes, nor is mind irrational, even if it never reasons: for it possesses in an instant what reason seeks over time. Nor is God mad, even if he does not have a mind: for he is that whole which mind strives to have, indeed, to become.

WHEREFORE it is truly ineffable. [A]
For whatever you say, you will have said something
specific. But that which is above all things and
above the most venerable mind, separated from
all things, has no other true name, nor is it any
of all things. And absolutely no name is its,
because nothing is said of it: but we, as far as
we can, try to signify something of it to ourselves.
But when we thus hesitate, saying, for example,
"thus therefore it least perceives itself, thus it
neither notices itself, thus it knows nothing at [B]
all of what it is," then indeed it is fitting to
consider that we, as often as we say such things,
are turned back to the opposites. For we do as
much as is in us

LIBER TERTIVS. 511

**A** is, that being itself is manifold, when we bring it to be known, and attribute knowledge to it: for when we attribute intelligence, we make it so that it needs intelligence; and if intelligence comes to be together with it, it will be superfluous for it to apply intelligence to itself. For intelligence seems altogether to be a certain agreement of the whole, where many things converge into one, when something understands itself, which indeed is proper and principal intelligence: but any single thing itself **B** is something, nor does it seek anything. But if intelligence extends to external things, it will be needy, nor principal intelligence. But that which is altogether simple, and truly sufficient, needs nothing: but that which is sufficient in the second place, but needy of itself, this indeed needs intelligence of itself; but that which is needy with respect to itself, by the whole itself renders itself sufficient, having obtained sufficiency from all things, dwelling with itself, and turning into itself by understanding: since indeed it itself

| A. Ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο δεῖ τι εἶναι, καὶ πᾶσαν δύναμιν, καὶ δύναμιν ἀμήχανον, καὶ ἐκ πάντων τῶν ἄλλων τοῦτο πιστοῦσθαι, ὅτι οὐδὲν τῶν ἐσχάτων ἀδυνατεῖ γεννᾶν. Νῦν δὲ λεκτέον, ὅτι ἐν τοῖς γεννωμένοις οὐκ εἰς τὰ ἄνω ἡ πρόοδος, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς τὰ κάτω, καὶ οὕτω γε εἰς πλῆθος ἀεὶ πλεῖον, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πανταχοῦ ἀρχὴ ἑκάστου. | A. But indeed it is necessary that something exists after the First, and that it is all power, and an immeasurable power, and this is to be affirmed from all other things, that nothing, not even among the lowest, is unable to generate. But now it must be said that among generated things, the procession is not upwards, but downwards, and thus always into a greater multitude, and for this reason, the principle of each thing is everywhere. |
| B. Ἀλλὰ πῶς ἔχει τοῦτο τὸ πλῆθος; Ἢ ὅτι ἓν ὄν, καὶ τοῦ

514 PLOTINI ENNEAD. V.

[Left Column - English Translation]

simpler, and remaining the same in itself, while a progression into multiplicity occurs. Wherefore, that which created the sensible world is not the sensible world, but is Intellect and the intelligible world; and therefore similarly, that which is superior to the intelligible world and its origin is neither Intellect nor the intelligible world, but simpler than Intellect, simpler than the intelligible world. For multiplicity does not come from multiplicity, but this multiplicity proceeds from non-multiplicity. For if that too were multiplicity, it would certainly not be the principle, but something else superior to it. Therefore all things must be gathered to that which is truly one, beyond all number and any simplicity, if indeed it is truly simple, and in it finally our ascent must stop. Furthermore, it must be considered by what reason that which is made from it is already a manifold and complete reason, while that (the First) is not reason. But if it is not reason, by what condition can reason come from non-reason? And in what way can the good-like proceed from the Good, or having what of it, be called good-like? Is it therefore considered to have a certain good-form because it has a certain state that is in accordance with the same things, and similarly disposed? But what do these things contribute to the Good? Seeing that we are accustomed to demand such a state that is in accordance with the same things and similarly disposed only when good things are present; and we first desire that from which one should never depart, because it is good; but if it is not good, it is better to depart from it. Is it therefore to be desired by us as good, namely, to live always in the same way, remaining spontaneously in the Good itself? If therefore this is especially to be desired by the mind, namely, to live thus, then it certainly requires nothing further, and it is certainly clear that that state, always similarly disposed, is sought for this reason, because the present things suffice. But with all things now present to this (mind), to live is to be desired as the highest good; I say, present to it in such a way that they are not different from it. If therefore all life is present to this (mind)—life, I say, vigorous and clear—now all soul and universal mind are perfect in this, and nothing is lacking to it, neither life nor intelligence. It is therefore self-sufficient, and desires nothing further. But if it demands nothing, it already possesses in itself that which, if it were not, it would certainly seek. Therefore it has the good in itself, the good, I say, either such as we have called life and mind, or something else pertaining to these. But if this is the Good itself, then certainly nothing will be superior to these; but if the Good itself is superior to these, then certainly the good for this (mind) will be life tending towards that (Good), and entirely leaning upon it, and possessing substance from it, and entirely directing itself towards it; for that is its principle. It is necessary therefore that that (Good) be more excellent than life and mind; for only thus will life, vigorous in mind, turn towards it, inasmuch as it is a certain imitation of that which exists in the Good, and lives and follows according to it. And the intelligence of this (mind) will turn as a certain imitation of that which exists in the Good, whatever that itself may ultimately be.

...self-sufficient and most simple. Nor is being simply desired, but well-being, nor to live in any way whatsoever, but well: nor to understand in any way, but well, and good things, and in such a way that it may be profitable to you: nor do we simply desire truth: for we do not desire a true fever, but a true good. Therefore, the Good itself is the end and the beginning of all good things. The end of our life is to see the Good itself through itself: but since this is most stable and most simple, we do not reach it by the discourse of reason, nor by the action of the intellect composing or discerning, but by a certain sudden and simple intuition. Moreover, the sign of this fruition for us is, when, beyond the usual and by no customary contrivance of the mind, a light suddenly flows into us, that is, a joyful clarity, which is a certain splendor of clarity subsisting in itself, which is God himself. Moreover, it flows in when, dedicated to it by its grace, we remove all things, that is, inclinations concerning all things from appetite, images from imagination, discourses from reason, intellectual species, and compositions, and discretions from the intellect. Of these things, both Plato and we have spoken enough in Plato's great epistle.

How that which is after the First comes from the First, and concerning the One.

*Things in the universe, diverse among themselves, would not have harmony, order, and union with each other, unless all proceeded from the One. Chapter I.*

*Which indeed, finally, is not this or that one, but simply the One itself. Which again, on account of its supreme simplicity, has the characteristic of being the First, most sufficient, most powerful. And it is itself the power of all things, through which other things are potent for action, and the more potent they are, the more they do. Whence it appears that this first power itself makes all things, has the widest dominion over all things everywhere, and is most present to all things.*

For that certain things are closest to it, necessity itself demonstrates: then indeed it is necessary that what generates the rest, be the most excellent of the subsequent things. Moreover, that which is generated most closely from it, and holds the second place, is more excellent than the others.

*Intellect depends on the intelligible almost, just as sight depends on the visible, therefore it is not the first. Chapter I.*

*Here it touches upon a twofold intelligible: one conjoined with the intellect, the other superior. Consider in the eye of an animal seeing by itself day and night, the very lucid substance of the eye, and the power of seeing depending on it, which is indeed formless by itself, but is formed by the lucid substance conjoined to it. Think of such a first intellect, even when it contemplates itself, just as if a very lucid eye, pressed in some way by a finger, were to look at itself. Now indeed in the first intellect its own substantial unity is its own intelligible, from which the power of understanding, turned towards it, depends and is formed from it. Such a power, together with its conversion, is an indefinite duality: but defined by its intelligible, it becomes intellect in act and an all-form idea. From this also it is converted through its unity to the simply one itself: which is also named the more excellent intelligible, which Plotinus here does not entirely deprive of cognition, but only of intellectual cognition.*

[Greek subtitle]
That the intelligibles are not outside the intellect and concerning the Good.

That the intelligibles are not outside the intellect: likewise concerning the Good itself.

*Just as sense, which is the lowest form of knowledge, perceives only external things: so intellect, which is the highest form of knowledge, inspects only internal things. Chapter I.*

[Decorative initial S]Just as therefore in sense there are only images of things which are sensed, so in the intellect are the things themselves which it understands: otherwise, if it were to receive images from the intelligible things, it would neither adequately know the things themselves by means of knowledge formed through images, which are far inferior to the things themselves, nor would it be certain to have a sincere judgment about the things: inasmuch as images, transferred into the nature of the recipient, do not present the pure nature of the object. Placed above discursive reason, the intellect, acting stably, has present objects at its disposal. Therefore, it possesses within not only certain principles of arts and things, but also, within these principles, whatever necessarily follows from them. Nor should you think that the intelligibles themselves are propositions, and as it were certain utterances, but rather reasons and essential forms: nor that they are certain spectacles disjoined from each other, but forms within one certain immaterial form: just as all sensible forms are in unformed matter; finally, that intelligible forms are much more united with the intellect than sensible forms with matter: and celestial forms with the substance of heaven. But that the forms of things are naturally infused into our souls, we discuss more broadly in Theology.

A This indeed is justice, but that rather is something else. Finally, the strongest point of all is this: namely, if anyone were to admit outright that these things are external, and that the mind [Marginal note (Greek: τὸν νοῦν): the mind] contemplates them as such, it necessarily follows that the mind does not possess the truth of these things, but is deceived and lies in contemplating each one. For truly the things will be external: it will therefore look at them, and will not possess them themselves, but will possess images of them in such knowledge. Since therefore it does not possess truth [Marginal note (Greek: αὐτῷ): to it/itself], but holds certain images of truth within itself, it will undoubtedly not accumulate truths, but rather will bring back falsehoods. If therefore it knows that it possesses only falsehoods, it will undoubtedly confess itself to be devoid of truth: but if it is ignorant of this too, and though not a participant in truth, yet believes itself to be master of truth, it will then be doubly deceived by falsehood, and will be very far from truth: for this reason (as I believe) truth is not [Marginal note (Greek: ἔνεστιν): is in] in the senses, but opinion: because the condition of sense is concerned with receiving, whence 'opinion' (doxa in Greek) took its name from 'receiving': and therefore it receives something other than itself, since that from which it possesses what it has received is also something other. If therefore truth is not in the mind, such a mind [Marginal note (Greek: μὲν ὁ): indeed the] will neither be truth, nor truly a mind, nor altogether a mind: indeed, truth will not reside anywhere else either.

The objects of the intellect are not images of things or certain imaginings, but truly existing things: since even the objects of sense are certain things. Chapter II.

*For as much as the intellect is more excellent and truer than sense, by so much are the objects of the intellect more excellent and truer than the objects of sense, as Timaeus says. Moreover, intelligibles are in the very essence of the intellect, since it does not seek by arguing, nor does it wander outside, but turns inward and stably contemplates as if possessing: and it penetrates and defines the very substance of each thing. But truly, through images of things, it could only infer qualities and external aspects.*

A THEREFORE it is not fitting to seek intelligibles outside the intellect, nor to admit that figures of things are inherent in the mind, nor to deprive the mind of truth, by conceding that the mind itself is ignorant of intelligibles, and that the intelligibles themselves (which are offered) do not exist in the order of things, and thus we abolish the mind itself. But it is necessary to attribute everything to the true mind, if indeed it is necessary to introduce knowledge and truth, and to preserve beings themselves, and that knowledge by which each thing is known for what it is, and not to acquiesce in that knowledge which merely apprehends what each thing is like, when namely we have only a semblance and trace of the thing to be known, and do not hold it itself, nor dwell with it, nor conspire with it into one. For [Marginal note (Greek: δὴ): indeed] by that reasoning the mind will know, and will truly know, nor will anything escape it, nor will it ever forget, nor will it wander about everywhere searching: but truth will be in it, and the seat of things, and it will live and understand. All these things indeed must be present in the most blessed nature, otherwise where will anything honorable and venerable be? Then truly by this reasoning it will neither need demonstration, nor faith to be persuaded thus. For the intellect itself is that which is entirely thus: it is entirely manifest to itself: and if anything before it is similarly discovered, that it is from that: likewise if anything is after that,

that it itself is this very thing, and no one is more worthy of trust to it than itself, and indeed it has explored that this truly exists there. Who then can refute it? And from where will one bring a refutation? Indeed, any argument that is brought forward will revolve back to the same point as the previous arguer. *Just as the innermost light of the sun pours forth light around itself, filled with innumerable rays and powers, so the principle of all things generates an all-form intellect within itself, this [intellect generates] a similarly all-form soul.          Chapter III.*

*The ancients named that [first principle] Heaven, this [intellect] indeed Saturn, and finally this [soul] Jupiter. All intellectual souls can sometimes ascend through their intellect to the divine intellect. They can and also ought, both through their own unity and also through the divine intellect, sometimes progress to the principle of all things.*

THEREFORE, this one nature of intellect is all beings: it is also truth: it is also a great God, indeed, not some God, but all [God]: [Marginal note: these things (ταῦτα)] nor does it unworthily consider itself to be all these things. Therefore, this nature is God: a second God, I say, presenting itself to those who seek, before they behold that higher one: namely, that higher one sits more eminently on this splendid throne of his, depending on him. For it was fitting that he should not encounter us in some inanimate chariot, nor again immediately in a soul walking, but that an inestimable beauty should wonderfully shine forth before his sight, just as before the aspect of a great king. For thus it is arranged by nature, that to those progressing towards him, lesser things first occur, and then greater and more excellent things gradually offer themselves to those proceeding further, and those who stand around the king are more royal, and then the rest in a similar order. But after all these things, that great king suddenly shines forth: and the rest indeed reverently worship the king himself, as many, that is, as have not retreated from there before having progressed all the way to the ultimate, just as those are accustomed to whom the things shining forth before the king are thought to be sufficient. Therefore, another king rules there, and those who subsequently appear before him are certainly different from him. Nevertheless, that supreme king does not rule as over strangers, but has a most just and natural dominion, and he has a true kingdom: since he himself is the king of truth, and by his very nature is the master of all his offspring together, and of the divine assembly: indeed, king of the king and of kings, and also called father of the gods by a more just name. Indeed, Jupiter also imitated him in this respect, that he did not entirely rest in the contemplation of his father, but proceeded beyond to his grandfather, as if to his act into the very (so to speak) subsistence of essence.

*Since by speaking of species or essence, you conceive and define something with the intellect, know that this is not the true principle: for that cannot be comprehended in any way. Chapter VI.*

*The One itself or Unity is a name invented by the Pythagoreans, by which they might, to the best of their ability, designate the simplicity and eminence of the principle of things, indeed denying all multitude, composition, and every determination whatsoever from it, affirming nothing in the interim, which they also confirmed by the name of Apollo. Just as the sensible genus has a proportion with sense, so the intelligible with intellect. Therefore, the principle of things, not having a proportion with intellect, transcends the intelligible genus: therefore, it is superior to being.*

THEREFORE, seeing in act occurs in two ways, just as it happens with the eye. Indeed, one spectacle for the eye is the species of the thing itself to be perceived: but the other is that through which it sees the species of that thing: which itself is also sensible to it, certainly different from the species itself: but the cause by which the species itself is perceived, and existing in the species, and immediately seen with it: for which reason it is not seen very clearly then, since the eye directs itself more intently towards the illuminated object. But when there is nothing else besides it, it will contemplate it with a sudden and whole intuition all at once, although even then it will perceive it adhering to another: but if it alone is joined to absolutely nothing, the sense will not be able to receive it: since the light of the sun, vigorous in the sun itself, would perhaps escape the sense, unless the more solid mass of the sun itself were joined. But if someone says that the whole sun is light, someone might perhaps accept that as a declaration of what is said: for light will be in no other species of things that are seen, and perhaps only visible and luminous, for other visible things are not only light.

In a similar way, the mind's gaze indeed sees, through another light, things illuminated by that first nature, and in them it truly sees that light: yet, by turning itself more intently towards the nature of the illuminated things, it perceives less of the light itself in the meantime. But if it sometimes dismisses the things seen, and intently regards that light through which it sees, it will then perceive the light itself and the principle of light. Since the mind ought not to contemplate such light as something external, let us return again to that eye, which itself also sometimes sees not an external light, nor an alien one, but rather contemplates an internal light before an external one: some proper and brighter light shining through in a certain inviolate and pure seat, or sees a certain ray projecting itself from itself before it at night in the darkness: or when, wishing to see nothing else, it restrains itself with the covering of its eyelids, and meanwhile produces light from itself. Or when someone pressing the corners of the eyelids, inspects the light that was hidden within, then indeed by not seeing it sees, and then most of all it sees: for it sees light: but the other things it had seen before were indeed luminous, but were not light. Thus, therefore, the mind, separating itself from other things and restraining itself inwards, seeing nothing, immediately perceives light, not one thing in another, but itself alone, pure, shining forth repeatedly from itself.

**A** This happens in such a way that it occasions doubt as to whence this light shines forth: whether from something external, or rather from something internal; and when it has departed, it happens that one says, "this was intimate," and again, "not intimate." **B** just as the eye awaits the rising of the sun, which the sun itself, rising from the horizon and, as the poets say, from the Ocean, presents itself to be seen. **C** standing firm and as if filled with vigor, it first looks at itself, now made more beautiful, and now shining, since it is now close to the highest. **D** because, truly, He remains in nothing, and if the intellect could also be nowhere—not merely in a place, I say, for it itself is not in a place, but entirely nowhere—it would undoubtedly always behold Him; even if not beholding, it would attain Him, but by abiding in Him; nor indeed as two separate entities. But now, since it is intellect, it sees when it sees, precisely because intellect is not in Him. And truly, it is wonderful how He is present without approaching, and in what manner
**E** He exists, being nowhere, and for that very reason, is everywhere in the meantime. Indeed, it happens that one marvels at this from its very condition, but to one who has known the thing itself, it would rather be a cause for wonder if the opposite were ever said; nay, it cannot be otherwise, so much so that one would marvel more intensely: thus indeed it is.

*Since all things depend on God, but He on none: therefore all things are in Him, but He is in none: He contains all things, He is not contained. Chapter IX.*

*Because He is contained by none, He is nowhere: but because He contains all things, He is present to all. Thus the body of the world is in the soul of the world, this in the mind, this in the Good, and not vice versa. Just as therefore the soul, as if free, is entirely present simultaneously to each part of the body, so the Good, absolute from all limits, is present to all. Indeed, whatever does not depend for its existence on a certain subject, or place, nor on a certain nature, is everywhere and nowhere, just like the soul, and the mind, and God.*

**A** Thus, therefore, nature is arranged, that ultimate things are always in penultimate ones: and again, prior things similarly in prior ones, and always one thing in another, until one arrives at the highest. The highest principle, however, as that to which nothing further presides, cannot be in another. But since it itself is not in another, while other things are inherent in superiors, it clearly embraces all remaining things. Embracing them, it is neither dissipated into them, and it has entirely without being had: and indeed, since it has, and is not had, there is nowhere that it itself is not: for if it were not present, it would not have: and again, if it is not had, it is certainly not present.

**B** Therefore, it is present, and it is not present: namely, from the fact that it is not comprehended, it is by no means present: but from the fact that it is free from everything, it is nowhere prevented from being present: for if it were confined, it would certainly be defined by another, and the things that follow would be left devoid of it: and God Himself would reign only up to this point, and nothing more would be in Him, nor would He exist in Himself, but He Himself would now serve others.

**C** Whatever, therefore, are in something, are properly there, belonging to its own jurisdiction. But whatever are not properly somewhere, are such that there is nowhere where they are not. For if something is not here, another place certainly contains it, and it is in some other as in a place, wherefore it is false that it is nowhere. If, therefore, it is true that it is nowhere, and false that it is somewhere, lest perhaps it be in another, then it is absent from nowhere.

**D** But if it is absent from none, certainly existing nowhere, it will be everywhere in itself: for not one part of it will be here, and another there, nor yet the whole only there, wherefore it will be everywhere whole: since it has no single "somewhere" for itself, nor again does it not have it; rather, it has in such a way that it is truly had (possessed) more. Come now, consider this world: here indeed, if there is no other world, *the principle* is superior to *it* (the world), *and the principle* is not in the world, nor again in a place. For what place existed before the world? The parts of the world are reduced to it, and located in it.

**E** But the soul is not in the world, but the world in the soul: for the body is not the place of the soul, but the soul is in the mind, and the body in the soul. Finally, the Mind exists in another, which indeed does not depend on another, in which it is therefore compelled to rest: therefore, it properly rests in nothing, and for this reason it is said to be nowhere. Where then are other things? Undoubtedly they are in it. Therefore, it is neither absent from others, nor again is it in them, nor is there anything that has it, yet it contains all things. Wherefore, and for this reason, it is considered the good of all: because all things are through it, and are referred to it. I say, one thing is referred in one way, another in another, and therefore some things are better than others, because some are more "to it" than others.
