A BUT truly, I beg you, do not look at God through other things, otherwise know that you will find not God, but His trace: but consider with yourself what this most powerful thing is, which it is right to perceive as existing only in itself, pure, mixed with nothing: where certainly all things indeed participate in it, yet nothing possesses it: truly nothing else can be such, and undoubtedly it is necessary for such a thing to exist. Who then can apprehend all of its power at once? For if anyone apprehends all of it at once, how will he be considered to differ from it? Does he then receive it in part? But indeed, looking at it, you will contemplate it with a certain whole, simultaneous, and unique stroke, yet you will not report the whole to yourself, otherwise you will be an understanding intellect, if you have achieved anything at all: but God will immediately flee from you: indeed, rather, you will flee from God. Moreover, when you look, behold the whole: and when you first understand this, whatever you have preserved of it in memory, remember that it is the good itself. For it is the cause of wise and intellectual life: since it is the very power from which life and intellect are born, indeed it is the author of essence and being, because it is the one itself. For it is simple, and it is the first, because it is the principle. From it indeed all things flow: from it the first motion arises, yet it is not in it: from it also comes rest, because it itself needs nothing: for it neither moves nor rests, since it has nothing in which to rest, or in which to revolve. For around what, or to what especially, or in what particularly will it either move or rest? For it is itself the first. But neither can it be defined, otherwise by whom could it be defined? Nor again is it infinite in the way an immense mass is usually conceived. Then indeed, where should it proceed? As if it were said to proceed in order to bring back something from there, it who needs nothing at all. But this power itself has infinity: for it is not otherwise infinite, nor does it ever behave otherwise, nor will it ever fail: since whatever does not fail, properly has this very thing from it.

The First Principle, on account of its inestimable simplicity and eminence by which it is called one, is neither externally nor internally finite. Cap. XI.

It neither rests, nor moves, nor has figure, nor form: it is infinite in power, not in quantity. Those are mistaken who think that bodies, because of quantity, especially exist, and exist as the greatest: for because of the same [reason], it is permissible to say infinitely that neither this part nor that part is the whole itself: and also to say infinitely that this part in this [body] is small, and that [part] is small: therefore a body is infinitely not itself, and is infinitely small. Finally, we distrust the truth of separated things, due to excessive commerce with matter: souls indeed dream in this body, outside they are vigilant.

A AND YET this infinite is called infinite from the fact that it is not more than one, nor has anything to which any of its own might be terminated. Nor again does it have figure, because it has neither parts nor form. Therefore, do not seek it with mortal eyes, that is to say, entirely such as reason approves. A But as for the beautiful, not everyone thinks they will be sufficiently satisfied. B For all strive to acquire especially for themselves that which is first of all. What shall we say to these things? That souls contend with the beautiful as if with a certain desire for victory? As if it itself were made from elsewhere, just as they are made from elsewhere. As if someone inferior to the king should strive to make another, who immediately follows the king, equal in dignities: inasmuch as he depends on the same one as that other, ignorant, of course, that he too depends on the king, and that the other precedes him.
C But the cause of the error is this, that both are principles of the same thing, and one is prior to both. It is moreover established that the good itself by no means needs the beautiful, but the beautiful needs the good. Therefore, the good itself is gentle, mild, calm, delicate, and usually occurs as each desires. But the beautiful either renders the soul dull, or excites it and mixes pleasure with pain. Finally, it is accustomed to often turn unwary souls away from the good, just as a lover often separates the beloved from the father.
D For the beautiful is younger, but the good is older, not indeed in time, but in truth, which indeed also has prior power. For it has all power: but what is after it does not possess all, but only so much as is after it and from it. Therefore, that father is also the master of this power, in no way needing those things which are generated by him, but sending forth everything and the whole that is generated: because it absolutely needs this under no condition, but exists absolutely the same as it was even before it generated this from itself: and indeed it would make no difference to it if this had not been generated: since, even if something else could have been generated from it in addition, it would not have begrudged it also the gift of being.
E But now nothing further can be made: for nothing remains that has not already been procreated, since all things have now been made. But God himself does not exist as all things, for thus he would need all things: but transcending all things, he was able to establish all things, and permit all things to themselves, he himself indeed excelling above all things.

All beings, more or less good among themselves, terminate in some supremely good being; this finally resolves into the good itself, that is, goodness itself simply, superior to being. Cap. XIII.

When you name this itself, do not think of two things, that is, a certain thing together with goodness: otherwise the principle of things will be composite, and it will not be absolute goodness, but a certain goodness, and as if a participant of the good: it will finally be referred to a higher good, not good beyond participation. Of essence, life, mind, evil can sometimes be predicated, or at least not good, or certainly more or less good. But such things cannot be predicated of goodness itself simply. The nature therefore of goodness itself is both other and simpler, and therefore prior to the nature of essence, life, mind. Do not therefore imagine God first to be contained in the common order of beings under the common notion of being, and moreover to have his own goodness, otherwise he will be composite, and good not formally, but by a certain participation of a higher and simpler good. Finally, the good itself, which is desired by all essences, lives, minds, and perfects and effects them, is not to be said to properly have essence, life, mind, just as we do not say the sun properly has in itself those things of which it is the cause in the elements, that is, heat of that kind and growth and generation, and similar forms and figures.

532 PLOTINUS ENNEAD. V.

A When indeed God is good itself, not merely good, it is necessary for it to have absolutely nothing in itself, since it does not even have good. For if it has anything, it will either have good, or not good: but neither in that which is properly, principally, primarily good, can there be non-good, nor does good itself have good. Therefore, if it has neither non-good nor good, it has absolutely nothing: finally, therefore, if other things are either good, but not good itself, or perhaps not good, and it has neither of these, certainly having nothing by having nothing, it is good itself.

B If therefore anyone adds anything to this, whether essence, or mind, or beauty, by that very addition, he subtracts from it that which is good itself, taking away all things, and affirming nothing about it, nor lying in any way as if something were with it, rightly allows only what is, to be said: testifying nothing about it of those things which are not present.

C In this matter, indeed, many are accustomed to err, who, when they do not know how to praise someone, detract from the glory of those praised, by adding to them things which are inferior to their dignity, being ignorant, of course, of how to apply true praises to the praised persons. Wherefore we also, first of all, must be careful not to add anything posterior or lesser, and to thoroughly observe that God, excelling all these things, is the cause of them, yet He Himself does not exist as these things.

D Now, indeed, the nature of the good is not to be either all things, or something of all things. Certainly, if it is something of all things, it will be under one and the same [category] together with all things. But if it is under the same [category] together with the others, it will certainly differ from others by some proper distinction and by some addition. It will therefore be two now, not one, of which one part is non-good, namely that which is common to it with the rest: the other part, however, is good. It will therefore be mixed from good and non-good at the same time,

E and therefore it will be neither purely nor primarily good. But that will be primarily good, of which this, being a participant beyond its common condition, has now become good. This, therefore, will be good by some participation: but that of which this is a participant, is none of all things: wherefore none of all things is good itself. But if this good is in it, for it is the difference by which this composite is good, it is necessary for this to depend on another, which indeed is entirely simple and only

F good. This, therefore, as if manifold, depends on that which is merely good. Wherefore that which exists primarily, and is good itself, is established to be above all beings, and good alone, having nothing in itself, but entirely unmixed with anything, excelling all things, and being the cause of all things. For beauty does not come from evil, nor are beings from evil, nor again from anything that is indifferent: for the maker is better than the made. For it is more perfect.

**BOOK VI.**

**On not understanding that which is beyond being, and what is primary intellection, and what is secondary.**

**That that which is above being does not understand: and what is primarily understanding, and what is secondarily understanding.**

*Intellect is both united with the intelligible thing and distinct from it. Chapter I.*

If it knows external things by looking outwards, there is a manifest diversity between the intellect and the intelligible, and the intellect assumes a foreign form; meanwhile, however, through this form, the intellect is united with the intelligible. But if it understands itself, the essence of the intelligent and the intelligible is indeed the same. Yet, there is an opposing relation between the former and the latter; therefore, they are formally distinct. Add to this that the nature of the intelligible itself is superior to the nature of the intelligent, just as the nature of light, or of the transparent, or of purer and less pure light. For the relation of the intellect to the intelligible, when it understands itself, is like that of a certain nascent light striving to receive absolute light, to which it may be equated as far as its powers allow.

the purer part of the same: then let him make the seeing light equal to the light seen, since he no longer has any difference by which to separate them, he will assert these two to be one, which indeed is intelligent precisely because it exists as two; but it is now seeing precisely because it is now one: he will therefore thus apprehend the intellect and the intelligible. Wherefore we indeed, by our reason, have made one out of two; but that (the intellect) on the contrary exists as two from one, because it understands by making itself two; nay, rather, because it understands by existing as two: likewise, because it is one, it can understand.

**The Intellect understanding itself has multiplicity within itself. Chapter II.**

Every intellect is in some way intelligible, but not every intelligible is necessarily an intellect. The concept of the intelligible, therefore, is different, more common, and prior to the concept of the intellect. The intellect, therefore, understanding itself, has diverse aspects within itself. Furthermore, in the very order of beings, essence is also prior in time to intelligence; deservedly, therefore, in the first being, it is at least prior in origin. Essence itself, therefore, in the first sign of origin, according to itself, is not yet actually intelligent, nor actually intelligible, unless a faculty of understanding arises in it, which faculty indeed is not actually intelligent unless it is coupled with the intelligible. Conclude, if the very essence of being does not need intelligence for its perfection of existence (for it precedes intelligence), much less does that which is superior to being. But that which is superior is that in which there is no prior and posterior: nor an absolute duality of principles, as we find in being and intellect.

IF, therefore, one thing is primarily intelligent, and another is intelligent in a different way, certainly that which is superior to the primarily intelligent does not understand: for it would be necessary for it to be an intellect in order to understand: but if it were an intellect, it would need to have an intelligible; and if it understood primarily, it would need to have the intelligible in itself: it is not, however, necessary for whatever is intelligible to have an intellect in itself, and to understand: for it would be not only intelligible, but also intelligent. And since it would then be two, it would certainly not be the first. Now, indeed, the intellect which possesses the intelligible could never subsist if there were not the essence of that which is pure intelligible, which will then be intelligible to the intellect. But according to itself, it will properly be neither intelligent nor intelligible: namely, what is called intelligible is judged intelligible to another: and indeed the intellect has that power by which intelligence strives, empty, unless it has received and comprehended the intelligible itself which it understands. For it does not have intelligence without the intelligible: therefore it is perfect when it already has it. But it must have a perfect essence within itself before it understands. That, therefore, from which it exists perfect according to essence, is itself prior to intelligence: wherefore this (the First Principle) has no need of intelligence, since it exists sufficiently before it, and thus does not understand. There is, therefore, something supreme that does not understand: there is, moreover, that which understands primarily: and finally, there is that which has a secondary intelligence. Furthermore, if that first principle of all things were to understand, something would already be present to it: therefore it would not be first, but second: nor one, but already many, and indeed as many as it would understand: nay, even if it only understood itself, it would again become many.

**How far do you imagine the intellect, by the very fact that it understands either itself or other things, to become so multiform, that there are in it many forms formally distinct from each other by the very nature of the thing, even if no relation has accrued to them there, you have not yet discovered the simplicity of the principle. Chapter III.**

Again, wherever many things are composed together, and one is made out of many, such a multitude is posterior to the One itself. Finally, every multitude which is something other than unity itself, and in some way is opposed to unity, ne-

-ty, is necessarily after the one itself, and is a participant of the one. These Platonic ideas do not oppose Christian Theologians, among whom the first principle does not have multiple forms, by understanding multiple things, however it may understand, but by looking at itself through one form of itself in a single act, it perceives all things, namely, considering its most simple form to be imitated differently by different things and in different ways. Furthermore, the divine Trinity (as Dionysius the Areopagite confirms, and Gregory Nazianzen asserts) is the same there as unity itself: indeed, just as light and heat are indeed distinct and two things under the sky, in the sky they are one. Moreover, progression and rest are indeed diverse here: but there, rest is found in progression, and progression in rest: thus in the divine nature, in so far as it is infinite, motion coincides with rest: for if you imagine infinite velocity of motion, you resolve it into rest, indeed, infinite slowness and velocity, while they end in rest, also converge into one another. For infinite power, suddenly uniting all things to itself, unites them in itself and mutually, so that

nor [should we] imagine there such a thing as would make there a composite, or add intelligence to goodness, so distinct there that it is not goodness itself. P L O T I N U S
FIFTH ENNEAD,
BOOK VII.
[Greek text]
Whether there are also Ideas of individuals.

[Bottom section]
As many men are born in the great year of the world, so many seminal reasons of men are in universal nature, almost as many ideas of men in the divine mind. Chapter I.

AND EACH rational soul naturally has numbered within itself that which it is about to produce various lives from itself. But just as when we say that all celestial things are on earth, and conversely all terrestrial things in heaven, we understand all things according to the nature of the place, that is, in heaven indeed by a celestial reason, on earth again by a terrestrial quality: so when we hear that our soul is all things, we ought to accept it according to the property of the human and rational soul. Therefore your soul will never produce lives and figures proper to brute animals, but always human ones: although similar in some way to brutes, and sometimes to demons. Therefore your soul can produce few changes of lives in the great year of the world: especially since it leads a very short life on earth, but a very long one above the earth. In the following year of the world, however, there is no change of lives, but an absolute resurrection of the same men. Meanwhile, men differ among themselves, not only by their materials, but also by their own forms and figures, and various modes of generation. But formal and ordered difference, since it arises neither from matter nor by chance, depends on certain formal reasons, which exist both in nature and in the universal mind, and are not infinite in number. For finite forms are generated in the great year of the world, but in the following (year) the same ones return, with the same causes, namely, returning. But in what way are things in matter more numerous than in the soul, and in the soul again more numerous than in the mind? Thus indeed, because certain things in matter differ from each other in number, either through a defect of form arising from matter somewhere, which form is more perfect elsewhere: or through a division of quantity. But simply formal differences are equal to seminal reasons. However, such reasons are more numerous in the soul than ideas in the mind: because in the nature of the soul there is always an absolute distinction of reasons: the mind

but the mind has a smaller number of ideas absolutely different from each other. For the mind can refer the same idea to diverse things through an act of intelligence and will simultaneously, referring, I say, outwards in different ways as imitable. From this relation, indeed, many things arise, while the idea itself remains undivided.

**A** IS there also an idea for each individual? Perhaps if I and each individual are reduced to the intelligible order, there too is the principle of each individual. Perhaps also if Socrates always exists, and the soul of Socrates will be Socrates himself, inasmuch as the soul is individual, so there Socrates and each individual: but if
**B** Socrates does not always exist, but the soul sometimes becomes something else in a certain way, so that the mind which is now Socrates, was previously Pythagoras or another, and will be another, then no longer is each of those who are here, also there. However, if the soul of each individual has seminal reasons for all things which it executes and fulfills, again all are there. For we confess that as many reasons as the world has, so many individual souls also possess. Therefore, if the world embraces reasons not only of man, but
**C** also of individual animals, the soul also contains the reasons of individuals. Therefore, an infinite number of reasons will follow, unless a restoration to the same occurs in certain courses of time. Thus, indeed, infinity itself will finally be finite, when the same things are restored to the world. But if the things that come into being are altogether more numerous than the exemplar, why then must there be reasons and exemplars for all things that come into being in one revolution of the world? For it seems sufficient
**D** one man for all men, just as numbered souls for forming innumerable men: but indeed there cannot be one reason for different things, nor is one man sufficient as an exemplar for many men differing among themselves, not only in matter, I say, but also in very many proper differences. For these things are not as images of Socrates to an exemplar, but a different effect must necessarily proceed from different reasons.
**E** But the universal revolution embraces all reasons: and the same things are regenerated again through the same reasons. Nor indeed is it to be suspected that an infinite multitude might follow from this in the intelligible world: for there the whole multitude is contained in a certain indivisible, and as it were, individual things proceed from there when it acts.

*Every soul and particular nature contains within itself the seminal reasons of all things that are to be generated from it, distinguished among themselves by formal differences. Chapter II.*

However, these things can be distinguished in this way, even if they are commonly reckoned in the same species. But such a proper distinction of forms is prescribed even in the very intention of universal nature: because in such a distinction also consists the order, beauty, and good of the universe. Matter, however, brings no proper variety of forms, but a defect of form. Quantity, moreover, by its division in homogeneous things, creates number somewhere, but nowhere variety. Finally, in one world-year, whatever heterogeneous things are generated in natural order are formally dissimilar among themselves, and therefore are produced by different reasons: but in the subsequent year, all the same things are recreated by the same reasons under the same causes.

BOOK VIII.

On intelligible beauty.
On intelligible beauty.

That beauty is natural in the human intellect also appears, because it renders raw
matter beautiful. Chapter I.

Nor does it achieve this only by imitating natural works externally, but also by using inner principles, when namely it corrects certain defects of nature. Hence we conclude that form and beauty are more excellent in the mind than in any work of art. Add that it is more powerful, because in a work it is indeed dispersed, but in the mind it is entirely united.

[Decorative initial Q containing a figure of a person]
WHEN we admit that the soul
which contemplates the intelligible world
and beholds the beauty of true
intellect can sometimes also
perceive the father of this, who is
superior in mind: come now, let us
try with all our might to discern
and express to ourselves,
B as much as such things can be explained, by what particular reason we may be able to perceive the beauty of the mind and of that world. Imagine therefore two stone masses placed near each other: one of which is indeed uncomposed and devoid of artistic work: while the other, through art, is already sculpted into a statue, whether divine or human: and if divine, let it be a statue of some Grace, or a Muse: but if human, let it not be of some particular man, but rather of someone whom art has gathered from all beautiful things.

The stone, therefore, arranged by art into the beauty of a form, A
will immediately appear beautiful, but not
because it is stone: otherwise, the other
mass would also be similarly beautiful: therefore, it is because it
possesses the form which art applied. This form, then,
the matter did not possess, but it was in the
conceiving mind before it came into the stone:
And it was in the artist, not by virtue of his
having eyes and hands, but because he was endowed
with art. Therefore, this beauty was B
much more excellent in art. For the form itself,
existing in art, does not come into the stone,
but that [form] indeed remains, while another, lesser one,
proceeds from it in the meantime, nor does it remain pure in itself, nor such as
the artist desired, but only insofar as the matter
obeyed the art. If, however, art makes that which it is and possesses such a thing,
and it makes beautiful according to the reason
by which it also acts: then surely, art,
possessing beauty, is more truly and genuinely
beautiful, greater and more excellent than all that which proceeds C
externally. For insofar as the form, proceeding into
matter, is now extended, it is by that much weaker than that
which remains in unity. For whatever suffers dis-
tance in itself, departs from itself: if strength, in strength:
if warmth, in warmth: if power altogether, in
power: if beauty, entirely in beauty.
Now, first, every efficient cause must be
more excellent than its effect: for it is not
the musician in music, but music that makes, and music
in sensible sound creates music above D
sense. But if anyone should despise the arts, because
they imitate nature, it must be answered,
first, that natures also imitate other things:
then, that the arts do not simply imitate what is seen by the
eyes, but recur to the very reasons, from
which nature consists and acts: moreover, many things
they make from themselves, and add something besides,
where anything is lacking to perfection, inasmuch as they
have beauty in themselves. Finally, Phidias E
himself could have fashioned Jupiter, not by
properly imitating any spectacle with his senses,
but by imagining him such as Jupiter himself would appear,
if he ever wished to encounter our eyes.

_Beauty in a natural work is a certain form, not impressed upon matter in just any way, but then impressed by nature itself, when nature more excellently dominates matter. Chapter II._

_For this work is not beautiful by reason of matter or quantity: otherwise, that which was more material or larger would also be more beautiful, but by reason of a certain more excellent form, as if already rendered immaterial. Hence it happens that a form first captivates you as beautiful when, having entered sight, it has already become spiritual there: and then especially when it is more intensely contemplated. Finally, form in morals and disciplines, which is entirely immaterial, captivates us with love as beautiful. But immaterial beauty in nature is much more wonderful than natural beauty. For nature, neither by some adventitious habit, nor by laboring externally like art, but by its own essence and by dominating internally with wonderful ease, exhibits beauty to matter._

BUT for the present, let us set aside the arts. A
Let us consider the naturally beautiful works
which they are said to imitate, namely, all rational
and irrational animals, especially whatever
among these are more perfectly finished: where,
of course, their maker and fashioner, having dominated
the matter, applied the form he desired. What then
is beauty in these? Not blood and
menses, but color and figure distinct from these, or
nothing, or something without figure and incongruous, or
as that which contains something simple, like matter.
Hence

--- Page 587 ---
**BOOK EIGHT. 543**

Whence then arose the beauty of Helen, for which such a great contest was stirred up? Whence shone forth other forms similar to Venus? And indeed, whence arose the very form of Venus? Or if any human is entirely beautiful, or a God, whether of those who come into our sight, or of those who do not come, they nevertheless have conspicuous beauty in themselves. Is not this form everywhere, descending into that which is born from that which generates it, just as it is said in the arts that beauty proceeds into works of art from the arts themselves? What then? Are the works indeed beautiful, and is the principle (of beauty) in the matter itself? But the principle which is not in matter, but in the agent, primary and free from matter, is not *a* beauty, but this very principle is brought into a single unity. Moreover, if mass, by virtue of being mass, were beautiful, it would certainly follow that the active principle itself, since it is not mass, would not be beautiful: but if, whether in a small or in some large mass, the same form similarly moves and affects the mind of the beholder by its power, certainly beauty is not to be attributed to the magnitude of the mass. Hence again the same argument is taken up: because insofar as form is outside the mind, we do not perceive it, nor are we moved by it: but when it is already conceived in the mind, it affects us. But indeed, through the eyes, the mere appearance of things flows in; otherwise, the largest things could not penetrate through the narrowest (aperture). But magnitude is also contracted, not great in mass, but rather great in form. Furthermore, the cause of a beautiful effect must be either deformed, or indifferent, or beautiful. If it were deformed, it certainly would not produce the contrary: If indifferent, why would it make something beautiful rather than deformed? But indeed, nature, the artificer of such beautiful things, is much earlier and more beautiful. But we, since we are accustomed to inspect nothing intimate, and are entirely ignorant of intimate things, naturally follow external things, meanwhile ignorant of that which lies hidden intimately and moves us, just as if someone seeing his own image, and ignorant whence it came, should follow that very image. But that there is something else that attracts those who pursue it, and that beauty does not consist in magnitude, is testified to us by the beauty which is in disciplines and duties, and entirely in the soul: where certainly beauty truly flourishes more, when namely in a certain soul you contemplate wisdom, and having contemplated it, you are delighted and love it, not then looking at the face of the body, which perhaps may not be beautiful, but having set aside the entire form of the body, pursuing intimate beauty. But if that soul does not yet move you to call it beautiful, nor, having looked into your inner self, will you delight in yourself as beautiful. Therefore, thus affected, you will in vain seek true and intimate beauty: for thus you will search not with something pure, but with something base: and therefore words about such matters are not for everyone. But if you too have looked into yourself as beautiful, from this you will now remember beauty itself.

*Beauty appearing in matter is a certain image of beauty, which flourishes more excellently in nature: But that image of it which is in the intellectual soul is greater: This finally (is an image) of that which is primary in the divine mind. Chapter III.*

But the splendor of beauty shines forth from the divine intellect into the intellect, the chief part of the soul, just as light from the Sun always (shines) into a star, and then into the virtue of the rational soul, as into a lamp, insofar as it is turned towards higher things.
                                                                                                                                                                Z 2

--- Page 588 ---
544 PLOTINI ENNEAD. V.

But in vain does the soul seek what beauty itself is, if it has not rendered itself most beautiful through such a conversion. But if it has rendered itself so, then, contemplating its own beauty, it will thence behold a higher beauty: and through its intellect, now purified, as through a certain gold that was in a mass, it will contemplate the divine intellect as universal and pure gold; otherwise, it is not to be sought. Finally, the first beauty is the first fullness of intelligence. The simply intellectual gods are beautiful and gods through participation in that [first beauty]: through the same, also the celestial gods, that is, all the mundane ones, who indeed, as celestial gods, know divine things by a direct intuition, but look upon and govern human things with a deflected gaze. Finally, the simply intellectual gods who are in the intellectual heaven are said not to govern, at least in the way they are there, but to contemplate. Whatever is in the intellectual heaven is likewise an intelligible heaven, and there indeed are all things.

**BOOK EIGHT.** 545
Above the corporeal heaven, in the incorporeal heaven, there are twofold gods, namely, intelligible and intellectual ones. The former indeed are ideas, but the latter are all intellects, blessed by the eternal contemplation of ideas. Chapter IV.

The divine intellect thus derives itself into ideas, so that the whole is preserved in each, but with a different property in different ones. Nor is it so much to be said that ideas are in the intellect, as that the intellect itself exists as the ideas themselves, namely, wonderfully proceeding as multiform from its uniform self. If heaven similarly derives itself into stars, in each star both the whole heaven is present and all the stars, but with a diverse property. Therefore, what Anaxagoras says, "everything is in everything," applies not so much in the subcelestial world (where unity is minimal) as in the supercelestial world (where unity is maximal); and in a certain way also in the celestial world, where unity is moderate. But where Plotinus proves that the contemplators of divine things will never depart from there, consider what Porphyry and Iamblichus asserted: that even our souls can attain a similar blessedness. It will not be moved

*Since art imitates nature, and nature God, and art indeed acts through a certain wisdom, but God through*
*wisdom itself simply, it follows that nature acts through a certain wisdom inherent in itself. Chapter V.*

*If all things derive their essence through their wisdom, it follows that primary wisdom is primary essence. Wisdom through*
*industry acquired, which is human art, depends on wisdom innate in us, and imitates the wisdom of nature. But*
*these three wisdoms, because they are in another, must be referred to the primary wisdom, which is in itself, where namely wisdom*
*itself is essence. Indeed, the wisdom of human art is accumulated from many acts of meditations and discourses:*
*but wisdom naturally inherent in us, and the wisdom of nature itself and of God, is a certain single form presenting*
*itself as all-form, like a single countenance, not like a single speech or disputation: for before the one accumulated from many, there is*
*the one which unfolds itself into many, and before this, the simply one itself.*

WHATEVER things are made either by art or by nature,  **A**
a certain wisdom makes them, and everywhere wisdom guides the action.
But wherever a certain wisdom may come to be,

LIBER OCTAVVS. 547

A If it is said to have it from another, we will again ask about that other; and if it has it from itself, then we will rest there. Therefore, if they take refuge in the mind itself, there again it must be investigated whether the mind generated wisdom. If they admit this, from where shall we ask? But if it conceived it from itself, it cannot have done so unless the mind itself is wisdom. True wisdom, therefore, is essence: and true essence, conversely, is wisdom, and the very B dignity of essence is claimed by wisdom. For it is established that true essence comes from wisdom. Therefore, whatever essences do not have wisdom, they are indeed essences because they were made through some wisdom: but because they possess no wisdom in themselves, they are not true essences. Therefore, no one should imagine that in the intelligible world either the gods themselves, or other more-than-blessed inhabitants there, contemplate certain rules of propositions, but rather that each thing said to exist there offers itself to those who behold it as certain exemplars and beautiful spectacles, such as one might perhaps imagine to exist in the mind of a wise person. But I speak not of depicted images, but of existing things: for which reason the ancients called ideas "beings" and "essences."

*Egyptian priests, to signify divine mysteries, did not use small letter characters, but whole figures of herbs, trees, animals: because, namely, God has knowledge of things not as a complex cogitation about a thing, but as a simple and firm form of the thing. Chapter VI.*

*The cogitation of time among you is manifold and mobile, saying, namely, that time is indeed swift, and by a certain revolution joins the beginning again with the end: it teaches prudence, brings forth things, and takes them away. But the Egyptian comprehends the whole discourse of this kind in one certain and firm figure, depicting a winged serpent grasping its tail in its mouth: and other similar figures which Horus describes.*

A But it seems to me that the wise Egyptians, whether by a certain consummate wisdom or even by a natural instinct of the mind, when they decided to signify the mysteries of wisdom to us, did not use figures of letters signifying discourses of speech and certain propositions, and imitating the sounds and pronunciations of rules, but rather, by describing the individual images of things, and depicting them, they signified in sacred silence the discourse of the thing itself: B namely, that each image or exemplar, and that whole spectacle gathered together as a subject, is a kind of science and wisdom, and is neither a cogitation nor a deliberation. Afterwards, however, from that very exemplary image or wisdom, whole at once, an image is already unfolded in another, and speaking in a certain discourse and finding the causes for which things are thus established, while, namely, the disposition of things, that it is so well, moves admiration. C Hence, he says that whoever considers how wisdom itself, not having causes of its essence for which it should be or act in such a way, presents itself as being in the way that those things which are made according to it are, will admire wisdom. Therefore, this very thing which can be called the disposition of things, that it is well as it is, which indeed becomes manifest from inquiry scarcely at last or in no way—namely, that things ought to be so, if anyone should only find this very thing, I say—it must be so and stand firm in the intelligible world before all inquiry and argumentation: but let us now take it in one great thing that I speak of, which is also agreeable to all.

The knowledge of God is not like argumentation or deliberation, but rather like a natural disposition. Chapter VII.

For it does not, having posited a principle, subsequently gather a conclusion through intermediate steps, nor, having established an end, consequently choose ways and means to achieve that end, and then act as it deliberated: but because it is by its very nature disposed in all ways, therefore it also acts naturally thus: just as a seed, being affected in a manifold way, thus generates manifold offspring. But that all-form nature of God is its very intelligence, marked with all ideas, not like a tablet with figures, but like the heaven with stars, which are themselves the heaven. Indeed, it acts most easily, because it acts by its very nature, and is itself the universe. Our soul acts almost similarly, when it recalls itself to an all-form habit.

A DO we perhaps think that this universe,
which we confess to be from another, and to exist as such, was composed by its maker in such a way that he thought to himself about the earth, and that it ought to rest in the middle? then water continuous with the earth, and the rest subsequently arranged in order up to the heaven: then indeed all animals, and such and so many forms of individual living beings as each now possesses, and the disposition both of their internal organs and of their external parts and mem-
B bers? then, as he had arranged each thing within himself, did he thus proceed to arrange them by the work itself? But certainly, such consideration could not have existed in him. For whence would it have occurred to him who had not yet seen such things? Nor indeed could it happen that he, receiving from some other, would fabricate, as our artisans now fabricate, using hands and instruments: for hands and feet come later.
It remains therefore that all things are in another, and since
C nothing interposes itself as a medium, by the very proximity of the being itself to another, as if suddenly its image and likeness shine forth, whether from itself alone, or through a ministering soul. For at present it makes no difference whether through a particular soul, but indeed all these things have flowed entirely from there, and are more beautiful there. For here they are mixed, but there they are pure. But this universe, having proceeded from there, is comprehended from beginning to end by forms.
D First indeed, matter by the forms of the elements, to which other forms are added, and to other forms similarly others, so much so that it is difficult to find matter hidden beneath many forms. But since it also has a certain ultimate form, it can easily undergo every form. But that maker, with whom the exemplar of the work is form, produces all forms, and these indeed without any difficulty or violence, because the agent there
E is the universe, and essence, and form. Wherefore, for this reason too, the fabrication was easy and without labor, and the structure of the whole existed, just as the maker himself is the universe: therefore there was no impediment, and even now in fabricating he freely dominates. And although other things are here and there an impediment to others, yet nothing can obstruct the fabrication of the universe itself, not even now: for it stands as a whole. Indeed, I believe that if we ourselves were the first exemplars of things, and at the same time essences and forms, and the very
F form which makes here were our essence, our fabrication would dominate without labor: although man, as he is now made, fabricates a form different from himself. For now, having become man, he has ceased to be the universe: but when he ceases to be man, as Plato says, he raises himself to the sublime, and governs the whole world. For having become the whole, he also makes the whole. But to return to our subject, you can

A You can indeed offer a reason why the earth is placed in the middle, and why it is round; or why the oblique circle is established in a certain region: but in the divine mind, it was not deliberated thus because it was necessary, but rather because it is as it is, therefore these things are also well as they are: as if, before an argument running through causes, the conclusion itself would stand firm without any propositions. For nothing there depends on consequence, nothing becomes certain from consideration, but before consequence, before consideration, the whole is established.
B For all these are posterior: reason, demonstration, faith. For by the very fact that the principle exists, from it by its own nature all these things are, and are thus arranged. Now indeed what is said, that the causes of the principle are not to be sought, is rightly said thus, especially concerning such a principle that is perfect, which is the same as the end: namely, that the principle is simultaneously the beginning and the end, and this whole (universe) is simultaneously both, lacking in no part.

*Since beauty itself is a certain multiform shape, adapted to sight, deservedly the first principle is superior to beauty. Chapter VIII.*

*The divine mind is the first whole, therefore in every part of itself it is whole: and it is the first beauty, therefore in every part of itself it is whole beauty. There are three most beautiful things under the Good itself: the divine mind, the soul of the world, the body of the world: just as in the heavens are the Sun, Jupiter, Venus. Those captivated by Venus do not realize what they are experiencing, because they do not notice that they admire the lower beauty on account of the higher.*

A THIS therefore is beautiful first: it is whole: it is whole everywhere, so that there is no defect of beauty even in any part. What then is to be called beauty itself? Certainly nothing that is not the whole itself, but either has only a part, or has nothing of it. Indeed, unless that is beauty itself, what else can it be? For that which is before it, does not wish to be beautiful: for that which first comes into sight, because it is a species, and a spectacle for the mind, this is lovable and pleasant to behold.
B Therefore Plato, wishing to signify this to us, introduces the architect of the world approving his perfect work to something somewhat more manifest to our intellects, wishing to show by this the very beauty of the exemplar and idea as lovable. For whenever someone admires a work crafted according to another exemplar, they admire the exemplar itself most of all. Nor should it seem strange if in the meantime one is unaware of what they are experiencing: since both lovers, and indeed all who admire this beauty of ours, are unaware that they are affected in this way on account of the supernal beauty: and indeed they are thus affected on account of it.
C But that Plato refers to the divine exemplar, when he says that the architect of the world loved his work, he declares that he was delighted by the spectacle itself, where he deliberately adds thus:
D For he says, he was indeed delighted with his handiwork, and also wished to make it more similar to the exemplar itself: demonstrating by this very fact what kind of beauty the exemplar possesses, because he says that this work is beautiful from that, because it is its image: namely, unless that were wonderfully beautiful, possessing inestimable beauty, what could be more beautiful than this whole visible universe? Therefore, those who detract from the beauty of this world do not think correctly, unless perhaps in their detraction they mean that this world is not supernal.

When you have grasped this whole variety of worldly forms at once, immediately remove the local dimension, while preserving their forms and their motions. You therefore have the soul of the world, in which all things are present in every form. Then remove the motions, with the forms preserved in their state, and you now have the divine mind, where every idea contains all others. Finally, with the diversity of ideas resolved into a single light, you have attained the first principle. Chapter IX.

The corporeal world is not truly great, because everywhere it depends on small things. The incorporeal world is infinite. For one may say infinitely, 'in this idea are all things.' And with all these reckoned, again all in each, and similarly thereafter. Since the first essence and beauty are the same, deservedly, insofar as something participates in beauty, to that extent it also participates in essence, and vice versa: likewise, since the first essence is simply form itself, doubtless all things have essence through participation in form.

| A LET US therefore conceive of this world of ours as being such in thought, that each part indeed remains what it is, but that each is in the other. Let us imagine, I say, all things gathered together into one with all their might, so that whatever of the individual things first presents itself to the eyes, as if it were an outer sphere, immediately the spectacle of the Sun also follows, and at the same time the image of the other stars, and within, the earth, sea, and all animals are seen as if in a certain sphere B everywhere transparent: and finally, in reality, it happens that all things are seen in each. Let there be, therefore, in the mind a certain clear imagination of a sphere containing all things within itself, whether agitated, or remaining, or partly mobile, and partly stable. But you, keeping this in mind, imagine another besides, taking away mass from it: also remove place, and at the same time completely expel every imagination of matter far from yourself: yet do not, in the meantime, imagine one to be smaller in mass than the other: then C indeed, invoking God himself who made it, whose image you now have, humbly implore him to come. He will come suddenly, bringing his world and its adornment with him, together with all the gods who are all in it: he will come existing as one and at the same time as all: each one will meet, bringing all with him, converging into one. There indeed all the gods are varied among themselves in powers, but by that one power, all are very many, one God; indeed, one God is all: nor D indeed does the one himself diminish, so that all those might be born. But at the same time all are present, and each one again is separate from another in a state in no way distant, presenting no form subject to the senses: otherwise, one would indeed be elsewhere, and another elsewhere, nor would each exist as all in itself: nor again does any of them have parts different from others or from itself: nor again is each one there a divided power, existing only as great as the measured parts are: indeed, it is E the whole, a universal power, proceeding indeed into infinity, and into infinity in virtue. And yet that world is so immense that its parts also become infinite again. For where can anything be said to exist which he has not preceded? *Three degrees in divine contemplation, and three preparations for it. Chapter XI.*

*He who is to enjoy God ought first to conform himself to a certain divine likeness through a common notion of God and faith: then to strive with the whole intention of his thought towards God: thirdly, to ardently love God alone with his whole will. To him, therefore, thus affected, God flows in, as light, everywhere present, immediately made clear. Then indeed the soul occupied by God, as long as it is still less united to God, perceives and thinks itself to be breathed upon and filled from above. But when it is more closely united, it perceives God himself inspiring, and now considers by what reason He flows in. Finally, when it is entirely united to God, it no longer considers the occupied or the occupier in a distinct condition: but rather beholds something as one with a simple act. Nor does it properly behold, or hear, or know by similar thought: indeed, through a certain universal, intimate, hidden sense, it enjoys itself and God equally as one, and is conscious to itself then at last that it is in the best possible state. Which consciousness of itself is not a distinct perception, but is almost the same as this very best state of well-being.*

BUT IF ANY of us, unable to see A
himself, being entirely comprehended by that
God, should bring forth into view a spectacle or
sight, he certainly brings forth himself, and sees
his own image made now more beautiful. But
letting go of the image, however beautiful, and
conspiring together with Him into one,
separating nothing further, he exists as one with
all things together with that God, who silently
and quietly flows in: moreover, he is with Him
as much as he can and wills. But if he returns
to two, and meanwhile is pure, he then dwells B

He places himself outside. But the soul, about to perceive such a divine power, must have a certain form of it, and thus persevere, while it strives to clearly know it, and thus knowing what and how great a thing it enters, and confidently trusting that it will enter a most blessed thing, then finally immerse itself completely to such an extent, that it emerges as a spectator, now a specimen of another seen by it, such as comes forth from there, abundantly refulgent with notions. But in what way will anyone be B in beauty itself, unless he sees it? Indeed, if he sees it as another, he will not yet be in beauty: but if he himself is made beauty, thus he will be in beauty most especially. If, therefore, vision looks to an external thing, it is not expedient for vision to be there, or to be in such a way that it exists as the same with that which is seen. But this is like a certain consciousness of oneself and a consensus, warning lest perhaps if it wishes to perceive more, it should depart from itself. Nor should it escape us that the sensations of evils indeed have greater C pulsations, but cognitions are lesser, inasmuch as they are shaken out by a certain force of pulsations. For disease pulsates and excites more vehemently: but health, dwelling more quietly with us, exhibits a plainer knowledge of itself, indeed silently resides and is tranquil, as if familiar and conspiring with us into one. But disease has nothing domestic, but is entirely alien, therefore it occurs more manifestly, because it appears to us as most different: but those things which are ours, which D are ourselves, are within us even without manifest sensation. Thus, truly having ourselves, we are known to ourselves most of all: since we have thus made our knowledge and ourselves one. Therefore, in the divine world, when we use our mind knowing to the utmost, we seem in a way to be ignorant, namely, by suppressing the passion of sense: which indeed says it has not seen at all: for it has not seen: nor can it ever see such things.

Therefore, that which distrusts having seen, is sense: but the other is that which has seen. Or if that one also distrusts, neither will it believe itself to exist. For neither can it, when it has placed itself outside, behold itself as something sensible with the eyes of the body.

*Whoever entirely enters his own intellect, through this he also enters the divine: which indeed is the son of the Good itself, but the father of the soul of the world. Chapter XII.*

On Intellect & Ideas & Being.

The soul contemplating divine things is now in its homeland. Active men and pleasure-seekers are exiles: but active men return to their homeland more easily than pleasure-seekers.

A [Marginal note]
[Large decorative woodcut initial Q depicting a figure in a landscape]
SINCE all men, immediately upon being born, use sense before mind, and necessarily first encounter things pertaining to sense, and apply their affection (to them), some indeed, persevering in the same habit, thus pass their lives:
considering these things both first and last, and what is troublesome in them, evil; but what is
B [Marginal note] pleasant, they judge to be good. And thus finally they think enough has been done for themselves, if throughout their whole life they pursue pleasant things, and reject the contrary. Therefore, whoever among them claim some reason for themselves, judge this to be wisdom: being affected precisely like heavier birds, which, when they have seized many things from the earth by whose weight they are burdened, cannot fly higher through the sublime (regions), although they have received wings from nature. But others are somewhat
C [Marginal note] raised from lower things, whom the better nature of the soul itself recalls from pleasure to what is honorable. But since they cannot behold the supernal (realm), and therefore have nothing else where they may rest, they are transferred, along with the very name of virtue, to the actions and choices of lower things, from which they were trying to raise themselves at first. Finally, the third kind of men is divine, in which indeed are those who, relying on greater power and keenness of sight, keenly look up at the supernal light, and to it
D [Marginal note] they completely raise themselves, having perceived it, transcending the lower mists and darkness, and when they have transcended, they remain there, completely despising all these (lower) things, nor do they delight in the supernal region as true and proper (to them) any differently than a wanderer, after long errors, finally restored to his rightful homeland.

**A** Every species that lies in another, also depends on another, and is referred to that, and is an image of it. Furthermore, if it is necessary for the intellect to be the artisan of this universe, it certainly will not understand those things which exist in that which is not yet, in order to create it. Therefore, before the world, those things must exist not as figures impressed by others, but as certain principal exemplars, and the primary essence of the mind. If some, however, say that seminal reasons suffice for this, they will undoubtedly **B** bring forth eternal ones: and if they are eternal and far removed from all passion, they must exist in the mind, and indeed in such a mind, which exists prior in habit, and nature, and soul.

For these are in a certain potentiality, and consist in its power. The mind therefore is beings themselves, according to the true mode of being, not understanding those things which are elsewhere: for these are neither before it, nor after it: but the mind is as the first legislator, indeed, it is the very law of its own being.

**C** Rightly therefore it has been said: truly, to understand is the same as to be: likewise, the knowledge of those things which are without matter is the same as the thing itself.

Again, I have indeed investigated myself as one of the beings: reminiscences testify to the same.

For none of the beings is outside the mind, nor again in a place: but they remain perpetually in themselves, not subject to change or destruction, and therefore are considered to be beings by the true mode of being: otherwise, if they arise and perish, **D** they would acquire an adventitious being: nor would these any longer be beings themselves, but rather that very being, namely, what is perceived, are by a certain participation that very thing which they are said to be: since the subject nature receives form from elsewhere, just as bronze receives form from the art of sculpture, and wood from the art of carpentry, while art, namely, proceeds into such materials through an image: but art itself meanwhile outside matter **E** perseveres in the same state, and has in itself the true statue and couch.

Thus, therefore, this whole in the genus of bodies, being merely a participant of images, clearly testifies that beings themselves are different from bodies: for the former are immutable, while the latter change: the former consist firmly in themselves, needing no place: for they are not extended by any magnitude, but have an intellectual substance sufficient for themselves: for the nature of bodies always needs some other preserver.

But the mind, since by a wonderful nature it sustains and preserves those things which by their own nature fall, is rightly not compelled to desire where it itself should be founded.

*Ideas in the intellect are properly certain powers of it, by which it is defined in one way or another. Chapter VI.*

*But since the faculty of understanding and generating is the same there, therefore ideas there are not only as various notions, but also as many seminal powers in the soul: from this, indeed, they are called exemplars, but from that, principles of things, reasons, and species everywhere. Therefore, wholly material qualities, heat, cold, and similar ones, cannot have mutual union without confusion: for either they remain separate, or if they are mixed, either one confuses the others, or all are confused by each other, so much so that some other thing results from all. Less material qualities like flavors can unite, like those, indeed with confusion, but not so much. But odors, as if still less material, unite in the same medium, differing, and one confuses the other somewhat less. It still confuses, however. Different voices unite still more in a medium, and are less confused, because they are less material. But species of colors, even contrary ones, because they are immaterial, unite in the same point, and exist there most distinctly without any mutual confusion, from which it is concluded...*

*Notions of sensibles recently acquired or produced in the soul are not the sensibles themselves: But absolute notions of intelligibles coming into the rational faculty from the intellect are, in a certain way, the intelligibles themselves. Chapter VII.*
*Because, namely, the intellect is most intimate to the soul, both proper and common: in the proper, notions and intelligibles are more identical, in the common, they are most identical. The proper intellect (as Plotinus often says) is in the soul as a form: but the common intellect is present to the soul as an agent. But since the intelligible itself relates to intelligence almost as a mover, and therefore in a certain way precedes it, we should not say that the intellect becomes the intelligibles after it has understood them, but rather the converse: especially since otherwise intelligences would arise by some chance, and would be, as it were, certain fictions.*

[Marginal note: A] THEREFORE, the sciences that are in the rational soul, which indeed pertain to sensibles—if indeed these notions are to be called sciences by us, since it is more fitting to call them opinions—these, I say, being posterior to things, are also images of them: but those that pertain to intelligibles, which are truly sciences, coming from the intellect into the rational soul, understand nothing sensible. But insofar as they are sciences, they are themselves the very things they understand, and they have the intelligible and intelligence from within: [Marginal note: B] because the intellect is most intimate, which is the first itself, dwelling perpetually with itself, and existing as act: neither directing its gaze as if it did not possess, nor acquiring anything, nor discursive

A through things it did not previously have ready: for such conditions seem to belong more to the soul, but it rests entirely within itself, existing as all things at once, nor using intelligence for this purpose, that it might bring individual things into being within itself. For it did not become God when it understood God: nor did it become motion after it understood motion. Therefore, what is usually said, that species are intelligences, if it is said in such a way that after it understood this very thing, it became or exists as this very thing, it is not rightly B said: for what is understood must exist prior to this act of understanding. Otherwise, in what way will it proceed to understand it? For it does not fall upon it by some chance, nor does it strive rashly or in vain.

*Indeed, intellect taken absolutely is all ideas. But any given idea is not intellect taken absolutely, but intellect of a certain kind. Likewise, any given idea differs from intellect only by a certain intellectual reason. But ideas differ among themselves by the nature of the thing and by formal reason. Chapter VIII.*

*For it is more permissible to say: The idea of man is intellect, and the idea of horse is intellect, than to say the idea of man is the idea of horse: although under the act of each idea, the others exist virtually or by a certain consequence, just as propositions arranged consecutively in geometry relate to geometry and to each other. Furthermore, since being in a certain natural order precedes intellect, the necessary distinction of being into its modes of existing and into beings in a certain way precedes the use of intelligence: a distinction which neither Platonists nor Christians readily admit in the first principle of things. Just as we consider there the nature of being and common intelligence, so in any idea we consider a certain proper nature of being and proper intelligence, which are as it were two things, not like matter and heat, like the diaphanous and light, but like heat and to be hot, like light and to shine, of which each is an act, and therefore in reality they are one. Although, therefore, intelligence is the innermost act of being, nevertheless, each is an act.*

A SINCE, therefore, what is understood is intimate, this very intimate thing is one something, both species and idea. What then is this? Indeed, it is intellect and intellectual essence, and any idea does not differ from intellect, but each one is intellect, and altogether intellect itself is indeed common to all species: but each species is each intellect. Just as a whole science is all its contemplations and notions: and any notion B is a part of the whole, not divided by place, but each having its virtue in the whole. This intellect, therefore, rests within itself in the same state with itself, an eternal fullness of all things. But if intellect itself were conceived as prior to being itself, it would then be necessary to say that intellect, by acting and understanding, generates and perfects beings. But since it is necessary to conceive being as prior to intellect, it must be confessed that beings themselves are primarily inherent in intelligence, and that act and intelligence C accrue to beings themselves, just as the act of fire accrues to fire already existing, so that beings, being thus intimately implanted in intellect, have in themselves, as it were, their own act. But being itself is also act. Therefore, there is one act for both: nay, rather, both are one. Therefore, being itself and intellect are one nature, wherefore beings and the act of being and such intellect are one, and such intel- lections are species and form and acts D of being. Nevertheless, when we divide such things, some are conceived there before others: for the dividing intellect is one thing, but that which is indivisible and minimally dividing is being itself and all things.

of man: although concerning man it must be especially considered whether there is also a singular idea there.

564          PLOTINUS' ENNEADS. V.

A singular [idea], I say, because it is not the same A
or does not have one singular thing after another. This one indeed
is snub-nosed, that one truly is aquiline. Such
properties, however, are to be placed in the form of man,
as certain differences of forms,
just as an animal also has its own differences. But from
matter they proceed, that this one indeed is in this condition,
that one truly is rather aquiline in that condition: and similarly,
we must consider some differences of colors to consist
in reason and form, while others arise from the diversity of matter and place.

*Every material thing relates to its idea as an image or painting to a living substance. Chapter XIII.*

*Souls, however, minds, and their perfected virtues exist as true things outside the idea, just as in the
idea: nor are they the same by an equivocal rather than a univocal denomination: nor do they differ as a painted man from a living one, but rather as a boy from a man.*

IT REMAINS to inquire whether only A
those things are there which are contained in the sensible order: or
whether, just as our man here is one thing,
and Man himself is another, so there also the Soul itself is one thing,
and this soul is another: similarly, this mind, and Mind
itself is another. Therefore, it must first be said that
not all things that are here are to be considered
mere images of exemplars, nor is the soul an
image of the Soul itself, yet one excels the
other in dignity: and it is also here: per- B
haps, however, not insofar as it is here, is it the Soul
itself. Since every soul truly is, there is
also a certain justice and temperance in
the souls dwelling here, and moreover true
knowledge, not merely images nor
likenesses of those things as if moving in a sensible
place, but those very same things existing here in some other way:
for those things are not determined in a specific place.
Therefore, when the soul emerges C
from the body, those things are there too: for the
sensible world is determined by only one place: but the
intelligible world is everywhere. Whatever
such a soul has here, it has the same again
there. Therefore, if those things which are said to be in the sensible
place are understood to be those which are counted in the genus of
visibles, not only those things which are in the
sensible world are also there, but many more exist
there. But if they are said to be in the world in such a way that
both the soul and what is inherent in the soul are comprehended
simultaneously, then indeed all things that are there are also here.

*Many things, through decay and a certain chance, occur besides ideas and are deformed: because the vegetative part of the soul, which is
the lowest of divine things, cannot entirely overcome matter. Chapter XIV.*

*Nor do those things have ideas which sometimes converge into one without a certain order directed to an end. In the very
idea of man are contained ingenious and necessary arts. The Soul itself is the idea of the soul: closest to this is the soul
entirely formed by intellect. Further removed, however, is the same soul sometimes imagining the universal providence of the world within itself;
farthest of all, finally, is the same soul now devoted to particular providence.*

THEREFORE, should we consider this nature, A
containing all things in the intelligible genus, to be
the Principle itself? But in what way?
since the Principle itself is truly entirely one
and simple, but in the very plenitude of beings there is
necessarily a multitude. But again, in what way
is such a nature and plenitude, besides the
One itself, from the One? And how did this multitude flow
from there? And under what condition are all these things?
Also, why does the intellect have these, and from where? Indeed, these things must be discussed elsewhere, with a different kind of beginning.

--- Page 609 ---
**BOOK NINE.** **565**

**A** But when it is asked whether there is a species of those things also which are made from putrefaction, and of difficult and very troublesome things, likewise of filth and mud, it must be said: that as many things as the mind derives from the First Principle are all best, in which species these certainly are not present: nor does the mind receive from these, but the soul indeed receives many things from the mind, and moreover admits very many things from matter, in which these things occur.

**B** But concerning these things it will be explained more clearly, if we return to that question by which it is asked, how a multitude flows from the One. Now indeed it is established that those composite things which are made rashly and in vain, and which flow together not by mind, but by a certain impulse of their own in this sensible kind, are least of all contained in the species themselves. Moreover, those things which are made by putrefaction happen by a certain power of the soul, then perhaps not being able to do otherwise: otherwise it would have undoubtedly made something more agreeable to nature. Therefore it acts where and how it can.

**C** It is also clear that those arts are contained in the higher nature of man itself, whatever refer to those things which are natural to the human race: and that this former (nature) is more universal than the others, and that the soul itself, or life in the Mind, is prior to the universal (principle) before it emerged as soul, so that this soul may be made from it, and it happens to call that especially the soul itself.

LIBER I.

ABOUT the kinds of being.
Of the kinds of being.

*He touches upon many questions concerning the kinds of things: but he seems to define nothing in this chapter. Chap. I.*

[Decorative initial V containing a face and figures] Indeed, the ancient question is, how many and what are the things said to be. For some said there is only one, others indeed many but definite, and others finally infinite; and each of these, some brought forward something else, whether they posited one, or finite, or infinite.
But since such opinions have already been sufficiently examined by later thinkers, we must dismiss them for the present. And only the opinion of those must be considered, who, having discussed the older [opinions], posited certain determined kinds of things: who indeed neither accepted one, because they saw that there are many even among intelligible things, nor again wished to admit infinite [kinds], because neither could that be done, nor would there be any science at all.
But reducing finite [things] to their number, since they could not correctly call these elements—because they would comprehend many things subject to themselves—they rather called these certain kinds: some indeed ten, others fewer. Perhaps there would not be lacking those who would moreover bring us more. There is also a difference in the kinds: for some wished the kinds to be principles, while others [wished] the things themselves to be so many in kind.
First, therefore, the opinion of those who divided all things into ten seems to us to be accepted, as we investigate whether they mean there are ten kinds having a common name of being, or ten predicaments. For they themselves also admit that being itself is not univocal in all things, and they rightly admit it: indeed, that must first be asked, whether those ten are similarly present in intelligible things as well as sensible things, or rather all in sensible things? But in those things which pertain to intelligence, some indeed are, but others by no means. No one, however, would certainly say that these things are conversely. For here, indeed, it seems to be investigated which of the ten especially agree with the intelligible nature. And how...

--- Page 611 ---
LIBER PRIMVS. 567

And whether what is there should be collected under the same genus as these things of ours, or rather whether what is there and what is here is called essence equivocally? But if equivocally, there are more genera; but if univocally, it is immediately absurd for essence to signify the same thing, both in those things which are primary and in those which are posterior: since there is not one common genus in them, in which one thing is indeed prior, and another posterior: but they do not speak about things pertaining to intelligence according to division. Therefore, they did not want to divide all things whatsoever that exist, but rather they dismissed those which are most truly existent.

*It is not easily to be conceded that incorporeal and corporeal things simultaneously, likewise form and matter, and the composite, and the singular and the universal, agree in one genus of substance. Chapter II.*

A  AGAIN it must be asked, now what these genera are to be considered: and how substance is one genus. For it seems that one must begin entirely from this: Indeed it has been said that one genus of substance cannot be common to intelligible and sensible nature. For in that case there would also be something else predicated commonly of both intelligible and sensible substance, which would be neither corporeal nor incorporeal: otherwise, if that genus were cor- B poreal, it would follow that what is called incorporeal under it would be corporeal; or if it were incorporeal, it would again follow that what is called corporeal under it would be incorporeal. Furthermore, in those things which are called substances by us here, it must be asked what is common to matter and form and the composite. For they say that all these are substances, yet they are not equally substances: since form is called substance more than matter, and rightly so; although others might perhaps say that C matter is more substance. Moreover, what will the substances called primary have in common with the secondary substances? since secondary substances derive from primary ones the very fact that they are called substances. But altogether, it is not possible to explain among them what substance is. For even if someone assigns to us a proper characteristic of substance, he will not have thereby grasped what it itself is: and perhaps what is assigned as a proper characteristic of substance, namely that one and the same thing in number can successively receive contraries, seems to agree with all substances.

*It is more probable that what the Peripatetics call substances are arranged in a single series, successively dependent on one, rather than agreeing in the same nature. Chapter III.*

A  BUT should we say that there is one predicament, under which we commonly comprehend intelligible substance, and form and matter, and the composite? Just as if someone were to say that the Heraclidae are one genus, not as if there were something common to all, but as if they descended from one. For that [primary substance] is substance first: and the rest are of a second degree, and less so. But what prevents all things whatsoever from being B one predicament? For what prevents all other things that are said to exist from being from substance? Or perhaps the other things are indeed certain affections of substance itself, while substances themselves are arranged successively in some other way?

*Number, continuum, place, time, which the Peripatetics place in one genus of quantity, do not seem to have one nature equally common to all, but rather to be arranged in a certain common series, one after another, through degrees reduced to a primary quantity. Chapter IIII.*

*Number alone indeed seems to be quantitative per se, and quantity itself, in this, unity itself defines each successive unity: dimension, compared to this, is measured as to how much it is: place and body are measured by dimension.*

A They certainly say that number is primarily quantitative, and all continuous magnitude, and place and time: and whatever other things they call quantitative, they refer to all of these. Thus they say that motion is quantitative, and the time in which it is completed. Although perhaps it seems that it should be treated conversely: since time receives its continuity from motion. Now indeed, if they say that the continuum, in the respect that it is continuous, is quantitative, it will follow that what is discrete is not quantitative:
B but if the continuum is quantitative by accident, what will be common to both in the very fact that they are quantitative? For they are accustomed to understand passion in two ways, saying that it leads either to worse, or to better, or to neither.

*The same motion, if referred to the agent, can be called action: if referred to the patient, it can be named passion.
