A  PERHAPS, then, suffering indeed occurs from the fact that something has motion within itself, a motion, I mean, of alteration, by which it is altered in some way; but to act is either to have an absolute motion in oneself and from oneself, or to produce a motion from oneself passing into another: which also begins from that very thing which is said to act. And indeed, motion is in both; but the difference distinguishing acting from suffering is such that acting itself is fervent, as acting is free from passion: suffering, however, is when
B  something is affected differently than before, while the essence of the patient itself acquires nothing pertaining to its essence, but rather suffers something else in the meantime, when some essence is generated. Therefore, the same thing, in one relation, is to act, but in another relation, to suffer. For in respect to this, it will be considered acting, when the motion is the same: but in respect to that, it will be suffering, because that (thing) is now thus affected. Both, therefore, seem to be referred to something, inasmuch as the condition of acting
C  relates to the property of suffering: namely, the same thing in respect to this is to act, but in respect to that to suffer, and both are certainly considered, not so much according to themselves, as together with the agent and the patient, where the former indeed moves, and the latter is moved, and both are two certain categories. And indeed, the former transmits motion to the latter, and the latter in turn receives motion: wherefore transmission and reception and reason occur there.

**A** It remains to dispute concerning the predicament which they name 'to have'. Indeed, if they say 'to have' in many ways, what prevents all modes of having from being equally reduced to this predicament? Therefore, quantity itself will easily be reduced here, since it has magnitude: likewise, quality will be referred to the same place, because it **B** has color. Again, father and family: because both the father has a son, and the son has a father: and in summary, all possessions, and furnishings which are had. If they should say that whatever else is had is in its own predicaments: but arms and shoes and clothes are in this proper predicament of 'having', first indeed someone will ask, for what reason this happens: then why indeed 'having' these things constitutes one distinct predicament. But burning them, or dividing them, or hiding them, **C** or throwing them away, does not again constitute another predicament, or other things. If they respond that a predicament is made for this reason, because they are wrapped around the body, it will follow that if a garment is placed on a litter, another predicament arises from that, and again another if someone is completely covered by a garment. But if they assert that the predicament itself is made according to the proper act of containing and having, indeed thus it will be necessary for all other things, which are denominated 'to have' according to this very thing, to be referred here under the same condition, and all those things, wherever the habit itself occurs, will have to be reduced to the habit itself. For it will make no difference what that is which is had. Therefore, if in describing a predicament of this kind, it is not to be said 'to have quality', because quality itself has already been spoken of in its own place: again, nor 'to have quantity', because quantity has previously occupied its place: likewise, nor 'to have parts', because substance has already been properly described. Why then is it permissible to say 'to have arms', when substance has already been defined, in whose genus arms are properly contained? For shoes, clothes, arms are substances. Furthermore, in what way is this very thing simple, and of only one predicament, when we say, namely, 'he has arms'? For that signifies what is called 'to be armed', or 'to be in an armed state'.

In the first place, indeed, they gather the prior things together with the posterior things into a single entity, whereas otherwise it cannot happen that in the same genus one thing is prior and another truly posterior. For in those things in which there is prior and posterior, that which is posterior certainly has its essence from the prior; but in those things which are under the same genus, each has an equality of being with respect to the same genus. Clearly, this must be the genus, which is predicated of the species in its essence; since they themselves (B) will confess, as I believe, that all other things have their essence from matter. *If primary matter is subject to all things, both movers and forms, it cannot be the principle of things. Chapter XXVII.*

*Nor does matter, formless by itself, give birth to forms, nor can any form lying in matter exist from itself, since it can never subsist in itself: nor is their principle some form mixed with matter, otherwise it will not be able to dominate matter. But the most efficient mover must finally be free from material impediments. But if anyone imagines matter to be the principle of forms, he will deny that it is subject, and will affirm that all forms exist through its essence. And finally, whatever truly exists in the world is matter, and forms are certain imaginings. But in reality, since a form cannot be produced from naturally formless matter, much less life, which is a more excellent form: and least of all mind, the most excellent form. Finally, the principle of material form is a certain power not springing from matter, although it is infused into matter. And the principle of this life is life itself, far surpassing matter.*

And altogether, when they say 'quality' and 'how it is disposed,' either they add nothing beyond matter thus disposed, or they do add something: if nothing, it will truly be a single category: if something else, they never explain what this something is when asked: nor do they ever distinguish between qualified matter and matter how it is disposed, by this distinction, namely, intending to make more categories. **CONCERNING THE KINDS OF BEING, SECOND.**

Concerning the kinds of being.

We consider only that to be true being, to which the opposite of being is not mixed, that is, the defect and privation of becoming. Chapter I.

Therefore, it ought to be whole in its nature, and always remain. It is not fitting to place false being together with true being under the same genus, just as not the image of Socrates with Socrates. Plotinus will indeed proceed to discuss the genera of beings in the Platonic manner: But you, Magnanimous Laurentius, will now receive a very brief interpretation of these things from your Marsilio. For you have sometimes heard, and perhaps sometimes will read, your and my friend Pierleone, treating such mysteries with a certain divine instinct, as he usually does with other things.

*Just as fire does not exist first, then its light, and heat, and dryness, and lightness: but these four are simultaneously with the essence of fire, as both its properties and concomitant acts, even when it exists in act; so too do its innermost motions, and state, and identity, and alterity relate to being itself. Chapter XV.*

In what way, therefore, do the four genera complete the essence, not yet making it a qualified essence: for they do not yet make a certain essence. Therefore, what has already been said about primary being itself, namely that motion is not another being, nor even a state, nor again alterity, nor identity, is sufficiently clear. Moreover, that this motion does not bring about quality there, is perhaps manifest: but if it is stated, it will also become manifest. For if motion is an act of essence, and being is an act, and universally those things which are primary are acts, then deservedly motion is not an accident there, but since it is rather the act of being truly existing in act, it should certainly not be said to complete the essence, but rather to be the essence itself. Therefore, it did not accede to the place of something posterior, nor in place of a quality, but was established in the order of something simultaneously accompanying. For being does not first exist, and then move. Nor must it be said that being exists first, and then rests. For state (rest) is not a passion there. Furthermore, identity and alterity themselves are not posterior, because that being did not later become many, but was already this very thing which was one and many. But if many, then alterity was there. Furthermore, if from the beginning many are one, then identity is also there simultaneously. And these indeed suffice for essence. But when there is to be a progression from there to lower things, then other things arise, which no longer make essence, but 'what kind of essence' and 'how much essence', and certain genera of this kind are indeed formed, but not primary ones.

*Relation, place, where, when, time, position, habit, action together with passion are neither primary genera, nor among them. For they are adventitious, and signify composition and defect. Chapter XVI.*

Therefore, how can relation, similar to some adventitious offshoot, be established among the primary things? For relation is of one thing to another, and it is not a relation to itself, but always to another. *Just as in the intelligible world, so in this sensible world, five genera of things are to be posited; yet they are not to be arranged under a single genus. Nor should it be thought that these genera agree in the same nature with those higher ones, although they may correspond by a certain proportion. Nor is the substance of the intellectual soul to be placed under inferior genera. Chapter I.*

[Decorative initial D] Indeed, it has already been said concerning being, and what seems most likely to us, and how it accords with the Platonic doctrine; but after this, we must consider the other nature, whether we should posit the same genera here as there, or assert that there are more and other genera here in addition to those, or entirely different ones here and there, or posit some of the same here and there, but others in a different way. And when we posit the same genera here and there, we must understand it as speaking equivocally and by analogy. This will become clear then, when these things are known individually. Our beginning, therefore, will be as follows: Since our discourse is concerning sensible things, and every sensible thing is in this world, it is necessary for us first to inquire concerning the world, dividing the nature of this world, and dividing the things of which it is composed, to arrange them into genera, just as if we were to divide an indefinite sound into a certain number, making that which is the same in many things into one, and again another, and again another, until we place each thing in a certain number, that which is in each, calling it a species. And speaking of genus as being in species, in the case of sound, it was possible to gather each species, and all things within it, into one, and to predicate a vocal element or letter or sound similarly of all. But in the things now being investigated, it is impossible to predicate similarly, as we have shown above. Therefore, it is necessary to seek more genera, and to assign different ones to this universe than to that, since this whole is also different from that, and does not agree with that univocally in reason, but is homonymous and an image. A [certain degree of] being cooked, to the extent that a pot or tile is scarcely made. Perhaps indeed matter and species are not from the same [principle]. For there is a difference even in those.

When we speak of sensible substance, it is better to take the composite than matter or form. But it is generally characteristic of composite substances that they are indeed subjects, and are not in subjects. Cap. VIII.

Incorporeal substance is pure substance, because it does not depend on accidents: but corporeal [substance] is not pure substance, because it is constituted by certain accidents, at least intimate and proper ones, otherwise it will not be the sensible corporeal substance which we are currently seeking.

**A** BUT perhaps it is fitting now to omit dividing into elements, especially when we are discussing sensible substance, which it is fitting to grasp by sense rather than by reason, and not to add from what it is composed. For those are not substances, or certainly not sensible substances. But it seems worthwhile to comprehend in one certain genus what is common to stone, and earth, and water, and moreover to those things which are composed from these, namely plants and animals, insofar as they are sensible:
**B** for thus neither matter nor form will be omitted by us in the meantime: for sensible substance has these in itself. For fire and earth and their intermediates are both matter and form: but composite substances are already many substances brought together into one: and indeed this very thing by which they are separated from others is common to all these. For these are subjects to other things, and are not in a subject, nor are they considered to be dependent on another. And in general, whatever we have recounted as proper to substance rightly applies to this. But if sensible substance does not exist without magnitude and quality, in what way shall we separate these accidents from it?
**C** For separating these, magnitude, figure, color, dryness, humidity, what then shall we further posit it to be? For these are, as it were, qualitative substances. But there is certainly something around which these very things converge, which together bring it about that what was only substance becomes such a substance:
**D** and thus fire will not be entirely substance, but something of it, as it were a part, will be judged to be substance. But what will this be? Perhaps indeed matter. Is sensible substance therefore a certain collection of qualities and matter? And all these mixed together in one matter are substance.
**E** But each one taken separately from there will be one thing of a certain quality, another of a certain quantity, or many qualities. Then indeed, that which among these is such that if it is ever lacking, it leaves the essence imperfect, exists as a part of this essence. But that which happens to an already complete essence obtains a certain other proper order, and is not included in that mixture which constitutes this aforementioned essence. Nor indeed do I say at present that something of this kind, while it is there together with the rest, is essence or substance, while namely
**F** it properly completes one mass so great and of such a kind. But where it does not complete something of this kind, it is rather a quality. But I say that not even whatever is there is substance: but the whole gathered from all is substance. Nor should it be taken ill if we compose sensible substance from non-substances: for that whole is not true substance and essence, but rather imitates true essence.

But if it is asserted to the same point, that generation is nothing other than a certain alteration or permutation, and some augmentation, because generation is of certain things which are permuted or altered, and in some way augmented: certainly, he who says these things will bring forward what precedes generation.
F But generation must be understood as another species in these matters: for generation and coming-to-be do not consist in something being passively altered in some way, such as becoming warm or becoming white. For it can happen that these things have already occurred, yet generation in the simple sense has not yet been there. And if you ask what we then say happens, we will answer, this very thing which we say is altered, or has been altered. But then at last generation occurs, when an animal comes to be, or a plant, or something similar, when, namely, a certain species is received there. Therefore, one will be able to argue that it would be reasonable to place transmutation rather than motion in the species, because the very condition of transmutation signifies something else coming to be in place of another, or for another: but the nature of motion also has a certain transition from its own (state), like local motion.

--- Page 682 ---
628        PLOTINUS  ENNEAD.  VI.

If someone is less inclined to that, at least the very act of learning, or the striking of a lyre, or indeed any movement arising from a habit, will be of this kind. Therefore, transmutation itself, or change, since it is a kind of motion, positing something beyond itself, will rather be a species of motion.

*Common to all motions is a certain progression from potentiality to actuality, whether this actuality be primary, like form; or secondary, like some action or passion. Motion proceeding into a natural habit can be called a certain species: but proceeding into an unnatural habit, it is the fall of one species to the advent of another. Moreover, motion, especially natural motion, is most similar to life: but most especially proper to motion is alterity, that is, being otherwise than before, consequently proper also to time. Chapter XXII.*

A BUT let there be indeed the notion of permutation or alteration, insofar as something else follows motion: what then must motion be said to be? Let motion therefore be, so that we may speak summarily about it by way of analogy, an exit from potentiality into that which is said to be able (to be). For when something is in potentiality, through which it may proceed into some species, as a statue in potentiality, and again something in potentiality by which it may emerge into actuality, like something progressive; when that indeed proceeds into
B a statue, the process itself is motion: and when that which is progressive executes the act of progressing, the progression itself is motion: likewise, a jump in one who is able to jump, when he is now jumping. But in some motion, namely in that which leads to a statue, a species is produced other than the motion itself: but in some, as in a jump, the jumping itself is a simple species of the potentiality for jumping, and has nothing after itself,
C after the motion itself has ceased. Wherefore, if someone were to call motion a vigilant and awakening species, opposed to other species as if dormant, insofar as some indeed are at rest, while others are not at all: and were to call it the cause for other species when something is produced after it, he would not err at all. Furthermore, if someone were to call this motion of which we are presently speaking a kind of life of bodies,
D he himself would not seem far from the truth. For we must call this motion equivocal to the motions of mind and soul. Therefore, one will no less persuade himself that motion is a genus for this very reason, that it is neither easy, nor perhaps possible, to encompass it by definition. But how then is motion a species when it declines into something worse, or is altogether passive motion? Perhaps indeed this is almost so, just as heating under the sun sometimes increases some things, but decreases others,
E and motion itself is something common and the same in both cases: but according to the subjects, it receives the apparent difference. But from this it seems to follow that sickness and recovery are the same. But indeed, insofar as they are motions, they seem to be the same, but by what will they differ? By subjects? Or rather by something else? But this will be treated in what follows, when we consider alteration: but now it must be observed what is the same in all motions: for thus it will be able to be a genus. But perhaps it is said in many ways, and it is so, just as one might say "becoming" is a genus. But to that concerning which principally

A Those things which are moved are said thus to acquire a certain mixing, and a tempering and constitution into one: that, I say, which consists in that act, while something is being constituted, not in a certain state, after something has already been constituted. B just as anyone easily finds local motion to be the principle of increase, but that there a motion proper to quality soon follows. So here too, a certain local motion indeed begins, but concretion or discretion does not necessarily follow: but when things that meet each other embrace each other, concretion happens, whereas conversely, discretion follows. Often indeed, where discretion occurs, local motion also follows,
C or happens there simultaneously. *Status is in eternal things, where there is no motion: but quies is in temporal things, namely a certain privation*
*of some motion, or a very slow motion. Chapter XXVII.*

Since therefore quies is a certain privation, it is not a genus in itself: but motion is not simply the privation of quies, but is an effective act taking away something and bringing something. Status in eternal things is not a privation of motion, for neither is there status there by the cessation of motion, nor are those things naturally inclined to motion. Motion has two opposites, namely both motion which seeks different terms and quies, especially if quies is considered in the term from which motion now departs.

EPILOGUE OF THE CATEGORIES.

      Indeed, it has been said by us in the foregoing that
to act and to suffer are motions. But some motions
are indeed absolute, while others are partly actions,
and partly also passions. Furthermore, it has been said
that the other things which are called genera, ought to be
referred to these of ours. It has also been said concerning
relation, namely, that it is the disposition of one thing to another,
and that both concur simultaneously. Finally, it has been
said concerning relation, when namely the disposition itself
constitutes substance, that which is referred is not a relative
in the sense of being substance: but in the sense of being some
part, like a hand, or a head, or a cause, or a principle,
or an element. It is also permitted to divide relatives
according to the custom of the ancients, so that some are
as it were effective, others as it were certain measures:
some are found in excess and defect, and finally others
are distinguished by similarities and differences. But let these things
already said concerning these kinds suffice.

A but every body throughout its whole is as it were illuminated by the soul. Indeed, nothing ought to seem surprising, if that divine universal, since it is not in a place itself, is present to everything that is in a place: on the contrary, it would be both wonderful and moreover impossible, if that [being], having its own proper place, were present to something that is in a place, or if it were present at all, and were present in the way we speak of presence. But now B reason dictates that it is necessary that it, since it does not have a place, be present whole to whatever it is present to: and since it is present to the universal, it must be present in such a way that it is present whole to each individual: otherwise, one part of it would be here, and another there, to such an extent that it would be both divisible and a body. Now indeed, it is permissible to ask, how would you divide it? Would you divide life? But where you have divided it, if the whole was life, a part will not be life. But would you divide intellect, so that one part is in one thing, and the other C in another? But neither of those would be intellect. Or then, would you divide its being? But indeed, a part would not be being in that way, if the whole existed as being. What then? if someone objects that a divided body also has parts, which are themselves also bodies: but certainly the division was not of the body, but rather of such a body: and each body is made and called a body by its species. But this, especially as it pertains to species, does not properly have a certain quantity, indeed, D not even any quantity whatsoever.

*The one primary essence, that is, the divine mind, is whole everywhere, similarly the one soul of the world: nor does the multitude of worldly parts prevent it from being one and whole everywhere: nor does the unity of the primary mind and soul prevent there from being many other minds and souls besides. Chapter IIII.*

*Nor is the soul compelled to be manifold and divisible by the many members of the same body: nor do many souls arise through many bodies: for there are both minds and souls differing among themselves in their own properties, and also bodies: and they are joined to each other by a certain natural kinship and community of function, and yet distinct by the otherness of property and essence, not by place.*

A BUT how then is it permissible to speak of being and beings, and many minds, and many souls? If being is one everywhere, and not one merely as something conformable: likewise if mind is one, if soul is one: even though we have received that the soul of the universe is one thing, and the other souls are others. For these things seem to contradict what has already been said: and what has been said, if perchance it has some necessity, nevertheless does not bring persuasion, B since the mind considers it incredible that one and the same thing is thus whole everywhere. Perhaps therefore it is better to divide that one whole, yet in such a way that that from which the division is made is not diminished thereby: or rather, to generate certain things from it, to speak more correctly, and to permit that [original] to subsist in itself: and to consider those things which are generated from it as if parts, to be souls already completing all things. But if that being rests in itself for this reason, precisely because it seems incredible for some one whole to be simultaneously everywhere, the same C reasoning will certainly likewise doubt concerning souls. For these [souls], in which bodies they are said to be whole in wholes, will no longer be so: but either they will be divided, or if they remain whole in a certain part of the body, they will properly rest there, and from there diffuse their powers through the members. And the same [reasoning] applies to the powers themselves, [namely that] it is whole everywhere. Moreover, one member of the body will have the soul, while another will have only a power. But first of all, it must be investigated in what way

A If from the higher realms there are many souls, many minds, many beings besides the One. Now, indeed, those things which flow from the prior principles, yet in such a way that they are not magnitudes but numbers, will similarly raise the question of how they fill the universe. Therefore, nothing clearly discovered by us from such a flowing multitude contributes to explaining the difficulty. Since we concede that Being itself is many by a certain otherness, but not by place. For Being as a whole is B simultaneously, although it is thus manifold: namely, as Parmenides says, being approaches being, and is simultaneously the whole. Moreover, Intellect is manifold by otherness, not by place, but is simultaneously all. Do souls also behave in this way? Perhaps souls too. For that which is said to be divisible concerning bodies is again considered to be indivisible according to its nature: but bodies having magnitude are present C to them, namely, by the nature of the soul itself: nay, when bodies are formed there, and insofar as that nature of the soul itself, which is concerned with bodies, appears, extending through every part, it thus happens that the soul is considered divisible in relation to them. For that it is not D distributed into parts along with the parts of the body, but is present everywhere as a whole, is clearly evident to us from the fact that nature is truly found to be one and indivisible. Therefore, from the fact that the soul is one, it is not removed that there are many: just as the One Being does not prohibit there being beings, nor does multiplicity there contradict unity: nor is it necessary for life to fill bodies through a certain multiplicity: nor, because of the magnitude of the body, E must we suppose that a multitude of souls comes into being, but rather that many souls exist even before bodies, and as one. For in the whole itself, many already subsist, not indeed in potentiality, but each already in actuality. For that one whole does not prevent many from existing within itself: and many, in turn, do not impede the one. For they are distant from each other, yet not distant; and they are present to each other, yet not alien. For they are not separated from each other by any boundaries: just as many sciences gathered in one soul are not separated: but the soul itself is such that it contains all within itself. Thus, precisely such a nature is infinite.

_The Soul of the world, like the Mind, is individual and universal at the same time, therefore it is entirely everywhere in the world. Chapter V._
_Since the Soul does not have quantity, it is not smaller or larger in quantity than the world, but in power, which the world cannot even entirely contain. The same soul, however, suffices for a larger as well as a smaller body because of the magnitude of its power._

A THEREFORE, the magnitude of this nature is not to be estimated according to bulk: for bulk is a small thing, destined to fall towards nothing if one subtracts from it. But from that nature it is neither right to subtract, nor, if by chance you were to subtract, would it in any way diminish. If it does not diminish at all, there is no need to fear that it might be absent from anything anywhere. For how could it be absent from anything, since it suffers no defect, but is an eternal, non-flowing nature? Otherwise, if it were to flow, it would proceed only as far as it could flow. B But since it does not flow at all, nor indeed has it anywhere to flow, it already completely comprehends the whole. Nay, it is itself the universe, and is something greater than can be estimated according to the magnitude of corporeal nature. For it is rightly considered a small thing to attribute to this universe: insofar, namely, as this is able to bear of that. But it is necessary neither to call that higher universe smaller, nor to place it as smaller according to bulk, lest...

The multitude of numbers flowing from one, and of lines flowing from a center, do not prevent that one or this center from being indivisible and unique. Similarly, the soul is not compelled to become divisible, or multiple, on account of diverse members or bodies. Indeed, just as the guiding power is whole in every part of a weight, and the same indivisible light is whole in every part of the air, so also is the soul. Chapter VII.

A BUT let us say again how the same thing is through all things: and this is similar to asking under what condition each of many sensible things scattered everywhere participates in the same nature. Indeed, it is certain that it is wrong to divide the one itself into many on account of the multitude of things, but rather it is fitting to rightly gather the many divided things into one: which, however, would not apply to these. But because these [things] are scattered, they have compelled us to suppose that that [one] is also, B in a certain way, scattered according to these [things]: as if someone were to think that what surpasses and contains, together with what is contained, should be divided into equal parts. Although a hand can indeed contain a whole body and a piece of wood many cubits long, and anything else. Where indeed the very force that contains is active everywhere in what is held, yet it is not divided into equal parts along with what is held by the hand: although it appears that insofar as the hand reaches, to that extent C the power is circumscribed. But the hand, meanwhile, is described by its own quantity, not by the quantity of the body that is suspended and held: and yet if you add another length to the suspended body, and the hand is able to sustain it, the very power of guiding will also guide that, not, of course, cut into as many parts as the body has. What then? If someone were to imagine the corporeal mass of the hand secretly stolen away from the midst: but meanwhile leaves there the same force that previously sustained the weight, and was formerly in the hand, D will not the same indivisible force be in the whole weight similarly through every part? Moreover, if you fix a certain small and luminous body somewhere as a center, and place around it some larger spherical and transparent body: so that the light of the inner body shines through the whole surrounding [body], where there is no other earth for the external mass, shall we not say that that inner light, while suffering nothing, but remaining, has proceeded through the entire E external mass? and that the light, conspicuous there in the small body, has thence entirely embraced all that surrounds it. Since indeed the light itself did not emanate from the corporeal mass of that center, for it did not possess light insofar as it is a body, but insofar as it is a luminous body, namely through another incorporeal power. Tell me now, if someone were to remove the mass of that body, but preserve the power of light there, would you still say that the light is properly F somewhere? Will it not rather be equally both within, and throughout the entire outer sphere? nor will you any longer fix in thought where it was previously placed, nor will you say any longer either whence, or where the light is: but concerning this you will be ambiguous and utterly astonished: at the same time you will see the same light both here and there throughout the globe. Now indeed, can you say concerning the sun whence especially the light illuminates the entire air? You do not, of course, direct your gaze into the body of the sun, and at the same time you behold the same light everywhere and undivided. This indeed is testified by the very divisions that are made from light, which certainly do not render light elsewhere than from the region whence the light had flowed out, nor do they cut or diminish the light.

*Since the soul is prior to every corporeal thing, it rightly depends on nothing: therefore it needs no place, is bound to none, and thus relates to every place indifferently and equally: therefore it is commonly everywhere and nowhere, unless some soul applies itself to something specific through its own affection. Chapter VIII.*

*Likewise, since it is indivisible, wherever it is, it exists whole. Whatever therefore receives it, receives it undividedly, in a way, as a whole, although it may not fully enjoy all its powers. The soul of the world, just as it is not itself a body, or a passion, or a proper form of a body within bodies, so it is not manifold, nor is it divided, nor does it suffer. And since it is enslaved to none, it is readily present to all.*

A But if the sun itself were some sole power segregated from a body, and poured forth light, and neither originated entirely from here or elsewhere, nor would you indicate whence it is sent; but it would be entirely light existing everywhere, one and the same, neither originating nor having a principle from anywhere.

A INDEED, since light is something of a body, you can easily say whence it came: since you can indicate where that body is. But if something is devoid of matter, and does not need a body, since it is naturally prior to every body, founded in itself, indeed, not needing such a foundation: this, I say, endowed with such a nature, having no principle from which to originate, nor dwelling within any place, nor existing as something of a body—B how then will you be able to say that something of it is here, and something of it is there? For thus it would both have a source from which it originated, and it would exist by another's right. It remains therefore to assert that if anything receives it, the very power of the whole receives it entirely, and that it does not thereby become something else or divisible. For it is fitting for that which has a body, although often by accident, yet rightly to suffer. And for this very reason, it can be judged passive and C divisible: inasmuch as it is something of a body, either as a passion or as a species. But that which is of no body, but exists entirely in such a way that a body desires to be of it, it is necessary that it admits none of the other passions of a body into itself, and especially that it can in no way be divided. For division is a passion of a body, and primarily, and insofar as it is a body. If therefore, insofar as it is a body, it is divisible, then surely, insofar as it is not a body, it exists entirely indivisible. D For by what condition will you divide that which has no magnitude? If therefore that which has magnitude participates in it in any way, that which has no magnitude perceives it undivided: otherwise, it would again have magnitude. When therefore you say that one exists in many, you do not say that it itself has become many, but rather you attach the passion of many around that one, observing it simultaneously in many. But that one in them is to be understood in such a way that it has not yet become the effect of each of them, nor of all of them together: but that it is its own master, and exists by itself. And since it exists by itself, it is nowhere lacking to itself, nor does it admit any defect. Nor again should it be thought that it is properly as much as the sensible universe, lest it be only as much as some part of the universe: for it is in no way quantitative at all.

*In what way, therefore, will it properly be so much or so great: for such a measure is fitting for a body: but to that which is not a body, but endowed with another nature, no such measure is to be applied in any way: since it is not even such a thing. Therefore, it is not to be placed anywhere: nor thus here and there, otherwise often*

it would be somewhere. If, therefore, division according to place is appropriate when something of the thing itself is here and something there, it follows that for that which it is not appropriate to be somewhere, division is in no way fitting. Wherefore it is necessary for that to remain indivisible in itself, although many things affect it and even attain it. If, then, many desire it, it is clear that they desire the whole of it; and so if they can attain it, they attain the whole of it according to their powers. Wherefore it is necessary that those which participate in it, participate in it as if they do not participate, since it itself has become the property of none. For thus it remains whole in itself, and at the same time, in those things in which it is observed, it remains whole and appears. Otherwise, unless it remains whole there, neither will it itself exist, nor will the things themselves participate in that which they desire, but rather in something else which they least desired.

*The first Soul, while exhibiting itself whole to many parts of the world, is neither multiplied into many equally primary souls (for these would in no way differ among themselves), nor into parts; for it is indivisible. Otherwise, where it approaches to govern a mass, it would utterly fail, being weakened. Chapter IX.*

*It adapts its powers to the members of the world; but these powers are so essential and proper to it that they are inseparable from it. Therefore, it itself is whole everywhere. Furthermore, even if it imparts only images of its powers to the world, it itself is similarly present to the whole, to govern its images everywhere. Finally, just as in us, so in the world, unless the same life flourished everywhere, there would not be such a wonderful agreement and sympathy of the parts among themselves and with the whole, everywhere. And what we say about the soul of the world, understand to be said similarly about the divine intellect.*

**A** THEREFORE, if that common one is thus divided into parts in many things, so that each part is as it were the whole itself, it follows that there are many primary things, and each one is primary. Moreover, by what means will these many primary things be distinguished, lest all be one simultaneously? For they will not be separated by their bodies; for it is impossible for them to be species of bodies, since these too are similar to that first one from which they emanate. But if what are

For if they abandon it, it is clear that they left it somewhere, while they themselves proceeded elsewhere. Likewise, whether these powers, which have been made here in the sensible realm, are still in that, or not. If parts, then what remains there will be parts; but if whole, then the same ones that are there are also here, in no way divided; and thus it will again be the same everywhere, in no way divided. Or these powers are that whole, having already become many individually, of which each is whole, and such powers are similar to each other. And thus,

*Our soul is wholly present with its full powers to every member, although other members receive other powers from it, more or less: similarly, the soul of the world and the divine mind relate to the parts of the world. Chapter XI.*

*Corporeal things often differ from each other by external boundaries: incorporeal things, however, although they do not differ from each other by external boundaries, are distinguished by their intrinsic properties: thus ideas from ideas in the mind, sciences from sciences in the intellectual soul, mind from soul, minds from minds, souls from souls. Indeed, body is not easily present to body, body easily to soul, soul more easily to soul, and minds most easily to mind. Easier indeed is the union of light to light, than of light to the diaphanous. And this is easier than of quality to quality or to body: and again, that is easier than the interaction of bodies among themselves.*

A Therefore, it must indeed be said that the soul descends and insinuates itself into the body, just as we said it is infused into the body; and this is to hand over something from itself to this (body), yet in such a way that the soul does not escape the body. But to depart from the body, that is, for its body to participate in nothing. Furthermore, it must be considered that an order of communion of this kind exists for the parts of this universe; but the soul itself, as if placed at the extreme degree of the intelligible B realm, frequently bestows something from itself, inasmuch as it is close in power and in shorter intervals, and therefore bestows by a law of this kind of nature.

But a union of this kind is evil, while divorce is good. But why so? Because even if the soul was not properly of this (body), yet when it is said to become of this (body) in any way whatsoever, it somehow becomes particular from the universal. For its action is no longer directed to the whole, although it itself is of the whole, just as it happens in one who, though he possesses all knowledge, acts only according to a certain notion C of it.

But the good of the knowing one itself was to act not through some part of its knowledge, but through the whole which it possesses. Now, when the soul itself existed as part of the whole intelligible world, and concealed a part within the whole, it sometimes broke forth from the universal into a part, since that into which it exerted itself was a part, just as if fire, powerful enough to burn the whole, is compelled to burn some small D thing, although it possesses all its power.

For each soul, when it is completely separated from here, is not merely each one properly speaking; but when it is separated not by place, but by act, and becomes something singular, it is then a certain portion, no longer universal, although in another way it also subsists as if universal. But when it properly presides over nothing, it is entirely universal, inasmuch as it is then to be judged as a part by a certain power. Therefore, what they say about the soul going to the underworld, if they mean the name of the underworld to signify something hidden, then to go to the underworld is nothing other than to be apart. But if by this name they designate a certain inferior place, what is surprising? since even now where our body is, and in what place, there the soul is said to be. But when the body no longer exists, what is it for the soul to be in the underworld? Perhaps, if the soul's image is not entirely torn away, why should we not think the soul is there, where the soul's image is? But if philosophy completely dissolves (it), the image alone departs to an inferior place; but the soul itself lives very purely in the intelligible world, with nothing then excepted from it, or led forth outside. And so indeed let that image be which is produced from such a thing. But when it itself shines forth as if within itself, by a certain nod towards those things which are alien from here, then it is already contracted to the whole, and neither exists in act, nor even perishes. But let these things said suffice concerning these matters; but let us again resume the discussion proposed from the beginning.

<center>CONCERNING THE FACT THAT BEING, BEING ONE AND THE SAME, IS SIMULTANEOUSLY WHOLE EVERYWHERE, AND INFINITE.</center>
<center>That being, one and the same existing, is simultaneously whole everywhere.</center>

Natural judgment, which cannot be mistaken, declares that there is one God whole everywhere. Likewise, the natural appetite of all things, recalling all things to one good, testifies that the entire nature of beings depends on one simply good, and through it possesses mutual union. But the first receptacle of this one good is the first being itself: which indeed, together with itself, is simultaneously one whole everywhere. Chapter 1.

The sensible world is dispersed in three principal ways: by local extension and division; likewise by temporal succession; again by mutual contrariety of qualities. But the intelligible world, that is, the first fullness of ideas, admits no such division. Likewise neither the world of life, that is, the assembly of intellectual souls wonderfully united with the first mind and its ideas.

**Chapter II.**

But lest on account of the union, here and above and below, more frequently celebrated by Plotinus, you suspect that neither minds nor souls are plural in number, pay attention to what I say. For here he says that all beings are one, which it is clear are not one by the unity of individual essence; but he says they are one because they are from one, and flow together to one by a certain unity of natural desire; likewise because all separate things which he calls beings, are in one another with no spatial boundaries preventing it.

Likewise because inferior things among the grades of beings perform their principal action under the form and act of superior things.

A if it were no longer one, just as if some magnitude were divided into many: for thus it would be dissipated, nor would all parts exist as that whole of another. Again, if B we say that nature is infinite (for we would not concede it to be finite), why especially infinite, unless because it never fails? For if it could not be present, it would certainly fail, and there would be something where it was not: Now indeed, even if we say that something else exists after the One, again it must be simultaneously with it: and that which is after it, must revolve around it, and strive towards C it, and be its offspring connected to it, so much so that what participates in that which is after it, also participates in it. Therefore, since there are many things in the intelligible world, and there are first, second, and third in rank, and all subsequent things are, as it were, simultaneously affixed to the center of one sphere, nor are they separated from each other by any intervals, but all things are there simultaneously, deservedly wherever the third things are, there also the second and first are equally present, but let us explain this matter more clearly hereafter.

*Often he takes the first being and intellect for the intelligible world, in which, as in a common center, are the ideas of things, as certain proper centers. Often also he takes that for what I have said, but by joining to those ideas, as centers, immaterial forms depending thence as lines, which, as they are connected there, are one, as they are produced thence, are many. And this whole collection is the intelligible world, more one than the collection of material forms annexed to one matter, which is called the sensible world: but that intelligible world is more one, because immaterial forms are assigned more closely and firmly to their ideas, and through ideas to the intellect, than material forms to their beginnings, and through them to matter. Also, because that world is one by the unity of the highest form, while this one is one by the unity of the lowest matter: also because here local distance of parts, repugnance of qualities, and total temporal transmutation impede union: but there these impediments do not exist. Also, the intelligible world is compared to a very ample sphere, within whose circumference circumferences are contained, and to whose center the centers of immaterial forms are reduced, as if of spheres thus contained in the first form, just as smaller spheres in a larger sphere. Such a union does not prohibit distinctions of essences, just as neither the union of forms in matter, nor the annexation of lines to centers and to the center, nor the collection of spheres in a sphere. Chapter 5.*

LIBER VI.
ΠΕΡΙ ΑΡΙΘΜΩΝ.
On Numbers.

If the one itself and the good are the same, deservedly the multitude, the further it departs from the one and from unity, the worse it becomes. Therefore, if a multitude is imagined either as infinite, or in any way devoid of unity, it will be evil itself. Cap. I.
Any separate species and the idea of each is most united with itself, because its essence is simple and individual. A natural species extended through the parts of the body is less united with itself, even as long as it preserves its continuity: therefore, less good. A discrete multitude, contingent on the dissolution of the continuous, has the least unity: therefore, evil. That which is imagined to preserve no unity at all is called the greatest evil.

A <img src="decorative_V.png" alt="Decorative initial V depicting a figure" width="20" height="20"> IT seems to be feared, first of all, whether multitude is a departure and distance from the one, and therefore infinity itself is the extreme departure from unity, because this is an innumerable multitude, and for this very reason infinity becomes evil, and we are evil when we are multitude.
B For then anything becomes a multitude, when, unable to remain in itself with the same, it is diffused and already extended as dispersed: and when in that very diffusion it is entirely deprived of the one, it becomes a multitude, where that which unites one part with another is lacking. But if some conciliator is present, then what is diffused becomes magnitude by remaining. But what

Since if this were deprived of beauty itself, insofar as it is great, it would have appeared also ugly, and thus this very greatness is the material of beauty, because it is much that needs adornment. Therefore, that which is great, if separated from beauty, is more unadorned and more ugly.

Chapter XIII.

*For 'one' is predicated equally of non-man and of man, and man is a kind of multitude just as he is one. 'One' itself predicated of man is not merely negative, as if it only signifies this man and not another: for after you have perceived this man to be truly one, you immediately judge that there is no other man there who is also one in himself. Furthermore, the nature of 'one' itself is so firm that its opposite, that is, multitude, can neither exist without one, nor be understood; indeed, all things whatsoever exist by union: as if 'one' itself exists most especially by itself, and is supreme among all things: without its participation, no thought arises or remains in us: and likewise, with the participation of unity, even a discrete multitude becomes something one, and a continuous thing becomes more one, and an individual thing is most one: certainly 'one' itself possesses its own existence. Furthermore, the Peripatetics confirm that 'one' signifies something entirely undivided and undifferentiated in itself, and that it is affirmative, not negative. For they say that the opposite of this meaning is something divided in itself: in which division multitude occurs together with privation: both because prior essence defines it thus, and also because when multitude occurs, we now say negatively, 'neither is this that, nor is that this'. Since, therefore, the meaning opposite to 'one' is negative, it follows that the meaning of 'one' is affirmative. Finally, 'one' is so affirmative that it even posits multitude, and not vice versa: and just as Avicenna proves in his Metaphysics, 'one' is perceived and conceived by the intellect before 'many', although perhaps it can happen differently to the imagination.*

For it brings forth all-form ideas within itself, by its own certain motion, I say, a numerous motion, otherwise it would by no means

*Bodies indeed are resolved into dimensions, and these into numbers. In the primary exemplar, therefore, numbers indeed*

*Indeed, before the natural body is the body itself simply: therefore, the principles of the former are before the principles of the latter.*
*Dimensions, therefore, which are the boundaries of a body; likewise, numbers, which are the measures of dimensions, are conceived before the proper principles of natural things: wherefore they are also known without sensible matter. A body, indeed, is properly a body neither by matter nor by quality, but by quantity: for unless this is added, both are incorporeal.*
*Numbers, therefore, since they are the principles of quantity, are probably called the beginnings of bodies by the Pythagoreans: for they have the property of principles, inasmuch as they are constituted by the first and smallest differences, and proceed immediately from the simplest unity. This unity, freely pre-eminent, precedes the point assigned to a position: indeed, the super-essential unity itself precedes every essence designated by species. The first essence is considered primarily as living, then it is recognized as intellectual: but when it is primarily intellectual, it is simultaneously defined as a living intellectual, or an intellectual animal: numbers and figures, previously enfolded there, are then unfolded together with the intellectual animal there.*

Two

--- Page 738 ---
694 PLOTINUS ENNEAD. VI.
Two most important things are usually asked about anything: namely, what the thing itself is, and why it is. The former is explained by definition, but the latter is declared by assigning the efficient and final cause; and both are joined to each other.

Chapter II.
Sense, indeed, seeks neither; but reason seeks both separately; but intellect possesses both simultaneously. And in this, reason simultaneously obtains both: namely, when it has first defined what the nature of the thing itself is, it soon discovers its efficient and final cause in that very definition; and conversely, when it has first apprehended such a cause, it comprehends the nature of the thing itself therein. Furthermore, in an animal, both cosmic and any other, the members are so interwoven with each other, and the whole comes forth simultaneously, that when any part is inspected, its cause is immediately perceived, and vice versa. Much greater is the connection of both in the divine world, where in any idea, the others are connected. And the mind itself, holding simultaneously the 'what' and the 'why' of each thing, is each idea itself. Finally, fire

Chapter VIII.

Therefore, a horse is not conceived there so that a horse may be made here: otherwise, that [horse] would depend on this [one], and a horse would be known there before it was known. Then indeed the multitude of forms there seems to be enumerable to the extent that whatever you take in that which is after the One itself, always appears as multiple. The first fullness, indeed, whatever it has, has everything equally full within itself.

[A] But let the faculty of sensation indeed be so. But in what way does that whole horse, and any animal there, not look to these our [animals]? since, so that a horse or any other animal may be generated here, that intellect would have come to the very notion of a horse, even though it is impossible to know that it, already willing a horse, then thought of making a horse. For already, without a doubt, [B] the intellection of a horse would have existed, if it merely wished to make a horse. Therefore, it is not given that it made it think, but it is clear that the ungenerated horse existed first, before the horse that would be here. If therefore it existed before generation, and the intellect was not for it to be generated, then indeed, not looking to these our [things], it had the horse within itself, which possesses the horse there: nor did it have the horse and other things in order to make these; but those things indeed existed, and these things necessarily followed from those: for it was not given to proceed only up to those things and [C] stop there. But they proceed always letting go of something, and in letting go, they always suggest other things, and still other things: and because of the need of the animal now emerging, from the fact that it suffers defect, they contrive to apply something else: as if because there is no longer sufficiency for life, a claw and a beak appeared, horns, teeth appeared. Therefore, wherever the mind itself descends, there again the sufficiency of its nature receives itself from above and emerges, and finds in itself the exposed remedy for what is deficient.

*First life and intelligence, and the most perfect animal, contain all the grades and species of life, intelligence, and animals, however many can be conceived. Chapter X.*
*Since there is the first multiplication there, deservedly what is better is multiplied into species, which are greatly united with each other, and equally distinct. Indeed, in dark matter, the forms of things are scarcely united with each other, and soon are confused among themselves: but in the first form, they are most effective and at the same time most clear. All forms of things, together with their common nature, wonderfully preserve their properties, and the whole there appears uniformly and omniformly.*

BUT in what way is there any defect there? What about horns there? Is it not for the sake of defense? Certainly, certain such things are there for its very self-sufficiency and perfection, as if of the animal itself. For just as the animal ought to be perfect, so too the mind, perfect; so too life, perfect. Therefore, if not this, yet that. And the difference itself indeed is from the fact that one thing is for another, so that from all there may be the most perfect animal, the most perfect mind, the most perfect life: but individual things are also perfect as individual things. Then indeed, even if it consists of many, it must again be one, and conversely: otherwise, it is impossible that it should indeed be from many, but that those many things should be the same among themselves: otherwise, one would have been self-sufficient. Therefore, it must consist of things always differing in species, just as every composite: yet in such a way that individual things are properly preserved, such as are forms and principles. For forms, such as the form of man, ought to exhibit as many differences as they consist of: although something in all is one, where some things are better and some worse in relation to each other, like an eye and a finger: nevertheless, they are members of one and the same, of which each is inferior to the whole. But for the matter to be so is undoubtedly better; moreover, reason is an animal, and something else besides which is not entirely the same as an animal. Virtue also has something common in itself and something proper, and the whole is beautiful, where what is common, is equally common.

For it causes that intelligent beings everywhere understand, and living beings live, inspiring mind, inspiring also life, inspiring being at least, where life cannot be received.

*To be desirable is not so much the very nature of the good, as a certain condition consequent to the very nature of the good. It is debated what is the very nature and reason of the good, and what follows the good: whether they obtain only pleasure from it, or also something else besides: and by what certain sign we may be able to discern the true good to be present. Chapter XXIV.*

A It would remain to inquire what it especially does towards us. But again we are about to speak of light: what is the light by which the mind is illuminated, and of which the soul is also a participant. But it is better for the present, deferring this to the future, first to investigate whether the good itself is and is called good because it is to be desired by another: and that which is desirable to someone, is also good to someone: but that which is to be desired by all, we would affirm to be the good itself.
B Or rather, should someone judge this to be a sign of the good, and that what is desirable should be that nature by which it may rightly claim such a designation for itself. It must be asked furthermore, whether those desiring it desire it by receiving something from it, or merely by rejoicing in it? And if they receive something, what is that? But if they only rejoice, why only in this, and not in anything else? Where indeed this also must be investigated, whether the good is to be weighed by its own proper reason, or by something else?
C Then indeed, whether the good is entirely for another, or whether the good itself is also good for itself? Or rather, for whatever it is good, it is not good for itself, but necessarily for another? Likewise, for which nature it is especially good: for there is some nature for which nothing is good. Nor do I think that should be passed over in silence, which perhaps some stubborn and contentious person might object. Why, O men, will he say, do you adorn your subject more gloriously by looking up and down? You call life good, and mind also good:
D although above these you establish the good itself. Tell me, I pray, what is the mind itself as good? what good does it have, understanding the forms themselves, while it contemplates what each thing is? It can perhaps happen that, deceived by the delight of these, he calls it good: similarly also he considers life good as something sweet to himself. But if by chance he is in such a state that he is touched by no pleasure, why then will he affirm these to be good?
E Or perhaps he will think it good, namely, to exist? But what fruit will he perceive from existence itself? Or what difference will it make to him to be, or not to be at all, unless someone asserts that a certain friendship towards oneself is the cause of these? So much so that on account of this deception naturally inherent in us, and the fear of death, the estimation of goods has been introduced.

*The good is indeed form to matter, but soul to body, intellect to soul, and to intellect, and to all simultaneously, the principle of all. Chapter XXV.*
*Form exhibits act and order to matter as good: soul gives life and motion to the body, intellect gives virtue to the soul, the principle gives to the intellect vital and intellectual act, and inestimable light: just as it follows the nature of fire that it illuminates distant things, but also warms nearby things: indeed, just as the center attracts and holds heavy things, so this condition accompanies the nature of the good, that it indeed attracts distant things through desire, but holds and delights present things.*

But that someone has already attained good can undoubtedly be believed when, namely, they are better off, are not affected by regret, but are fulfilled, and remain in it, and seek nothing else. Therefore, pleasure is not sufficient in itself: for he who is affected by pleasure does not desire the same thing. For even if he is said to desire pleasure itself, he will not yet be convinced to seek the same thing: for that

It is certainly necessary that the good which someone primarily desires is not some passion or affection by which he who attains it is inwardly affected: whence he who judges the affection itself to be good can remain empty, when he has only the affection, which another would similarly possess with the good present. Therefore, no one will primarily choose to be affected in such a way *without* having some good, as another *with* having it: as if to rejoice as if he has a son, when he does not have one. Nor do those who desire to fill their belly choose as good to be delighted in such a way, not eating as if they were eating. Nor do those who completely indulge in Venus choose as their good merely to be suffused with pleasure, without possessing the beloved object, nor performing the act, just as if they possessed and performed it.
Neither appetite nor pleasure makes something good, but the very nature of the good indeed attracts appetite from afar, and soothes it with pleasure up close. Similarly, not some particular familiarity is the cause that something is good for itself.

For it is impious to think that those things which are truly beautiful would immerse themselves as they are into the mud of bodies, and defile themselves, and disperse.
E Now indeed, when it considers that what are thought beautiful among us are in perpetual flux, it entirely apprehends that what shines forth in them is obtained from elsewhere. After this, it is entirely uplifted, being able, namely, to finally attain what it loves, nor does it cease before it attains it, unless perhaps someone uproots love from it: where at last it sees all beautiful and truly existing things, and filled with the life of Being itself, it is greatly strengthened: and it itself becomes truly Being itself, and dwells there, truly comprehending, and dwelling most closely, it clearly perceives what it has long sought.

Chapter XXXIII.

That all-form beauty of the divine world, and though very much to be admired, is nevertheless something defined; nor is it to be loved supremely, but goodness itself is better than all form. For even in the divine world, although each thing is a certain form, there is nevertheless something there compared to another as if it were matter. Hence both this and that are something defined. Therefore, beauty in the divine world, as the splendor of the Good itself, even through love, recalls the soul (which is to be admired there) to the Good itself; similarly, beauty in the soul, as the splendor of intelligence, secretly invites through love to love the intellect. Beauty in the body, like an image of animal beauty, exhorts one to desire incorporeal beauty.

A WHEN therefore beauty is spoken of, we must flee far from such a form, nor must it be placed before our eyes, lest we fall from that which is truly beautiful into something which is called beautiful by a small participation; namely, an unformed species is truly beautiful, if only it is a species. And indeed, inasmuch as you proceed by separating from matter into every form, as if to the seminal form itself, in which we say one thing differs from another: just as justice and temperance are distinguished from each other, because the intellect understands something proper in these:

C Now indeed, if you have proceeded thus far, it will be necessary for you to consider further what that most important thing to be conceived is, which is certainly superior to this very thing, beautiful everywhere and distinguished by all-form variety, yet itself distinguished by no variety: which the soul indeed desires, yet never expresses why it desires such a thing. Reason indeed dictates that this is truly to be loved by us, since the nature of the best and most lovable itself consists in that degree which surpasses every species.
D Wherefore, whatever you show to the soul referring to a species, in this very thing it always seeks something else that has formed it. The passions of lovers attest to this. A It must therefore be supposed that the intellect has a twofold
power: one indeed for understanding, by which it perceives its own internal things: but the other by which it gazes upon higher things with a certain glance of intuition and a certain perception: by which intuition and reception, it previously saw only, and by seeing, it afterwards received intellect, and becomes one. Indeed, that is the vision of a sound mind: but this itself is the loving mind. For when it raves, utterly drunk with nectar,
B then it is seized by love, spreading itself out in a blessed affection and sweetness through satiety. And indeed, it is better for it to be occupied with this intoxication than to live soberly far from such a draught. But does that mind in turn contemplate some things first, others later? Not at all: although discussion, for the sake of teaching, introduces it as if contemplating in alternating turns. But the intellect itself always exercises an act, by which it
C properly understands: and again, it does not properly understand, but beholds God by some other mode. For when it beheld God, it then conceived offspring within itself, and perceived them as already born and inherent, and while it contemplates these, it is said to understand: but it gazed upon God with that power by which it was subsequently intellect. Therefore, the soul, as if confounding and obliterating the intellect remaining within it, gazes upon God: nay, rather, the intellect itself beholds first, but the vision is also transmitted to the soul: and the two become one there. But the Good itself,
D propagating itself through these things, and applying itself to their constitution, hovers over them, and joining two into one, presides over them, bestowing a happy sense and blessed contemplation. Furthermore, it elevates these to such an extent that they are no longer in a place, nor in anything else, under any condition whatsoever that one thing can be in another. For God himself is not in anyone/anything. But the intelligible place is

in it, but He Himself exists in absolutely nothing. Wherefore the soul is not moved then, because He is not moved: nor therefore is the soul properly, since it does not properly live: because He does not properly live, but exceeds the function of living: but neither is it intellect, because it does not understand. For it must be assimilated, but it does not understand Him, because it does not even understand.

*The ladder by which one ascends to the Principle has seven steps: the first is the purification of the soul: the second, the knowledge of divine works compared individually: the third, the contemplation of the order by which lower works are gradually reduced to higher ones: the fourth, a certain proportional comparison from an order of this kind referring itself to the divine order: the fifth, negation, by which you separate all that you conceive from the Principle: the sixth, humble prayer to God, that He, the father of the intellectual world, may render you an intellectual world in act: for this world is potentially from the beginning: the seventh, that when you have become the intellectual world itself, further moved by the love of the Good, you may be transformed from the intellectual state into the Good, which is superior to intellect. Chapter 36.*
*Since the Good is far superior to intellect, and therefore its enjoyment cannot rightly be called intelligence, it seems it should not even be called knowledge. For it is more natural and more desirable than knowledge. Nevertheless, we call it, as best we can, vision because of its light and purity, and also touch because of the greatest union. It is also called taste because of the sweetness thoroughly infused into the soul there, nourishing it healthily and wonderfully transforming it for the better.*

a certain congruence of propositions: likewise negations: again, the cognition of those things which are made by it: finally, a certain ascent proceeding ritually by steps. We arrive at it by purifications, prayers, worship adorning the soul, ascent to the intelligible world, and perseverance there, while the soul feeds on the banquets of that world, whatever is beheld simultaneously becomes a spectacle, both of itself and of others: and having become essence and intellect and the universal living being, it no longer looks at itself externally, but having finally become that, it now approaches the highest. This highest, indeed, is there undoubtedly nearest, shining from above throughout the entire intelligible world: where certainly, all disciplines having been dismissed, the soul, led thus far and placed in beauty, understands up to that point in which it is: but then, as if lifted by a wave of that same intellect, and raised higher by it as it swells and overflows, it suddenly perceives, not knowing how. But this intuition itself, filling the eyes with light, does not indeed cause something else to be seen through it: rather, the light itself is entirely what is seen. For in it there is not this visible thing, and this its light, nor intellect and the intelligible: but this law operates there, generating in what follows, and allowing to remain with itself. Yet light alone exists, generating intellect, and is not extinguished by generating: but while it remains, something else follows from the fact that it exists. For unless it existed thus, nothing else would subsist from it.

[Marginal note: B]

Since Plotinus once defined intelligence as the reflexive act of a living essence dependent on the Good, and its striving to seek itself and its cause simultaneously, and living both its own parts with itself and itself by virtue of the cause, he denies that the principle of such intelligence needs aids. Chapter XXXVII.

Indeed, it seems that just as sight relates to light, so intelligence relates to the light of the Good, and is similarly distinguished: nevertheless, intelligence differs much more from the Good than sight from light: inasmuch as the Good seems to transgress intelligence by a greater altitude and latitude than light does sight. Therefore, since the reasons for the Good itself and for intelligence are so distinct, and thus are two in nature, when you rightly call the Good first, so that you preserve it as simple and self-sufficient, do not attribute intelligence to it, which indeed follows essence and life: but the Good exceeds both. For to be and to live is desired only by the reason and grace of the Good. Yet God is not mad, though superior to mind: nor is anything hidden from Him, through whom all things are manifest.

WHOEVER, therefore, in their arguments, have attributed intelligence to the supreme principle of things, have entirely removed the cognition of lesser things and of those that proceed from it. Although this also seems absurd to some, that God should in no way know other things. But they, indeed, finding nothing more excellent than it, believe that the cognition of itself attributed to it will be more venerable as a gift, and that the gift of intelligence itself is more excellent than the principle, while this very thing exists only as it is: as if that (principle) does not bestow all dignity upon intelligence, but receives it. Therefore, it must be asked, in what does God himself rather have his dignity: in intelligence, or in himself? If he acquires dignity through intelligence, then by himself he is either not venerable at all, or certainly less so: but if he possesses his dignity by himself, he is certainly perfect before intelligence, and is not made perfect by understanding. And if anyone should say that, because God is not potency but act, therefore he must understand, we will immediately distinguish thus. Either God is an essence always understanding, or only an act of understanding. If an essence always understanding, etc.

*In the first principle of things there is neither intelligence of itself, nor of others: if indeed intelligence is a certain kind of knowledge, having conditions of this sort. Chapter XXXIX.*

Plato, therefore, speaking about essence, says: 'He will indeed understand essence, but for that reason the most venerable itself will not exist.' As if essence indeed understands, but that which it does not understand, may be able to exist as primarily venerable. In these words, Plato says 'to exist' or 'to consist,' because he was not able to express it otherwise. Augustus, however, considered that which surpasses understanding to be truly august and venerable.

He considers every action both to belong to something and to be concerned with something else; then he wants intelligence to be an action; then he considers essence to be the foundation of action and intelligence. Rightly, therefore, he denies action, intelligence, and essence in principle, because it neither underlies anything nor is it in any way concerned with anything else. If goodness itself has been posited, then you attribute intelligence to this: either you think it differs by nothing, or by something. If by nothing, you name intelligence there in vain; if by something, when you mix it with the highest good, it is less good. --- Page 777 ---
It is something. For it introduces nothing into itself, but undoubtedly it suffices itself. Wherefore it is not good for itself, but for others. For other things always need it, but it does not need itself. For that would be ridiculous: for thus it would be in need of itself. Therefore it does not look at itself: for there would need to be something that comes into being for it on account of the act of looking at itself. Indeed, all these things seem to have been easily conceded to subsequent arguments, and it appears that none of the things that belong to others belong to it anywhere, just as essence is not present to it either. Therefore, not intellection either: since essence concurs with intelligence, and both are simultaneously the first and principal intelligence, and being itself in harmony. Therefore, for these reasons, Plato says that neither discourse, nor sense, nor knowledge can be had of the First: because, namely, nothing can be predicated of it as an accidental attribute.

Chapter IV.
Furthermore, if it understands, wills, chooses, acts according to its own nature, it is not therefore said to be compelled, because this very thing is primarily voluntary for it: nor is it led to this by external forces: nor should intellectual action be said to serve intellectual nature.
