*The Intellect lives freely in contemplation, and by a free decree determines to refer all private and public actions to contemplation. Chapter V.*
*It also knows many inconveniences which it would less desire, if they were often to come to its body and also to its soul. It has deliberated and twice applied opportune remedies according to its strength. All this disposition in the mind so far is voluntary, and does not depend on anything else: but the actions which follow daily, assisting involuntary inconveniences, do not exist so much by their own right, but depend in a certain way on opportunity.*

Is freedom and free will therefore placed only in the pure and intelligent intellect? Or also in the soul operating according to the intellect and acting according to virtue? Now, if we attribute this to the agent, perhaps it should not be attributed as far as attainment is concerned. For we are not masters of attaining. But if we designate it for honorably arranging its duties, perhaps it will be rightly said. But how can that be in us? As if it were said, 'because war presses, we exercise the duty of fortitude.' But I say, how can we judge an action frequently performed at that time to be in us, since unless battle surrounded us, we would not be given to use such an action: similarly in other actions composed by virtue, virtue itself, namely, always compelled to do this or that according to what arises. For if anyone were to give an opinion to virtue, whether it would wish, in order to obtain an opportunity for action, that adversities happen to us, such as battles impending, so that it demonstrates the duties of fortitude: and that injuries be perpetrated so that it defines what is right and dissolves disputes, and that poverty presses, so that it displays the gifts of liberality. Or rather, with all things duly pacified, would it choose to act quietly, undoubtedly a cessation of such actions, with no one, namely, needing any cure from it: just as if a legitimate physician, such as Hippocrates, would wish no one to need his medicines. 742 PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

that we may speak rightly, much less by predicating anything of it,
but neither by adapting any proper reason to it.
For all things, both beautiful and venerable, are posterior to it.
For that is the principle of all these things,
although in another way it is not a principle,
since we separate all things from it, and therefore
that free will of operating, or that which is accustomed
to be said to consist in it, we separate from it as something posterior.
For that seems to signify action tending towards another:
tending, I say, without impediment. Likewise, that there are other things
which strive towards the same without impediment: but altogether
it is proper to refer the First itself to nothing by speaking.
For this very thing exists even before all things,
since also that which is called being, we separate from it:
and therefore, to be in any way among beings we rightly deny.
Hence, neither will we say it exists thus, as it is naturally
instituted. For this too is posterior. And if it is spoken of concerning
superior things, certainly it will be spoken of concerning those which
are from another. Therefore, concerning the first essence

NOS, indeed, we think that the gift of freedom
does not belong to it as some accident,
but from the gifts of freedom which are attributed
to others, namely by the subtraction of contraries, we conceive it
in itself, for itself, while lesser things from

--- Page 787 ---
LIBER OCTAVVS. 741

A Over what follows the principle, necessity rules;
nor indeed does it inflict violence upon them.
But this unique and singular thing possesses from itself.
This very thing, therefore, is not something else: but what was ex-
pedient or ought to be. Therefore, it did not happen thus,
but it was necessary thus. But this very thing which is called
'necessary' is the principle of all things that must be.
This, therefore, is by no means as it happened, for it does not
exist as if by chance, but as it had to be. Indeed, not even that which o-

B ught to be. Now indeed, it is fitting to expect other things,
what things may appear to them at some point, and to assert absolutely
that which exists itself, certainly not as it happened to appear,
but truly a king, truly a principle, truly good.
Nor acting according to the good, for thus it would seem to follow
another, but this one very thing which is existing entirely.
And so, not acting according to the good, but existing as good itself
entirely. If therefore not even in being itself is there anything
contingent: otherwise, it would be a certain being,

C and certainly something would befall a certain being, yet
being itself did not happen in any way, nor did being itself
by some chance come to be thus: nor did it receive from another
to be thus as it is, but the very nature of being is to exist as being.
How then could anyone think that this condition, namely, that it
happened or occurred thus, exists in that which is superior to being?
since that [superior thing] generated being itself, which indeed did not
happen thus, but is as it is, essence itself existing, this very thing
which is essence, and this very thing which is

D intellect: otherwise, someone might by similar reasoning say
that intellect also happened thus, as if intellect could have been
something else, besides that which its nature exists as.
Therefore, that which does not transgress its own nature, nor ever
deviates from itself, one might most easily say that this very thing
exists as it is. What then will he say who has transcended
even this, and has beheld the highest? Will he say that as he
saw it to be, so it also happened? But certainly

E neither thus nor in any way whatsoever should it be said to have
happened, indeed, nor to have occurred at all and simply.
Can it then be said only thus, and not otherwise, but merely thus?
Indeed, not even this very thing which is called 'thus,' or 'in this manner,'
is to be assigned to it: otherwise, in that way, you would circumscribe
it, and render it something specific. For indeed, he who perceives
it, ought neither to say 'thus,' nor 'not thus,' otherwise you would
have said it is something from the number of things to which this very
thing, that it could be said 'thus' or 'in this manner,' belongs.
It is therefore other than all things which are said to be 'thus' and

F 'in this manner'. But you, when you have found it to be
infinite, will indeed be able to speak of all things that are after it.
But you will say that it is none of them, but as a universal power, truly mistress of itself, and existing as it wills.
Indeed, projecting this very thing which it wills into things themselves, while it is evidently more excellent than every act of will, and subjects such acts to itself. Therefore, it itself did not will this very thing, which is said to be thus, so much so that it said it to itself, nor did anyone else make it to be thus.

*Since the principle imposes form and limit and order on all things, and rational order is contrary to fortune, deservedly, if a fortuitous principle were to befall things, no order would remain anywhere. Because the principle is uniquely and firmly, and remains this very thing which already exists, nor does it derive from elsewhere: for this is its very nature. Nor is any weakness the cause, so that it could not have come into existence otherwise, nor proceeded to another. For to be and to remain immense goodness and power, this itself is the highest freedom and power alike. Chapter X.*

**BOOK EIGHT. 743**

For if you inquire what it is, you will contract and confine it to the narrowness of your understanding, and it will immediately escape you. But then, when reason has found the principle above essence, it cannot further inquire what it is: since such a question defines into essence. Nor is it right to investigate *why* concerning the principle: indeed, this question resolves into the principle itself. Finally, since you are going to deny essence concerning it, much more so accidents, in what way will you be able to affirm a contingent lot in it?

**A** But what is to be said of this which does not properly subsist or exist? But indeed, it is fitting for us to depart from here in silent uncertainty, and to inquire no further. For what will anyone inquire, when nothing further is revealed for him to proceed? Since every question refers itself to the principle, and finally rests in such a one. To this is added, that every question inquires either what something is, or **B** of what kind, or why, or whether it exists or not. Moreover, to ask what kind it is, is nothing other than to inquire what happens to it, to which absolutely nothing happens. But will was not devoid of reason, nor was it carried rashly and in vain, nor did it happen by chance immediately, but rather as was fitting: since nothing there is rash and vain. Hence Plato called it the fitting and the opportune, wishing in whatever way he could signify F that God is most remote from fortuitous chance, but that this very thing, which is itself, is fitting. But if this fitting itself exists, certainly it does not exist without reason. And if it is opportunity itself, whose property especially dominates in what follows, indeed, opportunity is present to itself much earlier. Therefore, it does not exist as it happens: but rather it is that which, as it were, He Himself willed: since fittingness wills, and there is one, the fitting itself or the opportune, and the action of the fitting. And the fitting is not like a subject, but as a primary action, properly bringing itself into light, which also was fitting. Forgiveness must be granted to our words. For thus we must speak of God, since we are unable to speak of Him as we wish.

PLOTINUS
ENNEAD VI.
TREATISE IX.

ON THE GOOD OR THE ONE.

Whatever exists apart from the First is composed of many parts or powers, which have been reconciled into a single form of the whole.

Chapter I.

Insofar as unity prevails in the multitude of each thing, so long does its essence endure; for if unity is lost, the essence is destroyed. Unity, therefore, preserves essence; it is this, then, that constitutes both essence and being. Unity, dominating in the multitude opposed to itself, neither exists from itself nor proceeds from the opposing multitude. It proceeds, therefore, from a pure unity, which simply subsists in itself, above the everywhere varied essence. When you speak of one body and one soul, one heat and one cold, the unity predicated here is neither one body (for it would not then apply to the soul), nor cold (for it would not then apply to heat). By a similar line of reasoning, you will find that the One itself is more eminent than any essence, and by its power, those things that are more unified also participate more in essence. Furthermore, the highest perfection of being consists in identity of state; and this is founded in unity, just as difference and motion are founded in number. Unity, therefore, which stands as the cause of being's perfection, is superior to being. Consequently, you either say that being is identical with unity, or distinct from it. You will certainly affirm that unity is the foundation of identity. Therefore, if you assert the former, namely that Being is identical with Unity, then Unity itself exists prior to this unity, through which Being is identical. But if, on the other hand, you assert the latter, that is, that unity is distinct from being, then unity itself is first identical with itself *per se* before it is distinct from being. Indeed, it will first be absolutely primary in itself through absolute primality, that is, through its own nature, before it is prior to being, or related to being. Nor is it permissible to say that being is so distinct from unity as to be primary in accordance with unity. For if it is said to be distinct from unity, it will not first be identical with itself, I mean through unity. Moreover, nothing can be conceived as higher than its simplicity. And this is Unity itself. Unity, therefore, is not only the first of all things, but is also Primality itself.

--- Page 801 ---
BOOK NINE. 757

primacy, by reason of which it is everywhere prior to other things. Through this, being itself is also prior to what follows, namely through unity both conjoined to itself and also superior to being itself. Nor is it permissible to say that being in the first sign is neither one nor not one. For unless it is one, that is, most simple, it will not yet be in the first sign. That it is there, therefore, it seems to have through unity. Consider being and unity concurring simultaneously: being, indeed, since it is capable of multitude, does not compel itself to be one: but unity itself compels being to be either unique or united. Rightly, therefore, Boethius says, "The cause and reason of being is unity." And Avicenna and Averroes confess that unity is the nature of each thing.

[Decorative initial O containing a figure]

ALL beings are beings by unity itself, both those which are primarily beings and also those which are in any way numbered in the order of things. For what would they be, unless they were one? Indeed, deprived of unity, they are no longer what they were previously said to be. For there will be no army, unless it is one: nor a chorus, nor any flock, unless they are similarly one. Then indeed, neither a house nor a ship will exist, unless they possess unity: for a house is something one and a ship is something one, which indeed if they cast away, neither will the house any longer be a house, nor will the ship similarly be a ship. Consequently, therefore, magnitudes will never exist, unless unity is inherent. When therefore they are divided, inasmuch as they lose unity, they also change their being. Furthermore, the bodies of plants and animals, which are each one, if they ever flee unity, that is, are dissipated into multitude, they will immediately lose their essence which they had, and will no longer be what they were before: but will immediately become other things, which indeed are themselves, inasmuch as they are also one. Then moreover, health flourishes, when the body is reconciled into one: then beauty blooms, when the power of unity connects the members: then virtue reigns in the soul, when the mind conspires into one, and into one agreement. But since the soul leads all things to unity, fabricating, shaping, forming, at the same time ordering, should we, having proceeded thus far, assert that it indeed supplies unity to things, but that it itself already exists as unity itself? But indeed, just as by suggesting other things to bodies, it is not so much itself what is transmitted, as if by transmitting form and species, but those things which are attributed by it are other than the soul: so it must be considered that, even if it bestows unity, unity is nevertheless different from the soul, and that the soul itself, looking towards unity, makes any given thing one, just as by looking towards man, man is rightly fabricated. At the same time, however, assuming unity along with man, the unity itself is found in man. Of those things indeed which are called one, each is one to the extent that it possesses this very thing within itself. Therefore, lesser beings possess less unity: but the more they are, similarly the more they are also one. Now indeed, although the soul is other than unity, nevertheless, inasmuch as it is more and more truly, to that extent it possesses more unity, yet it does not exist as unity itself. For the soul is one, where unity is, as it were, contingent. And these two are, namely the soul and unity, just as the body and unity. Indeed, what is discrete, like a chorus, is most remote from unity: but what is continuous, is closer to unity: but the soul is also much closer, itself also partaking of unity. But if anyone objects that the soul is entirely the same as unity, because there is no soul unless it is one: we will respond, first indeed, that other things also similarly exist individually, and at the same time exist as one: nevertheless, something else...

Therefore, speaking of God with the most exact reason, it is not right to say either this or that: but we, as if wandering around from outside, try to interpret our affections or pas-
B sions there as best we can. And sometimes indeed we approach closer to this very thing, but at other times, uncertain, we stray further due to ambiguity.

Access to God. Chapter IV.

The Principle of things is entirely incorporeal, immobile, one. Since therefore we cannot attain it through opposites, deservedly we do not attain it by imagination contriving corporeal things, nor by mobility always devising something mutable, nor by intelligence, by its very nature manifold, always meditating on something varied. But we attain it at last by a certain unity of the soul with a higher intellect, when we flee to it, entirely separated from the multitude, both internal and external. Then first we have the sign of God, everywhere and always present, now perfectly present to us, especially threefold: new light, unaccustomed love, inestimable joy. To achieve this, two things contribute: doctrine indeed as a path, and the said segregation as a preparation of the soul.

[Right column]
C But doubt and deficiency happen to us concerning knowing God, especially because we do not know Him through any science, nor through any intelligence, as we are accustomed to know other things which are called intelligibles, but through a certain presence, better than knowledge. But the soul escapes far from the One, nor is it entirely one, when it assumes knowledge of something. For knowledge is a certain discursive reason, but reason is manifold.
D Therefore it transgresses the One, having fallen into number and multitude. It is therefore necessary to transcend knowledge, nor in any way to deviate from that which is the One: but to be called away from knowledge and things to be known, and from everything else, and from beautiful spectacle. For every beautiful thing is both posterior to it, and from it, just as all daylight is from the sun. Wherefore Plato says that the highest God can neither ever be understood, nor be spoken of.
E We write and speak of Him frequently, so that at least by our discussions we may stir up the soul and direct it to the divine spectacle, as if showing a certain path to one desiring to see something. Doctrine indeed extends its powers as far as the way and the journey: but to see God is now the work of him who wills to see. He certainly neither comes to the spectacle, nor sees its light, and therefore is neither affected by it, nor tastes in himself the loving affection or
F passion accustomed to proceed from intuition, if ever a lover now rests in the beloved, where indeed true light is received, illuminating the whole soul drawing nearer: he, I say, does not attain such things, who strives to ascend thither, still weighed down and drawn back from behind by those things which are spectacles for those who behold. Nor does he ascend thither alone, but meanwhile drags with him that which separates him from it, or rather, he is not yet entirely reduced to one. For God is never absent from anyone,

--- Page 806 ---
762 PLOTINI ENNEADIS VI.

He is present only to those who can grasp him, and are so prepared that they can harmonize with him, and as it were, touch him, namely, through a certain inherent similarity and power, akin to the gift bestowed from there, when indeed the soul is altogether so disposed, just as it was when it proceeded from there; and therefore it can now see, just as God himself is by nature to be seen. He, I say, has not yet reached that point, who is drawn back from there because of these obstacles, or even prolongs delays on the journey, because reason is lacking, and discipline leading to that point, and making faith concerning divine things: but indeed, as far as other obstacles are concerned, each person would rightly place themselves in fault: namely, one ought to strive to be far from all things, and to emerge alone. But as far as reasons are concerned, which perhaps one believes less, one who is about to make progress should finally consider thus.

764 PLOTINI ENNAED. VI.

A But the One itself resides neither in another, nor in a divisible thing: nor is it individual in the sense of being a minimum. For it is the greatest of all, not indeed in magnitude, but in power. For this reason, when it is called individual, we mean indivisible power: since even those things that are after it are judged individual not according to masses, but according to forces. Moreover, we must call God infinite, not as if it were a certain magnitude or multitude that cannot be traversed, but because it is a power that you cannot comprehend.
B For although you might conceive of it as exceeding your powers, like intellect or God, yet there remains something far more excellent. And again, when you lead it supremely to the one in thought, then too it surpasses this unity conceived by you in simplicity. For you were reducing it to the highest unity of your intelligence according to your powers: but it surpasses beyond measure. For it remains in itself, nor does anything ever
C happen to it. Moreover, one can nevertheless prove the supreme unity of God by that which is called self-sufficient. For the supreme principle of things must in no way be needy, but most sufficient of all, and most content in itself. Whatever, however, is not one, but many, is necessarily needy: since it itself is not one, but becomes one from many. Therefore its essence needs to become one.
D But the One itself does not need itself: for it already exists. Moreover, that which is many in itself, needs as many things as it is composed of. And whatever of the things that are in it, since it is not in itself, but together with the others, certainly needs others, and therefore both according to each one and according to the whole, it declares itself to be something needy. If therefore it is necessary for something to be most self-sufficient, it must also be one: existing as such alone,
E so that it is needy neither of itself, nor of anything else. For it does not seek anything so that it might exist at some time, nor again so that it might be well, nor even so that it might be founded there: since it itself is the cause both of being and of well-being for others, deservedly this very thing which is, and is well, it does not have from others. For what good could accrue to it from elsewhere? Therefore, well-being itself does not happen to it: for it itself exists as this very thing. Likewise, there is no place for it, for it needs no
F foundation, as if it could not sustain itself. For that which must be founded in another is judged empty of life, and a tottering mass, unless perhaps it is supported. And other things are established because of it, through which they both came into existence simultaneously, and obtained a place where they might be orderly placed. But that which seeks a place is undoubtedly needy. But the principle certainly does not need those things that follow: therefore the principle of all things needs absolutely nothing. Now indeed, that which is needy, is judged needy because it seeks a principle. But if the One itself should need something, it would seek to be no longer one: therefore it would need a destroyer. Nevertheless, whatever is called needy, is in need of a good state and a preserver. Therefore, nothing is good for the One, nor therefore is there any will, but it is (so to speak) beyond good: and it itself exists as good not for itself, but for others, if indeed anything can participate. Nor is intelligence present in the One, lest there be diversity in it from that. Again, there is no movement: for it is superior to movement and intelligence. For what would it understand? Perhaps itself? But if that were so, then before understanding it would be ignorant,

he established laws in its likeness, being instructed, namely, by that divine communion for establishing laws. Perhaps indeed some soul might consider civil institutions less worthy of divine intimacy, if it preferred to persevere in the heights. Which indeed seems rightly to happen to him who has contemplated very much. He says therefore, that God is not outside anyone, but is within all who are least knowing: For they themselves flee outside God, nay, rather, outside themselves. Rightly therefore, they cannot apprehend Him whom they flee. And those who have already lost themselves are not able to seek out another. And indeed a son, placed outside himself by a certain madness, will not recognize his father: but he who has learned himself will rightly know also from whence he is.

**Access to God. Chapter VIII.**

God is as it were the indivisible and immobile center of the universe, from whom and to whom all things depend. Similarly, divine intellects and intellectual souls created thence have their own certain centers, that is, essential unities superior to intellect. Therefore, in divine intellects, besides such a center, there exists one orb, that is, the proper intellect: but in the soul beyond its center there are three orbs, intellect, reason, imagination. The center indeed is always connected with the center of the universe. The intellectual orb perpetually revolves around the same: but the rational and imaginal orb sometimes revolves around its own and the divine center, sometimes as if it is broken, and deviates obliquely to other things. Meanwhile, while we lead a life similar to beasts, not turned to God by reason or intellect, at least secretly we revolve around God. There remains moreover a certain affection in reason, which will sometimes recall us to God by its own stimuli: to whom when we are entirely united, because we are joined to Him through essential unity, we enjoy more inwardly and far more fully than one who possesses anything by knowing it. But it is probable that we, joined by such a union, will by no means depart thence. But the union is most intimate when the incorporeal is joined to the incorporeal, if only one of them has already laid aside its formal diversity, by which alone it certainly differed from the other.

IF therefore any soul has known itself at some other time, and has recognized that its motion is not straight, unless perhaps when it suffers some breaking, but that its natural motion is as it were circular around something, not external indeed, but around a center: and that center is that from which the circle proceeds, it will certainly move around this very thing from which it exists: and bringing itself from all sides to it, it will apply itself entirely to that to which all souls ought to bring themselves. But the souls of the Gods are always carried thither: and for that reason they are Gods, because they are carried to that: for God is whatever is joined to Him. But that which stands far off is man, and man is manifold and brutish. What therefore is as it were the soul's center, is this very thing that which has been diligently sought? But certainly something else must be considered, into which all centers, as it were, converge. But it is necessary to remember that the appellation of this center and circle is adduced here according to a certain comparison of analogy. [Marginal note in Greek: τὰ κύκλα] For the soul is not a circle in this way, as a figure: [Marginal note in Greek: ὡς τὸ χῆμα] but because in it and around it is the ancient and principal nature. And the soul depends on such a thing, [Marginal note in Greek: ὑπὸ] and even more so when the entire soul is separated. But now, after some part of us is submerged in the body, just as if someone has their feet in water, but with the rest of the body above the water, being raised higher by that very part which is not submerged in the body, through our center we are joined with that which is as it were the center of all: just as we often are accustomed to entirely affix the centers of many circles to the center of the surrounding and containing sphere. If therefore the orbs of souls were corporeal orbs, certainly by some condition of place, by a common position, the orbs of the soul would revolve. But since the souls themselves are intelligible, and that is superior to intellect—

768 PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

**A** The soul is free from evils, after it has returned to a place free from evils: here it truly understands, nor is it subject to any passions: here alone does it truly happen to live. For what is now said to be living without God, is a trace of life imitating the supernal life: but to live there, is an act of the mind. But this act also generates gods, while it touches God with a certain hidden and tranquil touch. But it generates beauty, and generates justice, and also generates virtue itself. For the soul, pregnant with God, gives birth to these things:
**B** and that is the soul's beginning, and end. A beginning indeed, because from there it proceeds: but an end, because there is its good, and arriving there, it becomes that very thing which it was. For what it is here, in these things it is involved in, is a kind of fall, and flight, and loss of wings. But love itself, innate in the soul, indicates that our good consists there, just as love is joined to souls both in writings and fables: namely, because the soul is other than God, and yet is from Him, it necessarily loves Him. Now indeed when it lives there,
**C** it has a celestial love: but here it becomes common and vulgar. For celestial Venus reigns there: but here Venus becomes vulgar, as if already (so to speak) adulterated. But every soul is Venus: which indeed, although in obscure words, the birth of Venus indicates, and of love born together with Venus. Therefore the soul, established in its natural state, loves God, desiring to be mingled with God, as if striving for beautiful virginity with honorable love.
**D** But after it has fallen into generation, it is deceived by certain quasi-marriages, and changing its love, it brings back the perishable instead of the divine; then, as if separated from its father, it becomes wanton: but again, hating human wantonness, and withdrawing itself chaste from these things, it sometimes returns to the father

--- Page 813 ---
LIBER NONVS. 769

A But indeed, the light itself, pure, light, sublime, then made God, nay, truly already existing, then indeed kindled. But if the burdened soul should again slip away from there, it is then as if again extinguished.

The Enjoyment of God. Chapter X.

*The soul, finally having completed its preparation, as close as possible to God, who possesses an infinite power of attracting from infinite good, conceives an infinite love for Him: therefore, it is so transformed into God on both sides, that to the beholder it soon appears no longer as a soul, but as God: just as if air is rarefied into light, which perhaps happened to fire from the beginning. Hence that saying of our Paul: 'He who adheres to God becomes one spirit.' Plotinus indeed granted that our intellect, once placed in God, never deviates from Him. He also grants that reason is converted to intellect, when, discursive thought being laid aside, argumentation in it suddenly becomes intuition. He would also have granted that reason perpetually contemplates there, especially when entirely freed from the body, which he seems to have touched upon here while speaking.*

B Why then does the soul not remain there? Certainly because it has not yet entirely emigrated from here. But there will also be a time when continuity of intuition will be granted, namely when the body will in no way disturb the intuition. But there is one who saw, not what is properly disturbed, but something else. And indeed, he who saw, then especially refrains from vision, when knowledge, which is occupied with demonstrations, conjectures, and the discursive reasoning, does not refrain from it:
C but that which is seeing itself and the seer himself, is no longer a certain reason, but something more excellent than reason, and preceding reason. And if in any way it is in reason, it is there rather as something seen: Whoever therefore sees himself, certainly while he sees, he inspects himself thus affected: nay, truly he will adhere to himself thus disposed, and will perceive himself as such, now entirely made simple. Perhaps indeed it should not be called seeing, but rather becoming the vision itself.
D Indeed, these two must be considered as certain things, namely the seer and the seen, nor are both one: although this statement seems bolder. Then indeed he neither properly sees, nor as a seer himself discerns, nor imagines two distinct things: but the soul then, as if already made another, no longer itself, nor merely bringing itself there, but gives itself to it, and having become entirely of it, immediately becomes one, as if joining center with center.
E For here, things that meet become one, but then they are two, when they are separated from each other. Thus we also now say 'the other'. Therefore, this spectacle is very difficult to describe. For in what way will someone declare as 'the other' that which, while he saw it, he did not see as 'the other', but as entirely one with himself?

The Enjoyment of God. Chapter XI.

*By the virtue of the One itself, union occurs everywhere: nor for any other reason do things more similar to each other unite more easily, than because they are one in quality. The soul, therefore, is then most intimately united with the One, the very principle of things, when it itself becomes most especially one within itself: and this is achieved when, stripped of the multitude that pertains to imagination, reason, and intellect, it becomes its sole unity, and by this very unity, through an amorous affection, it enjoys divine unity, thus joining its own center with the center of the universe. Plotinus asserts that a soul thus affected has transferred its intellectual form to unity: and likewise transferred its rational form to the intellectual. Hence, he would therefore have granted that the rational form should now be considered as intellectual, and that this, like the other, would perpetually remain there: especially since he says that the soul, constituted in an immobile state there, has as it were already become a state, and has transcended not only mobile nature, but also the first essence itself, where it acts without movements and labors. We, indeed, Magnanimous Laurentius, now bring an end to our labors on Plotinus, with God's help: thus humbly adoring Almighty God.*

*We give thanks to You, highest God, illuminator of minds, and author of good things, because You have supplied us with strength by Your grace, beyond our merit, to complete such a great work. I implore, most merciful God, infuse true prosperity into the pious Reader, and moreover, light, by which he may everywhere discern the true from the false, lest anywhere, either by meditating or by acting, he should dissent from Your will.*

This, therefore, the institution of such A

entered the inner sanctum of a certain sacred adytum, leaves behind D
all the statues arranged in the temple, which indeed, to him who is
soon to exit from the adytum, first again meet him after that
intimate spectacle. After which the communion itself is not directed
to statues, not to images, but rather to that very thing which the
statues, which the images represent: which indeed are to be judged
as certain subsequent spectacles. But perhaps it itself is not to be
judged a spectacle: but there is a certain different way of seeing
there. Namely, a certain exit from oneself, and a certain wonderful E
diffusion and progress, and an eagerness to touch, and finally, rest.
And every thought there strives entirely towards union, if one only
perceives what is in the inner sanctum. But he who looks otherwise
brings nothing back from there. Therefore the wise men of the
Prophets wrap such imitations of divine things in obscurities,
indicating by what reason that God is perceived: But the wise F
priest, explaining the hidden mystery, and having entered the adytum,
attains true contemplation there: but if he has not yet entered,
then considering the adytum itself as something invisible, and a
source, and a principle, he will know it very much as a principle.
But having entered there, he sees the principle itself, and is joined
to it, and perceives like by like, neglecting none of the divine
things, as many as the soul can attain. Now indeed, before the vision itself, he desires that which remains for the vision. But for him who
has already transcended all things, there remains that very thing which surpasses all things. For the nature of the soul will never come
into something entirely non-existent: but having fallen, it will indeed descend into evil, and thus it is judged to rush into non-being, not
because it can be precipitated into something entirely non-existent. But if ever a way contrary to this should proceed, the soul will not
indeed come into another, but will arrive at itself:

--- Page 815 ---
LIBER NONVS. 771

A to itself: and thus since it is not in another, it should not therefore be judged to be entirely in nothing, but rather to subsist in itself: and to be in itself alone, and not in being, is nothing other than to be entirely in God. For it becomes something itself, not essence, but also superior to essence, insofar as it entirely insinuates itself into God. If therefore anyone should ever see himself having become that, he will certainly have himself as a kind of image of that. And if he passes beyond himself, as an image translated to the very
B archetype, he will then have attained the very end of the journey. But if he should ever fall from contemplation, again exciting the virtue inherent in himself, and perceiving himself entirely cultivated, he will again be raised to the sublime, while he proceeds through virtue into the Intellect, and through wisdom advances to God. This therefore is the life of the Gods and of divine and blessed men, altogether neglecting human pleasures, and the flight of the alone to the Alone.
